*Shipped 2026-09-02* across four commits: =e4c60ce= (lint), =d0adb2f= (the functions and their tests), =ea762f3= (the file mutation), =b378b1f= (the ongoing half).

*The prerequisite had already been met, and was checked rather than assumed.* All 210 keyworded headings in DONE.org carry =CLOSED:= — the 39 this body measured on 2026-08-28 were backfilled by [[id:b7b46a26-2fd6-4784-bed3-d0112a917c0a][b7b46a26]] after it was reopened. That check was the one condition under which this heading should have stopped instead of building, so it ran first.

*The lint had to be widened before the tree existed, which is [[id:e30d52d7-960b-44f3-ab92-93846c81a1bd][e30d52d7]]'s own rule applied to the case it predicted.* Its closing note — measured hours after that rule shipped — said a =datetree/= archive location would produce four errors per archived item. Materialising it confirmed the shape exactly: year, month and day at levels *1-3* rather than 2-4, the task at level 4, and no =:DATE_TREE:= property anywhere.

*It cannot be given one, which settled the design question without a judgement call.* =org-archive-subtree= calls =org-datetree-find-date-create= on the widened buffer with no restriction (=org-archive.el:343=), and that function never consults the property — so the tree is built at top level, outside this project. CLAUDE.md already names this exact case: where another system owns the thing, read the contract it publishes. Depth is now measured from the file root when there is no anchor, and the day-node =:ID:= exemption is *gated on the absence of an anchor*, because the two trees want opposite things — org writes the archive's day node bare, while the meta-work tree's day node is what time is assigned to.

*The conversion ran clean, verified against invariants recorded before it rather than by reading a 24,554-line diff:* 210 keyworded and 210 =:ID:=s before and after, no duplicate ids, all 155 tasks under a day node matching their *own* =CLOSED:= with zero mismatches, and years, months and days each descending — 2026-09-01 first, 2026-07-28 last, across 1 year, 3 months, 22 days. =bin/lint-org=: 0 errors, 123 warnings against 124 before, the lost one being a =:CATEGORY:= check that only applies at level 1.

*The ongoing half is where the real defect was, and it would have corrupted every future archive.* =claude-code-ide-org-archive-finished= binds =org-archive-reversed-order= to =t= — the mechanism that made the *flat* archive read newest-first, by inserting at the beginning of the target location. In a datetree the target location is the day node, so inserting at the beginning puts the entry **before** it: a level-4 heading parented to the month, and an empty day node left after it. The sort that follows then fails outright with "Region to sort contains a level above the first entry".

Isolated to that single variable: plain =org-archive-subtree= into the same populated tree nests correctly with it =nil= and malforms with it =t=, nothing else changed. It is now off for a datetree target only, and nothing is lost — ordering is =claude-code-ide-org-sort-datetree-descending='s job, and it orders every tier rather than only the insertion point.

*Worth recording that this was found by wiring the directive up rather than by reasoning.* The one-time conversion was correct and fully tested before the defect existed to be seen; it lives entirely in the *steady state*, which is the half that rots silently because each individual pass looks correct.

*Three traps hit and worth not rediscovering.* A =.replace= that matched nothing looks exactly like a mutation the tests caught, so every mutation now asserts it applied — two "passing" mutations were non-events. The undated-heading refusal test was *structurally incapable* of failing for its own reason: with the guard deleted a nil =CLOSED:= still throws =wrong-type-argument= from inside =encode-time=, so a bare =should-error= passed either way; it now asserts the message. And a fixture written to disk under a buffer the test macro had already opened makes the next =find-file-noselect= ask whether to reread, which in batch is a *hang*, not an error.

*One docstring claim was corrected rather than kept.* Reading =CLOSED:= without the inherit flag does not prevent a parent taking a child's date — property inheritance searches *upward*. What actually guarantees it is that only level-1 headings are filed, so a story moves whole. Mutation-tested both ways: adding the flag changes no test, filing every heading fails three.

*Twin of [[id:42ba0a80-61c5-49bd-b6a2-9da76a53ff64][42ba0a80]], split from it because the fix is
different and neither fix alone is sufficient.* That one is about the
window's left edge; this is about what the window is allowed to sweep up
once its bounds are right.

*The rule as written.*
=claude-code-ide-org--slice-incidental-ids= subtracts only two things
from everything closed in the window: the slice itself, and the slice's
own declared members. Its docstring defends the breadth explicitly —
"that this sweeps in genuinely unrelated workstreams is a *feature*: the
list answers 'what else was going on', which is the question worth
asking of a plan."

*That defence is sound for unowned work and says nothing about this
case.* Work that no slice claims is genuinely incidental to whoever was
running at the time, and deriving it beats curating it. But another
slice's *declared checklist* is not unowned — it is planned work, merely
planned elsewhere. Listing it as this slice's incidental work asserts
something false about who planned it.

*Measured 2026-09-01:* of [[id:f9fe9fac-a423-4ede-bc42-1d201c2c3d82][f9fe9fac]]'s 26 incidentals, 21
are [[id:b36e6369-a210-4540-adc7-0c0c188e9791][b36e6369]]'s declared planned members. The remaining
five are claimed by *both* slices' incidental lists at once, so any
count that aggregates incidental work across slices double-counts them.

*This is the declared-versus-inferred error, mirrored.* CLAUDE.md's rule
is that inferring a declared grouping is the same mistake as declaring
an emergent one — and this infers membership for work another slice
explicitly declares. The previous slice closed that gap in one
direction; this is the other.

*Why it survives 42ba0a80's fix.* Bounding the window to actual work
fixes f9fe9fac, which has none. It does not fix two slices worked
*concurrently*, or one worked during another's long tail: the second
would still absorb the first's declared members, and a closed slice's
incidental list is exactly the artefact meant to be read as fact
afterwards.

*The likely fix, not chosen:* subtract the declared members of *every*
slice, not just this one's — every =:KIND: slice= heading's member list
is already enumerable by the same function that reads this slice's. Open
questions that a fix has to answer rather than assume: whether a member
of a *cancelled* slice counts as declared; whether an id declared by a
slice that has not started should shield it from a slice that is
actually working; and whether the exclusion should be reported rather
than silent, since a slice's incidental list going quiet is the same
class of failure as it going noisy.

:END:
*Shipped 2026-09-02 as =b6bcdc9=.*
=claude-code-ide-org--other-slices-declared-ids= collects every slice's
planned members across the tracked files, and
=--slice-incidental-ids= subtracts them.

*Only the planned half is read, never the generated incidental list* —
otherwise two slices whose windows overlap would each shield the other's
incidentals and both lists would empty out. That is the same
self-reference trap =--slice-planned-member-ids= exists to avoid, one
slice further out, and it was worth stating in the docstring because the
obvious implementation reads all members.

*The three open questions, decided:*

- *CANCELLED slices are skipped, and it is the only real judgement here.*
  A =DONE= slice's declaration stays true as a historical claim — that
  slice did plan this work — so its members keep their owner. A
  cancelled plan was abandoned, so its declarations no longer speak for
  anything and work closed in someone else's window really is incidental
  to them.
- *An unstarted slice's declaration still shields.* The question the
  list answers is *who planned the work*, not who got to it. A member
  completed by someone else is still that slice's member, and its
  checklist showing it done is correct rather than a false claim of
  credit.
- *The exclusion is reported.* A derived list that quietly *shrinks* is
  as wrong as one that quietly grows, and only one of those is visible —
  which is the whole reason this heading exists. Named rather than
  counted, following the =unrendered= precedent in the same report: a
  count sends the reader hunting, an id says which.

*Live effect, measured:* =b36e6369='s incidentals went 13 → 11, dropping
=478d6ec9= and =9651d4c8= — both declared by the *previous* slice
=979e02b6=. Neither was ever incidental to the current slice; they were
its predecessor's planned work, closed inside the current window.
Refreshing twice reports identically, so the report variable does not
accumulate across calls.

*Verified by mutation, three ways.* Recording the exclusion without
applying it, letting a cancelled slice claim, and dropping the report
each fail *exactly* their own test — 506 ran, 1 unexpected, in every case
— and the suite restores to 506/506. Each test also asserts a positive:
=incid-002= must *stay* incidental, so none of them could pass on a
function that returned nil.

*Closes the twin.* [[id:42ba0a80-61c5-49bd-b6a2-9da76a53ff64][42ba0a80]] bounded the window;
this bounds the exclusion set. Neither alone made =f9fe9fac= right, which
is why both were filed rather than one.

*Filed 2026-08-21, not built.* The 2026-08-21 cross-artifact audit found that prose conventions recur (UUID-from-memory, clock-in-at-drift) while mechanically checked ones fail loudly and get fixed -- and that duplicated conventions drift into contradiction (four found in CLAUDE.md, one in a memory, one in the next-session prompt). =bin/check-org-dev-skill= already embodies the fix for one file; generalize it: the CLAUDE.md and org-skill transition tables agree; every cited =:ID:=, defcustom, and function name resolves (=git grep= the symbol); every "is live"/"not built" claim carries a greppable anchor (e.g. =config.el:2792=) that still matches. Wire into =bin/hooks/pre-commit= beside the existing lint. Not a prose rule about keeping prose fresh -- that is the anti-pattern recursing.

*Prototyped 2026-09-02 before writing anything, and one of the three
proposed assertion families has nothing to check.*

The three this heading names are: the CLAUDE.md and org-skill transition
tables agree; every cited =:ID:=, defcustom and function name resolves;
and every "is live"/"not built" claim carries a greppable anchor (e.g.
=config.el:2792=) that still matches. Measured across the five documents
a check would cover — CLAUDE.md, =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md=,
both =SKILL.md=s, and =.claude/commands/next-session.md=, 3101 lines
together:

- *Ids: 73 distinct 8-character tokens, 0 unresolved.* Every one
  resolves to an org heading or a git object. The assertion is true
  today, so it can be wired into =pre-commit= without a backlog of
  pre-existing failures — which is the property that decides whether a
  check is adoptable at all.

  *The extraction needs a tighter boundary than the obvious one.* A bare
  =[0-9a-f]{8}= matches *inside* full UUIDs — the trailing segment of
  =9d2fcdad-9bf7-47b6-8018-223b13ec4577= reads as the token =223b13ec=
  — and produced five phantom failures. Requiring the run not be
  adjacent to a hex digit or a dash removes all five. Git short SHAs are
  seven characters here and pass by resolving as git objects, so the
  same check covers both citation kinds without telling them apart.

- *Anchors: zero, in any form.* No =file:line= references, and no "line
  NNN" prose, anywhere in those 3101 lines. For contrast, TODO.org
  bodies carry 12.

  *And that is deliberate rather than an omission.*
  =bin/check-org-dev-skill='s fourth check exists precisely because the
  org-dev skill "describes the tool-registration block by anchor … not
  by line number, specifically so a =config.el= edit that shifts line
  counts can't put the doc out of date", and verifies the claim
  *structurally* instead. So this heading proposed asserting a
  convention the project had already decided against.

  *The residue is real but it is somewhere else.* The 12 anchors live in
  org bodies, which do rot and which nothing checks. Whether a check
  should cover them is a decision this heading has to take rather than
  inherit — and it is a different check, over different files, from the
  one described here.

- *Transition tables: not yet measured.*

*What this changes about the work.* The harness plus the id assertion is
small and demonstrably green. The anchor assertion is not work but a
*decision*, and the honest options are to drop it, or to re-aim it at
org bodies as a separate check. Recorded here rather than silently
dropped, because a heading that quietly loses a third of its scope reads
afterwards as though it was always smaller.

:END:
*Shipped 2026-09-02 as =5d42fc5=. The harness is the deliverable; two of
the three assertion families landed with it, and the third became a
separate heading.*

=bin/lib/check.fish= holds the failure accumulator, the report format
and the exit-code discipline. Both =bin/check-conventions= and
=bin/check-org-dev-skill= source it, so the second check family added
*assertions* and nothing else — which is this heading's own argument
made concrete rather than asserted. The plumbing is also where the bug
was: the block-local =set= that made =check-org-dev-skill= exit 0 while
printing FAIL lived there, and writing it twice would have meant
debugging it twice.

*What shipped:*

- *Ids resolve.* Every 8-character token the docs cite resolves to an
  org heading or a git object. 73 distinct, 0 unresolved.
- *The keyword set agrees* across TODO.org's =#+TODO:= header, the rules
  file, the org skill's transition table and the =org_set_todo= tool
  description — compared as a *set*, since the orderings differ
  legitimately and a string comparison would fail on a difference nobody

- *Anchors: split out as [[id:5fc7b934-28ec-4eeb-9f90-f1becec353f0][5fc7b934]].* The docs carry none
  and deliberately so; the twelve that exist are in org bodies, which is
  a different check over different files and a decision this heading

*Two things went wrong, and both were caught by testing rather than
reading.*

*The skill assertion false-positived on its first real run,* against
"This paragraph used to argue the point via =PLANNING= ownership … Both
are gone" — correct prose about a retired keyword, which a whole-file
set comparison read as drift. Scoped to table rows instead: naming a
dead keyword in history is legitimate, listing one as a live transition
is not, and only the table makes that claim. *The assertion was wrong,
not the prose*, which is the direction that is easy to get backwards
when a check fires.

*The wiring was worse, and is the more instructive one.*
=.githooks/pre-commit= has an early =exit 0= when no org file is staged,
and the block was appended *after* it — so it could never fire on a
CLAUDE.md-only commit, which is the exact case its own comment said it
existed for. It was found by staging a bogus citation and checking that
the commit was *refused*; every reading of the code beforehand had
looked right. A check wired where it cannot run is
[[id:542924c1-9152-4414-8da8-d530d3423611][542924c1]]'s class in its purest form — the check had no
way to fail — and it was introduced by the very commit meant to address
that class.

*Verified:* =bin/check-conventions-test= runs 7 cases and asserts *exit
codes*, never output, including a case where the fixture is correct so
the rest cannot pass vacuously; both false-positive guards (a full UUID,
a retired keyword in prose) are among them. End to end, a staged bogus
citation refuses the commit and leaves HEAD unmoved. =bin/test= 503/503,
=bin/lint-org= 0 errors.

*Known gap, stated rather than discovered:* the check reads the
*worktree* where the org lint beside it reads the *index*. Accepted for
now — these files are hand-edited and rarely partially staged — and
recorded in the script's own header. =pre-commit= passes =--docs-only=,
so a machine with no Emacs running can still commit.

That diagnosis is right and it generalises — the =:PLAN:= lifecycle ([[id:8bcd56f4-22a8-4673-bad6-a99433027b81][8bcd56f4]]) applies at =DONE=, so a *live* heading that has been accumulating for weeks has never met it.

*Measured 2026-08-28 across TODO.org: 90 live keyworded headings hold 4,027 body lines, and the ten longest hold 1,593 of them — 39%.* None carries a =:PLAN:= drawer.

*The eighth row is the joke and also the point.* [[id:b07df584-3adc-433c-ab49-e104f88aecf7][b07df584]] — "Heading bodies grow into narratives no human will read; decide what to stop capturing" — is itself 99 lines. Whatever this heading does should be reconciled with that one rather than done past it: that one asks what to *stop capturing*, this one asks what to do with what already accumulated. They are the prospective and retrospective halves of the same complaint.

*What worked on c954f650, for whoever picks this up.* Compress *first*, while the text is still body, then wrap. CLAUDE.md's rule says wrap first and condense in a separate commit, on the grounds that a bad pare inside =:PLAN:= is invisible because readers are told to skip the drawer. Compressing before wrapping inverts that: the pare shows up in the diff as ordinary body prose, where it is reviewable. The rule's *concern* is right and its *order* may be backwards — worth deciding here rather than assuming either way. 305 lines went to roughly 70 without losing an open question.

*The three things the rule says stay untouched still stayed:* every open question kept verbatim, the debrief kept whole, and anything whose seam was uncertain wrapped rather than pared.

*Not a backlog sweep.* [[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]] chose "wrap unedited" for the 30-heading archive pass deliberately, to keep it cheap. This is the opposite case by construction — ten headings, each one read and condensed, all of them live and therefore still being consulted, which is what makes the cost worth paying here and not there.

*Corrected by the user 2026-08-28, and the correction is narrower and better than what it replaces.* The paragraph above argued that compressing before wrapping may invert CLAUDE.md's order in general, on reviewability grounds. That overreaches. The order inverts *for this population specifically*, and the reason is a property of these ten bodies rather than of the rule:

*They were never revised as they were worked — only appended to.* Which is exactly what [[id:b07df584-3adc-433c-ab49-e104f88aecf7][b07df584]] is about, and why that heading sits eighth on this list rather than merely adjacent to it. So what "compression" does here is not *paring considered prose*, which is the risky act CLAUDE.md's separate-commit rule guards against. It is *collapsing an append-only transcript*, where later entries routinely supersede earlier ones outright and the superseded text is not a judgement anyone made — it is a sentence nobody went back to delete.

*So the rule stands unchanged for its own case.* A body that was drafted and revised should still be wrapped first and condensed separately, because a pare there discards someone's considered wording where no reader will see it. A body that is a transcript can be condensed first, because the diff is where the supersession becomes visible and there is no earlier judgement being overruled — only an earlier sentence that a later one already replaced.

*Which gives whoever picks this up a test rather than a preference:* ask whether the body was ever *revised*. If it was only ever appended to, compress first. c954f650 was a clear case — five distinct dates of accretion, each opening with a bold lead that qualified or reversed one above it, and nothing ever deleted.

*Measured 2026-08-31, and it converts this from ten judgements into nine mechanical compressions and one that needs care.*

This heading's own test is "ask whether the body was ever *revised*; if it was only ever appended to, compress first". That is answerable from git rather than by reading. Sampling 28 points across all 472 commits that touched TODO.org, with each heading's body bounded at the *next heading of any level*, and counting any drop of more than three lines as a revision:

| id | samples | max | now | shrinks | verdict |
|----+---------+-----+-----+---------+---------|
| 02aaae22 | 25 | 154 | 147 | 1 | *revised* |
| 9e627dc0 | 16 | 211 | 211 | 0 | append-only |
| 9ae4b17e | 17 | 169 | 169 | 0 | append-only |
| b5f94b88 | 20 | 128 | 128 | 0 | append-only |
| 0c8644ff | 25 | 141 | 141 | 0 | append-only |
| 2aeb65d6 | 21 | 123 | 123 | 0 | append-only |
| a1d63f52 | 24 | 94 | 94 | 0 | append-only |
| b07df584 | 13 | 95 | 95 | 0 | append-only |
| 2d9eeebd | 17 | 111 | 111 | 0 | append-only |
| d1cf852a | 19 | 90 | 90 | 0 | append-only |

*Nine of ten have never lost a line.* So for nine, the risky question — am I discarding someone's considered wording? — is answered *no* before any reading begins, and compress-then-wrap applies without a per-heading call. Writing each compression is still work; deciding whether it is safe is not.

*=02aaae22= is the exception and should be done last, or by a human.* It is also the only container in the list, so its single shrink may be a child moving rather than prose being pared — which is exactly the ambiguity that makes it the one to treat carefully rather than the one to skip.

*The first version of this measurement was wrong in two ways and is recorded because both are the same mistake.* It sampled only the most recent 40 commits — 2026-08-27 onward, five days of a five-week history — and it bounded each body with =find("\\n* ")=, which for a heading *with children* runs past them, so =02aaae22= came out as 5 lines against a true 178. Both errors flattered the answer: a shorter window and a truncated body both hide shrinks. A measurement whose errors all point the same way is worth re-running before it is quoted.

:END:
*Seven of the ten swept 2026-09-01. The population was never ten by the time it ran.*

=2d9eeebd= closed and was archived into DONE.org; the table above still
lists it =NEXT=, which is what a measurement kept as prose does. And
=9e627dc0= was handled earlier the same day by =org_divide= rather than
by this sweep — its body is now 15 lines and the design travelled into
the story's children. So the work here was seven bodies, and =02aaae22=
is the one left.

| heading  | before | now visible | in =:PLAN:= |
|----------+--------+-------------+-------------|
| d1cf852a |    105 |          26 |          32 |
| b07df584 |    115 |          34 |          63 |
| a1d63f52 |    123 |          33 |          64 |
| 2aeb65d6 |    139 |          13 |         114 |
| b5f94b88 |    154 |          53 |         100 |
| 0c8644ff |    163 |          74 |          66 |
| 9ae4b17e |    195 |          60 |         136 |
| *total*  |  *994* |       *293* |       *575* |

*Read that honestly: this was mostly relocation, not deletion.* 994 lines
became 868 — 126 lines actually gone, about an eighth — while 575 moved
behind a drawer. The visible body is 70% smaller, which is the effect
that was wanted, but nobody should cite this as evidence that the bodies
were mostly waste. They were mostly *prospective*, which is a different
claim and the one this heading actually makes.

*The sweep's real yield was not shorter bodies. Six of the seven carried
claims the code had already falsified,* and none of them announced it:

- =d1cf852a= proposed a bracket mechanism that had shipped in =6a81822=;
  its "denylist should be an allowlist" survivor is done, and
  =--work-in-progress-keywords= is =("DOING")=.
- =b07df584= said "no tool can rewrite a body today" — =org_amend
  replace= and =org_wrap_plan= both exist — and cited a CLAUDE.md rule
  against trimming old bodies that was reversed on 2026-08-24. Its
  =:BLOCKER:= had been satisfied without the body noticing.
- =a1d63f52= named =--trigger-auto-promote-sole-todo=, retired; and the
  CLAUDE.md rule it asked for was never written, so its convention is in
  force and undocumented — the exact condition it was raised to end.
- =2aeb65d6='s =pre-commit= option is now "extend a hook" rather than
  "add one", since =.githooks/pre-commit= exists.
- =b5f94b88='s step 3 shipped, for both capture and amend, while the
  body says in terms that no verdict was recorded and none should be
  inferred. Step 1 — =create-lockfiles= — never shipped and is still
  Doom's =nil=.
- =9ae4b17e= is *unblocked*: =befaed0a= is =DONE=, and half its plan has
  quietly happened project-scoped.

Only =0c8644ff= had no falsified claim, and it had something worse: a
link that still *resolved*. It cited =9e627dc0= for a conclusion, and
that heading's division earlier the same day carried the =:ID:= to a
child, so the link now landed on a narrow leaf rather than the argument.
Re-pointed at the story =f90d745e=. *An id link cannot go stale by
breaking; it goes stale by continuing to work,* which is why mitosis
needs a referrer sweep and nothing does one.

*One method correction, and it is a real amendment to this heading's
plan.* "Compress, then wrap" assumes the seam falls in document order —
prospective first, debrief last. It did for five. It did *not* for
=2aeb65d6=, which is a live TODO nobody has started, so every line is
prospective and wrapping the lot would have left the heading blank; the
fix was to write a short "where this stands" close and seam on that. And
it did not for =b5f94b88=, where CLAUDE.md explicitly names two passages
— the "epic wearing a child's clothes" reasoning and the
plan-file-overwrite incident — as *not design*, so the body had to be
reordered before =org_wrap_plan= could take the right half. The tool
takes everything above the seam; when the durable half was written
first, reordering is part of the condense, not a separate liberty.

*And a claim in this heading's own body is wrong:* =02aaae22= is not
"the only container in the list". =a1d63f52= is =[3/5]=. It does not
change the compress-then-wrap decision, which turned on append-only-ness
rather than on shape, but the parenthetical should not be relied on.

*=02aaae22= is left, and the recommendation is not to wrap it.*

Its 369-line body is not a superseded plan. It is an accumulating
*scope list* — "Added to scope 2026-08-11", "…-08-12", "…-08-13",
"…-08-14" — plus an audit of what is still owed. Wrapping that puts
eleven items of outstanding work into a drawer readers are told to skip,
which is the residue-goes-invisible failure CLAUDE.md warns about, not
the tidying this heading exists to do.

The better move is division: each "Added to scope" item is a candidate
leaf, and consuming the body into children is what CLAUDE.md says
happens to an engorged body. That is a judgement call about eleven
headings, so it is left for a human rather than taken here. If wrapping
is wanted anyway, the seam is *Promoted to =**= and split into children
2026-08-14* — but it buries the scope, which is the objection above.

*=02aaae22= is resolved, and not by wrapping. Closed 2026-09-01.*

The user rejected both moves this heading had on the table: drawering
was wrong because the heading is *in progress*, so its body is
outstanding work rather than superseded planning; and mitosis was wrong
because it is already a container, and division is what a leaf does when
it outgrows itself. Both objections are correct and neither was in this
heading's reasoning — the recommendation recorded here on the day was to
divide, which would have been the second error.

*What happened instead was redistribution:* 369 body lines allocated to
children, twelve of the seventeen scope items culled as already done,
one culled as a duplicate of a heading already =NEXT= in this slice, and
six new children filed for what survived. The body ended at 77 lines and
the cookie moved =[7/11]= → =[7/17]=.

*That makes the sweep ten for ten, by three different means* — seven
condensed-and-wrapped, one divided (=9e627dc0=, earlier the same day),
one archived before the pass reached it (=2d9eeebd=), and one
redistributed. Worth stating plainly because this heading's premise was
that one method fits a long body, and it does not: what fits depends on
whether the body is *finished thinking* (wrap), *one task that grew*
(divide), or *a backlog in prose* (redistribute). Only the first is what
=:PLAN:= is for.

*The finding is the same in every case, which is the part that
generalises.* Across the seven wrapped bodies, six carried claims the
code had already falsified. Across =02aaae22='s seventeen scope items,
twelve were already done. Nothing announced either. A long body is not
mainly a readability problem — it is a *staleness* problem, and length
is only the symptom that makes it survive unread.



**** DONE An unstarted slice accrues every heading closed since it was written down :code:
CLOSED: [2026-09-01 Tue 16:16]
:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       42ba0a80-61c5-49bd-b6a2-9da76a53ff64
:CREATED:  [2026-09-01 Tue 15:54]
:CATEGORY: Slices
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-09-02 Wed 08:56
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Slices
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-09-01 Tue 16:16] \\
  window bounded by first work; f9fe9fac corrected
:END:
:PLAN:

*Noticed by the user 2026-09-01, reading the session-start report:* why
does [[id:f9fe9fac-a423-4ede-bc42-1d201c2c3d82][f9fe9fac]], a slice nobody has started, carry a list
of =DONE= incidentals?

*Measured, and the answer is that none of them are its incidentals.*
f9fe9fac has =:CREATED: [2026-08-31 Mon 12:07]=, no =:CLOSED:=, state
=TODO=, and *zero CLOCK lines* — it has never been worked. It lists *26*
incidentals. Twenty-one are the *declared planned members* of
[[id:b36e6369-a210-4540-adc7-0c0c188e9791][b36e6369]]; the remaining five are that slice's own
incidental work. None of the 26 has anything to do with f9fe9fac.

*The cause is the window's left edge.*
=claude-code-ide-org--slice-incidental-ids= opens the window at the
slice's =:CREATED:= and closes it at =:CLOSED:=, and
=--closed-in-window= documents =END nil= as "up to now, which is the
case for an open slice." For a slice being *worked*, created-to-now is a
reasonable reading of "what else was going on". For a slice *composed in
advance and not started*, it means "everything anyone closed since I was
written down" — and composing a slice ahead of its turn is normal
practice here: b36e6369 itself was composed while its predecessor was
still running.

So the window conflates two different moments — when the slice was
*written* and when it was *worked* — and only the second bounds anything
a reader would call incidental.

*The visible damage is the statistics cookie.* f9fe9fac reads =[26/28]=,
92% complete, with both of its two real members still =TODO= and no work
done. A reader scanning the outline sees a nearly-finished slice. That
is this project's own recurring failure — the code knowing more than it
says — reproduced by a mechanism built during the slice named for it
([[id:0086614a-c95c-4618-bba0-c821589dd7f2][0086614a]]).

*Candidate fixes, none chosen.*

- *Start the window at first work* rather than at =:CREATED:= — the
  earliest CLOCK on any member, or the slice's own first =DOING=. A
  slice with no work has an empty window and no incidentals, which is
  the correct answer here. Needs a decision about which signal, since a
  slice may be clocked without its members being, and vice versa.
- *Refuse to compute incidentals at all until the slice has started.*
  Cruder, and it answers this case exactly; it says nothing about a
  slice worked in bursts with long gaps.
- *Leave the window and fix the exclusion set* — see the twin below.
  Insufficient alone: even excluding another slice's declared members,
  f9fe9fac would still absorb that slice's five genuinely incidental
  ids, because they fall in its window and nothing else claims them.

*Its twin, filed separately because the fix is different:*
[[id:5bfc1d38-e758-4ed7-bb32-f976031ff3da][5bfc1d38]]. That one survives this fix — a *closed* slice
running concurrently with another would still absorb the other's
declared checklist. Fixing either alone leaves f9fe9fac wrong, which is
why both are filed rather than one.

:END:
*Shipped 2026-09-01, same day, as =d577751=. Candidate 1 was taken:* the
window opens at the later of =:CREATED:= and first work, where first
work is =claude-code-ide-org--first-work-time= — the earliest CLOCK
start across the slice and its planned members. A slice with no clock
anywhere gets no window and therefore no incidentals.

*Why that signal rather than the slice's own =DOING=.* A slice may be
clocked while its members are not, and far more often the reverse: the
members carry all the time and the slice itself never gets clocked at
all. Scanning both subtrees costs one pass and needs no decision about
which is authoritative. The open question the body raised — "which
signal" — is answered by taking the union rather than choosing.

*Measured after loading into the live Emacs:* f9fe9fac 26 → 0
incidentals, and its cookie =[26/28]= → =[0/2]=, which is two real
members and no work. [[id:b36e6369-a210-4540-adc7-0c0c188e9791][b36e6369]] unchanged at 12, since it
was worked — the fix is inert for a slice actually being run, which is
what it should be.

*The five existing incidental tests failed, and they were right to.*
Their shared fixture built a slice with =:CREATED:= and no CLOCK, which
under the new rule is a slice nobody worked. The fixture now carries a
clock opening at its =:CREATED:=, which leaves every window bound in
those tests exactly where it was — the assertions did not move, only the
premise they rest on became explicit.

*Mutation-tested, since a fixture change that makes tests pass again is
exactly where a vacuous assertion hides.* Making the window ignore
=worked= — restoring the old behaviour in one line — fails
=claude-code-ide-org-test-slice-never-worked-has-no-incidentals= and
nothing else (503 ran, 1 unexpected), and restoring passes 503/503. The
new test also puts the clock *back* and asserts the window returns, so
it cannot pass by the fixture simply having become inert.

*The twin survives and is not closed by this.*
[[id:5bfc1d38-e758-4ed7-bb32-f976031ff3da][5bfc1d38]] is about the exclusion set rather than the
window: two slices worked concurrently, or one worked during another's
long tail, would still absorb each other's declared members. f9fe9fac
only stopped being wrong because it had done no work at all.



**** DONE Sort TODO.org by :CREATED: descending, after each archive pass :code:

:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       5f1068f9-1452-45e4-9253-568edfce2053
:CREATED:  [2026-08-28 Fri 13:39]
:CATEGORY: Meta
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-09-02 Wed 08:56

:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Meta
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "TODO"       from              [2026-08-28 Fri 13:40] \\
  for the next slice
CLOCK: [2026-09-01 Tue 09:03]--[2026-09-01 Tue 09:10] =>  0:07
- State "DOING"      from "TODO"       [2026-09-01 Tue 09:03]
- [2026-09-01 Tue 09:03]--[2026-09-01 Tue 09:10] sort TODO.org newest-first
- State "DONE"       from "DOING"      [2026-09-01 Tue 09:10]
:END:
:PLAN:

*Asked for by the user 2026-08-28, for the next slice.* After archiving the closed headings, sort what remains in TODO.org by =:CREATED:= descending, so the file reads newest-first.

*It became a one-operation job when the category tier went.* [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]]'s plan already named this and could not do it: sorting used to mean nine separate operations, one inside each level-1 category, with no ordering between them. Flattened, every task is a level-1 sibling and the whole file is one =org-sort-entries= call.

*Where it belongs is the load-bearing part.* The ceremony order is fixed for a reason — apply the queue, consolidate drawers, normalise separation, *then* archive — and this goes *after* archiving, for the same reason archiving goes last: sorting before it would order rows that are about to be removed. It is also idempotent and cheap once the file is already sorted, so it can join the ceremony rather than being a thing to remember.

*Two things to settle when building it, neither obvious:*

- *What to do with headings that have no =:CREATED:=.* Every heading created since the convention has one and =bin/lint-org= errors without it, but archived-in and hand-written rows historically did not — the same gap [[id:b7b46a26-2fd6-4784-bed3-d0112a917c0a][b7b46a26]] is about for =CLOSED:=. Sorting must not silently pile them at one end as though they were coeval.
- *The datetree anchor must not move or be sorted into.* =* Review and planning= is the one structural level-1 heading left, and its year/month/day children have their own ordering question ([[id:0c3f1319-67c0-4b29-a8e7-5ffa12948aaf][0c3f1319]], newest-at-top). Whatever sorts the file has to skip it.

*Adjacent, and worth doing in the same pass rather than twice:* [[id:33864a0f-5e13-4235-85a6-0bd9d2fe5252][33864a0f]] reorders DONE.org as a datetree descending by =CLOSED:=. Both are "make the file read newest-first after archiving"; they differ only in the key and in whether the result is flat or nested.

*Measured 2026-08-28, and two of the three anticipated exceptions do not exist.*

- *Recurring ceremonies are not an exception.* All three =SCHEDULED= headings — =96a51c2f=, =2aff1e6d=, =cbe282ec= — carry a =:CREATED:= as well. The worry that they would have "no CREATED, rather SCHEDULED" does not hold against this corpus.
- *The datetree anchor is the only level-1 heading without =:CREATED:=.* Exactly one, not a class.
- *And it needs no special handling at all.* Verified in batch org 9.8.7: =(org-sort-entries nil ?R nil nil "CREATED")= with point before the first heading sorts the level-1 entries descending and places the *undated* heading last, on its own. Subtrees travel intact.

*So the whole operation is one call, and org owns the comparator.* =?R= is "by the value of a property, reversed", and the =PROPERTY= argument takes =CREATED= directly — no =getkey-func=, no custom compare. Two preconditions worth knowing rather than discovering: point must be *before* the first heading (org signals ="Nothing to sort"= otherwise, which is how a fixture without a =#+= preamble failed here), and TODO.org satisfies that only because of its header lines.

*The "mostly sorted, so a light operation" premise is right eventually and wrong now.* Measured: of 135 dated level-1 headings, *85 of 134 adjacent pairs are already descending — 63%*, and the longest already-descending run is *17*. The first sort is a large reordering and should be its own commit. Afterwards the premise holds, because =org_capture= prepends and a promotion inserts one heading, so each later sort moves one or two entries.

*Approaches, with what each costs:*

| # | approach | for | against |
|---+----------+-----+---------|
| A | the single =?R= call, anchor last by absence | one line; org owns the comparator; the exception handles itself; idempotent | the anchor's position is *implicit* — it is last because a property is missing, not because anyone said so, and an anchor that ever gained a =:CREATED:= would migrate into the middle silently |
| B | A, plus a sentinel =:CREATED:= on the anchor so it sorts last deliberately | the invariant is declared rather than emergent; the lint's "level-1 task has no =:CREATED:=" rule would then apply uniformly | a fabricated timestamp in a file whose entire value is that timestamps are trustworthy — the shape [[id:7771fc63-9374-4c8a-9e80-24ceec21977c][7771fc63]] retired rather than kept |
| C | move the datetree to its own file | TODO.org becomes homogeneous, every heading a dated task; no exception anywhere; =--datetree-node-role= stops sharing a file with real tasks | a third tracked file for =org-agenda-files=, =--tracked-files=, id resolution and the archive target; every doc saying "two files" becomes wrong; and A already handles the anchor for free, so this buys tidiness rather than function |
| D | insert in place on capture/promotion, never sort | no bulk reorder ever; minimal diffs forever | =org_capture= already prepends, which is correct for a newest-first file, so this is only needed for *promotions*, which are rare — and it spreads ordering logic across every writer instead of one call |
| E | sort the view, not the file | zero churn | the stated goal is that the *file* reads newest-first, and capture's prepend already assumes file order carries meaning |

*Recommend A, with B's concern answered by a lint assertion rather than by a fake timestamp:* assert that the =:DATE_TREE:= anchor is the last level-1 heading. That makes the invariant checked without inventing data, which is the same move [[id:8bea4317-c8e7-4939-8224-834bb914d89c][8bea4317]] made for the cookie's position — read the corpus, assert the result, do not encode it as data.

*C stays open on its own merits*, and is worth deciding separately rather than as a side effect of sorting: it is really the question of whether meta-work belongs in the same file as the work, which nothing here has asked yet.

*Two distinct failures, one ceremony, and the second only appeared once the first was fixed. Both shipped 2026-09-01.*

*First: the read-only guard.* =archive-finished= was the only one of the three steps with no binding — its siblings use =(let ((buffer-read-only nil)) ...)=, which an initial grep for =inhibit-read-only= missed, so the first reading that "two are latently broken" was wrong. It binds =inhibit-read-only= rather than the siblings' mechanism, and that difference is load-bearing: they touch one buffer, while =org-archive-subtree= writes the *target* file too, so a buffer-local binding on the source would leave DONE.org guarded and fail halfway.

*The failure was not clean, which is the sharper finding.* =org-archive-subtree= copies to the target and *then* deletes from the source. A read-only source means the copy lands and the delete does not, so the 07:06 run left [[id:c31b6c76-8ad8-45d4-a87b-39e085e31368][c31b6c76]] as a heading in *both files*. A partially-applied archive, not a refused one.

*=bin/lint-org= does not detect a cross-file duplicate =:ID:=.* It reported *0 errors* the whole time the corpus held one. The archive's own post-condition caught it — reporting =Archived 20, but 1 id(s) now appear twice= — but only *after* writing, and it does not roll back. So the duplicate was found by a guard that fires too late, and missed entirely by the check that runs on every commit.

*Second: a fresh-session-only load-order bug.* With the binding in place the step reported =Defining as dynamic an already lexical var: org-archive-reversed-order=. =archive-finished= =let=-binds that variable without requiring =org-archive= first; under lexical binding, binding a symbol org-archive has not yet =defvar='d makes it *lexical*, and loading org-archive afterwards signals. Two other call sites in this file already require it.

*It hid because a long-running Emacs has org-archive loaded from any earlier archive.* It works there and fails on the first ceremony after a restart — which is exactly when the ceremony is most likely to run. Confirmed directly rather than inferred: =(featurep 'org-archive)= was =nil= immediately after the reload that fixed it.

*And =bin/test= cannot discriminate it.* The suite passed identically before and after, because the batch environment's load order differs from the live one. *Found 2026-08-31 by the user asking whether the ceremonies would run at the next session start.* They will not, and the reason is a seam rather than a bug.

*The report names three things it is waiting on and goes quiet on evidence of one.* Its text is "Waiting: N queued item(s) pending review, N :LOGBOOK: drawer(s) out of order, N finished heading(s) not yet archived". Its quiet test is =--ceremony-reviewed-today-p=, which looks for a =CLOCK:= line dated today on the =Review attention= heading — created by running the *apply* command and nothing else. On 2026-08-31 four applies produced four such lines, the report went silent, and *106 finished headings sat unarchived*, drawers unconsolidated, separation un-normalised.

*This is [[id:806ff394-3ede-4d67-82aa-9c44fe1cf86e][806ff394]] working and reaching slightly short.* That heading replaced "a model remembers to stamp it" with "the act leaves its own evidence", which is strictly more reliable and removed the model from the nag guard. But the act it chose is *apply* — the one step a human always performs, being the one they came to do — while the three that follow are precisely the ones that get skipped. The signal is derived from the step least in need of a reminder.

*Can the ceremony be automated? One quarter of it cannot; three quarters already can.* Mapped rather than assumed:

| step | surface | automatable |
|------+---------+-------------|
| apply the queue | =M-x claude-code-ide-org-review=, no MCP tool | *no, by design* |
| =consolidate-all-drawers= | elisp; from Lisp defaults to writing | yes, via =emacsclient= |
| =normalize-heading-separation= | elisp; same | yes, via =emacsclient= |
| archive | =org_archive= | yes, already a tool |

Apply is human-only because org's native state-change logging completes only inside a genuinely interactive command, and =WAITING(w@/!)= and =CANCELLED(c@)= carry =@= cookies that *prompt* — a non-interactive call hangs on exactly the two keywords. That is the constraint the whole queue exists to route around, not a gap to close.

*So the honest shape is: the human applies, the agent finishes, and the finish is reported.* CLAUDE.md already says the last three steps are "yours if they ask" — and on 2026-08-31 nobody asked, four times, which is how 106 accumulated. "If they ask" is the same remembering-dependency 806ff394 removed from the other half.

*Two changes, and they are separable:*

1. *The quiet test should attest to what the report claims to be waiting on* — pending items, drawer order, unarchived count — rather than to the apply alone. Cheapest form: go quiet when all three counters are zero, which is derived and needs no new signal.
2. *There is no completion report at all.* The ceremony prompts at =SessionStart= and never says what happened, so success and failure look identical from the outside — and a step that silently did not run is the failure mode this project keeps finding. A line per step, success or failure, said in-session when the agent runs them.

*Not proposed: automating apply.* And not proposed: the agent running the last three *unasked* — that is a policy question about the user's attention rather than a defect, and it should be decided rather than assumed.

:END:
*Shipped 2026-08-31.* Both halves the title names are addressed, and the heading is in =REVIEW= rather than =DONE= for one reason given at the end.

*The completion report.* =claude-code-ide-org-ceremony-finish= runs the three post-apply steps -- consolidate drawers, normalise separation, archive -- reports each one success or failure, and returns a summary line. A clean pass advances [[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]]'s own =++1d= repeater and stamps the ceremony done; a pass where any step failed holds both. The summary is written into the stamp file's body, so it survives the =message= that displayed it.

*The quiet test.* It keyed on *either* the stamp or a CLOCK line dated today on the attention heading -- and the second only attests that apply ran. That was right while the later steps needed a human. It is wrong now they run automatically, and it hid the case that matters most: a pass that ran, failed a step, correctly held the repeater and wrote no stamp, then was silenced by its own apply clock. Silence now requires the stamp. The clock is still read, but to *say* something: =:reviewed-today= separates "nobody has been here today" from "someone was, and it did not complete", and the report leads with the latter.

*Verified, not just implemented.* The sweep was rehearsed on scratch copies before touching anything, then run live against the backlog this heading was filed about: 65 finished top-level subtrees archived, with headings 308 -> 308, =:ID:= 307 -> 307 and CLOCK 696 -> 696 across both files, no duplicate ids, and the 21 finished headings that are children of *live* parents correctly left alone. 447 tests pass. Restoring the old disjunct fails the new test, so it discriminates.

*Two defects surfaced by running it*, both fixed here: =#+ARCHIVE:= is parsed once at buffer creation and never re-parsed, so the first live pass archived under the retired =* Done= while the directive on screen read the new one; and a pass reported 65 while writing 66, which is guarded by a post-condition and filed unexplained as [[id:381ea07d-633f-4640-abbb-89472a07acba][381ea07d]].

*Why =REVIEW= and not =DONE=.* Every ceremony run this session was invoked by hand. The =quit-window= advice has never fired on its own, and it cannot be made to before [[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]] next comes due, because apply is human-only by design. Nothing is owed from this side; what is left is the user seeing it fire, or not, and saying so.

*Judged 2026-09-01: the trigger fires. This heading's open question is answered, and answered by observation rather than argument.*

*It fired unattended.* The user applied, buried the review buffer, and the =quit-window= advice ran the ceremony with nobody asking it to — which is the one thing that could not be demonstrated before, because apply is human-only and [[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]] had not come due again. That was the entire reason this sat in =REVIEW= rather than =DONE=.

*Both halves the title names did their job, and the second proved itself immediately by catching a real failure.* The completion report said =archive: FAILED (Buffer is read-only ...)= instead of going silent, and the quiet test correctly *withheld* the stamp and held the repeater, so the next session would be told rather than shown a clean slate. Before this heading, that pass would have looked identical to a successful one from the outside — which was precisely the complaint.

*The failure it caught was real and was worth catching.* It exposed two defects in the sweep, one of them a *partially-applied archive* that left a heading in both files ([[id:13ea6770-88ba-484d-87bd-2d20c44dc610][13ea6770]]). The report is what surfaced it; the four applies that produced 106 unarchived headings on 2026-08-31 said nothing at all.

*So the mechanism is confirmed working under exactly the conditions it was built for* — an unattended run, a genuine failure, an honest report, and a stamp correctly withheld. Closing.

:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       0086614a-c95c-4618-bba0-c821589dd7f2
:CREATED:  [2026-08-28 Fri 12:52]
:CATEGORY: Slices

  filed from the user's proposal
CLOCK: [2026-08-31 Mon 18:03]--[2026-08-31 Mon 18:12] =>  0:09
- State "DOING"      from "TODO"       [2026-08-31 Mon 18:03]
- [2026-08-31 Mon 18:03]--[2026-08-31 Mon 18:12] generate a slice's incidental list
CLOCK: [2026-09-01 Tue 06:54]--[2026-09-01 Tue 07:01] =>  0:07
- [2026-09-01 Tue 06:54]--[2026-09-01 Tue 07:01] render the incidental section
- State "DONE"       from "DOING"      [2026-09-01 Tue 07:02]
:END:
:PLAN:

*Proposed by the user 2026-08-28*, after a scan of [[id:979e02b6-2a4c-4328-8b08-ffaec03bd02e][979e02b6]] found 36 headings closed since it opened, of which only 6 were members. Their correction, and it stands: *work that arose in the course of the slice is slice business* — listing it separately as *incidental* keeps that true without pretending it was planned.

*What this fixes is the denominator.* [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]] closed at =[27/27]=, and its own body records that its members were "mostly small defects found while doing other work". So the slice absorbed its incidentals *as members*, and 27-of-27 reads as a plan executed exactly when it was a much smaller plan plus nineteen things that fell out of doing it. Those are different facts and the single number hides the more interesting one — how much unplanned work a plan generates.

*Mechanics, following the rules a slice already has:*

- *A second list, under an =Incidental:= lead*, below the member list.
- *Plain =- = items with no checkbox*, exactly as a cancelled or deferred member is written. Incidentals are closed by definition, so a checkbox could only ever be =[X]= and would inflate both halves of the cookie. The cookie keeps meaning *plan completion*, which is the only thing it can mean and stay useful.
- *Not in the =:BLOCKER:=*, which names cookie-carrying members and must not gate a slice on work already finished.
- *Same link form as a member* — full-UUID target, 8-character description — with keyword and title as derived text alongside.

*The open choice, and it is the whole design.* How the set is picked:

| | rule | cost |
|--+------+------|
| *strict window* | every heading closed between the slice's =:CREATED:= and its close that is not a member | none to compute, zero judgement, cannot drift — but sweeps in genuinely unrelated workstreams |
| *curated* | the subset someone judges related | needs a judgement per heading, and a judgement that is re-made differently each time is the thing this project keeps getting wrong |

*Recommend the strict window*, and the recommendation is not about which list is prettier. An incidental list is *emergent*, not declared: it is derivable from the closing timestamps, so by this project's own axis it should be *detected* rather than written down, and a derived thing must have a rule that needs no opinion. The curated version reintroduces exactly the hand-maintained second copy that [[id:979e02b6-2a4c-4328-8b08-ffaec03bd02e][979e02b6]] exists to eliminate. That the strict window sweeps in the ceremony and footnote stories is a feature: it says truthfully what else was going on, which is the question the list answers.

*Which makes this generated, not maintained.* =claude-code-ide-org-refresh-slice= should compute the incidental list the same way it already regenerates member lines — on every refresh, from the corpus, discarding whatever was there. A hand-kept incidental list would go stale by the second day.

*Measured on the live slice 2026-08-28:* 36 closed in the window, 6 members, *30 incidental*. Five of the thirty are children of [[id:478d6ec9-1b99-4c6c-88e9-c793ad4b2f22][478d6ec9]], which the [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] plan named as one of its two prerequisites — its sibling prerequisite [[id:8183fc7c-905e-40c8-81cb-10c56158c6ce][8183fc7c]] *is* a member, so identical work is tracked one way and invisible the other. That asymmetry is what prompted the scan.

*Decided by the user 2026-08-28, and it overrules the recommendation above on one point.*

*Strict window: yes*, for the reason given — the rule needs no opinion, so the list cannot drift.

*Checkbox cookies: kept on incidental items too, and the denominator grows.* The "keeps the denominator honest" argument above is overruled as splitting hairs, and on reflection it was arguing for a distinction nobody asked the cookie to make. The user's reading is the simpler and more defensible one: *=[n/m]= says what was closed between =:CREATED:= and =CLOSED:=*, which is a clear statement about a bounded window rather than a claim about plan fidelity. A separate "plan completion" number would be a second statistic to keep true, and the whole point of the strict window is to avoid maintaining anything.

*The user's assumption — that splitting the list in two has no effect on the aggregate cookie — was verified rather than accepted.* Batch org 9.8.7, a heading with two sibling lists separated by a prose line, 3 planned (2 done) and 2 incidental (2 done):

: * TODO [4/5] A slice

*And =:COOKIE_DATA:= is not what makes that work*, which matters because the slice convention mandates it and a reader would credit it. The same shape with *no* =:COOKIE_DATA:= at all also yields =[4/5]=: org counts every checkbox in the entry regardless, and =checkbox recursive= governs *nested* lists and subheadings, not sibling ones. So the two-list layout needs nothing added.

*One consequence that still needs deciding, because it is an invariant rather than a preference.* =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= says a slice "carries a =:BLOCKER:= naming exactly its cookie-carrying members", and =bin/lint-org= reports a disagreement in *either* direction as an error. If incidentals now carry cookies, that rule pulls them into the blocker — roughly forty ids on this slice, every one of them already closed and therefore inert. Two ways out:

- *Narrow the rule to planned members*: "naming exactly its cookie-carrying **planned** members". The blocker keeps meaning "what still has to finish", which is its only job.
- *Leave the rule alone* and let the blocker carry the closed ids too. Harmless — =org-depend= blocks only on unfinished work — but it makes a machine-readable property forty entries long to express eleven facts.

Recommend the first. The blocker is not a record of membership; the checkbox list is.

*Inherits [[id:9651d4c8-6887-4b0a-91d9-562c3bc49a75][9651d4c8]], cancelled 2026-08-29 as superseded by this heading.* That one asked for a convention marking which of a *container's* children were in its original plan and which accrued during execution. The planned/incidental split answers the same question one level up — if the slice is the planning unit rather than the container, a container's children were never covered by its plan in the first place.

*So this heading now carries a capability that exists nowhere else*, which raises its stakes: until it is built, original-versus-accrued has no home in the files at all. That is why 9651d4c8 was cancelled as *superseded* rather than as unnecessary.

*The case study travels with it.* [[id:406e9200-c3e7-49ac-a8d0-d6ff8e061ce4][406e9200]] was planned with five children and had ten two days later, and its plan file still opens "Covers all five children" — true when written, false since, recorded once in a document nobody revises. Any convention that requires editing the container each time a child is added will drift exactly as that plan file did, which is the argument for the strict window: it is *derived* from closing timestamps and so cannot go stale.

:END:
*Half built 2026-08-31, and deliberately left at the seam. Detection is shipped; rendering is not.*

*What exists.* =claude-code-ide-org--closed-in-window= returns the ids whose =CLOSED:= falls in a range, read through =org-map-entries= rather than a regex — entries are bounded by construction and this scan is the input to a list a human reads as fact. =--slice-incidental-ids= applies it between the slice's =:CREATED:= and its =CLOSED:= (or now), minus the members it already names and itself. Archives are included, because work closed during a slice is often archived before the slice is, and a scan blind to DONE.org would report the window *shrinking* as the ceremony ran.

*Verified:* 485 tests, 0 unexpected. Each of the three bounds was mutated separately and each fails its own test — dropping the lower bound or the member exclusion fails the strict-window test, dropping the upper bound fails the bounded-by-close test.

*Measured against the live corpus:* [[id:b36e6369-a210-4540-adc7-0c0c188e9791][b36e6369]] currently shows 28 members and *7* incidental. Lower than the 30 this body measured on its predecessor, and for a reason worth knowing: most headings created during a slice are still *open*, and a strict window keyed on =CLOSED:= counts only what finished inside it.

*The "one consequence that still needs deciding" does not need deciding — it was already handled, and measurement says so.* This body worried that giving incidentals cookies would pull roughly forty ids into the =:BLOCKER:=. It does not: =--slice-blocker-ids= filters on *cookie-carrying and not yet done*, and an incidental is closed by definition. Tested directly — a slice with an =Incidental:= section of three =[X]= lines yields =--slice-members= of three and =--slice-blocker-ids= of *nil*. So neither =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= nor =bin/lint-org= needs changing, and the recommendation to narrow the rule to "planned members" is unnecessary rather than wrong.

*One edge case that survives, recorded rather than built:* an incidental whose referent is later *reopened* would regain a live cookie on the next refresh and enter the blocker — holding the slice open on work it never planned. Rare, and it needs the member parser to know which section a line sits in, which is the only reason that distinction would be worth adding.

*Why the rendering half was not attempted in the same session.* It is a body-region rewrite of a format =.githooks/pre-commit= validates, which is the exact class of edit this repo has two body corruptions on record from — the reason =org_wrap_plan= and =org_divide= exist as tools rather than as hand-rolled edits. Doing it unattended at the end of a very long session, with nobody able to react if the slice format came out wrong, is the wrong trade. The detection half stands alone, is useful on its own, and changes nothing a reader sees.

*What is left, concretely:* render an =Incidental:= lead below the member list, regenerate the lines beneath it on every refresh exactly as member lines are regenerated, and delete whatever was there before. The line form is settled by this body — same link shape as a member, checkbox kept, keyword and title as derived text.

*Rendering shipped 2026-09-01, completing the heading.* =refresh-slice= now generates an =Incidental:= section below the member list on every pass, discarding whatever was there — derived, not maintained, as this body required.

*The region is bounded on both sides before anything is deleted*, which was the whole reason the rendering was held back overnight. It runs from the lead to the end of the run of list items and blank lines beneath it, and never past the slice's own body, so trailing prose survives and a subheading is never crossed. A test asserts exactly that, and the mutation that removes the bound — deleting straight to the body end — fails it and nothing else.

*With no incidentals, an existing section is removed and none is written.* An empty lead states nothing and would be regenerated forever.

*Two defects the tests and the live run caught, both real:*

- *The list erased itself on the second refresh.* It is derived from "closed in the window that the slice does not already name", and =--slice-members= sees incidental lines as members like any other — so the second pass called every incidental already-named and deleted the section it had just written. Fixed with =--slice-planned-member-ids=, which stops at the lead. So the planned/incidental distinction *is* load-bearing after all, though not for the reason this body gave: not the blocker, but idempotency. Found by the idempotency test, which is what it was written for.
- *A =CANCELLED= incidental rendered =- [ ]=*, an *unchecked* box, because the renderer defaulted a missing mapping to a space. Wrong twice over: it inflates the denominator permanently, and it reads as a live cookie — so =--slice-blocker-ids= pulled it into the =:BLOCKER:=. That is precisely the failure this body feared, arriving through =CANCELLED= rather than =DONE=, and it was *not* caught by the earlier measurement that concluded the blocker was safe. Found on the first live run against the real slice, which is the argument for doing one.

*Verified live on [[id:b36e6369-a210-4540-adc7-0c0c188e9791][b36e6369]], twice, with the file copied aside first.* The second run: =1 slice refreshed, 0 member lines rewritten, 0 blockers updated, 8 incidentals listed=, cookie =[17/28]= to =[24/35]=, and a diff of *14 changed lines* — the cookie and the new section, nothing else. "0 blockers updated" is the assertion that matters: the =CANCELLED= incidental no longer leaks in.

*Verified in batch:* 485 tests before, 490 after, 0 unexpected. Four mutations, each failing only its own test: unbounded region, no lead-stop in the planned-id scan, writing a lead with nothing under it, and boxing a cookie-less keyword.

*One thing found on the way and filed rather than fixed here:* =refresh-slice='s own =ID= argument compares with =equal= against the full =:ID:=, so an 8-character prefix silently refreshes *nothing* — it reported "0 slices refreshed" and looked like a working no-op. Same shape as [[id:25e7b083-360b-4282-8fd0-bb768e2a0f13][25e7b083]], at another call site.

*Found and fixed 2026-08-31, four hours after [[id:c74f8663-b14e-4ab9-ad65-d99cb655b3fa][c74f8663]] shipped, and found by building something that depended on the invariant rather than by review.*

*The defect.* =org_capture= with =initial_state= writes the TODO keyword straight into the capture template, which is the whole point — it bypasses =org-todo= so a creation needs no queued transition. But =org-todo= is also what writes the =CLOSED:= planning line, so a heading born =DONE= or =CANCELLED= carried a done keyword and *no close time*.

*Why that is worse than cosmetic.* Every consumer of =CLOSED:= silently skips such a heading: =org-archive-subtree= uses it as the placement key, =bin/lint-org= as its archive threshold, and [[id:0086614a-c95c-4618-bba0-c821589dd7f2][0086614a]]'s new strict-window scan as the entire basis for deciding what a slice absorbed. A heading with a done keyword and no close time is finished work that the machinery cannot see is finished.

*And it fed a backlog that already has a heading.* [[id:b7b46a26-2fd6-4784-bed3-d0112a917c0a][b7b46a26]] exists to recover close times for the headings with no in-file evidence, and measured *39*. The count today is *42* — so three have accrued since, one of them mine, captured =DONE= this afternoon.

*The fix writes the line rather than refusing the state*, because capturing something already finished is legitimate: a decision recorded after the fact, which is exactly what the offending heading was. =CLOSED:= is stamped with the same timestamp as =:CREATED:=, which is honest — for a heading born finished, creation *is* the close.

*Scoped to the done keywords by =--outline-finished-keywords=.* A live keyword must not get a close time; that would be a false close, and a fabricated one is the failure [[id:7771fc63-9374-4c8a-9e80-24ceec21977c][7771fc63]] rates worse than an absent one.

*Verified:* 484 tests before, 485 after, 0 unexpected. One test covers both directions and both mutations fail it — writing no line at all, and writing one for any keyword.

*The one heading affected was repaired rather than left for the backfill.* =6e43120d= now carries =CLOSED: [2026-08-31 Mon 16:38]=, added through =org-add-planning-info=. That is not a guess and so not [[id:b7b46a26-2fd6-4784-bed3-d0112a917c0a][b7b46a26]]'s business: the close time was known exactly, being the moment this session captured it.

*Raised by the user 2026-08-31: "I have been ignoring the zero-minute spans. do we understand their origin and have a remedy in mind?"* The origin is understood and was measured rather than recalled; the remedy turns on a distinction [[id:31f766ab-90ed-4950-bc5b-787528c8fe84][31f766ab]] came within one sentence of making and did not.

*Origin, from this session's own queue.* Each zero-minute item is a *lone guidepost* — a =resume= or =pause= with no partner inside the clustering window — so start equals end and the item renders =0:00 span, no runs, 0 turns (a single point, not an interval)=. The four live today:

| ts | event | why it is alone |
|----------+---------+-------------------------------------------|
| 13:03:51 | resume | the session's first event; nothing precedes it |
| 14:05:43 | pause | stranded after a =clock_out=/=todo= pair consumed its neighbours into a clock-bounded span |
| 16:45:04 | pause | same shape |
| 17:37:56 | resume | genuinely in flight — the newest event in the queue |

*So there are two populations wearing one appearance, and only one of them is self-resolving.* =--review-nothing-reason='s docstring already says suppression was considered and rejected, on the grounds that "hiding the trailing in-flight span needs a liveness signal, whose only available form is queue-file mtime with an hour's idle threshold — so a crashed session's last span would vanish for an hour", and adds that "the in-flight case is self-resolving anyway: the next =pause= grows the cluster and the item stops being degenerate."

*That last claim is true of the trailing span and false of the other three.* 13:03, 14:05 and 16:45 have hundreds of later events behind them. They can never grow. They are *permanently* degenerate, and they have been re-offered on every review pass today — which is why ignoring them is the rational response and why they read as noise rather than as a question.

*The remedy is a test the earlier reasoning did not need and now does: does any later event exist in the queue?* If yes, the span is *stranded* and can never grow, so nothing is lost by not asking about it. If no, it is *trailing* and the liveness objection applies in full — keep offering it. This needs no mtime, no idle threshold and no guess about whether a session is alive; it is an exact property of the event stream, which is the kind of signal [[id:7771fc63-9374-4c8a-9e80-24ceec21977c][7771fc63]] says to prefer over a plausible heuristic.

*Scale, measured so this is not over-sold.* Across every queue file: 1563 guideposts, 1501 consumed into applied spans, 46 dismissed, 16 unresolved. So ~96% are absorbed and this is a small residue — but it is the residue that is *always on screen*, and today it was 4 of 9 pending items, which is why it feels larger than it is.

*Open: what to do with a stranded one.* Candidates, none chosen — drop it from the buffer entirely; render it without the =!= so it stops reading as a question needing a decision; or auto-dismiss it, which consumes the events and stops it returning. The last is the only one that also stops the queue file growing a permanent tail, but it writes without being asked, so it wants a deliberate decision rather than a default.

*Related but distinct:* [[id:31f766ab-90ed-4950-bc5b-787528c8fe84][31f766ab]] (DONE, 2026-08-18) made these items *explain themselves* rather than being silently degenerate, which is why the line says which kind of no-op it is. This heading is the next question — that an item which explains itself is still an item, and one that can never change still asks for a decision every pass.

:END:
*Shipped 2026-08-31 on the user's decision — "drop the stranded ones silently, if that's your recommendation" — and it was, for four reasons rather than one.*

*Nothing is lost.* The guidepost itself stays in the queue file, which is the durable record; only the *proposal* is dropped. This is not the shape this project regrets, where a queued event vanishes without trace — the event is still there, it simply stops being rendered as a question.

*The question had exactly one possible answer.* A stranded single point writes nothing and can never grow, so =d= was the only move; asking every pass is not a decision, it is a chore.

*The test is exact, not a heuristic.* [[id:31f766ab-90ed-4950-bc5b-787528c8fe84][31f766ab]] rejected suppression because hiding an in-flight span needs a liveness signal — queue-file mtime with an idle threshold — so a crashed session's last span would vanish for an hour. That objection is real and applies *only* to the trailing span. "Does any later event exist in the queue" is a property of the stream itself, needs no threshold, and cannot be wrong.

*And it repairs a second thing that was never diagnosed.* =--queue-drained-p= is "yields no review items" *and* idle — so a queue whose only remaining items were stranded points **never drained and therefore never archived**. That was a slow leak nobody had connected to this.

*Verified live, after reloading the module.* Pending went from 9 items to 1. The three stranded points — 13:03, 14:05, 16:45 — are gone, and the fourth demonstrated the other half of the split by *growing*: the 17:37 trailing point is now =[17:37]--[17:57] 0:20 span, 0:10 in 2 runs, 3 turns=, exactly the self-resolution =--review-nothing-reason='s docstring predicted for the in-flight case.

*Verified in batch and proved to discriminate on both halves*, which matters because they are opposite failures and one test would miss one: 480 tests before, 482 after, 0 unexpected. Dropping nothing fails only the stranded test; dropping the trailing one too fails only the trailing test.

*The other two candidates were not taken.* Rendering without the =!= leaves the item on screen, which does not fix the chore. Auto-dismissing writes to the queue unasked, and the drop achieves the same visible result without that — the events stay unconsumed, which is the more conservative record.

Residue from [[id:8d0716fe-ca88-429d-b46b-e2f880f5b2cc][8d0716fe]], filed 2026-08-31 rather than left in that heading's debrief — a decision named in a closed body is on the path to invisibility, which is the rule this heading exists to honour rather than an abundance of caution.

*What shipped.* =claude-code-ide-org-review-undo-refresh= restores the item list =g= last discarded, and the confirmation prompt names it. It is reachable by =M-x= only.

*Why it was left unbound*, and this is a real reason rather than a deferral: the review keymap's vocabulary is borrowed from dired on purpose — =m=/=u= per line and advancing, =t= to invert, =U= to clear — because that is the muscle memory a person arrives with. Adding a key to that map is a decision about which borrowed vocabulary to break, and it is worth making at the keyboard by the person with the muscle memory, not by a session composing a commit message.

*The obvious candidates are all taken or wrong.* =u= and =U= are unmark and unmark-all; =r= reads as "refresh"; =C-/= is undo, which is close enough to be tempting and wrong, since this restores a *list* rather than editing text and binding it would train a reflex that fails everywhere else in the buffer.

*Worth weighing before binding anything: whether the prompt makes a key unnecessary.* =g= now asks before discarding, so the undo exists for the case where a human confirms and immediately regrets it — which is rarer than the slip that prompted [[id:8d0716fe-ca88-429d-b46b-e2f880f5b2cc][8d0716fe]] in the first place. If that case is rare enough, =M-x= is the honest home and the legend line stays short. Leaving it as is, deliberately, is a perfectly good outcome for this heading.

*Decided by the user 2026-08-31: leave it unbound.* =M-x claude-code-ide-org-review-undo-refresh= is the whole interface, and that is the answer rather than a deferral.

*The reasoning that supported it, offered before the decision.* The =g= confirmation is a =yes-or-no-p=, which requires typing =yes= and so is hard to answer reflexively — it already catches the slip this all started from ("I hit =g= when I mean =x="). What the undo covers is narrower: the prompt names *counts*, not *items* — "Discard 3 marked, 1 assigned, 1 edited interval?" — so a human can confirm on an incomplete mental model, having forgotten an interval they edited twenty minutes earlier. Real, but rare enough that a key on a map borrowing dired's vocabulary is not worth spending.

*No code change.* The command exists, the prompt names it, and the legend line stays short — which was the point.

*What would reopen this:* evidence that the narrow case actually happens. If a =g= is ever confirmed and regretted, that is the datum this decision lacked, and it is worth saying so at the time rather than quietly reaching for =M-x=.



**** DONE Three conventions read as permission to grow a story where mitosis was owed :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-31 Mon 16:38]
:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       6e43120d-b9ed-4595-8309-ccd0cde8da59
:CREATED:  [2026-08-31 Mon 16:38]
:CATEGORY: Skill
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-09-01 Tue 08:17
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Skill
