:END:
:LOGBOOK:
CLOCK: [2026-08-31 Mon 16:18]--[2026-08-31 Mon 16:19] =>  0:01
- [2026-08-31 Mon 16:18]--[2026-08-31 Mon 16:19] assigned at review
CLOCK: [2026-08-31 Mon 16:24]--[2026-08-31 Mon 16:25] =>  0:01
- [2026-08-31 Mon 16:24]--[2026-08-31 Mon 16:25] assigned at review
:END:
:PLAN:

*Asked by the user 2026-08-31, immediately after the mistake:* "does the language of one or more conventions need to be revised to guard against this pitfall?" Yes — three passages, and between them they did not merely fail to forbid the error, they read as licence for it.

*The pitfall.* [[id:9e627dc0-d31b-42cc-857a-b1e5a77f44a5][9e627dc0]] was a level-1 leaf that had done real work — six CLOCK lines, a long body, and a shipped half. Its undone parts were filed as *children*, which made it a story. That is a legitimate shape for a heading that never did work of its own; it is the wrong shape here, because a container with live children can never close, so a heading whose own work is finished is held open by its group indefinitely. Mitosis exists precisely to avoid that: the original becomes the *child*, keeps its record, and closes.

*The three sentences, and what each contributed:*

1. =A task becomes one by acquiring keyworded children — however they arrived, whether grown or refiled.= This is the one that did the damage. It is a statement about *detection* and reads as one about *permission*, and "grown" names the wrong act as an ordinary route.
2. =Where a story comes from= describes mitosis correctly but never states the *direction* plainly, so nothing in it contradicts a reader who has already concluded that growing children is fine. The user's own question — "would it not now be a leaf, and the parent a new ID?" — is the sentence that was missing.
3. =The nine groupings carrying their own CLOCK lines today are history, not debt ... Nothing is to be migrated.= Written as amnesty for accidents; reads as a general blessing on the shape. It was the third thing I checked before deciding, and it said what I wanted to hear.

:END:
*What was added, 2026-08-31:*

- A *test* rather than a taxonomy: a heading that already owns work — a clock, a =:LOGBOOK:=, a body recording what it did — must not simply be given children, because that strands the record in something that cannot close. Only a heading with nothing of its own to strand may grow children in place.
- The *direction*, stated outright: after dividing, the original is the child and the new parent carries a new =:ID:=. "If the heading you started from is still the parent afterwards, you did not divide."
- The *ordering*, which cost a step in practice: divide first, then file the new leaves as siblings. Dividing afterwards carries already-added children down with it, since =org-demote-subtree= moves the whole subtree, and they arrive as grandchildren needing a refile.
- An explicit boundary on the amnesty: it covers what already happened, not a deliberate choice made today.

*Why this is worth a convention change rather than a note.* The error was not carelessness — three separate passages were consulted and each appeared to permit it. A rule that has to be *inferred* from a mechanism's description is a rule that will be got wrong again, and this one fails silently: the tree stays valid, =bin/lint-org= is content, and the only symptom is a heading that quietly never closes.

*Not claimed:* that the new wording is machine-checkable. A lint could plausibly flag "container with a clock and a body acquiring its first child", but that is exactly the shape the amnesty says to leave alone in the nine existing cases, so the check would need history it does not have. Left as prose deliberately.



**** DONE Auto-mark the state items that carry no judgement :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-31 Mon 16:01]
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Apply
:ID:       b6e229c7-3035-4c0e-943b-710a12bfd7d1
:CREATED:  [2026-08-24 Mon 19:08]
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-09-01 Tue 08:17
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Apply
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "TODO"       from              [2026-08-24 Mon 19:08] \\
  measure staleness rate before building
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-08-31 Mon 16:01]
:END:
:PLAN:

*Proposed by the user 2026-08-24, after a long review pass:* "it seems like state transitions never require any judgment anymore. could those be applied invisibly or at least marked automatically?"

*Mostly true, and the exception is the whole design.* A =state= item carries exactly one judgement: *staleness*. =--review-state-stale-p= exists because on 2026-08-07 applying a transition whose premise no longer held wrote plausible, correctly-formatted, wrong history -- and that is the failure this project exists to prevent. Everything else about a state item is mechanical.

So the rule is clean, and the predicate for it already exists: =--review-markable-p= encodes precisely "can be marked without asking the human anything". Auto-marking is that predicate applied at *render* time rather than when =M= is pressed.

- *Auto-mark* non-stale =state= items, so they arrive selected.
- *Leave stale ones unmarked*, exactly as =--review-set-all= already refuses them.
- *Do not auto-apply.*

*That last line is load-bearing rather than cautious.* Apply must stay human-triggered: org's native state-change logging only completes inside a genuinely interactive command, which is the constraint the entire queue architecture was built around, and a non-interactive apply hits the hang it exists to route around. Auto-*marking* removes keystrokes without touching that; auto-*applying* would dismantle it.

*A second reason, which the same afternoon supplied.* When an apply reported "Applied 0 item(s); 5 failed", the human had no independent expectation to compare against -- they had pressed =M= and did not know how many it had marked. Pre-marked items make the mismatch immediate: five marked, five failed, and the discrepancy is visible rather than inferred from a truncated message.

*Worth measuring before building:* how often a state item is stale in practice. On 2026-08-24 after two partial applies it was *every* item -- =markable 0= -- because the applies had already moved those headings to the states their events described. If that is typical rather than an artefact of a bad day, auto-marking buys less than it appears to and the honest answer is that the staleness check is doing most of the work.

*Measured first, as this body required, and the measurement changes the verdict.* Across the queue archive — 18 completed sessions, 450 queued =state= events:

| outcome | count | share |
|---------------+-------+-------|
| applied | 435 | 96.7% |
| dismissed | 15 | 3.3% |
| left unapplied | *0* | 0% |

*Zero.* Every state event that reached a review pass was either applied or explicitly dismissed; none was queued, refused as stale and abandoned. So a state item that reaches review is almost always one the human intends to apply, and the 2026-08-24 observation that prompted the caution — =markable 0= after two partial applies — was an artefact of that afternoon rather than the normal case. Auto-marking buys real keystrokes.

*(Limits, stated: the ledger records applied and dismissed, so "dismissed" may include items discarded precisely because they were stale, and staleness at the moment of an old review is not recoverable after the fact. The claim is about outcomes, not about how often the guard fired.)*

:END:
*Shipped 2026-08-31, exactly the three rules this body specified:* non-stale =state= items arrive marked; stale ones do not, as =M= already refused them; nothing is auto-applied. The last is load-bearing rather than cautious — org's native state logging only completes inside a genuinely interactive command, and auto-applying would dismantle the constraint the whole queue exists to honour.

*Scoped to =state= alone.* A span is not mechanical: it carries an interval a human may want to edit and, when unassigned, a heading only they can choose.

*Two things the build found that the proposal did not, both real:*

- *Auto-marking must happen once per item, never once per render.* Marks redraw on every keystroke, so re-deciding at render time makes =u= impossible — the mark returns on the redraw that follows it. Caught by the existing mark-advances and bulk-mark tests, which is what they are for. Guarded by an =:auto-mark-considered= flag.
- *An auto-mark is not judgement, and conflating them would have broken the guard shipped an hour earlier.* [[id:8d0716fe-ca88-429d-b46b-e2f880f5b2cc][8d0716fe]] makes =g= ask before discarding marks, assignments, notes and edited intervals. If a pre-mark counted, =g= would prompt on *every* refresh — turning that guard into exactly the decoration it was written to avoid. So marks carry =:auto-marked=, the judgement summary ignores them, and a hand =m= or =u= clears the flag because the line is then the human's. A mutation confirms it: counting auto-marks fails the instant-refresh test.

*The projection is re-run after auto-marking*, because the first pass judged staleness with those items unmarked, so a chain's later links were measured against a projection that stopped short. Skipping it would light a =STALE= flag on the very items just marked.

*The second benefit this body predicted is now available:* pre-marked items give the human an independent expectation to compare against, so "Applied 0 item(s); 5 failed" reads as a mismatch instead of an unanchored number.

*Verified:* 477 tests before, 480 after, 0 unexpected, exit 0. Three mutations, each a full 480-test run: removing auto-marking fails the three new tests; ignoring staleness fails the auto-mark test *and* the pre-existing bulk-mark test; counting auto-marks as judgement fails the =g= tests.

*Reported by the user 2026-08-26:* "I have a tendency to hit =g= when I mean =x= and I lose all of my review work." =g= and =x= are adjacent intentions -- refresh and apply -- and one of them is destructive.

*The loss is already documented; what is wrong is the assumption around it.* =claude-code-ide-org-review-refresh='s own docstring spells out the cost -- "every unapplied decision, not only marks: assigned headings, edited intervals, notes and stale confirmations all live in =--review-items= until =x= applies them, and a rebuild replaces that list wholesale" -- and then concludes: *"=g= is typed deliberately, so discarding here is correct; it just has to say so."* That conclusion is what this heading falsifies. It is typed deliberately and it is sometimes typed *instead of* =x=.

*This is the same loss the 2026-08-24 recovery already paid for once* ([[id:7148cddc-aca3-416e-8bcb-f164d4d2bba0][7148cddc]]): "Assignments and edited intervals live in =--review-items=, in memory, never in the queue. Rebuilding items from the queue restores the *events* and discards the judgement applied to them." The user lost a hand-made assignment and an edited interval then, and was told the rollback would "cost the review pass again" -- which sounded like keystrokes and meant decisions.

*Detectable, and checked before filing rather than assumed.* Three of the four kinds leave an unambiguous flag on the item plist:

| judgement | set by | flag |
|-----------+--------+------|
| marks | =review-mark=, =review-mark-all= | =:marked= |
| assignment | =review-assign= | =:assigned t= (and =:id=) |
| note | =review-edit-note= | =:note= |
| edited interval | =review-edit-interval= | *no flag of its own* |

*The fourth needs one line.* =review-edit-interval= overwrites =:start= and =:end= in place, and both keys exist on every span item straight from the queue, so presence proves nothing. It does set =:suggested nil= with the comment "an edited interval is a confirmed one, not a suggestion" -- which is *close* to the signal wanted but not the same claim, since an accepted-as-suggested span may also be confirmed. Adding an explicit =:edited t= beside it is the honest fix.

*So the predicate is:* any item carrying =:marked=, =:assigned=, =:note= or =:edited=. Cheap, exact, and it can also say *how much* is at stake -- "3 marked, 1 assigned, 1 note" reads better than a bare "are you sure?", because the answer depends on the amount.

*Prompt only when there is something to lose.* A confirmation on every =g= trains the reflex that dismisses it, which is how a guard becomes decoration. With nothing pending, =g= should stay instant.

*Worth considering instead of, or alongside, the prompt:* make the discard recoverable. The items are a list in memory; stashing the pre-refresh copy in a buffer-local variable and offering =C-/= or an =undo-refresh= command would make the slip cost a keystroke rather than a decision. That is strictly better than asking, and the two are not exclusive.

:END:
*Shipped 2026-08-31, taking both options this body offered rather than choosing between them — it said so itself: "strictly better than asking, and the two are not exclusive."*

*=g= asks, and names what is at stake.* =Discard 3 marked, 1 assigned, 1 note?= rather than a bare "are you sure?", because the answer depends on the amount. Declining signals a =user-error= and leaves the item list untouched.

*It asks only when there is something to lose*, which this body required and which is the difference between a guard and decoration: with no judgement pending, =g= stays instant. A confirmation on every refresh trains the reflex that dismisses it.

*The fourth flag was added, as diagnosed.* =:marked=, =:assigned= and =:note= already existed; an edited interval had none of its own, because =:start= and =:end= are on every span straight from the queue so their presence proves nothing. =review-edit-interval= now sets =:edited t= beside the =:suggested nil= it already set — the two are close but not the same claim, since an accepted-as-suggested span is also confirmed.

*And the discard is recoverable.* =claude-code-ide-org-review-undo-refresh= restores the stashed list; the prompt names it, so a human who confirms and immediately regrets it has a way back. The prompt stops the common case and the stash recovers the one that gets through. Deliberately left unbound: adding a key to a map whose vocabulary is borrowed from dired is a decision worth making at the keyboard rather than while the user is away.

*The conclusion in =review-refresh='s own docstring is now reversed rather than merely elaborated.* It said "=g= is typed deliberately, so discarding here is correct; it just has to say so" — and the docstring now records that this heading falsified it: it is typed deliberately *and* sometimes typed instead of =x=. Worth keeping visible, because that sentence was written by someone who had thought about the loss and still got the conclusion wrong.

*Verified:* 472 tests before, 477 after, 0 unexpected, exit 0. Three mutations, each a full 477-test run: never prompting fails the ask test and the undo test; dropping =:edited= fails only the flag test; never taking the stash fails only the undo test. The undo test also asserts a *second* undo errors rather than restoring the same list twice.

*Not done, and not needed:* [[id:7148cddc-aca3-416e-8bcb-f164d4d2bba0][7148cddc]]'s 2026-08-24 loss is the same shape and was paid for once already. Nothing here retroactively recovers that; this stops the next one.



**** DONE Apply logs a self-transition when a queued event's target already matches reality :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-31 Mon 15:51]
:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       05c71d99-2839-447b-a536-60eb4bf43b73
:CREATED:  [2026-08-28 Fri 07:56]
:CATEGORY: Apply
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-09-01 Tue 08:17
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Apply
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "TODO"       from              [2026-08-28 Fri 07:57] \\
  filed from the decisions pass
CLOCK: [2026-08-31 Mon 15:48]--[2026-08-31 Mon 15:51] =>  0:03
- State "DOING"      from "TODO"       [2026-08-31 Mon 15:48]
- [2026-08-31 Mon 15:48]--[2026-08-31 Mon 15:51] skip a state event that has become a no-op
- State "DONE"       from "DOING"      [2026-08-31 Mon 15:51]
:END:
:PLAN:

*Measured across both files 2026-08-28:* 4 of 463 =State= lines record a transition to the keyword the heading already held — 0.9%. Both =DONE -> DONE= cases are dated [2026-08-11 Tue], the day the staleness guard shipped, and they sit on =Build the interactive review-and-apply Emacs command= and — pointedly — on =Apply must not replay a state event that reality has moved past=, the guard's own heading. Since the guard: *2 in 17 days* — =TODO -> TODO= on 420816ec [2026-08-20], =DOING -> DOING= on 29439196 [2026-08-27].

*The staleness guard is blind to this by construction, not by oversight.* =--review-state-stale-p= asks whether reality moved *away* from what the event expected:

#+begin_src elisp
(and (not (eq current 'unresolved))
     (not (equal (claude-code-ide-org--review-normalize-from from) current)))
#+end_src

A self-transition is the one shape where the answer is emphatically no. =from= matches reality perfectly, which is exactly why it sails through — the event is a *correctly-non-stale no-op*.

*Cause.* Two events assert the same target. Post-cutover nothing moves an org file until apply moves it, so every =org_set_todo= in a batch reads =from= off an unmoved file; =--review-projected-staleness= then projects the batch forward and the second event sees =from= = projected current = =to=. On 29439196 the pair was almost certainly the =ExitPlanMode= hook's queued =todo DOING= plus an explicit =org_set_todo DOING= for the same heading.

*The fix is not in the staleness guard and should not be called one.* Stale means the event is *dangerous* — it would regress the record. This means the event is *redundant* — it would change nothing but still writes a log line. Conflating them would either let real staleness through or teach the reader that the flag means "harmless". Separate test, comparing =to= against the projected current state, skipping the item rather than refusing it.

*Worth deciding at the same time:* whether a skipped no-op is reported in the review buffer or silently dropped. Dropping is defensible — nothing was lost — but a queued event that vanishes without trace is the shape this project has repeatedly regretted.

*Related:* [[id:2d100d0d-2d04-43b9-af1e-f4d6b52bbada][2d100d0d]] is the same class of gap one layer down — a check that has to run *across* items in a batch rather than within one item.

*The queue-side half of this already shipped, and the dates say it does not cover this case.* [[id:cc0c17a7-a554-426d-afeb-09cbee7339f0][cc0c17a7]] — "A no-op TODO -> TODO transition should never be queued" — closed [2026-08-20 Thu 07:38], having taken the first of the two options its own body laid out: "=org_set_todo= could refuse to queue when =from= equals =to=", with the second, "apply could treat a no-op as satisfied rather than failed", left as defensible-but-not-done.

The =420816ec= self-transition is stamped [2026-08-20 Thu 07:49] — *eleven minutes after that refusal shipped.* So this is not the same defect recurring; it is the half cc0c17a7 explicitly deferred, arriving within the hour.

*Why the queue-side guard cannot reach it.* It compares =from= to =to= at *queue* time, against a snapshot of a file that then does not move until apply. The case here is a heading that arrives at =to= *in between* — because another event in the same batch lands it there, or a hand-edit does. At queue time the event is not a no-op by any test available then; it becomes one before it is applied. And org writes the state it *observes* as the =from= on the log line, not the one the event recorded, which is why the artifact reads =from "TODO"= even where the queued event said otherwise.

So cc0c17a7 owns "do not queue an event that is already a no-op" and this owns "do not apply an event that has *become* one". Same defect, two clocks, and only the second needs the projection =--review-projected-staleness= already computes.

:END:
*Shipped 2026-08-31, as a separate test rather than a change to the staleness guard — which this body was emphatic about and which the mutation testing confirms was the right call.*

=--review-projected-staleness= now annotates each state item with =:redundant= alongside =:stale=, comparing =to= against the *projection* rather than the file. That is why it can be computed here and nowhere earlier: the usual cause is two events in one batch asserting the same target, so at queue time the second is not a no-op by any test then available — it becomes one before it is applied. [[id:cc0c17a7-a554-426d-afeb-09cbee7339f0][cc0c17a7]] owns "do not queue an event that is already a no-op"; this owns "do not apply one that has become one", exactly as this body divided them.

*The two flags stay opposite, and the code says so at the site.* Stale means applying would *regress* the record; redundant means it would change nothing and still write a =State= line claiming the heading moved to where it already was. A test asserts the redundant item is *not* stale — its =from= matches reality perfectly, which is precisely why it sails through the staleness guard.

*Apply skips it and returns nil*, i.e. success, so the backing events are consumed and the item does not return every pass. The alternative — reporting a failure — would leave a permanently unapplyable item in the queue.

*The open question in this body is answered: reported, not dropped.* The line reads =state DOING 08-31 09:05 no-op, heading is already there --=, and carries *no* =!=, because nothing is wrong. Dropping it silently was defensible on the grounds that nothing is lost, but this body's own objection stands — a queued event that vanishes without trace is the shape this project has repeatedly regretted — and the reader is owed the difference between "applied" and "there was nothing to do".

*Verified:* 470 tests before, 472 after, 0 unexpected, exit 0. Two mutations, each a full 472-test run: never detecting redundancy fails both new tests, and detecting it but not skipping fails only the apply test — which is the pair that shows the annotation and the action are independently covered. The end state is asserted directly: the heading holds =DOING= with *exactly one* =State= line, not two.

- *=a= marks and advances*, collapsing the pair. One keystroke, but it makes assignment imply approval — and a human who wanted to assign, look at the interval, and *then* decide has lost the ability to.

The reader has to already know the convention to parse the line, and the line exists to tell them something they do not know.

*A person who reads this buffer daily read it as a bug*, which is the measurement that matters -- not whether the code is right but whether the reader can tell. Every candidate fix is a wording change and none touches the computation: ="writes 0:36 across 9 runs"=, ="writes 0:36 in 9 runs"=, or splitting the count onto the annotation where the runs are actually listed.

This is the first case the audit would have caught, found by a human the next morning instead.

*Worth doing in the same pass as that audit* rather than alone, since a one-word fix here and an unchanged wording three lines below would leave the buffer inconsistent in a way that is worse than uniformly terse.

*Decided 2026-08-28, and the decision is larger than the wording.* Every candidate above is a better label for the same claim — a prediction of what apply will write. That claim is the actual defect, and it turned up independently while judging a second, apparently unrelated bug: the figure is computed *before* =--subtract-intervals= runs, so the buffer can promise 0:11 and apply write less. The obvious repairs were to recompute per refresh (a file read per span item) or to flag items whose target already holds overlapping intervals. Both are features. The cheap answer is to stop making the claim.

*State the evidence, not the outcome.* The span envelope, the runs inside it, and the turn count are all in hand at render time and none of them can disagree with apply, because none of them asserts what apply will do. A readout that reports what was observed needs no recomputation and no staleness flag; the render/apply gap does not get fixed so much as it stops existing.

*This also repairs a misreading the current wording invites.* The user, who reads this buffer daily, took the span to be what lands in the =:LOGBOOK:=. It is not — the span is the envelope, and what lands are the =resume -> pause= runs inside it. The live pending item at the moment of this decision reads =writes 0:01 in 1= over the span 07:44--07:51: seven minutes of wall clock, one minute claimed. Nothing in the line says the other six were not lost, or ignored, or a bug. Reporting the envelope alongside the runs answers that without arithmetic.

That heading also supplies what the gap between envelope and runs *means* rather than leaving it as unexplained shrinkage — a dense run of turns is joint attention, the human reading and typing while the agent works, and the inter-turn gaps are not idle. Its recall-cue framing ("a number they must weigh is heavier than a word they can recognise") is the shape this readout should take, so the two should be built together rather than reworded twice.

*Found by the user 2026-08-26, from a readout they correctly refused to believe:* "I sense a contradiction. you just confirmed that [2026-08-26 Wed 13:05]--[2026-08-26 Wed 13:20] is my attention but something else says otherwise? who wins?"

*Nothing wins, because the two claims are about different intervals -- and the review buffer prints only one of them.* An unassigned span item carries:

- a *window*, rendered as its headline: =[2026-08-26 Wed 13:05]--[2026-08-26 Wed 13:22]=, 17 minutes, being the outer bracket of a guidepost cluster;
- a *payload*, rendered as =writes 0:01 in 1=: one CLOCK line of about a minute, extracted by =--span-work-runs= as the sole =resume= -> =pause= adjacency inside it.

*The two belong to different people.* The payload is agent activity, and [[id:b8e6007a-ae13-4b13-bb2e-a5df39435af0][b8e6007a]] correctly rules it inactive and out of the agenda. The remaining ~14 minutes of the window is the human reading a session report -- real attention, discarded by the extraction rather than recorded as anything. So b8e6007a never sees it, and the natural reading of the item ("this 17-minute range is about to be written down") is false in both directions at once: that range is not what gets written, and the part of it that *is* the human's is not written at all.

*Measured, on the item that produced the complaint.* Six guideposts back it and nothing else -- =pause= 13:05:50, =pause= 13:05:58, =resume= 13:20:21, =pause= 13:20:32, =pause= 13:20:43, =resume= 13:22:51. No =todo= or =clock= event falls inside, which is also why it is unassigned: there is no heading in the window to attribute it to.

*Why this is a readout defect rather than a pipeline defect.* The pipeline is behaving exactly as designed and every number it produces is right. What is wrong is that the item is *named* by a quantity it does not write, so a reader infers the headline is the record. The fix is presentational -- show the run(s) the item will actually write, or mark the window as a bracket rather than an interval -- and deliberately does not touch what is extracted.

*Distinct from the three neighbours it will be mistaken for.* [[id:5a6d2c75-9a42-4dd4-b4d6-670aeebc5b46][5a6d2c75]] wants the *evidence* that would make an unassigned span's heading obvious; [[id:98c302e0-ab1b-40bf-92d0-d2f2e16ac05d][98c302e0]] is about the units in "writes 0:01 in 1"; [[id:46e4ce2b-fdc8-447b-ad09-b4845602540f][46e4ce2b]] is about where the =:ID:= prefix sits on a line. All three are about a line that is hard to read. This one is about a line that is *misleading when read correctly*, which is the sharper failure and needs a different fix.

*Related but not the same*: [[id:996fd2bd-be90-44b3-b2c5-9018255940b3][996fd2bd]] proposes reclaiming a guidepost gap as the human's attention when an apply timestamp falls inside it. That is about *capturing* the missing 14 minutes; this is about not implying they are already captured. If 996fd2bd ships, this heading still stands -- a window and its payload would still be two quantities.

*Filed with a finding attached.* Writing this body hit [[id:478d6ec9-1b99-4c6c-88e9-c793ad4b2f22][478d6ec9]] live: =org_amend='s link checker expanded all four TODO.org prefixes above and refused =b8e6007a=, which is identical in form and differs only in living in DONE.org. So the expander is scoped to TODO.org, and a cross-file reference has to be written as plain text -- which is why one citation here is not a link.

:END:
*Shipped 2026-08-31, presentationally, exactly as this body specified — the extraction is untouched.* The span line now names its envelope instead of leaving it as an unlabelled headline: =0:11 span, 0:01 in 1 run, 6 turns=. The window and the payload are still two quantities, and now they are two *labelled* quantities rather than one label over two claims.

*The misreading this heading identified is answered directly.* "This 17-minute range is about to be written down" was false in both directions at once. It now takes no arithmetic and no prior knowledge to see that the range is the bracket and the runs are what lands: both appear, both named, on one line.

That is [[id:996fd2bd-be90-44b3-b2c5-9018255940b3][996fd2bd]], and as this body predicted, that heading and this one do not collapse into each other: if 996fd2bd ships, a window and its payload are still two quantities and still both need naming.

*Noticed 2026-08-24 when the user asked whether the day's new headings formed a group.* They do, and the grouping is not the one the categories suggest.

Six defects were found in a single afternoon, all in the review-and-apply surface, and every one has the same shape: *information existed at a boundary and was discarded there.*

| where | knew | said |
|-----------------------------+---------------------------+-------------------------|
| =--at-id= | the stack, the =:ID:= | a bare error string |
| apply's failure report | which item failed | five identical sentences |
| =M= (=--review-set-all=) | two kinds of refusal | "13 stale item(s)" |
| the group heading | four kinds of =:ID:= | resolvable or "unresolvable" |
| =e= (=--review-edit-interval=) | the bracket style typed | discarded at parse |
| the review buffer | the whole line | truncated at the window |

*None of these is a logic error.* Every one of those functions computes the right answer and then narrows it on the way out. That is why they survived so long: tests assert the computed value, and the loss happens after.

*The cost is not cosmetic, and the day priced it.* "13 stale item(s)" nearly led to dismissing six spans, three carrying real recorded time, with no undo. Five identical failure messages consumed an afternoon and three withdrawn hypotheses. ="Review a  (unresolved)"= made a working feature look broken. The truncation hid the tail of exactly the lines a human reads to decide something.

*Why this surface specifically.* The review buffer is the one place a human is *asked to judge*, so it is the only surface where a lost distinction converts directly into a wrong decision. Everywhere else in this project, discarded information is merely absent; here it is actively misleading, because the human acts on what the buffer says.

*The related-but-distinct heading:* [[id:2b050e7a-b0c4-45d3-835e-68befcebb7bb][2b050e7a]] names the same shape *within one function*, fixed three times. This heading is that observation one level up -- the =cond= there had the wrong shape for the same reason the messages here do.

*Proposed check, and it is cheap.* For each place the review buffer reports a refusal, a failure or an absence, ask: *does the code distinguish cases the message does not?* Every one of the six answers yes and is repaired by widening the message, never by changing the computation. That is a review-buffer-wide audit of perhaps a dozen call sites, not a redesign.

*Deliberately not a subtree.* Four of the six are already =DONE=, and refiling closed headings under a new epic would churn the file for a grouping that is a *lesson* rather than a work item. This heading holds the lesson; the instances stay where they are.

*Related:* [[id:b8e6007a-ae13-4b13-bb2e-a5df39435af0][b8e6007a]] and [[id:5ff5a4b8-2fee-472a-b5e1-c9de8cf96704][5ff5a4b8]] are earlier members of the same family -- both are about a readout that could not distinguish two things a human needed told apart.

:END:
*Audit performed 2026-08-31, and the wording fixed in the same pass* — deliberately not as two commits, because a one-word repair beside an unchanged line three rows down reads worse than uniform terseness.

*Method, as this body proposed:* for every place the review surface reports a refusal, a failure or an absence, ask whether the code distinguishes cases the message does not. Enumerated by scanning every =user-error= and =message= in the review-and-apply section — about two dozen sites. Four of the six original instances were already =DONE= and confirmed repaired in passing (=M='s stale-versus-unassigned split and =e='s bracket style both now carry their distinction). *Seven live sites remained*, every one repaired by widening the message and none by changing a computation, exactly as predicted:

| where | knew | said |
|-------------------------------+---------------------------------+--------------------------|
| =--review-item-at-point= callers (×6) | heading, evidence, legend or blank | "No review item on this line" |
| =e= on a non-span | the item's =:type= | "Only clock items ..." |
| =a= on a non-span | the item's =:type= | "Only a span can be ..." |
| =e= timestamp parse | *which* field failed, and the text typed | "Could not parse those timestamps" |
| =e= ordering check | both parsed times | "End is before start" |
| =a= chosen heading | which heading was chosen | "That heading has no :ID:" |
| =x= with nothing marked | whether anything is pending at all | "Nothing marked" |
| =restore-queue= | every archived session id | "No archived queue for X" |

*The six identical refusals are the same defect as the original table's "five identical sentences", one level down*, which is what makes the grouping this heading names load-bearing rather than tidy. A group heading, an evidence line, the key legend and a blank line are four situations with four different next moves, and the buffer *already tells them apart in order to draw them*. Fixing it needed one text property on the group-heading line — the only computation change in the pass, and it exists solely so the message can be specific.

*Two deliberately not widened.* =x= against a read-only buffer ("Left read-only; nothing applied, marks kept") and =d= on an eventless item already name their case precisely. Listing them here so a later reader knows they were considered rather than missed.

*Verified:* 465 tests before, 468 after, 0 unexpected, exit 0. Three mutations, each a full 468-test run with the run count checked first: disabling the group-line branch fails only the line-kind test, dropping the type from =e='s refusal fails only the type test, and collapsing the pending-count branch fails only the count test.

*What this heading does not claim to have finished.* The audit covers the *review buffer's own* messages. The span readout — a headline interval that is not what gets written — is [[id:44cef181-8dac-4735-8860-f123e132fdbc][44cef181]] and [[id:98c302e0-ab1b-40bf-92d0-d2f2e16ac05d][98c302e0]], and those two are a different question: not a message that discards a distinction, but a number that is honestly rendered and still misleads. The user's own reading on 2026-08-31, after applying a pass, was that much of the logged activity is bogus; that is filed as [[id:445ec1f1-095a-462b-abbd-7a3a00925ddb][445ec1f1]] and is about the data rather than the wording.

*The build [[id:ff1352b3-2732-4422-9f0d-4b3cb6fd8ff3][ff1352b3]] decided 2026-08-31*, filed separately because the decision is complete and the implementation is not.

*What it replaces.* Retrieving one heading currently takes three tools and hand-done arithmetic: =grep -n ":ID: 4f8500e6"= to find it, =awk= to locate the next sibling *at the right level* and so compute the subtree's end, then =Read= with the resulting offset and line count. The arithmetic is the fragile part, because the extent depends on finding the next heading at the right depth — which is exactly what org already knows.

*Nearly all plumbing.* =claude-code-ide-org--subtree-text-at-point= already returns a subtree from its heading through its last child without modifying the buffer; it is used on the clocktable path. Scope resolution — full ids, 8-character prefixes, and the shape-based error for an id that resolves to nothing — is shared with =org_outline= since [[id:2d9eeebd-4375-4790-8485-92b244236a21][2d9eeebd]].

*Returns the heading whole, drawers included, and does not filter.* That is the design rather than laziness: the property schema splits two ways, not three ([[id:ff1352b3-2732-4422-9f0d-4b3cb6fd8ff3][ff1352b3]] measured it), so there is no third surface for "metadata". =:CREATED:=, the plan link and the =ARCHIVE_*= provenance all describe *this* heading and travel with it; the caller extracts what it needs.

*Two things to decide while building, neither obvious:*

- *Whether it returns the subtree or only the heading's own body.* The primitive returns the subtree through the last child. For a leaf they are the same, and 92% of level-1 headings are leaves — but for a story the subtree can be hundreds of lines, and "show me this heading" usually means the heading. An argument, or two verbs, or default-to-own-body with an explicit opt-in.
- *What it does about =:PLAN:=.* Readers are told to skip that drawer. Returning it whole is honest and consistent with the above; suppressing it by default would be the first filtering decision the tool makes, which is the thing this design avoids.

*Deliberately out of scope:* shrinking =org_outline='s front matter. Build this first — at that point the front matter's remaining unique content is about one line, and the question answers itself.

:END:
*Shipped 2026-08-31 as =org_body=.* Both open questions decided the way this body leaned.

*Question one — own body, with =include_children= to opt in.* The heading's own text by default, stopping before the first child; pass =include_children= for the subtree. For a leaf the two are the same and most level-1 headings are leaves, but a story's subtree runs to hundreds of lines while "show me this heading" almost always means the heading — and a caller who wants a child can read it by its own id, which =org_outline= has already told them exists.

*Question two — =:PLAN:= comes back.* Suppressing it would have been the first filtering decision the tool makes, which is precisely what this design avoids. The tool *description* carries the warning instead: =:PLAN:= holds superseded design reasoning a reader is normally meant to skip, returned rather than hidden so that stays the caller's judgement. Same for =:PROPERTIES:= and =:LOGBOOK:=.

*Mostly plumbing, as predicted, with one correction to the premise.* This body said prefix expansion is shared "since 2d9eeebd" — true, but not where I first assumed. =--id-find= is the shared resolver and it expands prefixes itself, over an index of *tracked* files; =org_outline= gets the behaviour by calling it. Found by a red test: a temp fixture is not a tracked file, so a prefix minted inside one cannot resolve, and the prefix test had to move to the =--with-known-ids= fixture. What it now pins is the thing that actually matters — that =org_body= routes through =--id-find= rather than =org-id-find=, the same distinction that once left fourteen call sites accepting a prefix and one not.

*Read-only, and dispatched as one.* It goes through =--at-id=, never =--at-id-writable=; granting write permission to a query tool is exactly what that split exists to prevent ([[id:c8a97d9d-8b13-4b6a-a8b9-1a3f24b5e00b][c8a97d9d]]). A test asserts the buffer is neither modified nor narrowed after both paths run.

*One measured asymmetry worth knowing before it is mistaken for a bug.* On a *leaf*, own-body and subtree are not byte-identical: =--end-of-body= skips back over trailing blank lines and =org-end-of-subtree= keeps them, so =a0028a4e= itself returned 24 lines against 27. The content is the same; only trailing whitespace differs. Left as is — trimming is what makes repeated amendments not accumulate a gap, and it is the more useful answer.

*Verified:* 460 tests before, 465 after, 0 unexpected, exit 0. Proved to discriminate at the two points that can regress silently: making the own-body path return the subtree fails only =body-stops-before-the-first-child=, and swapping =--id-find= for =org-id-find= fails only =body-accepts-an-id-prefix=. Both full 465-test runs.

*Verified live too, against real headings* — after =load-file='ing the module, which is the precondition for the check to mean anything. =c8a97d9d= returned 119 lines own against 142 for the subtree, the difference being its one child.

*One thing this session could not check, stated rather than glossed:* whether =org_body= answers or hangs over MCP, which would be evidence for [[id:72463b68-9f08-44b2-8213-87f71298138d][72463b68]]. A newly registered tool is not in a client's tool list until the client reconnects, so the first session to start after this lands is the one that can test it. Worth doing deliberately then.

*Still deliberately out of scope:* shrinking =org_outline='s front matter, which this body defers and [[id:ff1352b3-2732-4422-9f0d-4b3cb6fd8ff3][ff1352b3]] sequences after this.

*CLAUDE.md's read-only tools table gained an =org_body= row in the same commit* — the table is read as the whole read surface, so omitting it would have made the document wrong.



**** DONE org_capture should accept an initial TODO state, so a heading is not keywordless until apply :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-31 Mon 15:20]
:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       c74f8663-b14e-4ab9-ad65-d99cb655b3fa
:CREATED:  [2026-08-28 Fri 17:36]
:CATEGORY: Tools

  companion question, filed on its own
CLOCK: [2026-08-31 Mon 15:15]--[2026-08-31 Mon 15:19] =>  0:04
- State "DOING"      from "TODO"       [2026-08-31 Mon 15:15]
- [2026-08-31 Mon 15:15]--[2026-08-31 Mon 15:19] org_capture gains initial_state
- State "DONE"       from "DOING"      [2026-08-31 Mon 15:20]
:END:
:PLAN:

*Raised as a companion question by [[id:36b811d9-8bd3-4a32-b67d-39ccfe0d66c1][36b811d9]] and filed on its own 2026-08-28.* =org_capture= deliberately writes *no* TODO keyword — its description says to set the state afterwards with =org_set_todo=, which *queues*. So **every heading captured in a session is keywordless on disk until a human applies the queue**, and a capture-then-set is two operations that land a review pass apart.

*The cost is not hypothetical and is not only cosmetic.* A =:BLOCKER:= naming a heading captured in the same session is *inert*: =org-depend= blocks only on an unfinished TODO keyword, and a keywordless heading has none. =bin/lint-org= reports it, [[id:36b811d9-8bd3-4a32-b67d-39ccfe0d66c1][36b811d9]] hit it within a minute of being written, and [[id:798bb7a1-d5a6-4c08-8cf0-cc91a82d08e6][798bb7a1]] is the same gap seen from the slice side — a member captured this session cannot be rendered or blocked on. Measured this session: roughly a dozen captures, every one of them keywordless for as long as it took to ask for an apply, and one =:BLOCKER:= error that cleared itself only when the queue was run.

*The tension, which is why this is a question rather than an obvious fix.* The queue exists because state transitions are the thing that caused every incident, and it is load-bearing that org's *native* state logging runs inside a genuinely interactive command. A capture that writes a keyword directly would write one state change without a =State= log line and outside the review pass — a small, silent exception to the rule the architecture is built on.

*Three shapes, none chosen:*

1. *An =initial_state= argument that writes the keyword with the heading.* Simplest and most useful; the exception above is real but bounded — a *creation* has no prior state to log a transition from, so nothing is lost that a log line would have carried.
2. *Capture queues a =todo= event alongside itself*, so the keyword arrives through the normal path. Keeps one rule, but does not fix anything: the heading is still keywordless until apply, which is the actual complaint.
3. *Leave it, and make the inertness visible instead.* =org_set_property= already warns when a =:BLOCKER:= names a keywordless heading ([[id:36b811d9-8bd3-4a32-b67d-39ccfe0d66c1][36b811d9]]); the lint already errors. This is the do-nothing option and it is not obviously wrong.

*Option 1 is the one worth arguing about*, and the argument turns on whether "a heading is created *with* a state" is a transition at all. If it is not — and a =State \"TODO\" from \"\"= line is arguably noise rather than history — then there is no exception, only a capture that finishes the job.

*Decided by the user 2026-08-31: option 1.* =org_capture= gains an =initial_state= argument and writes the keyword with the heading.

*The objection it overrides, and why that is sound.* Writing a keyword directly puts one state change outside the queue, and the queue is load-bearing because org's native state logging only completes inside an interactive command. But a *creation* has no prior state, so there is no transition to log: =State "TODO" from ""= is noise rather than history. Nothing is hidden from the review pass that the review pass wanted.

*What it fixes, measured:* every heading captured in a session is keywordless on disk until apply, so a =:BLOCKER:= naming one is inert, =bin/lint-org= errors, and =.githooks/pre-commit= refuses. That cost [[id:b36e6369-a210-4540-adc7-0c0c188e9791][b36e6369]] a commit on 2026-08-28 — the slice could not be committed until the queue was applied, because three of its own members were captured in the same session.

*Still queue-routed:* every *subsequent* transition. This is a creation-time argument only, and =org_set_todo= keeps its behaviour unchanged.

*Note for whoever builds it:* the argument should be optional and default to nothing, so a capture with no state still produces a keywordless heading. That is the current behaviour and some callers want it — a heading captured as a note rather than a task.

:END:
*Shipped 2026-08-31 as option 1, the decision recorded above.* =org_capture= takes an optional =initial_state= and writes the keyword with the heading. Omitting it still produces a keywordless heading, which the body asked for explicitly — a heading captured as a note rather than a task — and the empty string is treated as omitted rather than writing a bare =* =.

*Validated against the target file's own =#+TODO:= line*, the same gate =org_set_todo= applies and for the same reason: =queue-append= drops any reply starting with =Error:=, so this is the only thing between a bad call and a heading carrying a keyword org does not recognise — which org then reads as *part of the title*, invisibly and permanently. The error names the file's keyword set so the caller can correct itself. A shared =--file-todo-keywords= now reads that set per file, and the leading-keyword guard from [[id:2b2db914-c96e-416a-a80a-e31028308de0][2b2db914]] was refactored onto it rather than keeping a second copy.

*The deferred path carries the keyword too, which is the half that is easy to miss.* A capture whose target file is busy is queued instead of written, and =--capture-write= is deliberately shared by the immediate and apply paths so a deferred capture produces the heading it *would* have produced. That is only true if the state travels with the queued item, so: =bin/hooks/queue-append= records =initial_state= into the event's =state= column, the item parser carries it as =:to=, and =--review-apply-capture= passes it through. The review buffer now renders a pending capture as =capture "NEXT Title"= rather than hiding the keyword until it lands.

*Two keys, deliberately distinct.* A =todo= event names it =state=, a capture names it =initial_state=; they share the queue column so apply has one place to look, but a capture must not pick up a todo-shaped =state= key. Pinned by a =queue-append-test= check, alongside one asserting that a capture with no =initial_state= records =null= rather than the empty string — "no keyword wanted" and "keyword unknown" must not collapse, for the same reason =from= keeps ="none"= distinct from null.

*Verified:* =bin/test= 456 before, 460 after, 0 unexpected, exit 0; =bin/queue-append-test= 76 to 79 =ok=, exit 0.

*Proved to discriminate, once per moving part*, because the three pieces fail independently and a single test would have covered only the first: making =--capture-write= ignore the argument fails the immediate *and* deferred tests (2 unexpected); dropping the state in =--review-apply-capture= fails only the deferred one; disabling the validation fails only the refusal test. All three were full 460-test runs with the run count checked before the failure count.

*The error message from [[id:2b2db914-c96e-416a-a80a-e31028308de0][2b2db914]] now points here* — a title beginning with a keyword says "Reword the title, and pass initial_state if a keyword is what you wanted", which turns a refusal into a redirection.

*CLAUDE.md updated in the same commit.* Its caveat that a =:BLOCKER:= naming a same-session capture is inert was written as unconditional and is now conditional: true when the capture was keywordless, avoidable by passing =initial_state=.

*A last illustration of the cost, from this session.* [[id:445ec1f1-095a-462b-abbd-7a3a00925ddb][445ec1f1]] was captured about twenty minutes before this shipped, and is keywordless on disk with its =TODO= sitting in the queue — the last heading here that will need a round-trip through a human to acquire a keyword.

- State "DONE"       from "DOING"      [2026-08-31 Mon 15:14]
:END:
:PLAN:

*Open. Promised during 2026-08-26's session and not filed until the next morning* -- which is itself the pattern that produced the other six retcons.

*=org_capture= with a title beginning with a TODO keyword loses that word.* Capturing "NEXT belongs to containers; nominate rather than promote" produced =** NEXT belongs to containers; ...=: org parsed the leading =NEXT= as the *keyword*, so the heading acquired a state it was never given and its title lost its first word.

*The tool cannot prevent this by documentation.* Its description already says the heading is written with no TODO keyword, and that remains true -- the keyword does not come from the tool, it comes from the title.

*Caught only because =org_set_todo='s reply echoed the truncated title back*: "Queued todo -> DOING (was NEXT)" on a heading that had just been captured keywordless. Nothing else would have shown it; the heading looks entirely normal in the file.

*Cheap guard, since the tool already knows the keyword set.* Refuse, or escape, a title whose first word is one. Refusing is probably right: such a title is nearly always a mistake, and a silently renamed heading is worse than an error. Note =bin/lint-org= cannot catch it either -- the result is a well-formed heading.

:END:
*Shipped 2026-08-31. Refuses, as this body proposed, rather than escaping or silently renaming.* =org_capture= now returns =Error: title begins with the TODO keyword "NEXT", which org would read as the heading's state -- the title would lose its first word and the heading would acquire a state it was never given. Reword the title.= Because the reply starts with =Error:=, =bin/hooks/queue-append= drops it and nothing reaches the queue either.

*The keyword set is read from the target file, not from a global.* =org-todo-keywords-1= is buffer-local and derived from the file's own =#+TODO:= line, and capture can target a file other than the capture file when given an =:ID:=. A new =claude-code-ide-org--leading-todo-keyword= reads it there and *fails open* — a file that does not exist or cannot be visited yields nil, because refusing a capture on the strength of a keyword set we could not read would be worse than the defect being guarded.

*Deliberately narrow, and tested from both sides.* The match is against the whole first *word*, case-sensitively, because that is exactly what org treats as a state. So =NEXTGEN parser rewrite=, a lowercase =next steps for the parser=, =Decide what NEXT means for a container= and =TODOs are not TODO= are all ordinary titles and are captured unchanged. Anything stricter would refuse titles org handles perfectly well.

*Verified, and proved to discriminate in both directions* — which matters here because the two failure modes are opposites and a single test would miss one. 454 tests before, 456 after, 0 unexpected, exit 0. Disabling the guard (returning nil always) fails exactly =capture-refuses-a-leading-todo-keyword= and nothing else; making it over-eager (case-insensitive prefix match) fails exactly =capture-allows-titles-that-merely-look-keyword-ish= and nothing else. Both were full 456-test runs, run count checked before failure count. The refusal case covers every keyword the fixture's =#+TODO:= line declares, both sides of the bar, since a done-state keyword parses identically.

*Incidental fix, since writing the test surfaced it.* The capture fixture's comment claimed =target= is required, citing 2026-08-20 (=97696fc2=). That stopped being true on 2026-08-27 when a category became a =:CATEGORY:= property rather than a heading: passing ="Scratch"= as a target now errors with "there is nothing to file *under* by name". The comment was describing a requirement the code had already dropped, and it cost this session a red test run before the reply was read. Corrected in place rather than filed — it is a comment in the file already being edited, not work.

Raised by the user 2026-08-10. None of the MCP tools bind
=inhibit-read-only=, so any of them fails outright with a
=buffer-read-only= error against a buffer the user has toggled
read-only (=C-x C-q=). The standing workaround -- documented in
CLAUDE.md's "Read-only buffers" note -- is to clear the flag and
proceed without asking, since the user sets it to guard against their
own stray keystrokes, not to block Claude.

*The gap:* nothing ever restores it. Every clear silently disables that
guard from then on, and the user only finds out by noticing. The
workaround was written as a way past an error, and the other half was
never specified.

*Leading fix, not settled:* have the tool wrappers bind
=inhibit-read-only= t around their own writes, so the user's flag is
never touched at all. Strictly better than clear-then-restore, which
has a failure window (a tool erroring mid-call leaves the buffer
cleared) and races badly with concurrent sessions -- two of them
interleaving clear/restore can restore a flag the other still needs
cleared, or leave it cleared anyway. Binding has no window and no
shared state.

*The one thing it rested on is now verified.* Read-only guards
modification, not saving, so =save-buffer= ought to succeed under
=inhibit-read-only= -- but every tool here saves, and an unverified
"ought to" in the save path is how this project has acquired bugs
before. Confirmed in passing 2026-08-10: this very heading was inserted
into =TODO.org= while its buffer was read-only, using exactly the
proposed binding. The text reached disk, the buffer came back unmodified,
and =buffer-read-only= was still =t= afterwards. So the fix is a small
edit to each wrapper, not a research question.

Cheap and self-contained; no dependency on
[[id:b5f7c5c7-7ad6-4c68-9cce-3479db1f1644][b5f7c5c7]]. Note the
refactor does *not* make it moot: after the cutover the review-and-apply
command becomes the only writer of live state, and it writes to exactly
the buffers the user is most likely to be viewing read-only at the time.

Two documents encode the current half-answer and must be updated
together with the fix: CLAUDE.md's "Read-only buffers" paragraph under
the MCP tools table, and the =feedback-todo-org-read-only= memory.

*Raised in priority 2026-08-10 by the interactive apply hitting it.* The
first real =claude-code-ide-org-review= apply against a read-only
=TODO.org= failed outright; toggling =C-x C-q= and re-applying
succeeded. Two things make this a sharper case than the MCP-tool one
above, rather than another instance of it:

- *The gesture is the opposite of a stray keystroke.* Read-only exists to
  stop the buffer being edited by accident. =M-x
  claude-code-ide-org-review=, then =m=, then =x= is about as deliberate
  as an action gets, and it is the human's own hands doing it. The guard
  fires on precisely the case it was never meant to catch.
- *After the cutover this blocks the only writer there is.*
  [[id:feba67eb-35b3-48bd-a892-8ecd47ca52e0][feba67eb]] makes apply the
  sole path by which anything reaches an org file. A user who habitually
  keeps =TODO.org= read-only while reading it would then find the entire
  system silently unable to record anything, with a raw
  =buffer-read-only= error as the only clue.

So the wrapper fix above should cover
=claude-code-ide-org--review-apply-item= too, not just the MCP tools.

*One property confirmed by the failure, worth keeping:*
=--review-apply= records only items that returned no error, so the
failed attempt marked nothing applied and the retry was clean -- no
double-application, no half-applied batch. Whatever the fix, do not
regress that.

*A worse instance than the one this heading was filed for, 2026-08-25.* The read-only flag did not merely inconvenience an MCP tool -- it *failed the human's own review pass*. =M-x claude-code-ide-org-review=, =x=, and "Applied 0 item(s); 1 failed".

*The human pressing =x= is unambiguous authorisation to write*, which is what makes this different in kind from a tool call arriving unannounced. The guard exists so the user's stray keystrokes cannot edit the buffer; it is not meant to stand between them and a command they just invoked. So the apply path is the one place where binding =inhibit-read-only= is not a judgement call.

*Caused by the restore half of this heading's own subject.* The flag was cleared for an =org_amend=, restored immediately afterwards as the convention requires, and the next review pass hit it. Cleared and restored roughly eight times over the session; the failure came from doing it *correctly*.

*Diagnosed in one call because [[id:df1cf43c-749f-435c-9f45-3d8df1d725ad][df1cf43c]] shipped this morning*, which is the clearest return that instrumentation has paid here. The bare message names nothing; the captured record named everything:

: (:id "df001961-..." :message "Buffer is read-only: #<buffer TODO.org>" :backtrace nil)

*One limitation of that instrumentation is now visible:* =:backtrace nil=. Capture is additive on top of a plain =condition-case=, so a backtrace only materialises when =debug-on-error= is set -- which it is under ERT and is not in normal use. The item and the message carried the whole diagnosis this time, so the gap cost nothing, but it will not always.

*Verified no data was lost*, which was the real worry given [[id:21c91613-76e0-4590-affe-e2af9f1321ca][21c91613]]: apply writes the file and marks events consumed as two independent operations, so a failed write could still have consumed. It did not. The applied ledger's last entry was =2026-08-25T15:36:32= before and after the failure, and the day node's last CLOCK line remained =15:33--15:36=.

*Narrow fix available and worth taking before the general one:* bind =inhibit-read-only= around the apply write only. The general case this heading describes -- every file-touching tool binding it -- is a larger change with a real argument against it, since a tool call is not a human keystroke. The apply path has no such ambiguity.

:END:
*Shipped 2026-08-31 — the general case this heading was filed for, four months after its narrow child.* The write tools now bind =inhibit-read-only= themselves, so the flag is never touched and the clear/restore convention is retired.

*Two mechanisms, split on how a tool reaches its buffer.* A new =claude-code-ide-org--at-id-writable= binds and delegates to =--at-id=, and the six write tools that route through the dispatcher now call it: =archive=, =amend=, =sort-children=, =move-sibling=, =log-background-plan=, =wrap-plan=, plus =close-open-interval=. The four that reach their buffer directly — =refile=, =set-property=, =divide=, =capture= — bind in their own outermost =let=.

*=--at-id= itself deliberately does not bind, which is the design decision here.* It serves the read-only tools too, so binding there would grant write permission to code that should never write, turning a bug in a query tool into a silent edit of a buffer the user deliberately guarded. A test asserts the asymmetry directly, so a later "simplify these two into one" fails.

*Measured before and after, per tool, rather than assumed.* Against the pre-change =config.el=: =amend=, =divide=, =move-sibling= and =refile= all returned =Error: Buffer is read-only= and wrote nothing; all four pass now. =set-property= passed *both* ways — =org-entry-put= binds =inhibit-read-only= itself. Its binding is therefore defence in depth rather than load-bearing, and mutating it away fails nothing; that is recorded in a comment at the site rather than tidied away, because a reader who greps for the binding is owed the difference.

*A test defect caught by that same measurement.* The first draft asserted =move-sibling='s effect by looking for "Second heading" on disk — present before the move as well, so it passed against a tool that failed outright. Only the reply assertion caught it. Rewritten to assert the resulting *order*, and the whole thing restructured from one table into five independent tests so a failure names the tool.

*Verified:* 448 tests before, 454 after, 0 unexpected, exit 0. Run against the pre-fix =config.el=, the new tests give 4 unexpected — exactly =amend=, =divide=, =move-sibling= and =refile= — while every pre-existing read-only test still passes. Each case also asserts the buffer is *still read-only afterwards*, which is the assertion that would catch an implementation clearing =buffer-read-only= instead of binding: it would satisfy every write assertion and reintroduce the defect this heading is named for, by way of its own fix.

*Verified live, not only in batch.* This very amendment was written to a =TODO.org= whose buffer had just been deliberately set read-only, after =load-file='ing the module into the running Emacs — without that reload the check would have exercised the old code and passed for the wrong reason.

*Left alone on purpose:* =claude-code-ide-org--review-ensure-writable= still prompts rather than binding. That is a recorded decision with its own reasoning — apply is a human keystroke, and clearing a human's guard is the human's call when a human is present to make it — and this heading's own body agrees, calling the apply path the one place with no ambiguity. Not steamrolled.

*Both documents moved in the same commit*, as this heading required: CLAUDE.md's "Read-only buffers" paragraph now says there is nothing to do, and the =feedback-todo-org-read-only= memory was rewritten — it had itself said it should be revised once this landed. Both record that a =Buffer is read-only= error from an org tool is now a *defect to report*, not a flag to clear.

*Test scope, stated rather than left to inference:* five tools have their own read-only case — =amend=, =set-property=, =divide=, =move-sibling=, =refile=. The remaining write tools (=archive=, =capture=, =sort-children=, =log-background-plan=, =wrap-plan=) are not separately tested and this is deliberate, not residue: each reaches its buffer by one of the two paths already proven here, and the =--at-id-writable= asymmetry test pins the dispatcher itself. Not worth a heading. If a sixth path ever appears, that is what would need one.

*Shipped 2026-08-25, the same afternoon it bit.* =claude-code-ide-org--review-apply-item= binds =inhibit-read-only= alongside the re-entrancy guard it already binds, which covers both the capture path and the =--at-id= path in one place.

*Narrow on purpose, and the parent stays open because of it.* The general proposal -- every file-touching tool binds this -- has a real argument against it: a tool call arrives unannounced, and letting the flag stop one is defensible. Apply has no such ambiguity, because the human pressed =x=.

*A binding rather than a =setq=, which is the whole safety property.* The flag returns when the scope exits, including on a non-local exit, so a failure part-way through cannot leave the buffer writable. The test asserts exactly that: the buffer is still read-only *after* a successful apply. An implementation that cleared =buffer-read-only= instead would pass the write assertion and silently disarm the user's guard -- which is the defect the parent heading is named for, reintroduced by its own fix.

=claude-code-ide-org-clock-report= prefixes its table with =#+CAPTION: Clock summary at [2026-08-20 Thu 11:00], ...=. Two tests assert on durations with =(string-match-p "1:00" result)= against that whole string, so the caption's own clock satisfies the match.

Observed, not theorised: =test-clock-report-block-today= and =test-clock-report-explicit-tstart-tend= passed at 10:59:52 on 2026-08-20, failed at 11:00:12, 11:00:20 and 11:00:44, then passed again at 11:01. The failing assertion is the negative one, =(should (not (string-match-p "1:00" result)))=, which is the shape a green suite cannot catch: it only fires when the substring appears for the wrong reason.

Three minutes a day for this duration -- 01:00, 11:00, 21:00. Other durations asserted the same way have the same exposure at their own minutes.

Approach: assert against the table row, =| *Total time* | *0:00* |=, rather than the whole report. Stripping the caption would also work but matching the row is what the assertion means.

/Body restored 2026-08-20 by =org_amend=; the original capture silently discarded it -- see/ [[id:1cd2df62-35e9-47dc-bcce-dda7bae3c522][1cd2df62]].

*Fixed 2026-08-31, as the whole class rather than the two named tests.* Every duration assertion in the =clock-report= section matched a substring against the entire report; all five tests are now routed through two new helpers in =config-test.el=. =claude-code-ide-org-test--report-total= pulls the =*Total time*= cell out and the assertion becomes =equal= on it — strictly stronger than the substring match it replaces, and it covers both table shapes (=| *Total time* |= and the file-list =| ALL *Total time* |=). It *signals* rather than returning nil when no such row exists, so a report that never built cannot pass as an ordinary duration mismatch. =--report-body= strips the =#+CAPTION:= line, and every negative assertion runs against that.

*The caption cannot be stubbed, which decided how this is pinned.* org builds it in =org-dblock-write:clocktable= with =(format-time-string (org-time-stamp-format t t))= and *no TIME argument* (=org-clock.el:2836=), so the timestamp is read in C and =cl-letf= on =current-time= never moves it. Confirmed by measurement, not inspection: with time pinned to [2026-07-27 Mon 23:16] the caption still read the real wall clock. So the regression pin is =claude-code-ide-org-test-clock-report-assertions-ignore-the-caption=, which asserts against a *crafted* report whose caption reads =[2026-08-31 Mon 11:00]= — deterministic, and no clock games. It asserts that the naive match is fooled and that neither helper is, so it documents the defect as well as guarding it.

*Verified, and proved to discriminate:* 447 tests before, 448 after, 0 unexpected, exit 0. Mutating =--report-body= to a no-op — semantic, still parses — gave =Ran 448 tests … 1 unexpected=, that one being the new pin and nothing else. Run count checked before failure count.

*Done in one pass with its twin* [[id:c31b6c76-8ad8-45d4-a87b-39e085e31368][c31b6c76]], committed together in =811d180=.

: (string-match-p "1:00" "#+CAPTION: Clock summary at [2026-08-22 Sat 23:16], ...

Both are the same underlying habit -- a test whose fixture is pinned to =(current-time)= and whose assertion is a substring match over the whole report -- so they are worth fixing together even though neither is the other.

*"Now" is pinned to [2026-07-27 Mon 23:16]* — the hour, and the very minute, at which the defect was measured — so the test permanently runs at the time that used to break it rather than merely avoiding that time.

*The old failure was reproduced deterministically before the fix, not merely described.* Under the pinned clock at 23:16 the old fixture construction produced =*0:44*=, matching the =0:44= recorded in this heading on 2026-08-22 exactly.

**** DONE Decide whether returning a heading's whole body is a mode on org_outline or its own tool :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-31 Mon 09:48]
:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       ff1352b3-2732-4422-9f0d-4b3cb6fd8ff3
:CREATED:  [2026-08-28 Fri 17:24]
:CATEGORY: Tools

:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Tools
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "TODO"       from              [2026-08-28 Fri 17:24] \\
  surface decision, deliberately not built
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-08-31 Mon 09:48] \\
  decided: two tools; build filed separately
:END:
:PLAN:

*Filed 2026-08-28 as [[id:2d9eeebd-4375-4790-8485-92b244236a21][2d9eeebd]] closed.* That heading shipped *front matter without the body*; its complement — *the body, whole* — was raised in the same analysis and deliberately not built.

*The request it comes from is concrete.* Asked to "show me 4f85", the only route was =grep -n ":ID: 4f8500e6"= to find the heading, =awk= to locate the next sibling at the right level and so compute the subtree's end, then =Read= with the resulting offset and line count. Three tools and hand-done line arithmetic to retrieve one heading — and the arithmetic is the fragile part, since the extent depends on finding the next sibling *at the right level*.

*It is nearly all plumbing.* =claude-code-ide-org--subtree-text-at-point= (used on the clocktable path) already returns a subtree from its heading through its last child without modifying the buffer. And scope resolution — including 8-character prefixes, and the shape-based error for an id that resolves to nothing — is now shared, since [[id:2d9eeebd-4375-4790-8485-92b244236a21][2d9eeebd]] fixed it there.

*So the only real question is the surface, and the arguments genuinely cut both ways.* CLAUDE.md's design note says the tool surface should stay small because each tool's schema costs tokens on *every* request — which argues for a mode argument on =org_outline=. But a mode argument is itself schema paid on every request, which is the reasoning that kept front matter from being a flag; and a tool whose modes return *structure*, *front matter* or *raw text* is three tools wearing one name, which is how a schema description becomes something a model has to reason about rather than read.

*A third option worth weighing rather than dismissing:* leave it out entirely. =org_amend= can now *revise* a body wholesale, and a reader who needs the prose can be pointed at the heading with =RET= in Emacs. The measured cost was three tools and some awk in one session — real, but small, and the =grep= route is at least honest about what it is doing.

*Do not build it before deciding*, which is why this is filed rather than done: the implementation is an hour and the surface decision outlives it.

:END:
*Decided 2026-08-31: two tools, not three, and not a mode.* Add a body read that returns the heading with its drawers; add no front-matter tool; add no mode argument.

*The user's framing is what settled it:* treat the metadata as part of the body and let the agent reason about what to extract — with the counter-argument that the *outline* must carry blockers, since dependency linkage is structure. Both halves are right, and together they decide it.

*The property schema tips the scales, measured across both files:*

| property | n | nature |
|----------+---+--------|
| =ID= | 305 | identity; already on every outline line |
| =CREATED= | 290 | a fact about one heading |
| =CATEGORY= | 208 | grouping — already expressed as the outline's *grouping*, not as text |
| =ARCHIVE_TIME/FILE/CATEGORY/TODO/OLPATH= | 63 each | provenance, DONE.org only |
| =BLOCKER= | 23 | *the only property that names another heading* |
| =KIND= | 3 | class — already expressed as the outline's *behaviour*: a slice expands its members |
| =COOKIE_DATA= / =DATE_TREE= / =ARCHIVE= | 3/2/1 | org-facing machinery |

*Exactly one property is relational.* Everything else describes a single heading in isolation or is machinery. So there is no third *kind* of metadata needing its own surface — the split is two-way: **the outline carries relationships, the body carries everything about one heading.**

*Which turns the counter-argument around.* Because blockers belong in the outline and blockers are the only relational property, the outline needs nothing *else* — so the front-matter block added by [[id:2d9eeebd-4375-4790-8485-92b244236a21][2d9eeebd]] is the thing that should shrink, not the body read that should be split out of it. Of its five lines, =:CATEGORY:= and =:KIND:= are already implicit in the rendering, =:CREATED:= and the plan link are per-heading facts, and the =:BLOCKER:= value is nearly what =[blocked: ...]= already says — that marker filters to *unfinished*, which is the useful set.

*Not a contradiction of 2d9eeebd's schema-cost argument.* That argued a *mode or flag* is schema paid on every request, which is true and still true. A second tool with its own narrow schema is a different cost, and it is the one this buys.

*Sequenced rather than decided: whether =org_outline='s front matter then shrinks.* Build the body read first; at that point its remaining unique content is about one line, and the question answers itself instead of needing an argument.

*One observation from the same measurement, recorded because it bears on what the tool is for.* Of 145 level-1 headings, *134 are leaves* — 92% — with 11 carrying children. So beneath the ten synthetic =:CATEGORY:= headers the outline is a grouped *list* with eleven small branches, not a tree, and its only grouping is derived from a property rather than from the file. That is the flattening working as designed ("the rendered shape stays identical, only the source changes"), but it means the outline's value is now index, grouping and relationships rather than depth — which is the same conclusion the two-tool split reaches from the other side.
