- State "DONE"       from              [2026-08-31 Mon 08:56] \\
  lesson named in CLAUDE.md
:END:

*Observed four times in one session, twice on the same pair, for the same reason.* Responses cited =c31b6c76=/=5a5e87c9= as shorthand for *the twin asymmetry* — the pattern where two headings describe the same defect and only one gets scheduled — and the footnote hook refused every one of them.

*The failure is compositional, not one of discipline, which is why "be more careful" is not the fix.* The hook catches it every time, so enforcement is not the gap. What happens is that an id stops being a *reference to a heading* and becomes a *name for a lesson*: "the c31b6c76/5a5e87c9 asymmetry" is one idea, and the two ids are its spelling. Once a token is a name, the writer stops reading it as a citation. It still is one to a reader who does not have the earlier response on screen, which is exactly what the footnote rule protects.

*Distinct from [[id:2758f3a0-3c47-405e-9662-a7669dcb60cc][2758f3a0]], and the difference is the interesting part.* That heading found footnote discipline decaying on *re-mention*, where "every offender was correct the first time" — the id was cited properly and then abbreviated. Here it is never cited properly, because it was never being used as a citation at all.

*A testable claim, and it held on inspection:* every lesson in this project that has acquired a **name** stops being cited by id. "Declared versus inferred", "in the mail", "silence is not a pass", "a story is precipitated, never authored" — none of these are ever spelled with ids, because they do not need to be. The ones without names are spelled with ids every time, and every spelling is a footnote the writer did not intend to owe.

*It happened a third time in the response that filed this heading*, which is the strongest evidence in it. That response cited the pair as a spelling while arguing that citing them as a spelling is what trips the hook. So *the failure survives knowing about it* — the writer had the mechanism in mind, described it in the same paragraph, and still did not see two ids as two citations.

*And a fourth, of a different kind, in the same exchange.* The reply announcing the third occurrence said "I've added that observation to the body saved in the scratchpad". It had not been; the sentence stood in for the act. That is the shape [[id:46d225c7-7541-4867-af72-929a572df2a5][46d225c7]] was filed for — a source comment reading "Removal is filed" when nothing was — and it belongs here because both happened while writing *about* the discipline they broke.

*Resolved 2026-08-31 by naming the lesson*, which was the first of the two directions and the one the evidence favours: the second makes the citation cheaper, the first makes it unnecessary, and a named pattern can be taught where a footnote can only be looked up.

*The name was adopted, not coined.* =twin= is already this project's word for it — four uses, three of them in exactly this sense, and unlike =sibling= (164 uses, and org's own =org-get-next-sibling=) it carries no other meaning here. The user had also already adopted "the twin asymmetry" in conversation. That is [[id:9e627dc0-d31b-42cc-857a-b1e5a77f44a5][9e627dc0]]'s lesson applied: it searched for a name, found the term already in the file, and recorded that the session had drifted from it.

*Where it lives:* CLAUDE.md, beside the epic/story/slice vocabulary, not =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md=. The asymmetry bites while *composing* a slice or a session prompt, which is not always with an =.org= file open, and a path-scoped rule that does not load is a rule that does not apply.



**** DONE The :PLAN: lint asks a slice for a drawer it has no prospective half to fill :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-31 Mon 08:40]
:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       f89c912a-2ce5-4f77-b6be-67ae35901e7a
:CREATED:  [2026-08-31 Mon 08:26]
:CATEGORY: Tools
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:17
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Tools
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "TODO"       from              [2026-08-31 Mon 08:27] \\
  lint rule scoped to tasks, not slices
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-08-31 Mon 08:40] \\
  slices exempt from the PLAN lint
:END:
:PLAN:

*Raised by the user 2026-08-31:* what is the justification for wrapping a slice's pre-closure content into =:PLAN:= and writing a debrief? We did not do it for [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]], and it reads fine as it is.

*They are right on the facts, and I had asserted the opposite.* c44c2119 has *no* =:PLAN:= drawer — zero drawer lines; the =:PLAN:= strings in its body are prose mentions. My claim that it set a precedent came from a probe shaped =(save-excursion (re-search-forward ...) t)=, which returns =t= whether or not the search matched. A probe that can only answer yes. Fourth instance of the family [[id:542924c1-9152-4414-8da8-d530d3423611][542924c1]] collects.

*And the justification really is weaker for a slice.* [[id:8bcd56f4-22a8-4673-bad6-a99433027b81][8bcd56f4]] argued the =:PLAN:= lifecycle for *tasks*, on a specific hazard: a closed task's body holds design claims — "here is how this will work" — that the implementation may contradict, and a later reader consulting it for background repeats a superseded claim as current. The evidence was three headings whose design claims went wrong in one day against zero journal claims needing correction. *Design is the perishable half.*

*A slice has no design half.* Its body holds the argument for why these things belong together, a sequence, a *derived* member list and revision links. Once closed, nearly all of that is already retrospective — a true statement about what was grouped and why. The only prospective part is phase prose, which is a small fraction and carries no falsifiable claim, because a slice does not design anything. There is nothing waiting to be contradicted.

*So the pressure to wrap comes entirely from the lint*, which is applying a task rule to a heading class that is not a task. That is not a new shape: [[id:f421c5c3-f81f-4ebf-99c9-42c53cc00558][f421c5c3]] hit the same rule from the other side — it demanded a drawer from a *debrief-only* heading, and the answer was to invent the empty drawer rather than distort the body. A slice is a third case: a body that is prospective in *form* and retrospective in *fact*.

*Proposed fix, one predicate:* exempt =:KIND: slice= from the "finished heading with a substantial body and no =:PLAN:= drawer" warning. It stops the rule nagging about c44c2119 forever, and it is the same shape as =--slice-blocker-ids= already treating finished members differently from live ones.

*The alternative, if uniformity is preferred:* wrap slices with an *empty* =:PLAN:=, which is f421c5c3's answer and records that the question was asked. Worse here, in my view — an empty drawer on a heading whose body was never prospective states nothing, where an exemption states something true about the class.

*Not decided.* The user asked the question; this records the argument rather than settling it.

:END:
*Decided and shipped 2026-08-31.* The user's ruling: drop the =:PLAN:= wrap from the slice-closing steps.

*Shipped as the exemption rather than the empty drawer*, which was the choice this body laid out. =bin/lint-org= no longer asks a =:KIND: slice= heading for a =:PLAN:= drawer. One predicate, beside the existing finished-keyword test.

*Verified by mutation, both directions.* The test asserts a finished slice is *not* reported and that a finished *task* with an identical body and =CLOSED:= still is — an exemption that silenced everything would satisfy the first assertion while deleting the rule. Removing the predicate fails exactly that test and nothing else; 441/441 restored.

*What it clears immediately:* [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]], which the rule had been nagging about since it closed, and [[id:979e02b6-2a4c-4328-8b08-ffaec03bd02e][979e02b6]], which now closes without one.

*The reasoning, restated in one line for whoever meets this next:* the =:PLAN:= lifecycle protects a reader from a closed *task's* design claims, and a slice makes none — so wrapping one would file true, retrospective prose into a drawer readers are told to skip, which is the inverse of what the lifecycle is for.

-----

*Debrief, drafted 2026-08-29.* Opened [2026-08-25 Tue 15:29] with eleven members and closed with 24 planned and 27 incidental.

*The thesis held and got sharper.* The slice asked where this project *declares* something and its code *infers* it some other way. Four heading classes were named at the outset; three were settled and one was settled by refusing it. The category tier became a =:CATEGORY:= property on the task ([[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]]), the slice already declared itself with =:KIND:=, the epic stayed *derived* because declaring an emergent grouping is the error the axis exists to name — and the datetree node turned out to be a case the axis does not cover at all.

*That refusal is the most useful thing the slice produced.* [[id:2e660571-26df-41e4-bb64-b9d74a3d7efe][2e660571]] proposed giving datetree nodes a =:KIND:=. Measured before building: =org-datetree-find-date-create= builds year, month and day inside org, there is no creation hook, and the planned DONE.org datetree would be built by =org-archive-subtree= outside this project entirely. *A datetree node cannot declare itself, because nothing we control creates it.* So the axis governs *our own* conventions; where another system owns the thing, reading the shape it publishes is correct rather than a workaround. CLAUDE.md carries that as a third case now.

*The largest single change was structural.* [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] flattened 190 headings out of a nine-category tier, and the taxonomy that replaced it was chosen from a survey rather than from taste: one label had held 40% of the corpus, and the top six now sit between 12% and 18%. Two findings from that pass generalise — the label with a conjunction in its name was compound, *and so was one without* (=Skill logic= split 21/21), so the conjunction tell points true where it fires and is silent otherwise.

*A keyword was retired on evidence.* [[id:c954f650-b92f-4920-9967-ab6c44577b30][c954f650]] measured =PLANNING= across the project's whole history: 7 transitions in 432, absent from the three busiest days, and 84% of planned work never wore it. The premise it was built on — long spans of agent work in Plan Mode — held for one of seven. Nothing replaced it, deliberately.

*Six tools changed and two were built.* =org_divide= (task mitosis) and =org_set_property= are new; =org_outline= gained front matter at a scoped root, an honest error for an unresolvable id, and stopped orphaning a live child of a finished parent. =claude-code-ide-org-goto= makes an 8-character abbreviation typeable, which closed [[id:478d6ec9-1b99-4c6c-88e9-c793ad4b2f22][478d6ec9]] at ten of ten.

*What the slice taught about itself*, and this is the part worth carrying into the next one. Three conventions were written *because composing this slice broke them*: a member list under a subheading is invisible to the parser and fails to =[0/0]= rather than to an error; a =- [[id:...]]= prose bullet is indistinguishable from a deferred member; and a statistics cookie belongs after the keyword, which the corpus said 13-to-1 while the inserter said otherwise. Each was found by a mechanical check or by a user reading the file — none by re-reading the code.

*One member was cancelled rather than done.* [[id:9651d4c8-6887-4b0a-91d9-562c3bc49a75][9651d4c8]] was superseded by [[id:0086614a-c95c-4618-bba0-c821589dd7f2][0086614a]]: its gating condition, "an unstated task lifecycle", had become stated, and both questions it deferred were answered by prose written after it.

*Residue: none unfiled.* Everything named as unfinished during the slice's life became a heading — [[id:ff1352b3-2732-4422-9f0d-4b3cb6fd8ff3][ff1352b3]], [[id:c74f8663-b14e-4ab9-ad65-d99cb655b3fa][c74f8663]], [[id:542924c1-9152-4414-8da8-d530d3423611][542924c1]], [[id:46d225c7-7541-4867-af72-929a572df2a5][46d225c7]], [[id:0086614a-c95c-4618-bba0-c821589dd7f2][0086614a]], [[id:33864a0f-5e13-4235-85a6-0bd9d2fe5252][33864a0f]], [[id:5f1068f9-1452-45e4-9253-568edfce2053][5f1068f9]], [[id:8c662dfb-b4ab-4f4d-a5d4-8a4beda996a8][8c662dfb]], [[id:dbf70459-bde4-4550-bd81-0d4f9ebc50e3][dbf70459]] — and the successor slice [[id:b36e6369-a210-4540-adc7-0c0c188e9791][b36e6369]] sequences most of them.

Wrapping this body would have filed true, retrospective prose into a drawer readers are told to skip — the inverse of what the lifecycle is for. =bin/lint-org= now exempts slices ([[id:f89c912a-2ce5-4f77-b6be-67ae35901e7a][f89c912a]]), so the convention and the check agree.

**** DONE Reopening a cancelled member retroactively un-completes every closed slice naming it :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-31 Mon 08:32]
:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       30a340fd-c216-4231-a8d9-fff83c54b9f8
:CREATED:  [2026-08-31 Mon 08:26]
:CATEGORY: Slices
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:17
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Slices
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "TODO"       from              [2026-08-31 Mon 08:27] \\
  closed slices should not be refreshed
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-08-31 Mon 08:32] \\
  guard shipped, c44c2119 repaired
:END:
:PLAN:

*Observed 2026-08-31, and the user found it by reading the file:* [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]] is closed, and one of its members carries an empty checkbox — =[27/28]= on a =DONE= slice.

*The mechanism is the convention working exactly as designed, in a case nobody considered.* A slice member's checkbox is *derived* from the referent's keyword: =CANCELLED= means the cookie is deleted, so the member neither counts nor inflates the denominator; =TODO= means =[ ]=. [[id:b7b46a26-2fd6-4784-bed3-d0112a917c0a][b7b46a26]] was =CANCELLED= when c44c2119 closed, so it had no cookie and the slice read =[27/27]=. On 2026-08-28 it was reopened to =TODO= — legitimately, because its cancellation ground had become void once [[id:33864a0f-5e13-4235-85a6-0bd9d2fe5252][33864a0f]] gave it a consumer. Apply's settle phase then regenerated *every* slice's member lines, including a closed one, and restored the cookie.

*Traced to the commit.* c44c2119 reads =[27/27]= through [[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::7ba5ddf][7ba5ddf]] (08-28 10:35) and =[27/28]= from [[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::1f8719c][1f8719c]] (08-28 13:04) onward — the commit after the apply that carried the reopening. The cookie itself is arithmetically *correct* at every point; it is the membership that changed.

*What is wrong is not the arithmetic but the mutation.* A closed slice is a *record* of a bounded piece of work. Regenerating its lines forever means unrelated later work can reach back and alter it — here, a heading reopened two days after the slice closed silently un-finished it. Nobody decided that; it falls out of "member lines are derived" being stated without a scope.

*The conventions' own wording is where the gap is.* "A checkbox that disagrees with its referent means the slice is stale" was written for *live* slices, where the referent's current keyword is the thing worth reflecting. For a closed slice the referent's *later* keyword is not a fact about the slice at all.

*Proposed fix, one predicate:* =claude-code-ide-org-refresh-slice= skips a slice whose own keyword is terminal. That matches how =--slice-blocker-ids= already treats finished *members* differently from live ones, and it costs nothing else — a closed slice is not refreshed because there is nothing about it left to keep current.

*Worth deciding alongside:* whether c44c2119 should be repaired to =[27/27]= by deleting that member's cookie, or left as evidence. Deleting it would assert the member was cancelled, which is no longer true; leaving it asserts the slice is unfinished, which is also not true. A third option — the honest one — is that a *reopened* member of a closed slice should keep its line and lose its cookie, exactly as a deferred member does, because the slice is done with it either way.

:END:
*Decided and shipped 2026-08-31.* The user's ruling: *an un-cancelled task in a closed slice should not have its cookie restored — the task's own state transition history is there to answer any questions that arise.*

*That settles the objection recorded above.* The worry was that a cookie-less line asserts "this was cancelled", which stopped being true when the member reopened. It does not have to assert that: a closed slice's line is a statement about *the slice's* relationship to the member — done with it — and the member's own =:LOGBOOK:= carries what it is doing now. The slice was never the right place to ask.

*Shipped:* =claude-code-ide-org-refresh-slice= skips a slice whose own keyword is terminal. One predicate, using =--outline-finished-keywords= rather than =org-done-keywords=, which is buffer-local and nil outside a visited org buffer.

*Verified by mutation:* removing the guard fails exactly one test and nothing else, with the run count checked first. The test asserts a *live* slice in the same file is still refreshed — a guard that skipped everything would satisfy an assertion about the closed one while breaking the feature. 440/440.

*The damage turned out to be two-part, which strengthens the finding.* Repairing the cookie exposed a second symptom: =c44c2119= was also carrying a =:BLOCKER:= naming the reopened member. It cannot have had one when it closed — a cancelled member contributes no blocker id, so the property would have been deleted — so the same regeneration that restored the checkbox also *re-blocked a finished slice*. =bin/lint-org= caught it the moment the cookie was fixed, which is the lint doing exactly its job: the checkbox list and the blocker are two copies of one set, and it checks they agree.

*Repaired:* =c44c2119='s member line lost its cookie, its headline recomputed to =[27/27]=, and its =:BLOCKER:= removed outright. A closed slice blocks on nothing.

*Note the ordering that made the repair durable.* The guard had to ship *first*: without it the next apply's settle phase would have regenerated both the cookie and the blocker and undone the repair silently. Fixing the record before fixing the mechanism would have looked like it worked.

**** CANCELLED Find a convention marking which children a container's plan actually covered :code:research:
CLOSED: [2026-08-29 Sat 14:15]
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Skill
:ID:       9651d4c8-6887-4b0a-91d9-562c3bc49a75
:CREATED:  [2026-08-19 Wed 11:00]
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:16
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Skill
:ARCHIVE_TODO: CANCELLED
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "CANCELLED"  from "TODO"       [2026-08-29 Sat 14:15] \\
  superseded by 0086614a
:END:
:PLAN:

Wanted: a markup or convention showing which of a container's children
were in its *original* plan, and which accrued afterwards. Raised
2026-08-19, for future research — not now.

*The case study is exact.*
[[id:406e9200-c3e7-49ac-a8d0-d6ff8e061ce4][406e9200]] was planned with
five children (=290b6fc5=, =226ed53b=, =31f766ab=, =09c134c4=,
=507754ba=). Two days later it has *ten* — =e0904e93=, =98700ea3=,
=7d739afd=, =9202b39d= and =e0c55d26= all accrued during execution.
Nothing in =TODO.org= distinguishes the two sets.

*The information exists, in the wrong place, and is never updated.* The
plan file opens /"Covers all five children"/ — which was true when
written and is now false. So the provenance is recorded once, in a
document nobody revises, rather than on the headings themselves where it
would survive.

*What the answer has to survive:* containers grow by accretion, so any
convention that requires editing the container each time a child is
added will drift exactly as the plan file did. Something set at
*creation* of the child, and never touched again, is the shape most
likely to hold — a property, a tag, or the presence or absence of the
plan link itself.

*And it forces a question that is genuinely open.* Under the current
discipline every planned task carries a plan link, so a container that
doubles in size after planning implies plans for the follow-on children
too — doubling the planning overhead for exactly the work that was
unforeseen. Whether that discipline is warranted at that scale has not
been decided, and neither has the related question from the same day:
whether a plan is a *maintained document* or a dated snapshot of intent
that execution supersedes. Both bear on this and neither should be
settled by whoever picks this up first.

Adjacent to [[id:b07df584-3adc-433c-ab49-e104f88aecf7][b07df584]], and
gated the same way: the user has an unstated task lifecycle in mind that
likely reframes all of it.

*Constrained, not ungated, by the 2026-08-20 retention policy* ([[id:3063c3e5-0dd0-4354-8985-271b0313c5d1][3063c3e5]]). That policy says a closing heading's plan of attack moves into a drawer; it does not say which children the plan covered, so the question here is still open.

What it does settle is where the answer *cannot* live. If a body may be rewritten wholesale on closure, then prose in the body is not a durable marker — it is exactly the kind of content the policy exists to remove. The convention has to be structural: a property, a tag, or a drawer entry. That rules out the cheapest option and is worth knowing before the research starts.

*The user's hot take, 2026-08-28: slices are the new convention.* Then: should a heading's body carry a link to the slice it was worked in — how, and when in the lifecycle?

*The planned/incidental split already answers this heading's actual question, one level up.* What this asks for is "which children were in the original plan, and which accrued during execution". A slice now records exactly that distinction about its own members: planned members in the checklist, and everything that closed during the slice's life in an =Incidental:= section ([[id:0086614a-c95c-4618-bba0-c821589dd7f2][0086614a]], built 2026-08-28). Original-versus-accrued *is* planned-versus-incidental. If the slice is the planning unit rather than the container — which is the hot take — then the distinction this heading wants exists already and is generated rather than authored.

*So the container version may not need building at all.* That turns on one question, and it is the user's: is a container still a planning unit? If planning happens by composing a slice, then a container's children were never "covered by its plan" in the first place, and there is nothing to mark.

*On the back-link: recommend not writing one.* A slice already names its members by =:ID:=. A link in the member's body pointing back at the slice is a *second copy of a fact the slice already holds*, and this project's own rule is that a declared copy of something derivable is a copy that can disagree — the reason member lines are regenerated and never hand-set. Slice membership is derivable by scanning slices for a link to this heading's id, which is cheap and cannot go stale.

*What is genuinely missing is not a link but a lookup.* Reading a heading, you cannot see which slices touched it without scanning for it. That is a *tool* gap, not a convention gap, and it belongs where the other structural reads live — =org_outline= reporting a heading's slice memberships, or a small predicate beside =--slice-members=. Note the asymmetry that makes this the right shape: a heading may belong to several slices over its life, and to none, so a single-valued property was never going to fit anyway.

*If a link is written despite that, the lifecycle answer follows from the same rule:* it would have to be *generated*, at slice refresh — which already runs in apply's settle phase — and regenerated wholesale each time, exactly as member lines are. Never hand-added at any point, because a hand-added one is stale the moment the slice's membership changes, and slice membership changed twice today.

*Unchanged: the two questions this heading says should not be settled by whoever picks it up first* — whether every follow-on child warrants its own plan, and whether a plan is a maintained document or a dated snapshot execution supersedes. Neither is touched by the above.

:END:
*Cancelled 2026-08-29 as superseded by [[id:0086614a-c95c-4618-bba0-c821589dd7f2][0086614a]].* The user's reading, checked and confirmed: the "unstated task lifecycle" this heading gated itself on is not unstated any more, and this predates the slice concept that answers it.

*The dates settle the first half.* This was created [2026-08-19 Wed], and every component of that lifecycle postdates it — the =:PLAN:= drawer lifecycle ([[id:8bcd56f4-22a8-4673-bad6-a99433027b81][8bcd56f4]], created 08-22), composing slices by reference ([[id:8ca6541d-0fc7-45a2-a4d3-76e1608f658d][8ca6541d]], 08-21), the first slice ([[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]], 08-25), and =org_amend= gaining the ability to *revise* rather than only append ([[id:3063c3e5-0dd0-4354-8985-271b0313c5d1][3063c3e5]], closed 08-26). The append-only-to-revision move and the prospective/retrospective split are exactly what "reframes all of it" meant.

*The substance is the stronger argument, though, and it is not about dates.* This heading deferred two questions as unsettleable by whoever picked it up first, and *both are now answered* in CLAUDE.md prose written after it. Whether a plan is a maintained document or a dated snapshot: settled — readers are told to treat =:PLAN:= as an intention that may not have survived contact, which is a snapshot. Whether every follow-on child warrants its own plan: settled — "a task with no separate Plan Mode session simply carries no link, that's expected, not a gap to fill in." Its own gating conditions were met without anyone noticing.

*And the question itself moved up a level.* What this asked for — which children were in the *original plan* versus accrued during execution — is exactly the planned-versus-incidental distinction a *slice* now draws. If the slice is the planning unit rather than the container, a container's children were never "covered by its plan" in the first place, and there is nothing here to mark.

*Cancelled as superseded, not as unnecessary, and the distinction is load-bearing.* [[id:0086614a-c95c-4618-bba0-c821589dd7f2][0086614a]] is still =TODO= and unbuilt, so the capability this heading wanted has a *home* but not yet an implementation. Cancelling this without naming that would leave original-versus-accrued with nowhere to live at all.

*What it leaves behind:* the case study is still good. [[id:406e9200-c3e7-49ac-a8d0-d6ff8e061ce4][406e9200]] was planned with five children and had ten two days later, its plan file still opening "Covers all five children" — a fact recorded once in a document nobody revises. That is the shape 0086614a has to beat, and it inherits it.

This project made every heading =:ID:=-addressed, then made *the first
eight characters* the unit of reference — in prose, in commit messages, in
conversation, and as of 2026-08-18 in the footnote convention itself.
Every actual lookup still demands all thirty-six. The abbreviations are
readable and completely unactionable, which is not org's fault: it is the
cost of a convention this project adopted deliberately and then did not
finish.

*The gap is measurable by how it is worked around.* The user's method for
finding a heading is =C-s= in TODO.org. That is not ignorance of a better
way — =org-id-goto= exists but its interactive form is =(interactive
"sID: ")=, a bare string prompt with no completion against 162 live
=org-id-locations= entries, so a prefix does not work there. Plain text
search beats the id machinery at the project's own convention.

*Four children, two on each side of the tool boundary:*

- Reading, model-facing:
  [[id:2d9eeebd-4375-4790-8485-92b244236a21][2d9eeebd]] — a partial
  =:ID:= currently *misreports*, falling through to filename handling, and
  no tool returns front matter without a whole-body read. Measured at
  roughly fifteen times the cost of the answer.
- Reading, human-facing:
  [[id:915378ac-3bd4-461d-b0f0-83f67fbb3dac][915378ac]] — an interactive
  command that completes over titles and annotates each candidate with its
  8-character prefix, so both halves of the new footnote convention become
  actionable.
- Writing:
  [[id:36b811d9-8bd3-4a32-b67d-39ccfe0d66c1][36b811d9]] — the same front
  matter, from the other direction. Its absence was felt on 2026-08-18:
  setting a =:BLOCKER:= required a hand-written =org-entry-put= through
  =emacsclient=.
- The index itself:
  [[id:98908aff-63cc-4b71-b90b-817da361a23b][98908aff]] — =org_outline= is
  what every one of the above would query, and its =active_only= mode
  drops children of finished headings.

*Why these four and not more.* The =org_capture= items are about heading
*creation*, a different concern with its own tighter cluster.
[[id:c8a97d9d-8b13-4b6a-a8b9-1a3f24b5e00b][c8a97d9d]] — the read-only flag
left cleared — is tool hygiene rather than addressing, though it is the
most frequently *felt* friction of the three: every =org_amend= and
=org_refile= in this session cost an extra round trip to clear it. Worth
its own decision about grouping rather than being absorbed here.

:END:
*Closed 2026-08-29 at 10 of 10.* The title's promise — "for the model and the human alike" — is met on both sides, and the two halves turned out to need different things.

*For the model*, the work was resolution: expand a prefix at every surface that could invent a tail ([[id:49557477-e50c-496f-85df-82c65109832b][49557477]]), against =org-id-locations= rather than a table of our own ([[id:93f6c908-1c15-44e5-84f9-03f1ffb6d5db][93f6c908]]), reaching DONE.org ([[id:020d3688-f08d-460f-a3e8-931a1677074a][020d3688]]) through org's own archive derivation rather than a hand-rolled one ([[id:e6d1d810-5e88-4356-b002-bbb10cf19fc9][e6d1d810]]), without a corpus rescan on every short prefix ([[id:6c48d5a6-1c78-4ce5-ac97-5e1091bdb25c][6c48d5a6]]), and with the plain-text workarounds of the unresolvable era converted back to links ([[id:c69df700-dbba-4437-bb98-44cff81501f2][c69df700]]).

*For the human*, it was reach: a =completing-read= that makes an abbreviation typeable ([[id:915378ac-3bd4-461d-b0f0-83f67fbb3dac][915378ac]]), a tool that sets a property instead of an =emacsclient= call ([[id:36b811d9-8bd3-4a32-b67d-39ccfe0d66c1][36b811d9]]), and =org_outline= answering "what is this, what blocks it, what is under it" in one call ([[id:2d9eeebd-4375-4790-8485-92b244236a21][2d9eeebd]]) without orphaning a live child of a finished parent ([[id:98908aff-63cc-4b71-b90b-817da361a23b][98908aff]]).

*The recurring lesson across the ten, and it is not about ids.* Four of them were cases where **the absence of a signal read as a positive result**: a fabricated id that never blocks and never errors; a scoped outline reporting a missing *file* for an unresolvable heading; a filtered ancestor leaving its child misparented rather than absent; a prefix falling past a gate and silently rescanning the corpus. Each was found by something mechanical — a resolve-check, a lint rule, a scratch file — and none by reading the code, which is [[id:542924c1-9152-4414-8da8-d530d3423611][542924c1]]'s thesis arriving from a different direction.

*What this unblocks:* [[id:979e02b6-2a4c-4328-8b08-ffaec03bd02e][979e02b6]], which has been blocked on this container and on [[id:9651d4c8-6887-4b0a-91d9-562c3bc49a75][9651d4c8]] alone.

*No residue.* Every child closed; nothing was named as unfinished and left unfiled. The one adjacent question raised during the work — whether a body-returning read is a mode on =org_outline= or its own tool — is filed as [[id:ff1352b3-2732-4422-9f0d-4b3cb6fd8ff3][ff1352b3]] rather than left in this body.

*Shipped 2026-08-25*, commit =3a569ac=, 382 tests green.

*The rule was correct and did not work.* Nine uuids were fabricated
across two sessions, every one with a right prefix and an invented tail,
despite a standing "grep before writing" instruction that names the
failure exactly. The trigger is composing continuous prose that happens
to contain uuids, not forgetting the rule -- so the fix stops requiring
the tail to be produced at all.

*Two surfaces, found by asking where a tail actually gets typed.*
=resolve-id-links= expands =[[id:PREFIX]]= before =org_amend= writes and
refuses the whole amend if any prefix is unknown or ambiguous. =--at-id=
accepts a prefix wherever a full =:ID:= is accepted, which covers every
tool taking an =id= argument at once, including ones written later. The
second surface was the one nearly missed: link text is the visible case,
but a tool *argument* is where the 2026-08-25 slip actually landed.

*Both refuse rather than guess.* An ambiguous prefix resolving to a
plausible wrong heading is worse than one resolving to nothing, which is
the same reasoning that retired the stale-clock guess heuristic
([[id:7771fc63-9374-4c8a-9e80-24ceec21977c][7771fc63]]).

*One test assumption was wrong before the code was*, and it is worth not
repeating: the fixture's id is the literal =test-0001=, so
=(substring id 0 8)= is not hexadecimal and the expansion correctly
declines. A test written against the fixture id would have passed for
the wrong reason. The heading it uses now carries a real hexadecimal
uuid and is appended through the *visiting buffer*, because org-id
searches the buffer and a =write-region= behind it finds nothing.

*Arrives at the write boundary, not as the read tool* this epic's other
children describe -- the two are complementary, and the read half is
still open.

*The guard has a hole, demonstrated by this heading.* It was written by
a direct disk edit rather than through =org_amend=, and carried a
fabricated tail on the [[id:7771fc63-9374-4c8a-9e80-24ceec21977c][7771fc63]] link -- inside the debrief for the fix.
=bin/lint-org= caught it, as it has caught most of them. So the
expansion covers the *tool* path only, and heading creation by text
editing is sanctioned by CLAUDE.md and bypasses it entirely. Either
=org_capture= gains the same expansion, or the lint stays the real
backstop and the expansion is a convenience on one path -- worth
deciding rather than assuming the first fix closed it.

*Raised by the user 2026-08-14, from a concrete request the tools cannot
serve:* "show me the front matter of =f4e628ce= — sans body — and the
tree of anything below it." Both halves fail, for different reasons.

*What the surface actually offers.* =org_outline= returns *structure*
only: one line per heading with level, keyword, title, =:ID:=, tags and
a =[blocked]= marker. =org_query= returns *matches*: one line with
state, heading, tags, =:ID:= and file. Neither returns a properties
drawer, a =:BLOCKER:= value, a plan link, or any body.

*The partial-:ID: failure is worse than absence, because it misreports.*
=org_outline= with =scope= =f4e628ce= answered
=Error: no readable file at .../f4e628ce=: an unrecognised scope falls
through to being treated as a *filename*, so a truncated id reads as a
missing file rather than an unresolvable heading. Partial *titles* do
work — =org_query heading:"permission prompt"= resolved to the full id —
so title-to-id lookup exists and id-prefix lookup does not, which is the
opposite of how this project's prose, commits and conversation refer to
headings.

*Measured, because the cost is the argument:* =TODO.org= holds 111
headings across 10,251 lines — median heading 75 lines, mean 92, largest
405 ([[id:02aaae22-0958-4c0f-b5bb-2cbea32416ae][02aaae22]]). Front
matter is 5 or 6. So answering "what state is this in, what blocks it,
what is under it" by reading the heading costs roughly *fifteen times*
what the answer needs, and that read happened about twenty times in the
2026-08-14 session alone, twice as a 60-line window to see one =:ID:=
line.

*An honest deduction from that number, before it is used to justify
anything:* part of the waste was habit rather than absence. =org_query=
already answers "what state is X in" in one line and already resolves a
partial title; it was passed over for =awk= repeatedly that day. The
genuine gap is narrower than the measurement suggests — properties are
unreachable, and 8-character ids are unusable — and a tool built to the
full measurement would be built to the wrong size.

*Proposed shape: extend =org_outline=, do not add a third tool.*
CLAUDE.md's own design note argues the surface should stay small because
each tool's schema costs tokens on every request, so extending an
existing tool beats adding one:
1. =scope= accepts an =:ID:= *prefix*, resolving it when unambiguous and
   saying so plainly when not — and, either way, never reporting an
   unresolved scope as a missing file. No change to the output at all.
2. When =scope= resolves to a heading, that heading's front matter
   precedes the tree: =:CREATED:=, the =:BLOCKER:= *value*, the plan
   link. Today none of those three is reachable — the tree line carries
   keyword, title, id and tags, and a =[blocked]= marker that says a
   blocker exists without saying which ids.

*Root only, never per line, and not behind a flag.* Two corrections made
2026-08-14 while the proposal was being read back, both worth keeping
because the first reading was wrong in a way that would have damaged the
tool.

*Per-heading front matter would destroy what the tool is for.*
=org_outline='s stated value is being "roughly 40x smaller" than reading
the file; multiplying every line by a property drawer scales with heading
count — 37 lines scoped to
[[id:b5f7c5c7-7ad6-4c68-9cce-3479db1f1644][b5f7c5c7]], 111 unscoped.
Scope-root only grows the reply by a *fixed* four lines however large the
subtree is.

*And it should not be optional.* A boolean is itself schema, paid on
every request whether or not anyone sets it — which is the same argument
that ruled out a third tool, applied one level down. Four lines is below
the size at which a knob earns its keep, and a caller who names a single
heading by id is nearly always asking *about that heading*.

*Deliberately out of scope: semantic matching.* The user asked whether
title matching is semantic; it is not, and it should not become so here.
A fuzzy resolver that returns the wrong heading confidently is the same
failure this project has now measured twice — see
[[id:7771fc63-9374-4c8a-9e80-24ceec21977c][7771fc63]] on a guess that was
wrong more often than right, and the suggestion fallback removed the same
day. Prefix matching is decidable; semantic similarity is not.

*Sibling, not duplicate:*
[[id:915378ac-3bd4-461d-b0f0-83f67fbb3dac][915378ac]] is this problem for
the *human* at Emacs — an interactive jump-by-title command, which
already establishes that =org-id-goto= is exact-match by construction and
that this project's 8-character abbreviations are "readable and
completely unactionable". Same root convention, different consumer:
that one wants =completing-read= over titles, this one wants the MCP
tools to accept what the prose already writes.

*The complement of this request turned up 2026-08-15, and it is the same
missing surface.* Asked to "show me 4f85", the only route was
=grep -n ":ID: 4f8500e6"= to find the heading, =awk= to locate the next
=^\*\* = and so compute the subtree's end, then =Read= with the resulting
offset and line count. Three tools and hand-done line arithmetic to
retrieve one heading — and the arithmetic is the fragile part, since the
extent depends on finding the next sibling at the right level.

So both directions are absent from the same surface: this heading asks
for *front matter without the body*, and that request wanted *the body,
whole*. Neither is served, and they want the same scoping argument.

*The primitive already exists and is not exposed.*
=claude-code-ide-org--subtree-text-at-point= (config.el:1961) returns a
subtree from its heading through its last child as plain text, without
modifying the buffer. It is used on the clocktable path. Exposing it is
closer to plumbing than to design.

*And the scoping already exists too:* =org_outline='s =target= accepts an
=:ID:= to index only that subtree. Whatever resolves an id to a heading
there is what a body-returning tool needs, which is also what makes the
partial-=:ID:= failure above worth fixing once rather than twice.

*Worth deciding together rather than separately,* since one tool with a
mode argument may serve both: front matter only, body only, whole
subtree, or structure — the last being =org_outline= as it stands.

:END:
*Built 2026-08-28, and half of what this heading asked for had already shipped without it noticing.*

*Part 1 was done.* =scope= accepts an 8-character =:ID:= prefix today — [[id:93f6c908-1c15-44e5-84f9-03f1ffb6d5db][93f6c908]] and [[id:6c48d5a6-1c78-4ce5-ac97-5e1091bdb25c][6c48d5a6]] landed that under [[id:478d6ec9-1b99-4c6c-88e9-c793ad4b2f22][478d6ec9]] after this was written. Checked before building rather than assumed: =org_outline scope=f4e628ce= returns the heading.

*But its second complaint was still live.* An id-shaped scope that resolves to nothing still fell through to the file interpretation and answered =Error: no readable file at .../zzzzzzzz=, which reports the wrong failure — a missing file rather than an unresolvable heading. Now decided on *shape*: a scope containing neither =/= nor =.= was meant as an id, so it says so and names the three forms it accepts. Both interpretations have already failed by that point, so nothing is guessed.

*Part 2 is the new work: front matter at the scope root.* =:CREATED:=, =:CATEGORY:=, =:KIND:=, the =:BLOCKER:= *value* with each id's current keyword, and the plan file. The original request — "show me the front matter of =f4e628ce= sans body, and the tree of anything below it" — is now one call:

: :CREATED: [2026-08-11 Tue 15:52]
: :CATEGORY: Queue
: :PLAN-FILE: ~/.claude/plans/cheerful-riding-robin.md
: DONE pause/resume cannot see a turn blocked on a permission prompt  {f4e628ce-...}  :code:

*Root only and not behind a flag*, exactly as this body argued, and the argument held up: per-heading front matter multiplies by heading count and would destroy the 40x-smaller property the tool sells, while a boolean is schema paid on every request whether or not anyone sets it.

*One addition the heading did not name: =:CATEGORY:=.* It was not a property when this was written — [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] made it one, and post-flattening it is how a heading's grouping is expressed at all, so omitting it would have left the front matter missing the thing most likely to be asked for.

*The blocker rendering is the part that pays immediately.* The tree line has always carried a bare =[blocked]= marker saying a blocker *exists*; the front matter now names the ids **with their current keywords**, so a satisfied blocker is visible as satisfied without a second call.

*Verified by mutation, and one of the two attempts was itself a lesson.* Removing the front matter fails exactly one test. The first attempt at breaking the scope-error branch left the file unparseable, so =bin/test= exited 255 having run *nothing* — and a naive count of =FAILED= lines read that as "no failures", which is the same silence-is-not-a-pass trap this project has recorded before. Redone with valid syntax it fails the new test plus one pre-existing one, as it should. 438/438 restored.

*Also corrected: the test fixture used ids like =b-0001=, which =--lint-blocker-ids= rejects because it filters on a UUID shape.* The code was right and the fixture was unrealistic — worth recording, because the first reading was that the blocker rendering was broken.

*Left for its own decision, as this body proposed:* returning a heading's *body*, whole. The primitive exists (=--subtree-text-at-point=) and the scoping is now shared, so it is plumbing — but whether it is a mode on this tool or a separate one is a design question, and this heading's own argument for a small surface cuts both ways.

=org-id-goto= wants the *entire* ID, exactly, and offers no help getting
it. Verified against the installed org 2026-08-11: it is
=(interactive "sID: ")=, a plain string prompt with no =completing-read=;
=org-id-find= resolves through the =org-id-locations= hash, which is
exact by construction; and the file-level fallback calls
=org-find-entry-with-id=, also exact. A miss is worse than a fast
failure — =org-id-find= re-runs =org-id-update-id-locations= and tries
again, so a partial ID costs a full rescan before returning nothing.

*Why this bites here specifically.* This project is unusually
ID-centric: every heading carries an =:ID:=, headings cross-reference
each other as =[[id:...]]=, and both conversation and commit messages
routinely name headings by their first eight characters — =720b2dcf=,
=f9f61c04=. Those abbreviations are readable and completely
unactionable. The gap is not org's fault; it is the cost of a convention
this project adopted deliberately.

*Proposal:* an interactive command that =completing-read=s over the
known headings, displaying *titles* rather than UUIDs, and jumps via
=org-id-goto= with the full ID behind the candidate.

*One design detail worth getting right:* annotate each candidate with
the ID's first eight characters. Doom's completion styles match against
the whole candidate string, so typing =720b2dcf= would then narrow
directly — which makes every abbreviation in these headings, in commit
messages and in conversation immediately typeable, rather than
something to look up first. That is most of the value; titles alone
would be a lesser tool.

*Building the candidates:* =org-id-locations= maps id to file and knows
nothing about titles, so they have to come from a scan. Either =org-ql=
over =claude-code-ide-org--tracked-files= — already a dependency, and
the same path =org_query= uses — or a plain =org-map-entries=. Do not
cache without measuring first: the tracked set is two files and well
under a hundred headings, so a rescan per invocation is very likely
cheaper than any invalidation bug it would buy.

*Not a gap, a convenience.* =C-c C-o= on any =[[id:...]]= link already
works and needs no new code, because the links in the file carry full
IDs. Scope this accordingly — it is a small command, not a subsystem.

*Testing:* the candidate-building function is ordinary and testable
(given a file set, assert the expected id/title pairs). The completion
UI itself is the fuzzy part and should be a documented manual check,
per this project's own "reasonably feasible" rule rather than forced
into a deterministic test.

*Re-verified 2026-08-18, and the case got stronger.* =org-id-goto='s
interactive form is still =(interactive "sID: ")= — a bare string prompt,
no =completing-read= — against 162 live entries in =org-id-locations=.
Nothing has changed on org's side, and no user-facing jump command exists
in =config.el=; the only =goto= functions there are review-buffer
internals.

*What changed is the convention this serves.* The footnote rule was
inverted the same day: prose now refers to a heading by *the first few
words of its title*, and the 8-character id moves into the footnote. So
both halves of this heading's proposal are now load-bearing rather than
one being a convenience —

- *titles displayed* is what makes a heading findable from the prose,
  which is where the reader meets it;
- *the 8-char prefix annotated onto each candidate* is what makes the
  footnote actionable, since that is now the only place the id appears.

The user's current workflow is =C-s= in TODO.org, which is not a
workaround for missing knowledge — with no completion on =org-id-goto=, it
is genuinely competitive today. That is the measure of the gap: the
project's own reference convention is faster to search as plain text than
to resolve through org's id machinery.

*Sibling, not duplicate, of
[[id:2d9eeebd-4375-4790-8485-92b244236a21][2d9eeebd]].* That one is
model-facing — MCP tools that should accept a partial =:ID:= and return
front matter without a whole-body read. This one is human-facing — an
interactive command. They share one premise, worth stating once rather
than in both: this project made every heading id-addressed and then made
the 8-character prefix the unit of reference in prose, commits and
conversation, while every actual lookup still demands all 36.

:END:
*Built 2026-08-29 as =claude-code-ide-org-goto=, an interactive command with no MCP registration* — this one is for the human at Emacs, so it costs nothing on the tool surface.

*The design detail this body called "most of the value" is the one that decided the implementation.* The prefix goes *in the candidate string*, not in an annotation. An annotation supplied through =completion-extra-properties= is displayed but not matched by several completion styles, so typing =720b2dcf= would narrow nothing — and making this project's abbreviations directly typeable is the whole point.

*And it leads rather than trails*, which this body did not specify. That is [[id:46e4ce2b-fdc8-447b-ad09-b4845602540f][46e4ce2b]]'s argument for the review buffer applied here: the prefix is what a reader arrives with, so it should be the first thing both the eye and the completion pattern meet. The test asserts *both* claims separately, since only the first is obvious.

*Reused rather than rebuilt:* =--ordered-collection=, which declares =display-sort-function= as =identity= so Vertico does not re-sort the list by title length ([[id:85702dba-8d15-4924-84bd-2bb7efac093a][85702dba]]). Document order, not relevance — unlike the assignment dialog there is no time axis to rank against, and file order already puts recent captures near the top because =org_capture= prepends.

*Keywordless headings are candidates*, rendered with =-=. Excluding them would lose exactly the headings captured in the current session, which are the ones most likely to be jumped to.

*Verified:* 439/439, and by mutation — moving the prefix to the end of the string fails exactly one test, with the run count checked before the failure count. Live on the real corpus: 203 candidates, first line =b36e6369  TODO      [0/20] The code knows more than it says...=.

*Semantic matching stays out*, as this body asked. A fuzzy resolver that returns the wrong heading confidently is the failure [[id:7771fc63-9374-4c8a-9e80-24ceec21977c][7771fc63]] measured; prefix and substring matching are decidable and similarity is not.

*Not bound to a key.* The command exists and is =M-x=-reachable; choosing a binding is the user's, not something to decide on their behalf in a module they load.

*One incidental worth recording because it bit while verifying this.* The form-reading syntax check written into the previous session prompt — =(while t (forward-sexp))= — only terminates when the file is *broken*, so on a clean file it spins until killed. Corrected there to a bounded =(while (not (eobp)) ...)=. A verification recipe that hangs on success is the same family as the ones [[id:542924c1-9152-4414-8da8-d530d3423611][542924c1]] collects.


***** DONE Add a tool to set heading properties, starting with :BLOCKER: :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-28 Fri 14:07]
:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       36b811d9-8bd3-4a32-b67d-39ccfe0d66c1
:CREATED:  [2026-08-15 Sat 16:43]
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "TODO"       from              [2026-08-15 Sat 16:44] \\
  property tool gap, three incidents tonight
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-08-28 Fri 14:07] \\
  org_set_property shipped with validation
:END:
:PLAN:

None of the 14 registered tools sets a property. =org_capture= writes
=:ID:= and =:CREATED:= at creation and that is the whole of it, so every
later property change is a hand-edit or an =emacsclient= call.

*The gap has a behavioural cost, not just an ergonomic one.* CLAUDE.md's
convention says to prefer =:BLOCKER:= over a prose "depends on ..."
sentence, because a property is machine-checkable and a sentence is not.
But there is no tool to write one, while prose costs nothing — so the
*discouraged* form is cheaper than the *preferred* one, and the
convention loses by default. Evidence from the session that found this:
on 2026-08-15 a dependency was recorded on
[[id:4f8500e6-b468-4fd4-a0f6-ebf04c7a57ba][4f8500e6]] as the words
"Tracked separately", with no link and no property, and only got a real
=:BLOCKER:= when the omission was noticed on re-reading. Twice in the
same session a property had to be set through =emacsclient= —
=org-entry-put= on that heading and on
[[id:9ae4b17e-278c-482f-9114-df28b2254806][9ae4b17e]].

*Validation is the reason to build the specific tool rather than only a
general one.* A =:BLOCKER:= naming an ID that does not exist never blocks
anything and never errors — it simply does nothing, forever. A tool that
resolves each ID before writing turns that silent failure into a refusal
at the call site. The same session fabricated a UUID from an 8-character
prefix and caught it only by a link-resolution sweep afterwards, which is
precisely the failure this validation would have made impossible.

*Design questions, unresolved:*

- *General =org_set_property= or specific =org_add_blocker=?* The general
  one is obviously more flexible and validates nothing. The specific one
  encodes the convention, can resolve IDs, and can append to an existing
  =ids(...)= list rather than overwriting it — which the general form
  would silently get wrong, since =:BLOCKER:= holds a *set*.
- *Write immediately or queue?* A property is neither TODO state nor
  clock, so it is outside what the queue exists to defer. =org_amend='s
  model looks right: write through Emacs when the file is free, queue when
  the human has unsaved changes in that buffer.
- *What else needs setting?* =:ARCHIVE:= per-heading overrides and
  =:TRIGGER:= (the inverse of =:BLOCKER:=) are the other two the
  conventions name. =:CREATED:= and =:ID:= are already handled at capture
  and should stay there.

Distinct from [[id:087e73e9-bb24-43b6-a972-b7f103d04017][087e73e9]],
which is about *enforcing* =:BLOCKER:= once set. This one is about being
able to set it at all.

*Footnote to the above, written the same minute:* the paragraph arguing
that a fabricated =:BLOCKER:= ID fails silently was itself written with a
fabricated ID — =8ee85ba3-...=, invented for this very link, caught by
the resolve-check rather than by reading it back. Third occurrence in one
session. The lesson is not "be careful"; it is that the resolve-check is
the only thing that has ever caught this, and a tool that validates at the
call site would remove the opportunity entirely.

*A fourth design constraint, found by =bin/lint-org= within a minute of
this heading being written.* Setting =:BLOCKER:= on
[[id:4f8500e6-b468-4fd4-a0f6-ebf04c7a57ba][4f8500e6]] naming
[[id:df5afbbd-0eac-4032-be91-17cc22ef0cd7][df5afbbd]] produced:

: error: :BLOCKER: names keyword-less heading df5afbbd -- org-depend
: blocks only on an unfinished TODO, so this is a silent no-op

The linter is right, and the cause is architectural rather than careless.
=org_capture= deliberately writes no TODO keyword — its own description
says to set the state afterwards with =org_set_todo= — and =org_set_todo=
queues. So *every heading captured in a session is keyword-less until a
human applies the queue*, and any =:BLOCKER:= naming one is inert in the
meantime. Not wrong, but not yet in force, and indistinguishable from
working without the linter.

This sharpens the validation argument above. A property tool should
refuse, or at least warn, when the heading it is about to name carries no
keyword — the same check the linter already implements, moved from
after-the-fact to the call site. It also suggests a smaller companion
question: whether =org_capture= should accept an initial state, so that a
capture and its keyword do not arrive a review pass apart.

Worth noting the linter caught this and re-reading did not, which is the
same lesson as the fabricated ID above and the same remedy: mechanical
checks catch what looks correct.

:END:
*Built 2026-08-28 as =org_set_property=.* The four design questions this heading left open are answered, three of them the way it leaned and one against.

*General or specific: one general tool that special-cases =:BLOCKER:=.* The heading framed these as alternatives, and they are not. A single writer gets the flexibility — =:CATEGORY:= was set by hand ten times in the session that built this, which is the same evidence that produced the heading — while =:BLOCKER:= keeps the validation only a specific tool was thought to allow. Every token is resolved before writing, 8-character prefixes expanded, and anything unresolvable or ambiguous refused. =append= unions with the existing set rather than replacing it, which is the one thing a general writer would silently get wrong.

*Write or queue: neither. It refuses while the file is busy*, and that is a knowing departure from =org_amend='s model rather than an oversight. Queueing needs a queue kind, a hook branch and a review-buffer rendering, none of which exist. Refusing loses nothing — the caller retries — where writing into a modified buffer could lose the human's edits.

*Keyword-less blockers warn rather than refuse.* The heading's fourth constraint asked for a refusal-or-warning and the answer is warning, for a reason it half-anticipated: =org_capture= writes no keyword and =org_set_todo= queues, so *every heading captured this session is keyword-less until apply*. Refusing would make the tool unusable in the case it is most wanted. The warning is =bin/lint-org='s own check moved to the call site.

*Refused outright: =:ID:= and =:CREATED:=.* Identity, written once at capture. Rewriting an =:ID:= orphans every inbound link and every queued event naming it, silently.

*The test caught a real bug on its first run*, which is the argument for having written it rather than eyeballing the diff. The implementation took a shortcut — if =--id-find= resolves the token, use the token — and =--id-find= resolves a *prefix* too ([[id:478d6ec9-1b99-4c6c-88e9-c793ad4b2f22][478d6ec9]] built that). So =BLOCKER: aaaaaaaa= wrote =ids(aaaaaaaa)=, a malformed id that reads as unresolvable to everything downstream: exactly the silent-forever failure this heading exists to prevent, reintroduced by the tool built to prevent it. Now it always expands and never trusts the token.

*Verification:* 435/435, three new tests covering the plain write, both refusals, prefix expansion, the unresolvable refusal, append-versus-replace, and the keyword-less warning. Registered on the MCP surface and =fboundp= confirmed after =load-file= — though the *schema* is negotiated at session start, so it is callable from the next session, not this one.

*Not built, and worth its own heading if wanted:* the queue path, and =org_capture= accepting an initial state so a capture and its keyword do not arrive a review pass apart — the smaller companion question this heading raised at the end.

Indentation is the *only* thing =org_outline='s output says about
parentage: =claude-code-ide-org--outline-line= emits two spaces per
absolute =org-current-level=, and =org-map-entries= emits in document
order. A reader reconstructs the tree as "parent = nearest preceding
line with a smaller indent," which holds only while every intermediate
ancestor is present.

=active_only= breaks that. The filter lives in =--outline-line=, which
returns nil for a DONE/CANCELLED heading — it does *not* skip the
subtree in =--outline-map=, so that heading's still-active descendants
are emitted anyway, at their unchanged absolute indent. Verified
2026-08-12 against a scratch file:

: * Category
: ** DONE Finished parent
: *** TODO Active child

returns

: Category
:     TODO Active child

The indent jumps two levels, and a reader re-parents the child onto its
*grandparent* with nothing in the output marking that it did. Silent
wrong structure, not a visible gap.

*Not currently observable in this project's own files*, which is why it
took this long to notice: TODO.org's level-1 headings are categories
carrying no TODO keyword, so nothing on the path from a category to a
level-2 task can ever be filtered out. All 60 lines of a full-depth
=active_only= run were checked and no indent jump occurs. That is a
property of the top-level-heading convention, not a guarantee from the
format — the bug is one three-level task tree away from biting.

=max_depth= is safe by contrast: it only ever drops the deepest lines,
truncating leaves rather than severing an ancestor.

*Options, none chosen:*
- *Emit the elided ancestors anyway*, unfiltered, so the path stays
  intact. Keeps reconstruction sound and costs a few lines the caller
  asked not to see.
- *Re-indent survivors to their visible depth*, so indent means "depth
  in the returned tree" rather than absolute level. Cheapest output,
  but contradicts the deliberate absolute-level decision in
  [[id:9f3c35c7-0229-4cd6-908b-779267ec9b97][9f3c35c7]] that makes
  =max_depth= mean the same thing for a file and for a subtree.
- *Skip the whole subtree* when a heading is filtered out. Simplest
  rule, and the most likely to surprise — an active child of a DONE
  parent is exactly the thing =active_only= should be showing.

*Related, same output, separate defect:* in a multi-file call the
per-file label is a bare =file-name-nondirectory= at column 0,
structurally identical to a level-1 heading, which by this project's
convention also carries no keyword, no =:ID:= and no tags. Nothing but
"it looks like a filename" distinguishes them, so a reader that treats
the label as a heading turns each file into one spurious root. Worth
fixing in the same pass, since both are the same class of bug: the
format asserting less structure than the reader needs.

:END:
*Fixed 2026-08-28 by the first of the three options above — emit the elided ancestors — and two things had changed since the analysis was written.*

*The safety argument had expired.* This body said the bug was "not currently observable in this project's own files" because "TODO.org's level-1 headings are categories carrying no TODO keyword, so nothing on the path from a category to a level-2 task can ever be filtered out". [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] removed that: level 1 is now where tasks live, and a closed story with live children is an ordinary shape. The structural protection was gone; only the absence of instances remained, measured at zero the same day.

*And CLAUDE.md described the defect backwards.* It warned that =active_only= "drops live children of a finished parent". It did not drop them — it *emitted* them at their unchanged absolute indent with the parent missing, so a reader re-parents a live child onto whatever line above happens to have a smaller indent. Confirmed against a scratch file before touching anything: a =DONE= level-1 parent's live child came out at indent 4 while a genuine level-1 sibling sat at 2. Wrong structure rather than a visible gap, which is the worse failure — a missing line gets noticed and a misparented one does not.

*The fix.* =--outline-map= now collects two renderings per heading, the filtered one and the unfiltered one, then walks the records in reverse keeping a heading when it survives the filter *or* when it is an ancestor of something already kept. =need-above= carries the level of the shallowest kept heading, so anything shallower encountered earlier in the document is on its path and is emitted.

*Why option 1 and not the other two.* Re-indenting survivors to visible depth would contradict [[id:9f3c35c7-0229-4cd6-908b-779267ec9b97][9f3c35c7]]'s deliberate choice of absolute level, which is what makes =max_depth= mean the same thing for a file and for a subtree. Skipping the whole subtree is the simplest rule and the most surprising: an active child would vanish because its parent finished, which is the opposite of what =active_only= is asked for. Emitting the ancestor costs a line the caller filtered out, and that line carries its own =DONE= keyword, so it cannot be mistaken for a result.

*Verified by mutation.* Removing the ancestor-keeping clause fails exactly one test and nothing else; 436/436 restored. The test asserts the *parent is present* and that the child sits deeper than it while a real sibling sits level with it — asserting only that the child appears would pass against the broken code, since it appeared there too, just in the wrong place. Real corpus output is unchanged, as expected at zero instances.

*One incidental worth recording:* the test's first run failed because it wrote its fixture with =with-temp-file= onto the path the enclosing macro already had a buffer visiting, so =org-map-entries= mapped over stale text and reported the parent absent. A fresh path fixes it. That is the same buffer-versus-disk hazard the tools guard against in production and the tests do not.

*The user reports using short prefixes constantly.* Until this change every one of them failed: =--id-find= gated on =(= (length id) 8)=, so a four-character prefix skipped expansion entirely and reached =org-id-find= as a bare string that cannot match a full uuid.

*Uniqueness, not length, is what makes a prefix safe.* =--expand-id-prefix= already refused an ambiguous one rather than guessing, so the gate was the citation convention's *width*, never a correctness requirement. Measured over 282 ids: two characters collide in 73 groups, three in four, and **four in none** -- identical to eight.

*The expensive half, and why Emacs died.* A miss triggered a full re-index of every tracked file and its archives -- and that fired for *ambiguous* prefixes too, where it is worthless by construction, since more data can only add matches. The unresolved prefix then fell through to =org-id-find=, whose own miss path rescans again. Up to two full corpus scans per lookup. The user was looking up =a1d6= when Emacs pinned at 99% CPU and had to be killed.

*Three changes:* accept four to eight characters; rescan only for ='none=; short-circuit rather than hand =org-id-find= something it cannot resolve. A genuinely absent id still earns exactly one rescan, which is the case the rescan was added for. Ambiguity now carries its candidates, because "try again" is a poor answer when the tool is holding the list you need.

  build the division tool

  org_divide shipped and proved by mutation

:PLAN:

*The user's proposal 2026-08-25.* When a leaf inflates far enough that it is really a story, do not promote it in place. Create a *new* parent, move the original leaf underneath it carrying its clock, LOGBOOK, state history and identity, and derive one or more further leaves from the engorged body. Division rather than promotion.

*It dissolves the objection this repo had already recorded against migrating clocks.* [[id:3964c575-50bc-4cc9-abeb-bdd1c0162c2c][3964c575]] listed "migrate on promotion" as a candidate and called it dangerous, because "the time was spent on the parent's own work, and there may be no child it belongs to". Under mitosis there always is one, by construction: the child *is* the parent's own work. The danger was an artefact of promoting in place, not of moving clocks.

*And it makes the forward-looking rule enforceable.* A container that never acquires a clock can be asserted; one that acquires clocks retroactively cannot. Mitosis is what turns "containers carry no clock" from an aspiration into a rule -- for new work. The 45 existing lines across eight containers are unaffected unless those headings are divided deliberately.

*Today's own case has exactly this shape and was done the other way.* [[id:2758f3a0-3c47-405e-9662-a7669dcb60cc][2758f3a0]] was a clocked leaf until [[id:5787bfc6-3ba5-4d94-802c-f8a7879de68d][5787bfc6]] was refiled under it, promoting it in place and leaving its clock on the container. Mitosis would have made a fresh parent with both as children, and the hook-building clock would sit on the child that did the hook building. The delta between the two approaches is exactly one CLOCK line in the wrong place.

*One clause needs deciding before this is built, and it is not a detail.* The proposal says the leaf takes its =:ID:= with it. Measured over both files rather than assumed: *251 headings carry an =:ID:=, and only 67 of them -- 27 percent -- have no inbound* =[[id:]]= *reference at all.* The rest are referenced up to 39 times, and 38 headings are named by some =:BLOCKER:=. So the id is load-bearing for most headings, and identity and history pull in opposite directions:

| what needs it              | where the =:ID:= should go | why                                                          |
|----------------------------+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------|
| prose cross-references     | the parent                 | "see [[id:X]]" is about the topic, which after division is the story |
| =:BLOCKER:= entries        | the parent                 | blocking on X means "until X is finished", now the whole story |
| queued clock/state events  | the child                  | an event naming X must not land its clock on a container      |
| clock lines, LOGBOOK, body | the child either way       | they travel with the subtree text, not with the id            |

*So the history argument may not need the id at all*, which is the thing to check before building: LOGBOOK and CLOCK lines move because the *text* moves. What genuinely needs the id to follow the leaf is the queue -- and queue events are transient, consumed at the next apply. If that holds, the id stays with the parent, the child takes a fresh one, and the proposal survives intact everywhere except that clause.

*The counter-case to test:* a heading divided while it has unapplied queued events naming it. On any working day here that is not hypothetical.

*Wants a tool rather than a hand edit*, on this repo's own evidence: two body corruptions are on record, both range bugs, and =org_wrap_plan= exists precisely because hand-rolling that class of edit failed twice with =bin/lint-org= reporting zero errors both times.

*The =:ID:= clause is settled, and the proposal was right as originally stated: the id goes with the leaf.* The table above raised three objections and all three fail. Recorded rather than deleted because the way they failed is the useful part -- the first measurement taken was the wrong one.

*"27 percent of headings have no inbound reference" measured density, not damage.* It establishes that references exist; it says nothing about whether any would break. The user asked for an example, which is what exposed it -- a statistic about a population cannot answer a question about a mechanism.

*Prose links land in the general area, which is all they were ever doing.* The most-referenced open heading is [[id:02aaae22-0958-4c0f-b5bb-2cbea32416ae][02aaae22]] with 20 inbound links, and they read like this one: "prose, because it holds the four container rules as settled and pending transcription". A reader following that wants the topic, and after division the topic is the story -- but landing on the elder child reaches it in one keystroke.

*The =:BLOCKER:= objection is empirically empty, and not by accident.* Of the 38 headings named by some blocker, only 13 are still open and therefore still able to gate anything. *Their largest body is 53 lines. The smallest plausible mitosis candidate is 97.* The two populations do not overlap at all.

The reason they do not is structural rather than lucky: you block on a *bounded, specific* deliverable, and a bounded specific deliverable is precisely the kind of heading that never inflates enough to need dividing. The eight large headings that *are* named by blockers are all closed, so they gate nothing. Worth re-measuring if that ever stops holding, but it is not a coincidence to be nervous about.

*And the queued-events case actively argues **for** the proposal rather than against it.* A queued =clock_in= names a heading by id, and apply opens a clock on whatever holds that id. If the id moved to the new parent, applying a pending clock event would open a clock *on a container* -- the exact outcome mitosis exists to prevent. The id must follow the leaf for the queue to stay correct.

*So the counter-case flagged above -- dividing a heading with unapplied events naming it -- resolves too.* The events follow the leaf, which is where they belonged. The one residue is a queued state transition whose intent was the whole task: it will land on the elder child rather than the story. Small, visible at review, and the review pass is a human reading each item anyway.

*Crossed with the user's definition 2026-08-25 -- "a task that acquired keyworded children is a story, point of fact" -- and the two together stop being definitions and become a lifecycle.*

*Mitosis is how a story comes into existence.* The new parent this creates has keyworded children the instant it exists, so by that definition it *is* a story. Nothing is promoted and nothing is classified: a task divides, and what appears above it is a story because of what is now under it. That is the emergent definition doing real work rather than merely describing a state.

*So a story is never authored. It is precipitated.* This matters for where the project is headed because it removes the act that was always going to be got wrong -- deciding that something "is now an epic" and writing it down. There is no such decision. There is a task that got too big, and a division.

*And a story is born empty, which settles three open things at once by construction rather than by rule.*

- *No clock.* [[id:3964c575-50bc-4cc9-abeb-bdd1c0162c2c][3964c575]] wants containers to carry none and cannot enforce it, because a heading clocked honestly as a leaf becomes a container retroactively. A story created by mitosis has never been worked, so it has no clock to have earned. The 45 existing lines across eight containers are then exactly what they look like: pre-mitosis artefacts, not a rule being broken.
- *No history.* The =:ID:=, =:LOGBOOK:= and state transitions travel with the elder child, which is the task that actually did the work. The story has no past because it did not have one.
- *No body of actions.* The user's earlier claim -- that a story should have nowhere to describe an action to take, all actions being distributed among its children -- is not a rule to obey under mitosis. It is what happens: the engorged body is *consumed* in producing the new leaves. Whatever is left is the reason the group exists, which is the one thing a story's body should hold.

*Where this leaves the four words, which is the point of the crossing.* They are not a taxonomy of heading types to be assigned. They are a lifecycle plus two orthogonal labels:

| concept | what it is | how it arises |
|---------+------------+---------------|
| task    | a leaf, the unit of work        | written |
| story   | a task with keyworded children  | *precipitated by mitosis* |
| epic    | the grouping a task belongs to  | declared, as a =:CATEGORY:= value on the task |
| slice   | a sequenced set, by reference   | declared, cutting across everything |

*Note the epic column, because it is the payoff for flattening.* Since the label sits on the *task*, a story's children may carry different =:CATEGORY:= values, so a story spans epics for free -- no refiling, and no arrangement of parents to work around. That was the constraint [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] existed to remove, and mitosis plus a per-task label removes it without either mechanism knowing about the other.

:END:
*Built 2026-08-28 as =org_divide= / =claude-code-ide-org-divide=.*

*Scoped to the mechanical half deliberately.* The tool inserts a new parent above the heading and demotes it underneath, and does *nothing* with the child's engorged body. Splitting that into further sibling leaves is an editorial judgement, and a tool that guessed at it would be inventing headings. So =org_divide= guarantees the *record* survives a division; it does not guarantee the division was a good one.

*Composed from org's own primitives rather than region arithmetic*, which was the one implementation risk this heading named: =org-demote-subtree= plus a single whole-line insertion at beginning-of-heading. Nothing is deleted and no range is computed, so it cannot repeat the two body corruptions on record — the ones =org_wrap_plan= exists because of.

*The child is not touched, and that is the whole mechanism.* Its =:ID:=, =:LOGBOOK:=, CLOCK lines, state history and body all move because =org-demote-subtree= moves the *text*. Nothing had to be migrated, which is why the "migrate on promotion" hazard [[id:3964c575-50bc-4cc9-abeb-bdd1c0162c2c][3964c575]] recorded never arises here.

*The new parent is born empty*, as the design required: an =:ID:=, a =:CREATED:= stamp, the child's =:CATEGORY:=, a =[/]= cookie, and no clock and no history at all. Its TODO keyword defaults to the child's, so the group inherits the claim the task was already making rather than resetting it.

*Verified by breaking it, not by watching it pass.* The test asserts what *stayed* as well as what moved, and both load-bearing claims were falsified deliberately: removing the demote fails exactly one test, and stealing the child's =:ID:= onto the parent fails exactly one test. Restored, 432/432. Registered on the MCP surface, and =(fboundp 'claude-code-ide-org-divide)= confirmed in the running Emacs after =load-file=.

*One limit worth stating rather than discovering.* The MCP *schema* is negotiated at session start, so =org_divide= is not callable from this session even though the elisp is live — the next session gets it.

*CLAUDE.md's mitosis section said "designed and **not built**".* That is now corrected, along with the tool table, and the paragraph records the manual/mechanical split above so nobody expects the tool to produce the sibling leaves.
