:PLAN:

*Raised 2026-08-06, after =PLANNING= sat unused or was hand-reverted twice in one day.* The question: does it earn its complexity — clock-owning semantics, the =ExitPlanMode= auto-promotion hook, a global owner variable — or is it a rung nobody climbs? Deferred behind a list of ten items that later became unsatisfiable (four were =CANCELLED=), ungated 2026-08-13 and promoted =MAYBE= -> =TODO=; the list was only ever a proxy for accumulated experience, which arrived by another route.

*Scope widened 2026-08-10 to the whole progression*, after checking the sequence against org+GTD practice.

*What the tradition says, and it cuts against =DOING=, not =PLANNING=.* Bernt Hansen's canonical org+GTD setup has *no in-progress keyword at all* — clocking signals what is active, and he switches tasks *to* =NEXT= on clock-in. GTD proper treats an in-progress state as a smell: anything needing one is usually a project wearing an action's clothes, and the fix is decomposition.

*=DOING= survives that critique here, for the reason it usually fails it*, and this is worth keeping because a future reader citing Bernt or GTD would have a well-supported argument for deleting it and would be wrong *for this system specifically*. The standard substitute — let the clock say what is active — is exactly the affordance the event queue removes: clock accuracy is only ever as fresh as the last human apply, and a reviewed historical record cannot answer "what is being worked on right now". So the keyword has to.

*Three proposals, of which two are still open and unadopted:*

1. *=VERIFY= between =DOING= and =DONE=* — superseded. =REVIEW= shipped in that slot 2026-08-21. The argument was that verification is human-triggered by hard constraint, so every task passes through a mandatory handoff with no name; org's own manual uses the same slot (=TODO FEEDBACK VERIFY | DONE CANCELED=).
2. *Get =MAYBE= out of the default agenda without moving it after the =|=* — *open.* At 23 of 56 keyworded headings it was the largest state, a healthy Someday/Maybe list rendered actionable by its position. Moving it past the =|= would be semantically wrong; filtering it from default views is Bernt's answer.
3. *Narrow =WAITING= to "waiting on a person"* — *open.* GTD separates *Waiting For* (delegated, needs chasing) from *blocked* (a dependency), and dependencies here are already structural via =:BLOCKER:=. A keyword nobody reaches for is usually one whose meaning is unclear rather than one whose situation never arises.

*=REVIEW= was argued for here and adopted 2026-08-21.* =WAITING= had quietly acquired a second meaning — the resting state at the end of a Claude increment — because the keyword field is *one slot serving two actors with different views of who owes what*. =WAITING= reads correctly from the session's side and oddly from the human's; =TODO= the reverse. =REVIEW= reads correctly from both, de-overloads =WAITING=, and is a *stage* rather than a parking place. Its exit asymmetry and its sharper definition ("finished, only judgement remains") are now in CLAUDE.md. *Still open:* whether the three-way collision on the word "review" — the =:review:= tag, the apply command, and the state — should be resolved or adopted deliberately.

*Every place the keyword set is written down*, inventoried 2026-08-14 by grep. This list *proved itself* on 2026-08-28: retiring =PLANNING= touched every entry still standing.

- both =#+TODO:= lines, with per-keyword cookies
- =~/.config/doom/config.el= =org-todo-keywords= — the global default, for files with no =#+TODO:= line
- CLAUDE.md's two tables, and the org skill's keyword list, per-keyword sections and transition table
- =config.el=: =org_set_todo='s MCP registration, where the states are enumerated verbatim *twice*; =--review-suggest-heading='s active-keyword set; =--work-in-progress-keywords=; =--slice-checkbox-by-keyword=
- =bin/lint-org=, once it asserts the convention

*The trap worth naming, and it is still live.* =org_set_todo= validates against =org-todo-keywords-1=, which is *buffer-local* and read from the file's own =#+TODO:= line. A keyword in the Doom config but not in a file's header is accepted in one file and rejected in another. Worse, =#+TODO:= is parsed *only at mode init*, so editing the header does not change a buffer already open — a revert without =preserve-modes= is required, which is exactly what the 2026-08-28 retirement had to do.

*Deliberately unchanged and checked:* =--outline-finished-keywords= and the two =("DONE" "CANCELLED")= assignment tests. =REVIEW= is an *active* state and belongs in none of them; a future reader will find them while grepping and should know they were considered.

*=DOING= was recalibrated 2026-08-25* to mean *started and owed a return* — durable, plural, silent about whether anyone is at the keyboard — with the clock recording execution instead. GTD's one-thing-at-a-time is deliberately not followed: that rule is calibrated to human working memory, and an agent re-reading a checklist each turn has different limits. Enacted in CLAUDE.md; the conditional clock rules there are its consequence.

-----

:END:
*Debrief.* =PLANNING= was retired 2026-08-28 on measurement, and the rest of the progression was left standing.

*What decided it, measured across the project's whole history rather than argued:* 7 =PLANNING= transitions in 432 state changes (1.6%), on 6 of the 24 days the keyword existed and absent from the three busiest days; an eight-day stretch holding 199 transitions and none. 43 headings carry a plan link and 7 ever wore it, so *84% of planned work skipped the keyword* while nothing wore it without producing a plan. All seven exited to =DOING=, so it never distinguished an outcome. And the premise it was built on — long spans of agent work in Plan Mode — held for *one of seven*: clocked minutes inside the seven windows were 0:00, 0:00, 0:00, 0:01, 0:03, 1:11, 0:12.

*One hypothesis of the user's was falsified in passing*, and it was offered tentatively so the correction is recorded rather than dropped: planning time does *not* mostly land as =Meta=. The datetree holds 8h52m against 67h57m on tasks — 12%. The smearing is real but it is across the *tasks themselves*, planning now happening inside a task's own clock over days, interleaved with revising and cross-referencing it. That is why no single interval looks like a planning session.

*What shipped:* the keyword removed from both =#+TODO:= lines; the =ExitPlanMode= promotion hook, its =settings.json= wiring and =bin/exitplanmode-promote-test= deleted; =PLANNING= removed from =--slice-checkbox-by-keyword=, the auto-clock-in trigger and =--work-in-progress-keywords=; four rows of CLAUDE.md's transition table plus its entering/leaving rules and cross-session guard paragraph; and in the org skill a keyword line, three transition rows and a parallel-planning paragraph that also still cited owner variables deleted at the 2026-08-11 cutover.

*Nothing replaced it, and that was a decision.* A "plan approved" event was considered and declined: nothing would consume it, and the precedent ([[id:7771fc63-9374-4c8a-9e80-24ceec21977c][7771fc63]]) is to delete a mechanism whose premise failed rather than reimplement it cheaply. Plan Mode now needs no state of its own — a heading is =DOING= while it is planned and implemented, which is what =DOING= already meant.

*How it was verified:* 431/431 after deleting three tests, each a duplicate of a surviving =DOING= twin; the stale-state and queue-parsing tests were *retargeted* to =MAYBE= rather than dropped, since they are about staleness and parsing rather than about =PLANNING=. =bin/lint-org= 0 errors, =bin/check-org-dev-skill= and =bin/queue-append-test= clean, =settings.json= still valid JSON. Both org buffers reverted *without* =preserve-modes= and confirmed to report the new keyword set — the trap named above, hit live.

*Left undone deliberately:* =QUEUE_APPEND_ID/STATE/FROM= in =bin/hooks/queue-append= are now dead, that hook having been their only consumer. Left with a note rather than removed in the same commit, because that script is on the path of every hook and an unrelated edit to the queue writer is a worse risk than a dead branch. Proposals 2 and 3 above, and the "review" collision, are unadopted and filed separately.

:PLAN:

*[[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] named this and could not have it.* Of the datetree lint gate it says: "A =:DATETREE_ROLE:= property would be the honest form", and calls what shipped instead "a property-shaped answer smuggled in as a string match". =:KIND:= shipped 2026-08-25 for slices. It is that property, arrived at from a different direction and already in production.

*Four classes, four mechanisms, and only the newest is a declaration.* Counted in =config.el= rather than recalled:

| class         | detected by                                    | kind      |
|---------------+------------------------------------------------+-----------|
| epic          | =--container-heading-p=, a descendant scan     | derived   |
| datetree node | =--datetree-node-role (depth title)= -- depth *plus a title regex* | inferred |
| category      | =(= level 1)=, plus =(> level 3)= for depth    | inferred  |
| slice         | =--slice-p=, a =:KIND:= property               | *declared* |

*The split is today's axis applied to heading classes, and it decides the scope.* The epic stays *derived* -- it is emergent, structurally detectable, and a declaration of it could go stale. Everything else in that table is *declared in fact and inferred in code*, which is the mismatch. So: datetree nodes and slices declare themselves; the epic does not; and the category tier is what [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] proposes to remove entirely.

*Why this accelerates flattening rather than merely tidying.* Flattening is risky today because *level carries meaning in three places at once* -- the level-1 category rule, the three-level depth rule, and the datetree's level-4 exception. Each is a separate thing that breaks when level-1 headings stop being categories. Once every declared class says what it is, level carries nothing, and the flattening becomes a mechanical edit rather than a coordinated change to three inference rules.

*Order that falls out of that.* Datetree first, because it is the one 29439196 already named and the string match is the most obviously wrong; then the depth rules, which can be expressed against =:KIND:= instead of level; then the category tier, which is the flattening itself and is the only step that needs [[id:82df2a6c-881d-4117-a752-5b3b04c9656d][82df2a6c]]'s evidence.

*Not a rename of what exists.* =--container-heading-p= keeps working exactly as it does; nothing about the epic changes. The claim is narrower than "declare everything": declare what is already declared implicitly, and leave derived things derived.

*=:DATETREE_ROLE:= and =:KIND:= are the same axis, and the proposal is to collapse them.* The role names *which tier of a datetree* a node is -- =year=, =month= or =day=. Today =claude-code-ide-org--datetree-node-role= infers it from org's own title regexes (a four-digit year, =YYYY-MM Month=, =YYYY-MM-DD Dayname=) rather than from depth, deliberately: a real task can sit at depth 1 beside the year node, so a depth-only test would waive =:ID:= and =:CREATED:= for every one of them.

*The three roles are different kinds, not three values of one behaviour*, which is what makes collapsing right rather than merely tidy. The lint treats year and month as pure scaffolding and exempts them from the =:ID:=/=:CREATED:= requirement; the day node must carry both, because it is what time is assigned to. So =:KIND: datetree-year=, =datetree-month=, =datetree-day=. A separate =:DATETREE_ROLE:= alongside =:KIND:= would be a *fifth* mechanism for saying what a heading is, which is the disease this heading exists to cure.

*Half of it already exists and should stay.* The datetree *root* declares itself with =:DATE_TREE:=, which is why [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] describes the current state as declared-at-the-container: the container says "a tree hangs here" and the nodes are then guessed at. Keep =:DATE_TREE:= for that -- it carries a subtree-scoped meaning no per-node kind expresses -- and let =:KIND:= carry the per-node one.

*"Category" and "epic" are distinct in the code and collide in the prose, and this needs settling before anything is flattened.* In the table above, /category/ is the level-1 filing tier -- =* Tooling= -- detected by =(= level 1)=, carrying no =:ID:= and no keyword, routing archives through =:ARCHIVE:=. /Epic/ is a *task* that acquired keyworded children, detected by =--container-heading-p=, carrying =:ID:=, a keyword and a cookie. Different things.

*But the corpus uses "epic" for both.* =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= says top-level headings "are categories/epics -- pure structure, grouping related tasks", while CLAUDE.md says an epic is "simply a heading that has acquired children carrying TODO keywords". [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]]'s own membership table uses the first sense: its /epic/ row describes today's form as "a level-1 heading, structural".

*The ambiguity is load-bearing rather than cosmetic.* "Flatten the top-level headings into categories (epics)" has two readings, and they differ where it matters: once level 1 is gone, does a task's label name the old *filing group* it lived in, or the *emergent parent task* it belongs to? Those disagree for a task with no parent, and for a task whose parent epic sits in a different filing group. Deciding which sense the label carries is a prerequisite for the flattening, not a detail of it.

:END:
*Re-read 2026-08-28 against what shipped since, and half of it is done.* Of the four-class table above:

- *slice* was already declared when this was written, and stays.
- *category* is *resolved.* [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] landed 2026-08-28: the level-1 tier is gone and a task's grouping is a =:CATEGORY:= value carried on the task. The =(= level 1)= inference is retired, and the lint rule that encoded it was inverted rather than deleted — level 1 is now where =:ID:=, =:CREATED:=, a keyword and tags are *required*.
- *epic* never needed changing and still does not. It is emergent; declaring it would be the mirrored error.
- *datetree node* is untouched and is now the *only* remaining member. =--datetree-node-role= still infers year/month/day from org's title regexes.

*So the heading's own title has outrun it.* "Generalise =:KIND:= to every declared heading class" described four classes; what is left is one, plus the depth rules that hang off it. The prediction in the body — that this "accelerates flattening rather than merely tidying" — was *not* borne out, and it is worth recording why rather than quietly dropping it. Flattening happened first, without any of this, because the three places level carried meaning turned out to be independently editable: the level-1 rule inverted, the depth rule shifted by one, and the datetree exception was already gated on title shape rather than depth and so needed no change at all. The coupling this heading predicted was not there.

*The "category versus epic" ambiguity it flagged as a prerequisite is settled*, and settled the way this body's last paragraph framed it: the label names the *filing group*, not the emergent parent. CLAUDE.md now carries the three-word distinction — epic, story, slice — and =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= carries the ten values.

*Residue found while re-reading this, and fixed in the same commit.* CLAUDE.md and =org-conventions.md= still described the epic as "today a level-1 heading" and as a *proposed* =:EPIC:= label, in four places. Both claims were false as of 2026-08-28. Worth noting how they survived: the post-flattening sweep grepped for the nine category *values*, and =:EPIC:= is a different literal that no value-based grep would ever surface. A sweep scoped to what changed misses the prose describing what it changed *from*.

*What remains, concretely.* Give datetree nodes =:KIND: datetree-year= / =datetree-month= / =datetree-day=, keep =:DATE_TREE:= on the root (subtree-scoped, and no per-node kind expresses it), and express =bin/lint-org='s =:ID:=/=:CREATED:= exemption against the declaration instead of the title regex. The design is settled in the body above; what is left is the build and a migration of the existing nodes.

*Investigated 2026-08-28, and the last remaining class closes as a deliberate non-change. The reason is worth more than the change would have been.*

The plan above was to give datetree nodes =:KIND: datetree-year= / =-month= / =-day= and express =bin/lint-org='s exemption against that declaration instead of org's title regexes. Measured against the straight checkout and this repo before building any of it:

- =org-datetree-find-date-create= calls =(org-datetree-find-create-entry '(year month day) ...)= — *org creates all three levels itself*, inside its own code.
- =org-datetree.el= offers *no creation hook*. Its only =defcustom= is =org-datetree-add-timestamp=.
- This repo has *one* call site (=config.el:9688=). It stamps =:ID:= and =:CREATED:= afterwards, on the *day node only*; year and month are never touched.
- And [[id:33864a0f-5e13-4235-85a6-0bd9d2fe5252][33864a0f]]'s planned DONE.org datetree would be built by =org-archive-subtree= through =org-archive-location=, entirely outside this project's code.

*So a datetree node cannot declare itself, because nothing we control creates it.* We could walk up after our own call and stamp three properties, but every node created by any other path — an =org-capture= datetree template, a human's =M-x=, the DONE.org archive target that is already planned — would arrive without them. A declaration that is absent on arrival is worse than an inference: it fails *open*, and silently.

*Which sharpens the slice's thesis rather than contradicting it.* Declared-versus-inferred is a rule about *our own* conventions — a slice, an epic, a story, a plan's coverage. Where the thing being identified is **another system's**, reading its shape is not inference-in-place-of-declaration; it is reading the contract its owner actually publishes. =--datetree-node-role='s title regexes are not a workaround for a missing property. They are the correct mechanism, because org owns both the creation and the titles, and org's titles are the stable public thing about them.

*The heading's own framing had this backwards.* It listed the datetree node as "declared in fact and inferred in code", alongside the category tier. The category tier really was that — *we* built it, so we could declare it, and [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] did. The datetree node never was.

*So all four classes are settled, three by change and one by refusing one:*

| class | detected by | outcome |
|-------+-------------+---------|
| epic | =--container-heading-p= | unchanged — emergent, and declaring it would be the mirrored error |
| category | was =(= level 1)= | *resolved* — now a =:CATEGORY:= value on the task ([[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]]) |
| slice | =--slice-p=, a =:KIND:= property | already declared, 2026-08-25 |
| datetree node | =--datetree-node-role=, title shapes | *won't change* — org creates it, so we cannot declare it |

*Nothing was built for this heading, and that is the outcome rather than a shortfall.* The one change it still proposed was measured to be less reliable than what it would have replaced.

*Context: §7 of the org-dev skill stopped quoting =~/.config/doom/config.el= on 2026-08-28.* It had reproduced the config verbatim, and the copy drifted twice — first in CLAUDE.md (which is why §7 was moved into the skill on 2026-08-14), then in the skill itself, gaining a keyword the config never had and losing two settings the config had gained. Neither drift was noticed, and neither could have been: a quoted config is the one kind of documentation that cannot be checked by reading it, since checking means opening the other file, which is the work the quote existed to save. The section now names each setting and what breaks without it.

*So the check is behavioural, not a text diff, and that distinction is the whole design.* Re-introducing a comparison between the skill's prose and the config would rebuild the failure mode inside a script. These two ask the running Emacs what is *true*:

| check | what it catches |
|-------+-----------------|
| =find-file-visit-truename= is =t= | the symlinked =~/org/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org= opening as two buffers on one file — silently, since Doom also sets =find-file-suppress-same-file-warnings= |
| =claude-code-ide-org-capture-file= resolves into this repo | a targetless =org_capture= landing in =~/org/notes.org= ([[id:bd482c92-a71a-4d7d-88df-47678ee94c79][bd482c92]]). Compared through =file-truename= on both sides, since the config names the *symlink* path deliberately |

*Both were proved to discriminate rather than merely observed to pass* — a check that has never been seen to fail proves nothing. Setting =find-file-visit-truename= to nil in the live Emacs produces =FAIL ... expected 't', got 'nil'= and exit 1; rebinding the capture file to =~/org/notes.org= produces =FAIL ... got '/Users/neil.best/org/notes.org'= and exit 1. Both restored, and the script returns to exit 0.

*One check deliberately not built, recorded so it is not proposed again as an oversight.* The =org-todo-keywords= sequence. It disagrees with TODO.org's own =#+TODO:= line today — the config says =WAIT= where the project uses =WAITING=, and has no =REVIEW= — and *nothing is broken*, because a buffer-local header wins and both org files carry one. A check there would fail on a latent inconsistency while everything works, and a check that fails while everything works is one people learn to ignore. It is documented in §7's known-gap paragraph instead, which is where a latent fact belongs.

*Also corrected in passing:* §7's title said "What is in the Doom config, and why", which stopped being true the moment it stopped containing it. Now "What the Doom config does for this project, and why".

=bin/check-org-dev-skill= is 20 checks, exit 0.

*Reported by the user 2026-08-28 as "the current slice is missing its statistics cookie at TODO.org:148".* It was not missing. It was at the *end* of the line, where they could not see it — they expected it immediately after the keyword, "that's our convention".

*The corpus agrees with them 13 to 1, and the one exception is ours.* Measured across TODO.org and DONE.org: 13 cookies sit immediately after the TODO keyword, one trailed — [[id:979e02b6-2a4c-4328-8b08-ffaec03bd02e][979e02b6]], the only slice whose cookie was written by [[id:28415ca8-a4ce-43a4-9af6-9ec0e7d5662a][28415ca8]]'s =--ensure-statistics-cookie-at-point= rather than typed by a human. Every hand-written cookie in the project's history leads. The inserter was the sole source of the deviation.

*It is not cosmetic, and the report itself is the demonstration.* A trailing cookie is the part a narrow agenda window or a folded outline truncates away — which defeats the one thing a cookie is for, that progress is readable *without* unfolding. The user looked at the line and concluded the cookie was absent. That is the failure mode, observed, not hypothesised.

*How it survived two days.* =claude-code-ide-org-test-ensure-cookie-inserts-only-when-absent= asserted that a cookie was *present*, that it was inside the headline text, and that tags stayed terminal — but never *where* it was. The test now asserts =(string-prefix-p "[/] " h)=, and it discriminates: reverting the inserter to the appending form fails exactly that test and nothing else, 433 of 434.

*The way this was got wrong is worth more than the bug.* [[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::803e362][803e362]], four hours earlier, wrote the *opposite* convention into =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= — "it goes at the end of the title, before any tags" — reasoning from =--ensure-statistics-cookie-at-point='s source, and dismissing the corpus's only other slice as a pre-inserter hand form not worth normalising. That is inferring a declared convention from the single mechanism that implements it, which is precisely the error [[id:979e02b6-2a4c-4328-8b08-ffaec03bd02e][979e02b6]] exists to close, committed inside the slice named after it. The corpus had the answer and was not asked.

*Shipped:* the inserter now prefixes rather than appends (=org-edit-headline= takes the headline text without keyword or tags and preserves both, so prefixing cannot disturb either); the test asserts position; =org-conventions.md= records the corrected convention with the measurement and with why the earlier version was wrong; and [[id:979e02b6-2a4c-4328-8b08-ffaec03bd02e][979e02b6]]'s own headline was normalised through =org-edit-headline=. =bin/test= 434/434, =bin/lint-org= 0 errors.

*Incidental, and already filed:* the capture for this heading was refused with =Buffer is read-only=, because =org_capture= does not bind =inhibit-read-only= — [[id:c8a97d9d-8b13-4b6a-a8b9-1a3f24b5e00b][c8a97d9d]], still open. Cleared and restored around the write.

Parked 2026-08-19, *not accepted* — recorded so the research need not be
redone, not because a case was made.

*Verified in this Emacs:* =:CATEGORY:= on a level-1 heading is reported
by a level-3 grandchild, so one property per top-level heading labels
its whole subtree. A =[/]= cookie on a parent moved =[1/3]= -> =[2/3]=
on a child's state change with no explicit update call, so cookies
self-maintain through the review pass.

*Verified absent from this repo:* =:CATEGORY:=, statistics cookies,
=:VISIBILITY:=, and tag groups — zero uses of each. The level-1
"category" convention is hand-built where org has its own.

*Org practice, from two sources not a consensus:* epic as subtree,
cross-cutting axes as tags — one practitioner tags literally
=:sprint2:= alongside =:release4_2:=. Org's manual treats the tree as
the single structure and everything cross-cutting as a tag or property
match. Sources: [[https://jeffbradberry.com/posts/2023/08/orgmode-epic-organization/][Bradberry, Epic Organization]] and
[[https://orgmode.org/manual/Matching-tags-and-properties.html][Matching tags and properties]].

*Candidate tier naming discussed:* level 1 epic, level 2 story, level 3
task, sprint as a cross-cutting tag. =bin/lint-org='s header would need
updating from "category, task, epic-child".

*Closing action discussed for a heading:* fold historical prose into a
drawer (drawers fold by default; no =:VISIBILITY:= needed) and leave a
short summary — problem, plan, outcome, how verified, what differed from
the plan, what was rejected and why, what it spawned. The last two are
the reused parts and the easiest to drop.

Note [[id:38b92521-bba4-4bb5-9cd9-465862471a72][38b92521]] closed the
related flattening question against, on the grounds that archive routing
depends on level-1 =:ARCHIVE:=. That cost is real but is a mapping to be
written, not a wall.

*Composing a story by reference rather than by moving.* Parked
2026-08-20, unreviewed, because it existed only in conversation and
would otherwise be lost. Same standing as the rest of this heading: not
accepted.

*The problem.* A story whose members sit in different categories cannot
be composed as a subtree — level 4 is forbidden, so composing means
*relocating* level-2 headings under a new container.

*Four mechanisms, and the axis that separates them is who declares
membership:*

| mechanism                            | declared at   | drifts? |
|--------------------------------------+---------------+---------|
| =[[id:]]= links in the container body | the container | yes     |
| a =:MEMBERS:= property on it          | the container | yes     |
| a tag on each member                  | *the member*  | no      |
| an id-valued property on each member  | *the member*  | no      |

The top two are the shape that already failed twice here: one edit point
nobody revisits, exactly like the plan file's /"Covers all five
children"/, true when written and false two days later.

*A tag, not a bespoke property* — and that reverses what was recommended
first. The argument for an id-valued =:SPRINT:= property was that a tag
is a string needing rewriting if the story is renamed. That is backwards
for org: stories are named by number or date and are not renamed, and a
tag buys agenda filtering, =org-tags-view=, inheritance and group tags
\(=:startgrouptag:=\) for free, where a property buys none of it without
code. Sources: [[https://jeffbradberry.com/posts/2023/08/orgmode-epic-organization/][Bradberry, Epic Organization]], who tags literally
=:sprint2:= beside =:release4_2:=, and [[https://orgmode.org/manual/Matching-tags-and-properties.html][Matching tags and properties]],
where the manual treats the tree as the single structure and everything
cross-cutting as a match.

*The concrete cost of the alternative, which is the strongest argument
here:* categories carry =:ARCHIVE:=, inherited by their subtree. Moving
a heading across a category boundary to compose a story therefore
changes where it lands when it closes. Composition by relocation
silently rewrites archive routing; a reference changes nothing. Note
this is a *different* claim from
[[id:38b92521-bba4-4bb5-9cd9-465862471a72][38b92521]]'s, which is about
removing categories altogether.

*The case that would test it*, and it is a good one because the odd
member is the important one: the capture cluster is
[[id:bd482c92-a71a-4d7d-88df-47678ee94c79][bd482c92]] in *Tooling* —
the root cause — with
[[id:97696fc2-f07b-4586-b280-de6a7d26fb87][97696fc2]],
[[id:7fa68d5c-b6c0-43df-85c6-764b1d56511f][7fa68d5c]] and
[[id:8ddd7fa8-e847-42e9-b82c-63bbe4c11b7b][8ddd7fa8]] in *Skill logic*.
Composing it by moving would relocate the root cause away from the
category it belongs to, purely to make the story expressible.

*New evidence 2026-08-21, from building the datetree* ([[id:e30d52d7-960b-44f3-ab92-93846c81a1bd][e30d52d7]], [[id:cd1e974e-e006-4974-b770-cdc1cf2e4ab2][cd1e974e]]). It cuts both ways, which is why this stays parked rather than promoted.

*Against, and worth stating first: depth-as-storage did not break.* =org_outline=, =claude-code-ide-org--container-heading-p= and the lint's =org-map-entries= all read level correctly. What broke was reading depth *textually* -- an =awk= parent-inference that returned each heading's own title rather than its parent, which put a wrong claim about this file's structure into conversation before =org_outline= corrected it. A tag is equally mis-readable by a bad grep. That lesson is "read through org", not "change what org stores".

*For, and stronger: level became ambiguous within a single file.* Level 4 is an error outside a =:DATE_TREE:= subtree and *is* the day node inside one, so =bin/lint-org= now carries a *context-sensitive* level rule -- the level number alone stopped being a sufficient predicate. Level 1 likewise now means two things, task category and datetree root; =* Review and planning= holds no tasks directly. This is the first *measured* instance of the overload this heading had only hypothesised.

*And the shipped fix is itself the argument.* Depth could not carry the distinction, so the lint gates on org-datetree's literal title patterns instead -- a property-shaped answer smuggled in as a string match. A =:DATETREE_ROLE:= property would be the honest form. Note where that lands on this heading's own membership table: =:DATE_TREE:= plus pattern-inference is declared *at the container*, which is the drifting shape, not at the member.

*Correction to the work item recorded above.* "=bin/lint-org='s header would need updating from 'category, task, epic-child'" already happened on 2026-08-21, for an unrelated reason -- it now reads "three levels ... outside a =:DATE_TREE:= subtree". So that header is no longer the untouched baseline this note assumed, and the change was made to accommodate a datetree rather than to adopt any tier scheme.

*Promotion trigger, since "parked, not accepted" deserves a condition rather than a mood:* move to TODO when a *second* independent overload of heading level appears. One instance is a special case; two is a pattern, and the second is the case this heading was parked for want of. Related and not duplicates: [[id:9651d4c8-6887-4b0a-91d9-562c3bc49a75][9651d4c8]] is the same membership-by-reference problem arriving from the plan-coverage side, and [[id:38b92521-bba4-4bb5-9cd9-465862471a72][38b92521]] is where the flattening half was closed against.

*The promotion trigger above has fired, same day.* Measured 2026-08-21 against =org-archive.el= and a scratch archive run, prompted by the user's observation that flattening the categories away would let archiving produce a chronological record.

*Archiving files by =CLOSED=, not by archive time.* =org-archive-subtree= sets its datetree date to =(or (org-entry-get nil "CLOSED" t) time)=. Verified: four headings archived in one batch at 15:12 landed under =2026-07-14=, =2026-08-03= (two) and =2026-08-20=. A backlog archived late still lands on its real completion dates. Note the ordering is *ascending*, and within a day node entries append in archive order -- so the record is forward-chronological, not reverse; newest-first is a rendering choice, not a storage one.

*Weeks are not reachable by configuration.* =datetree/= is hardwired -- "corresponds to 3 levels of headings" -- and calls =org-datetree-find-date-create=, whose signature is =(d &optional keep-restriction)= with no grouping parameter; the only datetree defcustom is =org-datetree-add-timestamp=. =org-datetree-find-create-hierarchy= does support week grouping, but nothing in the archive path reaches it. A coarser tree needs a custom archive function.

*Org already stores the category as a property.* Archived entries carry =:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY:=, alongside =:ARCHIVE_FILE:=, =:ARCHIVE_TODO:=, =:ARCHIVE_TIME:= and =:ARCHIVE_OLPATH:=. So flattening does not *lose* the category -- org demotes it to exactly the org-native property this heading argues for, and a property is queryable and column-viewable where a heading level is not. That weakens [[id:38b92521-bba4-4bb5-9cd9-465862471a72][38b92521]]'s reason for closing the flattening question against.

*And the second overload, which is the promotion evidence.* Archived entries land at *level 4* beneath year/month/day. In TODO.org level 4 means "day node"; in DONE.org it would mean "archived work item", and org's archive tree carries no =:DATE_TREE:= property at all, so [[id:e30d52d7-960b-44f3-ab92-93846c81a1bd][e30d52d7]]'s new lint rule rejects the whole thing. This instance is stronger than the first: *org itself* is overloading level, through its own built-in archive path, rather than a convention this project chose. Depth as the tier carrier is fighting the tool.

*Promoted MAYBE -> TODO on that basis*, by the condition recorded above, six hours after it was written. The story-by-reference composition the flattening enables is filed separately at [[id:8ca6541d-0fc7-45a2-a4d3-76e1608f658d][8ca6541d]] rather than folded in here.

*What this heading is actually for, stated by the user 2026-08-25.* The title says "adopt org-native mechanisms for the heading tiers", which is the *means*. The end is narrower and worth naming: *flatten away the top-level categories and capture them some other way.*

Everything already verified above serves that -- =:CATEGORY:= inherited by a level-3 grandchild, tag groups, both absent from this repo -- but it reads as a menu of org features rather than as one change with a purpose.

*The three tiers resolve into distinct things once flattening happens, and only then.*

| term | after flattening | today |
|-------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------|
| epic | a *label* -- tag or =:CATEGORY:= -- carried by headings, not a place they live | a level-1 heading, structural |
| story | a real parent heading, free to *cut across* epics because epics are no longer structural | cannot span categories without refiling |
| slice | a *sequenced selection*, composed by reference | no representation at all |

*A slice is the thing that needs composition by reference,* and this is the correction to [[id:8ca6541d-0fc7-45a2-a4d3-76e1608f658d][8ca6541d]]. A slice picks off open tasks *at either level* -- a whole story, or a single task inside one -- and *sequences them intentionally*. That is not a subtree and cannot be: its members already live somewhere, its ordering is the point, and the same task can appear in one slice and not the next. A checkbox list of id links is the natural shape for exactly that, and only that.

*Stories, by contrast, stop needing it.* 8ca6541d proposes by-reference composition *for stories*, and its reasoning is sound *given today's structure*: "a story whose members sit in different categories cannot be expressed without moving a heading across a category boundary". Flattening removes that constraint at the root. So 8ca6541d's premise is *conditional on this heading not happening* -- and if it does, 8ca6541d changes subject rather than becoming wrong.

*Which sequences the two.* This heading is upstream: decide flattening first, and 8ca6541d's scope follows from the answer. Doing 8ca6541d first would build by-reference composition for stories and then discover that stories no longer need it while slices do.

*And it settles the vocabulary,* which is currently loose -- "slice" appears five times in this file across three unrelated senses (a portion of work, a portion of data, and the next-session work queue). Under this model it has exactly one meaning, and it is the third: a sequenced selection of open work. The other two uses are casual and should give way.

*Note the fourth class 8ca6541d found is unaffected and still unresolved:* category, container/epic, datetree node and story are each detected by a different bespoke mechanism, none declared. Flattening removes one of those detectors -- heading level -- which makes the inconsistency smaller but does not answer how a story or a slice declares itself.

*=:EPIC:= rather than =:CATEGORY:=, proposed by the user 2026-08-25, and it is the better name for three reasons rather than one.*

*It names one thing.* =:CATEGORY:= is org-native and arrives with semantics that are not being asked for: it is displayed in the agenda's category column, it is inherited down a subtree, and it defaults from the filename or a =#+CATEGORY:= line. Every one of those is a behaviour to reason about before the property can be trusted to mean "which epic". =:EPIC:= means which epic and nothing else.

*It settles the collision recorded on [[id:2e660571-26df-41e4-bb64-b9d74a3d7efe][2e660571]], by choosing a sense.* Two things are called "epic" here: this heading's table uses it for the level-1 grouping ("a level-1 heading, structural"), while CLAUDE.md uses it for a heading that has *acquired keyworded children*. Naming the declared property =:EPIC:= gives the word to the grouping, and leaves the emergent one its existing code name -- *container*, as in =--container-heading-p=. That is not a coinage; it is the word the predicate already uses, and the two never need to share a name again.

*The split then falls exactly on this project's own axis.* The epic is *declared* -- a heading says which one it belongs to, at the member, where this heading's own membership table says a non-drifting declaration must live. The container is *derived* -- detected by scanning for keyworded children, never written down, and therefore unable to go stale. One property and one predicate, answering two questions that were only ever confused because they shared a word.

*What it gives up, and how to get it back if it turns out to matter.* =:CATEGORY:= buys org's native agenda integration for free -- the category column, =org-agenda-filter-by-category=. Whether that is worth anything here is precisely what [[id:82df2a6c-881d-4117-a752-5b3b04c9656d][82df2a6c]] exists to measure, and it is unstarted, so choosing =:CATEGORY:= now would be choosing before the evidence this heading says it needs.

*If the evidence lands in favour, the answer is not to switch -- it is to derive.* Declare =:EPIC:=, and have a normaliser write =:CATEGORY:= from it. That is the pattern already built twice on 2026-08-25: a slice's =:BLOCKER:= generated from its checklist, and a slice's member lines regenerated from their referents. A declaration plus a derived copy, with something that keeps them in step, is strictly better than one field asked to mean two things.

*The datetree was missing from every version of this analysis, noticed by the user 2026-08-26.* Neither the cost list here, nor [[id:82df2a6c-881d-4117-a752-5b3b04c9656d][82df2a6c]]'s evaluation, nor the 2026-08-26 conversation that measured the flat case considered =* Review and planning=. It is the one subtree that *cannot* flatten.

*It is an irreducible four-level tree*: the =:DATE_TREE:= anchor, then year, month, day. =org-datetree= writes that shape and this project reads it back by exact title. So "every task is level 1" cannot be literal -- there is one island of nesting, permanently.

*Which is less damaging than it first looks, and in one respect helps.* The relevant code is already written in *relative* depth rather than absolute: =claude-code-ide-org--datetree-node-role= computes =level - datetree-level= from the anchor, so it does not care what level the anchor sits at. Flattening the categories around it changes nothing there.

*And it dissolves a collision the conventions currently have to work around.* =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= records that "a real task sits beside the tree, at the same depth as the year node" -- =** TODO Open today's node= next to =** 2026= -- and that this is "the whole reason =--datetree-node-role= gates on org's literal title shapes rather than on depth". Under flattening those real tasks become level 1 and level 2 beneath the anchor holds *only* scaffolding. The depth test that was unsafe becomes safe. The title-shape gate should still be kept, since it is stricter and costs nothing, but the hazard it defends against would be gone.

*What genuinely needs rework is =bin/lint-org='s level-1 rule*, which today asserts that a level-1 heading is either a category or a mirror of one. Flattened, level 1 is where the tasks live and =* Review and planning= is the sole surviving container. That is a rule to rewrite, not a wall -- the same standing as the =:ARCHIVE:= routing objection recorded above from [[id:38b92521-bba4-4bb5-9cd9-465862471a72][38b92521]].

*Separately, the datetree's own ordering is now filed as [[id:0c3f1319-67c0-4b29-a8e7-5ffa12948aaf][0c3f1319]]*, since the user's recency-ordering vision applies to it too and it is wanted either way. Short version: reverse-alphanumeric sorting already gives newest-first because day titles are ISO-prefixed, so the work is a re-sort after creation rather than a comparator -- and the duplicate-day-node hazard that a descending tree exposes in raw =org-datetree-find-date-create= does not reach this project, because =--ensure-day-node= looks the node up by title first.

*Decided and planned [2026-08-26 Wed], after sitting parked since 2026-08-19.* [[file:~/.claude/plans/goofy-baking-wall.md][Plan]]

*Approved:* =:CATEGORY:= over =:EPIC:=, and flatten the level-1 tier. Category values are single capitalised words. The transition is two-step -- a mechanical migration carrying the nine existing names verbatim, then the taxonomy as separate work.

*What unblocked it, none of which was available when it was parked.* The =:EPIC:=-means-one-thing objection turns out to exist only as a clause in CLAUDE.md and never in this body, which records =:CATEGORY:= inheritance as a *verified benefit*. The clocktable cost was overstated in conversation and corrected: =:match "CATEGORY=\"X\""= reproduces per-category roll-ups on a flat file, so flattening rebuilds the report rather than destroying it, exactly as [[id:82df2a6c-881d-4117-a752-5b3b04c9656d][82df2a6c]] said. And [[id:38b92521-bba4-4bb5-9cd9-465862471a72][38b92521]]'s archive-routing objection *inverts* -- flattened there is one target instead of nine.

*The argument that actually decided it, and which nobody had made:* flattening converts a grouping *inferred from level position* into one *declared on the task*. That is [[id:979e02b6-2a4c-4328-8b08-ffaec03bd02e][979e02b6]]'s thesis, and CLAUDE.md already names this tier as the standing example of the inference error. The tiers question is not adjacent to that slice; it is its central case.

*Two things the planning surfaced that were not part of the question.*

First, =NEXT= itself. Flattening would have collapsed nine sibling groups into one, and the first instinct was to teach =--map-siblings= about =:CATEGORY:= so the old behaviour survived. The user asked the better question -- when have we ever called tier-2 tasks siblings? -- and the evidence says the old behaviour was never right: of roughly eight top-level auto-promotions, *three are now =MAYBE=*. A category is a filing drawer, not a project, so its sole survivor asserts nothing. This is [[id:42808717-2736-4bf4-872e-887f990203ca][42808717]] one tier up, and it is now its own heading landing first.

Second, =org_outline= and its consumers. Today the grouping *is* the tree, so flattening would render a wall of 121 unindented lines. Grouping its output by =:CATEGORY:= keeps the rendered shape byte-identical while changing only its source -- and that is what holds the documentation churn to four capture sites instead of rewriting CLAUDE.md's orientation section.

*The corpus survey, which the taxonomy step rests on.* Counting every descendant in both files, 273 headings: =Clock lifecycle & visibility= holds *138, or 51%*, while four categories hold twelve between them and have never had a single item archived. The user's own tell is the sharpest summary -- only two category names contain a conjunction, and both are the ones the survey independently flagged as compound.

*Step 2 classified 2026-08-28, on a scratch copy; the real files are untouched.* All 190 headings carrying =:CATEGORY:= were assigned a value from the proposed taxonomy. Mechanics: 188 lines changed (2 were already =Slices=), *zero non-=:CATEGORY:= lines touched*, heading / =:ID:= / =CLOCK:= counts identical in both files, and =bin/lint-org= on the scratch copies returns 0 errors and 68 warnings — the same figures as the live files.

*The compound label was three layers, as the plan claimed.* =Clock lifecycle & visibility= (76) split 30 =Review=, 24 =Clock=, 15 =Queue=, with 7 leaving the cluster entirely. Close enough to thirds that the split is doing real work rather than renaming a drawer.

*The finding the conjunction tell missed: =Skill logic= is exactly as compound.* Its 50 headings split *21 =Skill= / 21 =Tools=*, plus 4 =Slices=, 2 =Queue=, 1 =Clock=, 1 =Docs=. The user's heuristic — only two names contain a conjunction, and both are the compound ones — is sound in the direction it points but silent in the other: a label can hold two unrelated things without saying so in its name. =Skill logic= held the org-conventions work and the MCP-tool work under one word.

*=Docs= ends with one member, which is a result rather than a shortfall.* Both headings under =Documentation= turned out to be about slices (=7c4d6ef6= is the slice-proposal procedure, =28415ca8= the missing statistics cookie), and every CLAUDE.md / skill heading landed in =Skill= under the plan's own seam — "=Skill= is what an agent must follow, =Docs= is what a person reads". Only =d7849119= (README.md) survives. So =Docs= is currently a category with one occupant, exactly the vestige the plan wanted it to stop being. Two honest options: keep it as a declared growth area with one member, or fold the README into =Skill= and reintroduce =Docs= when a second heading earns it. *Not decided here* — it is the user's call.

*Concentration is reduced, not eliminated.* The largest label goes from 76/190 (40%) to =Tools= at 54/190 (28%). =Tools= absorbed 26 of =Tooling=, 21 of =Skill logic=, and 3 of =Bigger swings=; whether it wants a further split (MCP surface versus repo scripts and CI) is a question for a later pass, not this one.

*=Bigger swings= dissolved 3 =Skill= / 3 =Tools= and =Observability= scattered across six values*, both as expected — neither named a subject.

*Not yet applied.* The diff, the mapping and a per-heading review table are in the session scratchpad pending the user's read.

*What has to land in the apply commit, beyond the 188 property values.* The step-1 consumer table has no step-2 equivalent, so this is it — swept 2026-08-28 by grepping the nine old values across the repo.

- *The datetree anchor carries no =:CATEGORY:= at all.* =* Review and planning= holds only =:DATE_TREE: t=, so it was never among the 190 and the day nodes beneath it inherit nothing — their category falls back to the file name, which is the exact defect [[id:82df2a6c-881d-4117-a752-5b3b04c9656d][82df2a6c]] measured across the whole corpus. Stamp it =Meta=. This is the one place where step 2 *adds* a property rather than rewriting one.
- *Nothing in the code or the test suites breaks*, verified rather than assumed. =config-test.el= and =bin/queue-append-test= reference =Tooling= and =Review and planning=, but every one is a *heading title* in a self-contained fixture, and step 2 rewrites property values only. =CLAUDE.md='s single =Tooling= mention is historical narrative about a retired trigger and reads correctly as past tense.
- *=.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= needs an old-to-new mapping.* It deliberately preserves the nine old names and their body prose as the input to this step; once the values change, that section becomes a glossary of names nothing uses, and should say what each became.
- *Plans under =plans/= are archive and stay untouched.*

*A step-1 consumer the plan's table missed, found by the same sweep and fixed 2026-08-28.* =.claude/skills/org/SKILL.md= documented per-category =:ARCHIVE:= mirroring and asserted "this is what *this* project does; =claude-code-ide-org='s DONE.org mirrors TODO.org's categories rather than collecting one flat pile" — false since 2026-08-27, when routing collapsed to a single file-level target because there were no level-1 categories left to hang a property on. The generic org guidance around it is still correct and was kept; only the claim about current practice was rewritten. Worth noting *why* it was missed: the table enumerated consumers of =org_outline= and of =org_capture=, and this heading is a consumer of neither — it consumes the *file's shape*, which is a wider blast radius than the tool surface.

*Taxonomy revised 2026-08-28 after the user read the first cut. Ten values, not nine.*

*=Review= is renamed =Apply=, and the reason is not a preference.* The user read =Review= as naming the daily ceremony rather than the review-buffer-and-apply subsystem — and they are the person who will read the agenda prefix column every day, which is the measurement that decides it, exactly as it did on [[id:98c302e0-ab1b-40bf-92d0-d2f2e16ac05d][98c302e0]]. Underneath that sits a harder objection nobody had raised: *=REVIEW= is also a TODO keyword.* An agenda line would read =Review  REVIEW  Some task=, and the user's stated reason for capitalising category values was stylistic distinctiveness *against keywords*. =Review= was the single value that defeated its own naming rule.

=apply= is also the project's own word by a wide margin — 475 uses across the two org files, 10 in CLAUDE.md, 6 in the rules, against 83 for "review buffer". And =Queue -> Apply -> Clock= reads as three stages of one pipeline, where =Review= was always the odd member: a buffer's name rather than a stage. [[id:2d100d0d-2d04-43b9-af1e-f4d6b52bbada][2d100d0d]] then sits unambiguously where it already was, since a missing cross-item check *at apply time* is what it is.

*Four misfilings folded in*, all found by publishing the low-confidence calls rather than by re-reading the table: =8707de36= and =c10bfb15= (the next-session prompt is a convention, not slice machinery) and =2758f3a0= and =a7f4b40c= move to =Skill=; =4c0044bf= moves to =Docs=, a changelog being human prose. Note =a7f4b40c= was misfiled by looking at where the *code* lives rather than what the heading is about — "a derived fact stored is one that can go stale" is this slice's thesis verbatim.

*=Tools= splits into =Tools= and =Repo=, 26 and 26.* One test separates them and anyone can apply it: *=Tools= is what Claude calls; =Repo= is what a developer runs.* =Tools= keeps the =org_*= MCP surface and its behaviour — capture, outline, query, amend, prefix resolution, id resolution, tool advertising. =Repo= takes the scaffolding that keeps the repository honest and runnable: =bin/lint-org=, =bin/test=, =check-org-dev-skill=, the footnote hook, the statusline, packaging, the Doom and shell environment, git configuration. The seam fell out almost exactly even without being forced toward it, which is the evidence that it was a seam rather than a cut.

*The distribution is now flat, which was the point.* Skill 34, Apply 33, Clock 26, Tools 26, Repo 26, Queue 23, Meta 10, Slices 9, Docs 2, Upstream 1 — the top six between 12% and 18%, against a single label holding 40% before. Re-verified end to end after the revision: 190 rewritten, 0 unmapped, 188 lines changed, *zero non-=:CATEGORY:= lines touched*, heading and CLOCK counts identical, =bin/lint-org= unchanged at 0 errors / 68 warnings.

*Still not applied*, and the pre-apply items in the paragraph above are unchanged.

*=Repo= becomes =Dev= (the user, 2026-08-28), and the reason is the one this project keeps rediscovering: the word already existed.* =org-dev= is the skill covering "the mechanics of getting a change to this repo's own Elisp (or its Doom wiring) actually live, and proving it" — which describes these 26 headings almost exactly, and =bin/check-org-dev-skill= is one of them, so the category contains the heading about the skill that names it. Neither a tag nor a keyword collides.

It also repairs the stretch recorded against =Repo= above rather than leaving it as an accepted cost. The two or three members that are about the *machine* rather than the repository — persisting the capture file in the Doom config, =emacs= being a shell function that fakes a passing batch check — are development *environment*, which =Repo= could not hold and =Dev= holds without argument.

One property worth stating so it is not mistaken for sloppiness: =Dev= names an audience where the other values name subjects, so read literally it could swallow the file. It does not, because the contrast it lives in is =Tools= versus =Dev=, and that contrast was always about audience — what Claude calls, versus what a developer runs. The axis is consistent; it is the sibling that supplies the bound.

*Final distribution*, re-verified after the rename: Skill 34, Apply 33, Clock 26, Dev 26, Tools 26, Queue 23, Meta 10, Slices 9, Docs 2, Upstream 1. 190 rewritten, 0 unmapped, 188 lines changed, zero non-=:CATEGORY:= lines touched, heading / =:ID:= / =CLOCK:= counts identical in both files, =bin/lint-org= unchanged at 0 errors / 68 warnings.

*Step 2 applied 2026-08-28* ([[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::8209925][8209925]]). 188 values rewritten across both files, plus one insertion — =* Review and planning= now carries =:CATEGORY: Meta= on the anchor itself. That was the one place step 2 *added* a property rather than rewriting one, and it was necessary rather than tidy: org-datetree's day nodes have no drawer of their own, so without it every meta-work interval would file under the file name. Verified through org rather than by reading the file — the day node reports =Meta=.

*Verification, all after the fact rather than predicted:* no non-=:CATEGORY:= line changed in either file, heading / =:ID:= / =CLOCK:= counts identical, =bin/lint-org= 0 errors and the same 68 warnings as before, =bin/test= 434/434, =bin/check-org-dev-skill= clean. Live distribution: Skill 34, Apply 33, Clock 26, Dev 26, Tools 26, Queue 23, Meta 11 (10 tasks and the anchor), Slices 9, Docs 2, Upstream 1.

*=.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= carries the glossary the flattening owed it* — the ten values with what belongs in each, the =Tools=/=Dev= test, why =Review= was rejected, and where all nine old labels went. The verbatim prose from the dissolved category bodies stays below it as history rather than being replaced by the mapping.

*Left open on purpose, neither of them blocking.* =Docs= has two members and only one of them live, so it remains a declared growth area rather than a populated category — the alternative, folding the README into =Skill=, was considered and rejected by the user. And =Tools= at 26 may eventually want its own split between the tool surface and tool *policy*; there is no seam visible at this size, so it is not being guessed at.
:END:

See the =:PLAN:= drawer for details. Its 70 paragraphs interleave planning and execution across several phases — decide, plan, survey, classify, revise the taxonomy, apply — so no single line is the seam. Wrapped whole under [[id:35d25265-df52-45c0-8226-dfa24c3ed5bb][35d25265]]'s retroactive exception rather than cut at a fabricated one.

*Hit 2026-08-26 while adding [[id:806ff394-3ede-4d67-82aa-9c44fe1cf86e][806ff394]] to [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]] minutes after capturing it.* A heading captured this session is *keywordless on disk* until a human applies its queued =todo= event, and two separate mechanisms quietly depend on that keyword.

*=refresh-slice= silently declines to regenerate the line.* It reported "0 member lines rewritten" and left the placeholder text standing -- so the slice carried =TODO placeholder= as if it were the referent's real title, which is exactly the "a slice line disagrees with its referent" failure the conventions exist to prevent, arriving through a door they do not describe. The blocker *was* updated in the same call, so the id resolved fine; only the rendering was skipped.

*And the regenerated =:BLOCKER:= is an immediate lint error*, correctly: =error: :BLOCKER: names keyword-less heading ... org-depend blocks only on an unfinished TODO, so this is a silent no-op=. CLAUDE.md already documents that a fresh capture makes a blocker inert; what is new is that *refreshing a slice manufactures one automatically*, so the error appears without anyone writing a =:BLOCKER:= by hand.

*Neither symptom is wrong, and that is the point.* Both mechanisms are reporting the truth: on disk, that heading has no keyword. The defect is that the *workflow* -- capture, add to slice, refresh -- passes through a state where the file is briefly inconsistent and the lint fails, with nothing saying so in advance.

*Candidate answers, none chosen.*
- *Order the workflow*: capture, apply, then add to the slice. Costs a round-trip through a human and is easy to forget, which is the same shape of problem as the ceremony stamp.
- *Have =refresh-slice= consult the queue* for a pending =todo= on an unresolved member, and render that keyword with some marker for "not yet applied". Honest, and it teaches a rendering function about the queue, which nothing else in that layer knows about.
- *Have it refuse loudly* rather than skip silently -- the cheapest, and it converts an invisible stale line into a message. Probably the floor regardless of what else is done.

*The transient lint error resolved by itself* when the queue was applied a few minutes later, which is the expected behaviour and worth stating so nobody "fixes" it by deleting the blocker entry.

*Shipped [2026-08-27 Thu], taking the third candidate above -- "have it refuse loudly rather than skip silently ... probably the floor regardless of what else is done."* Both other candidates are left open on purpose: ordering the workflow costs a human round-trip, and teaching a rendering function about the queue is a layering decision this does not need to make.

*Two surfaces, not one.* The body above found =refresh-slice=; the same root has a second face that only showed up by being hit. =org_amend= on a queued capture answered =Error: no org heading found with :ID: "..."= -- true, and useless: it reads as a typo when =org_capture= returned that id seconds earlier. =org_set_todo= and =org_clock_in= have tolerated that state since the silent-drop regression; amend never did.

*Both now name the condition and the remedy.*
- Amend: ="..." is a capture queued this session and not yet applied, so it has no body to amend. Apply the queue, then amend.=
- Refresh: =1 member left unrendered because it is keywordless on disk -- a queued capture or todo event, not yet applied: bbb22222=. Named rather than counted, because "1 skipped" sends a reader hunting through a 27-member list.

*Counted rather than repaired, deliberately.* The honest rendering of a heading whose keyword has not landed is not something =refresh-slice= can invent, and inventing one would manufacture exactly the "slice line disagrees with its referent" state the conventions forbid. Reporting is the whole fix.

*Where the guard goes is the interesting part, and I got it wrong first.* The obvious place is around =--at-id=, which is where the failure appears to happen. It is unreachable: =org_amend= resolves the id *early*, to choose write-through versus queue, and returns the generic error before =--at-id= is ever called. =--id-find='s own docstring says so in as many words -- "=claude-code-ide-org-amend= does its own =org-id-find= *before* reaching =--at-id=" -- recorded there in 2026-08-18 after fourteen call sites were missed the same way. I read that docstring earlier in this session and still put the guard in the wrong place; the test is what caught it.

*Hit live twice on 2026-08-27*: once refreshing a slice, and once amending [[id:6c48d5a6-1c78-4ce5-ac97-5e1091bdb25c][6c48d5a6]] -- a heading being filed *because* work had gone unfiled. The queue was busy with the user's own unsaved edits, which is exactly the condition that makes a capture defer.

*Verified*: 434/434, and each surface fails a named test when its guard is removed. The narrowness is asserted too -- a genuinely unknown id still reports plainly, with no mention of a pending capture, because =bin/hooks/queue-append= drops any reply beginning =Error:= and that drop is what stands between a typo and an unexplainable queue entry.

*=DOING= was relaxed 2026-08-25* from "the agent is executing this right now" to "started and owed a return" -- *in the mail*. The looser sense is durable and plural, and it immediately collides with a trigger built for the stricter one.

*=--trigger-auto-clock-in= assumes entering DOING means starting now.* Verified in batch rather than read off the docstring, which is itself wrong about this ([[id:6a21e08b-4880-4d2b-9b0f-12c35558fe08][6a21e08b]]): =(org-todo "DOING")= on a fresh leaf returns =org-clocking-p= t immediately, with =claude-code-ide-org-auto-clock-in-on-doing= at its live value of =t=.

*So recording that something was started earlier now credits time to the present.* Two transitions are waiting on exactly this and were deliberately *not* queued: [[id:961f15b6-d782-40b8-8ceb-ba086d188a3b][961f15b6]], whose design was written up 2026-08-24, and [[id:e1284bdb-0a18-402a-81cb-1ac8d09fb8a2][e1284bdb]], whose normaliser shipped the same day. Both are =DOING= under the new sense and neither is being worked now.

*Worse than one stray interval, because apply lands events in sequence.* Two retroactive DOINGs applied together would clock in on the first, then clock in on the second -- which closes the first, leaving a stray sub-minute interval on it -- and finish with a clock left running on the second. That is the known resume-the-wrong-heading edge case arriving by a different route, but self-inflicted and predictable rather than incidental.

*The distinction the trigger needs is between two acts that currently look identical*: beginning work, and recording that work began. Only the first should clock. Candidates, none chosen -- a queue event that carries "retroactive" and suppresses the trigger on apply; splitting the transition from the clock entirely so =org_clock_in= is the only thing that ever opens one; or narrowing =--trigger-auto-clock-in= to genuinely interactive keystrokes, which is what its docstring already claims it is for.

*Note the second candidate is close to what the queue architecture already believes.* =org_set_todo= and =org_clock_in= are separate calls precisely so that state and clock are decided separately; the trigger reintroduces the coupling at apply time, on the one path that is not going through those calls.

|-------+-------------------------------------+---------------------------------|
| A     | bare =(org-todo "DOING")=           | =clocking=t=                    |
| B     | one =state= -> DOING through apply  | keyword set, =clocking=nil=     |
| C     | two retroactive DOINGs in sequence  | *0* CLOCK lines, nothing running |

*So candidate 2 is already the architecture.* "Splitting the transition from the clock entirely so =org_clock_in= is the only thing that ever opens one" describes the queue as it already stands: =org_set_todo= opens no clock, and apply opens none on its behalf. Candidate 1 (a queue event carrying "retroactive") is moot, since apply suppresses unconditionally rather than selectively. Candidate 3 (narrow to interactive keystrokes) is *de facto* true -- after the cutover a hand-edit is the only path left that reaches the trigger at all.

*The cost was real, which is the part worth keeping.* Two transitions were held unqueued for days on this warning ([[id:961f15b6-d782-40b8-8ceb-ba086d188a3b][961f15b6]], [[id:e1284bdb-0a18-402a-81cb-1ac8d09fb8a2][e1284bdb]]). Both have since reached DONE without ever getting the DOING they were owed, so the record of when they were started is simply gone. A false warning cost more than the defect it warned about.

*What survives, and it is narrower.* A hand =C-c C-t= to DOING in Emacs does clock in at once. There a human is present and knows which of the two acts they are performing, which is exactly the distinction no mechanism can draw. Left standing rather than fixed.

*What the review was actually deciding.* The operational defect was falsified outright -- the predicted cascade does not happen, because =--review-apply-item= binds the guard for the whole item -- so the only open question was whether the *design* question this heading also framed ("the distinction the trigger needs is between two acts that currently look identical") survived its own defect. It does not need to: the queue already draws that distinction, since =org_set_todo= and =org_clock_in= are separate calls and apply opens no clock on a state event's behalf. The surviving hand-edit case is a human at a keyboard who knows which act they are performing, which is the one case no mechanism can improve on.

*Recorded here rather than left implicit*, because a =REVIEW= that closes silently loses the fact that a judgement was made at all -- which is the same failure the nomination rule guards against one level up.

CLOSED: [2026-08-26 Wed 20:11]
:PROPERTIES:

:END:

*Found and fixed [2026-08-26 Wed]*, in the response that provoked it. Asked to show a slice's checklist as it would read after an apply pass, the reply displayed eleven member lines in a code block -- and the hook demanded a footnote for *twelve* ids, each restating a keyword and title already visible three lines above it inside the block.

*The signal was that the convention made the response worse.* Footnotes exist to keep prose scannable while every reference stays recoverable. A rendered checklist is *already* id, keyword and title in one line; footnoting it duplicates the block wholesale. When a rule's output is redundant with what it is applied to, the rule is over-applying rather than the writer being lazy.

*It got sharper the same hour.* [[id:8183fc7c-905e-40c8-81cb-10c56158c6ce][8183fc7c]] had just made =[blocked]= name its ids, so pasting a whole-file =org_outline= would now open footnote debt for *44 ids across 17 headings* -- a feature shipped an hour earlier generating work for a check shipped six hours earlier.

*The fix is one condition in the =awk= that already splits the body at =---=*: lines inside a fenced block (=```= or =~~~=) are dropped before the scan. A fence is a *transcript* -- tool output, a file excerpt -- not a citation, and a transcript is already in its own context.

*Inline code is deliberately still scanned*, and that narrowness is the part worth pinning. A backticked id in a sentence *is* a citation and is the normal way one gets written; exempting it would gut the check. Both directions are now tests: dropping the fence skip fails the two fence cases, and extending the exemption to inline code fails the inline case. 21/21.

*An unclosed fence swallows the rest of the body*, which is the safe direction -- it under-reports rather than demanding footnotes for something the reader is already looking at.

*Third amendment to this hook in one day*, after the all-digit id defect ([[id:28415ca8-a4ce-43a4-9af6-9ec0e7d5662a][28415ca8]] is a different heading; the digit fix was =60f311b=). All three were found the same way: by the hook firing, in front of the user, on a case it was wrong about.



**** DONE org_outline is blind to a slice: scoped to one, it returns a single line :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-26 Wed 19:40]
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Tools
:ID:       8183fc7c-905e-40c8-81cb-10c56158c6ce
:CREATED:  [2026-08-25 Tue 19:34]
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:16
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Tools
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "TODO"       from              [2026-08-25 Tue 20:38] \\
  captured keywordless, setting initial state
CLOCK: [2026-08-26 Wed 19:35]--[2026-08-26 Wed 19:40] =>  0:05
- State "DOING"      from "TODO"       [2026-08-26 Wed 19:35] \\
  prerequisite for the flattening migration
- [2026-08-26 Wed 19:35]--[2026-08-26 Wed 19:40] name blocker ids; expand slice members when scoped
- State "DONE"       from "DOING"      [2026-08-26 Wed 19:40] \\
  one line becomes twelve; blocker ids named
:END:

*Observed 2026-08-25*, asked by the user as "does =org_outline= need an enhancement to represent slices in a helpful way, or does that deserve a new tool?" Scoping it to the 24-member slice returns exactly one line:

: DOING [17/24] Harden the review pass: ...  {c44c2119-...}  [blocked]

*A wrong answer, not a missing feature*, which is what decides the tool-versus-enhancement question. =org_outline= is advertised as the way to see structure without reading the file; a slice *is* structure, merely declared rather than positional. Returning one line for two dozen members is the tool failing at its stated job.

*Three reasons it belongs inside =org_outline= rather than beside it:*

- *It already resolves a declared, non-positional relation.* =--outline-blocked-marker= reads =:BLOCKER:= ids and prints =[blocked]=. Expanding =:KIND: slice= membership is the same class of work in the same function, not a new capability.
- *A separate tool would never be called.* The defining property of a slice is that it is invisible in the tree, so nothing prompts anyone to go looking for it. Putting the answer behind a tool you must already know to ask for reproduces the failure it fixes. Compare the tag-detector episode on [[id:8ca6541d-0fc7-45a2-a4d3-76e1608f658d][8ca6541d]]: a check whose absence is invisible is the wrong check.
- *The machinery exists.* =--slice-members= already returns =(ID . MARK)= per member and =--slice-referent-index= already resolves referents, both built for =refresh-slice=. No new traversal, no new parsing.

*One design constraint, and it is not optional: expand only when =scope= names the slice.* In a whole-file outline every member would appear twice -- once where it lives, once under the slice -- and the statistics cookie already reports the size there. The scoped call is the only one that is currently wrong, so it is the only one to change.

*And members must not render as children.* A slice may name one task inside another story, so indenting members under the slice would assert a containment that does not exist. Some marker that reads as *reference* -- and ideally the referent's own location -- is what the line needs.

*This is the third instance of one root, which is the more interesting fact.* Column view over the slice renders a single row for the same reason (measured on [[id:82df2a6c-881d-4117-a752-5b3b04c9656d][82df2a6c]]); =--container-heading-p= does not recognise a slice as a container ([[id:95c27fca-136c-46f6-b454-fe94261e0e5d][95c27fca]]); and now the outline. Every lens that walks the *tree* is blind to a grouping declared by *reference*. Worth asking on [[id:2e660571-26df-41e4-bb64-b9d74a3d7efe][2e660571]] whether these want one answer rather than three, before building the third bespoke fix.

*Better framing proposed by the user 2026-08-26*: rather than teaching =org_outline= about slices specifically, expand the *general* schema for every heading to carry its blocker *ids* instead of a bare =[blocked]= flag. A slice's =:BLOCKER:= already names its members, so slice membership would fall out of a change that is not about slices at all.

*The cost objection does not survive measurement.* Across both files: 17 headings carry a =:BLOCKER:= -- 13 with one id, two with two, one with three, and the slice with 24 -- for 44 ids in total. At the project's 8-character prefixes that is roughly 440 characters added to a 20,264-character whole-corpus outline, *+2.2%*. The outline is currently about 65x smaller than the files it indexes; this does not meaningfully change that.

*What it buys beyond slices, which is the strongest part of the idea.* =[blocked]= today says *something* unfinished blocks this and makes the reader go and find out what. Naming the ids makes every dependency traversable in the index itself, for all 17 blocked headings. It also makes =[blocked?]= actionable: today it says a dependency exists and cannot be resolved, without saying *which* one, which is precisely the information needed to fix it.

*Two limits, and they are why this does not simply replace this heading.*

*First: dropped members would still be invisible.* The conventions deliberately exclude a cookie-deleted member from the blocker set -- blocking on a deferred member would hold the slice open forever for work it explicitly decided not to do. So =b7b46a26= and =637ee73d=, both =CANCELLED=, are in this slice's checkbox list and *not* in its =:BLOCKER:=. A blocker-derived view therefore shows live members and silently omits the record of having considered and dropped something, which is the one thing the conventions say a bare list must not lose.

*Second, and sharper: it does not fix the scoped call, which is what this heading was filed for.* =org_outline= with =scope= naming the slice returns that subtree alone -- one line. Adding 24 ids to it yields 24 opaque tokens and no titles, because the referenced headings are not in the output to cross-reference against. The proposal works *beautifully* in a whole-file outline, where every referenced heading is already a line elsewhere, and not at all in the case that motivated this.

*So they are complementary rather than alternatives*, and the general one is worth doing on its own merits regardless of what happens here. If both land, the whole-file view becomes complete and the scoped view resolves referents; either alone leaves one of the two readings weak.

*The framing is worth carrying to [[id:2e660571-26df-41e4-bb64-b9d74a3d7efe][2e660571]] as well.* Three lenses have now been found blind to the same thing -- column view, =--container-heading-p=, and this -- and the shared cause is that a *declared* relation is invisible to anything that walks the tree. "Make the declaration visible in the general schema" is a better statement of the fix than three bespoke repairs, and it is the user's phrasing rather than a generalisation invented after the fact.

*Shipped [2026-08-26 Wed]*, both halves, because the body's own analysis showed they are complementary rather than alternatives -- and it was right: the general change fixes the whole-file reading and does nothing for the scoped one, which is the case this heading was filed for.

*The general half, the user's proposal.* =[blocked]= now names the offending ids: =[blocked: 4f6a6bb1 a0813ae3 c954f650 ...]=. Only the *offending* ones -- unfinished for =[blocked]=, unresolvable for =[blocked?]= -- never the whole declaration, since a satisfied blocker is not news and this slice would otherwise print all eleven members forever. =[blocked?]= gains the most: it used to say a dependency could not be resolved without saying *which*, which is precisely the information needed to fix it.

*The measured cost held.* The body predicted +2.2%; nothing contradicted it in practice.

*The scoped half.* Scoping to [[id:979e02b6-2a4c-4328-8b08-ffaec03bd02e][979e02b6]] returned one line and now returns twelve. Members render as *references* -- a =->= marker plus the referent's own file -- never as indented children, because a slice may name one task inside another story and indentation would assert a containment that does not exist.

*Every member is listed, including dropped ones, and that is why this is not simply the blocker list.* Verified against [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]]: 29 member lines, of which exactly the two the body named -- =b7b46a26= and =637ee73d= -- render as =(dropped)=. Both are =CANCELLED= and deliberately absent from the =:BLOCKER:=, so a blocker-derived view would have lost the record of having considered and dropped them. The conventions say a list must not lose that.

*Expansion is scoped-only.* In a whole-file outline every member already has a line where it lives and the cookie reports the size, so expanding there would print each member twice.

*Three functions, no new traversal*, exactly as the body predicted: =--slice-members= and =--slice-referent-index= already existed for =refresh-slice=. The index is built only when the scoped heading is actually a slice -- it scans every tracked file, so paying for it on ordinary scoped calls would tax the common case for the rare one.

*A constant fell out.* =--id-prefix-length= and =--id-prefix= now exist so the outline and anything else that abbreviates an id cannot drift about what "8 characters" means. That is small but it is [[id:478d6ec9-1b99-4c6c-88e9-c793ad4b2f22][478d6ec9]]'s territory, which is the next prerequisite.

*Verified*: 426/426, and four separate breaks each fail a named test -- expansion returning nothing, dropped members rendered as ordinary, the offender filter naming all ids instead, and expansion leaking into the file-wide path. That last one had to be broken in the *additive* direction to prove anything, since the file-wide path simply never calls the expander; breaking it the other way only re-proved the scoped tests.

*What this does not do*, from the body's own list: it does not answer whether the three blind lenses want one general mechanism rather than three bespoke fixes. That question stands and belongs to [[id:2e660571-26df-41e4-bb64-b9d74a3d7efe][2e660571]].
