*Step 0 of [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]]'s plan, and it stands on its own* -- flattening only *exposed* this; the fix improves today's file unchanged.

*What exposed it.* Flattening would collapse nine sibling groups into one, since =--map-siblings= walks with =org-get-next-sibling=, which at top level stops only at the file's boundary. The first instinct was to teach it about =:CATEGORY:= so the old behaviour survived. The user asked the better question -- *when have we ever referred to tier-2 tasks as siblings?* -- and the evidence says the old behaviour was never right.

*Three findings, none of them from reasoning.*

1. *The nominations were bad.* Of roughly eight promotions that fired at level 2, **three are now =MAYBE=**: worktree partitioning, "commit a newly-captured TODO", and "evaluate choice of shell". The trigger declared something next and a human later parked it.
2. *A category is a drawer, not a project.* GTD's invariant is that a live *project* has a next action. "The sole remaining TODO in Tooling" asserts nothing.
3. *The test fixture has no category tier at all.* =--with-heading= builds a level-1 task with level-2 children, so every trigger test already modelled the flat world -- and "top-level sibling" in [[id:42808717-2736-4bf4-872e-887f990203ca][42808717]]'s verification meant *task*, never *category*. The suite encoded semantics production never had.

*This is 42808717 one tier up.* That heading taught the trigger to refuse a *container*, because promoting one "declares a project to be an action, inverting the one thing =NEXT= means". It fixed the case where the promoted heading was the wrong kind of thing; this fixes the case where the *sibling group* is.

*What shipped.* =NEXT= is meaningful only inside a container. =--trigger-demote-conflicting-next= survives, scoped by "has a parent" -- which *is* the container test, since a keyworded heading with a parent makes that parent one by definition. Autonomous promotion is gone, replaced by =--nomination-candidates-context=: a =SessionStart= line naming every container whose live members include no =NEXT=. It names a sole candidate and merely *counts* several, because that is the case no rule can decide.

*163 lines of code retired, and the shape of them is the point.*

| retired                            | lines | existed only because…                     |
|------------------------------------+-------+-------------------------------------------|
| =--trigger-auto-promote-sole-todo= |    92 | it wrote to the file on its own           |
| =--review-settle-auto-promote=     |    41 | suppression skipped it mid-batch          |
| =--auto-promote-active=            |    16 | re-entrancy; 1201 mutations in nine seconds |
| =--review-applying=                |    14 | apply lands one event at a time           |

Both flags had *exactly one reader* -- the trigger itself. Each guard was added after an incident caused by the previous one's absence, and the plan was about to add a fifth. Advisory promotion leaves nothing to guard. Net across the change: **-172 lines**, including 235 lines of tests for retired code.

*Three redundant guards were written into the new function on the first pass, and all three were found the same way* -- by breaking them and watching the suite stay green. A =--grouping-heading-p= check (implied by having members), a =states= non-nil check (implied by =(assoc "TODO" states)=), and a finished-member filter (implied by selecting =TODO= downstream). All removed. The remaining conditions each fail a named test when broken.

*A defect the tests could not have caught.* The advisory returned *propertized* strings -- =#("..." 0 11 (...))= -- because =org-get-heading= carries text properties and =format= propagates them. Batch Emacs runs no font-lock, so every fixture came back clean. Found by reading the live output, which is the same trap =--outline-line='s own comment documents.

*Measured on the real corpus:* five containers with no next action, each a genuine un-nominated project. Not a wall, and unlike a =DOING=-container line each one disappears the moment somebody nominates -- so it is not the "permanent, never-changing line" that =session-context='s container filter exists to prevent.

*Verified*: 423/423; the demote guard, the quiet-when-NEXT-exists rule, the count-rather-than-pick rule and the slice path each fail a named test when broken. The live Emacs needed =remove-hook= as well as a reload -- the retired trigger was still registered on =org-trigger-hook= after =load-file=, which is exactly the org-dev skill's deletion warning.

- State "DONE"       from "DOING"      [2026-08-26 Wed 15:50] \\
  refresher inserts, lint asserts, 979e02b6 healed
:END:

*Found by the user 2026-08-26*, noticing that [[id:979e02b6-2a4c-4328-8b08-ffaec03bd02e][979e02b6]] carried no statistics cookie, and asking that this become part of slice creation and validation discipline.

*Three mechanisms could have caught it and all three declined, silently.*

1. =org-update-statistics-cookies= *updates* a cookie and never *inserts* one. Measured: a slice headline with =[/]= became =[1/2]=; the same headline without one came back byte-identical. So the refresher called it on every apply and found nothing to recompute, forever.
2. =bin/lint-org='s cookie rule asks =--container-heading-p=, which is "has descendants carrying a TODO keyword". A slice's members are links, so it has none, so the rule never fired. This is the same predicate-versus-meaning split as [[id:95c27fca-136c-46f6-b454-fe94261e0e5d][95c27fca]], surfacing at a third caller.
3. The convention is written down in =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= and depended on a human typing =[/]= at creation. [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]] has =[27/27]= only because somebody remembered; 979e02b6 ran a whole slice's life without one.

*Fixed as self-healing rather than as a creation rule, which is the point.* =claude-code-ide-org--ensure-statistics-cookie-at-point= appends =[/]= when the headline lacks one, and =claude-code-ide-org-refresh-slice= calls it immediately before =org-update-statistics-cookies=. Establishing the slot and filling it are separate acts, and only the second one org will do. Verified live on the real file: the refresher produced =[3/11]= on 979e02b6, counting three =[X]= of eleven members, correctly excluding the =[-]= for the =REVIEW= member and the two =orgit-rev:= prompt-revision lines that carry no checkbox.

*A discipline that depends on remembering is the thing this repo keeps discovering it cannot have* — so the lint clause is the backstop, not the mechanism. It is a *second* clause rather than a widened predicate: the container rule counts children and this one counts checkbox members, and they genuinely differ in what they count. Folding them into =--grouping-heading-p= would have made one rule assert two different things.

*The cookie regexp is now a shared =defconst=*, so the inserter and both lint clauses cannot disagree about what counts as a cookie already being present. It was previously an inline literal in one place.

*Placement detail worth not rediscovering*: the cookie is appended before the tags, since org requires tags to end the headline. =org-edit-headline= handles that; writing it at the end of the raw line would have produced =... :code: [/]=, which org does not read as a cookie.



**** DONE A container carries clocks it earned before it was one :code:research:
CLOSED: [2026-08-26 Wed 14:47]
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Clock
:ID:       3964c575-50bc-4cc9-abeb-bdd1c0162c2c
:CREATED:  [2026-08-25 Tue 12:59]
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:17
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Clock
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "TODO"       from              [2026-08-25 Tue 12:59] \\
  proposed by the user; blast radius measured first
- State "NEXT"       from "TODO"       [2026-08-26 Wed 13:03] \\
  member 4; last of the mechanical four
CLOCK: [2026-08-26 Wed 14:45]--[2026-08-26 Wed 14:47] =>  0:02
- State "DOING"      from "NEXT"       [2026-08-26 Wed 14:45] \\
  starting now; A+B-C+D approved
- [2026-08-26 Wed 14:45]--[2026-08-26 Wed 14:47] record the convention; measure the roll-up question
- State "DONE"       from "DOING"      [2026-08-26 Wed 14:47] \\
  declined with reasoning; research delivered its decision
:END:

*The user's proposal 2026-08-25:* slices carry no clock, so stories should not either. The argument is the one =--container-heading-p='s docstring already makes -- org rolls a subtree's time up natively, so clocking the parent adds a second quantity *inside* the one that already existed, where it can no longer be told apart. Measured there on [[id:b5f7c5c7-7ad6-4c68-9cce-3479db1f1644][b5f7c5c7]]: parent row 14:52, ten children summing 13:44, the 1:08 difference indistinguishable from a rounding artefact.

*Measured before proposing a rule, and the number is not zero.* Eight container headings across both files carry CLOCK lines of their own: 5, 13, 9, 4, 1, 1, 3 and 9 lines. So this is not a convention that merely needs writing down; it describes a state the corpus is not in.

*And the reason is structural rather than a discipline failure, which is the finding.* A container is *emergent* -- it becomes one by acquiring keyworded children. So a heading is clocked honestly as a leaf, grows children later, and becomes a container that retroactively "should never have been clocked". Nothing was done wrong at the time and no rule applied at the time.

*Demonstrated the same day it was proposed.* [[id:2758f3a0-3c47-405e-9662-a7669dcb60cc][2758f3a0]] carried one CLOCK line as a leaf. Refiling [[id:5787bfc6-3ba5-4d94-802c-f8a7879de68d][5787bfc6]] under it made it a container an hour later, and its clock line did not move. Auto-clock-in already exempts containers, so *nothing new* would have been added -- the line is purely historical.

*So the rule has to be about new clocks, not existing ones*, and the candidates differ in what they do to that history:
- *Prevent only*: refuse a clock-in on a container, leave existing lines. Cheapest, and matches what =--trigger-auto-clock-in= already does. Leaves the 45 lines misattributed.
- *Migrate on promotion*: when a heading becomes a container, move its clock lines to a child. Correct-looking and dangerous -- the time was spent on the parent's own work, and there may be no child it belongs to.
- *Accept and mark*: keep the lines, and have any roll-up report the parent's own time separately from the children's sum, which is the only reading that is not a lie.

*The third is the one the docstring's measurement actually argues for*, since its complaint is that the two quantities become indistinguishable -- not that the parent's time is fake.

*Not the same question as whether a container has a body.* That inference was drawn alongside this one and does not follow; see the note on [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]], which has no clock and a substantial body.

*Decided [2026-08-26 Wed]: declined, and the corpus is not in debt.* The user's approved shape was A + B − C + D — record the convention, fix the report, do not migrate, keep mitosis.

*What settled it was a decision already on record, which this heading did not consult.* =--container-heading-p='s docstring has said all along that the exemption is "deliberately narrow: it suppresses only the *automatic* clock, never a deliberate =org-clock-in= on a parent, since a parent's own coordination and planning time is real and a blanket \"only clock leaves\" rule would discard it." So the proposal here was not filling a gap; it was *reversing* a decision, and the reversal was never argued against that sentence.

*Re-measured 2026-08-26 rather than trusting the 2026-08-25 count.* Nine groupings, not eight, carrying 46 own CLOCK lines: 13, 9, 9, 5, 4, 3, 1, 1, 1. Four are still active and five are finished. They are *not growing on their own* — auto-clock-in exempts groupings, and as of [[id:95c27fca-136c-46f6-b454-fe94261e0e5d][95c27fca]] that now includes slices. The only path that adds one is a deliberate =C-c C-x C-i= on a parent, which is precisely the act the docstring blesses.

*So the 46 lines are history, not debt.* Each was clocked honestly while the heading was still a leaf; it became a grouping later by acquiring children or by a refile. This heading's own best finding says so — "nothing was done wrong at the time and no rule applied at the time" — and that argument, followed through, refutes the proposal it was written to support.

*C was rejected outright: relocating a true record to make a report readable is backwards.* It would also require inventing a child on nine headings purely to hold history, which fabricates structure rather than recording it.

*B was measured before being filed, and it is a real feature rather than a documentation line* — [[id:64d34a64-d336-40a8-a8e8-da8133d0da06][64d34a64]]. The parent's own time is not merely mixed into the roll-up; it is *printed nowhere*, recoverable only by subtracting every child, and =:maxlevel= truncation breaks that subtraction silently. That also explains the 1:08 on [[id:b5f7c5c7-7ad6-4c68-9cce-3479db1f1644][b5f7c5c7]] which this body called "indistinguishable from a rounding artefact": it was the parent's own two lines, indistinguishable only because the table declines to name them.

*D survives and gets stronger by getting narrower.* CLAUDE.md justified mitosis ([[id:a0813ae3-0c6d-43de-bae1-fb4414cdb519][a0813ae3]]) partly on this heading — "3964c575 wants containers to carry none and cannot enforce it" — an argument that conceded its own unenforceability in the same sentence. Declining A removes that strand entirely. Mitosis now rests only on the claim that carries weight: the =:ID:=, =:LOGBOOK:= and clock stay with the task that earned them.

*And note C and D are opposites, not variants of one idea* — the distinction that made the combination coherent. C *moves* a parent's records onto an invented child. D moves nothing: the original leaf stays itself, keeping its id, clock and logbook, while a new empty parent appears above it. Ruling out C does not weaken D; D is what makes C permanently unnecessary for every future division.

*Coverage divides with no overlap and no gap*: A and B handle the nine existing groupings — legitimised, then made legible — and D handles every future one, by never needing to move a record at all.

*Written down in three places*: CLAUDE.md's clock rules now state that a grouping may be clocked deliberately and that the existing lines are history; CLAUDE.md's mitosis bullet is re-pointed off the retired claim; and =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= now distinguishes a *story* (may be clocked deliberately) from a *slice* (may not, being a sequencing declaration rather than a place work happens).

=footnote-check= dropped all-digit 8-character tokens *before* the =:ID:= lookup, on the reasoning that "a bare number or date is not an id". True of a date, false of an id: *5 of 267* tracked ids are all digits, so 1.9% of the corpus was unenforceable.

**** DONE A slice gets clocked and auto-promoted, because its members are links not children :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-26 Wed 13:03]
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Clock
:ID:       95c27fca-136c-46f6-b454-fe94261e0e5d
:CREATED:  [2026-08-25 Tue 11:10]
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:17
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Clock

  measured against the first real slice
CLOCK: [2026-08-26 Wed 13:01]--[2026-08-26 Wed 13:03] =>  0:02
- State "DOING"      from "NEXT"       [2026-08-26 Wed 13:01] \\
  starting now on the shared-predicate fix
- State "NEXT"       from "TODO"       [2026-08-26 Wed 13:01] \\
  next slice member; --slice-p already exists
- [2026-08-26 Wed 13:01]--[2026-08-26 Wed 13:03] teach the two triggers about a slice
- State "DONE"       from "DOING"      [2026-08-26 Wed 13:03] \\
  grouping predicate; both triggers exempt a slice
:END:

*Measured 2026-08-25 against the first slice* ([[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]]), not reasoned about: =(:container-p nil :auto-clock-in t :would-clock t)=. Setting =DOING= on a slice by hand opens a clock on the slice itself.

*The cause is structural and will not go away on its own.* =claude-code-ide-org--container-heading-p= asks whether a heading has a descendant carrying a TODO keyword, and exempts containers from =--trigger-auto-clock-in= on the argument that org already rolls a subtree's time up to its parent. A slice's members are =[[id:...]]= links in a checkbox list, not descendants, so the predicate says =nil= and the exemption does not apply -- while the *reason* for the exemption applies with full force, since every referent carries its own clock. The predicate tests the mechanism, and the argument is about the meaning.

*Same shape, second consequence:* =--trigger-auto-promote-sole-todo= also refuses containers, and also will not recognise a slice. A sole =TODO= slice under =* Slices= would be promoted to =NEXT= as though it were an action. This is the reintroduction of [[id:42808717-2736-4bf4-872e-887f990203ca][42808717]] by a route its fix did not cover, which [[id:8ca6541d-0fc7-45a2-a4d3-76e1608f658d][8ca6541d]] predicted in the abstract before any slice existed.

*Not urgent today only because the first slice's =DOING= was written as text*, which fires no trigger. The moment a slice's state goes through the queue and apply -- which uses =org-todo= -- both hooks run.

*The open question is what the predicate should ask.* "Has keyworded descendants" and "is a grouping whose time lives elsewhere" have been the same thing until now. A slice is the first case where they part, so either =--container-heading-p= learns about by-reference members, or the two callers stop sharing one predicate.

*Shipped [2026-08-26 Wed] as [[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::2c4796e][2c4796e]].* =claude-code-ide-org--grouping-heading-p= is the new predicate; both triggers now ask it.

*The open question above is answered by taking neither of its two options.* It offered "=--container-heading-p= learns about by-reference members" or "the two callers stop sharing one predicate". The third way is that they keep sharing a predicate, and it is a *new* one: the union. Widening =--container-heading-p= would have made it contradict its own docstring -- it says it is derived from structure "rather than declared in a property someone has to remember to maintain" -- and =--slice-p= says the mirror image about itself. Both are right, so neither could absorb the other. A docstring made to lie about what it reads is precisely what [[id:6a21e08b-4880-4d2b-9b0f-12c35558fe08][6a21e08b]] closed three hours earlier on this same branch.

*=grouping= is not a coinage, which is why it is the name.* Searched before naming: CLAUDE.md already carries "a grouping is either *emergent* or *declared*", and =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= already says "a slice is a declared grouping". The word existed and the code simply had no function wearing it.

*Reproduced first, and the fix verified not to overreach.* Four probes, batch, on scratch files:

| behaviour             | before      | after            |
|-----------------------+-------------+------------------|
| DOING on a slice      | =clocking=t= | =clocking=nil=   |
| DOING on a plain leaf | =clocking=t= | =clocking=t= (unchanged) |
| sole TODO slice       | -> NEXT     | stays TODO       |
| sole TODO leaf        | -> NEXT     | -> NEXT (unchanged) |

The two "unchanged" rows are the point. An exemption is only right if it is also *narrow*, and a predicate returning t for everything would have passed the first and third rows alone.

*Four of five call sites moved, and the fifth is the interesting one.* The two triggers are this heading's tracked defect. =--queue-heading-divergence='s abandoned-DOING report and =--review-suggest-heading='s filter are the same defect seen from two other surfaces -- a DOING slice is no more abandoned, and no more suggestible as an unassigned span's owner, than a container is -- so they moved too, and =--container-id-p= was renamed =--grouping-id-p= because its question moved with it. =bin/lint-org='s statistics-cookie rule *keeps* the narrow predicate: there the subject really is TODO children, and a slice carries a checkbox cookie over links instead. Different convention, not this one's business.

*Three tests, each proved discriminating* by reverting the union to its container half: all three fail, all three pass either side. 425/425.

*The payoff is immediate and this heading is where it lands.* [[id:979e02b6-2a4c-4328-8b08-ffaec03bd02e][979e02b6]] -- the slice this is a member of -- has been held at TODO precisely because setting it DOING would have clocked the slice itself. That constraint is now lifted, and the slice is set DOING in the same pass: at least one member is in the mail, which is what the word means one level up.

*[[id:42808717-2736-4bf4-872e-887f990203ca][42808717]] is now closed by route as well as by case*, and [[id:8ca6541d-0fc7-45a2-a4d3-76e1608f658d][8ca6541d]]'s abstract prediction -- made before any slice existed -- is confirmed and discharged.

- State "DONE"       from "DOING"      [2026-08-26 Wed 12:56] \\
  three sites fixed, regression test proved discriminating
:END:

*The docstring of =claude-code-ide-org--trigger-auto-clock-in= reads* "Off by default since 2026-08-18 (TODO.org :ID: 226ed53b, step 2(c)): the first thing tested is =claude-code-ide-org-auto-clock-in-on-doing=, which is nil, so in normal operation this function does nothing at all."

*It is not nil.* The =defcustom= two hundred lines above is =t=, and the running Emacs returns =t=. So the docstring describes a configuration that was reversed and never re-described, and it does so in the most misleading possible way -- by telling the reader the function is inert.

*Caught 2026-08-25 while reasoning about whether a slice would be clocked*, and it very nearly landed the wrong answer in a heading body: the docstring was read first and taken at face value, and only a direct evaluation of the variable contradicted it. CLAUDE.md, for once, was the accurate source.

*Worth a sweep rather than a one-line fix.* A docstring that contradicts its own =defcustom= is invisible to every test and to =bin/lint-org=, so if this one drifted, the reversal that produced it may have left others. Check what else references =226ed53b='s step 2(c).

*Shipped [2026-08-26 Wed] as [[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::24df841][24df841]].* Three docstrings re-described, two test comments corrected, one regression test added.

*The sweep found exactly three falsified sites, and the test that bounded it was tense rather than topic.* =--trigger-auto-clock-in= (the tracked one), =--blocker-clock-running-p='s "Rarely reached since 2026-08-18" paragraph, and the =defcustom='s own tail -- "What a human gives up", "Set this to t to have the old behaviour back", and the list of what turns quiet. Every *other* =226ed53b= reference in both files is a historical claim about the double-counting repair, which was never reverted, so all of them stay. That distinction is what kept this from becoming a rewrite of eleven sites.

*Verified against the running Emacs rather than read off the =defcustom=*: =(:live t :standard t)=. Both readings matter -- the docstring's "which is nil" was false of the default *and* of the live value, so no local customisation could have excused it.

*The blame is precise and worth keeping.* [[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::eca3a77][eca3a77]] re-enabled the variable on 2026-08-19 and updated the =defcustom='s opening line but not its readers. So the drift lasted a week, past a green suite and a clean =bin/lint-org=, in the most misleading available form: inertness asserted of a live function.

*Measured a consequence rather than reasoning about it, and it is easy to state backwards.* With the trigger on, =C-c C-t= to DOING opens a clock -- and =C-c C-t= to DONE on that same heading is then *refused* by =--blocker-clock-running-p=: the keyword stays DOING and =org-block-entry-blocking= names the heading. =org-clock-out-when-done= does not rescue it, because =org-blocker-hook= runs before any after-state-change hook. So the hand-edit path is close the clock, *then* set DONE. That now lives in the blocker's own docstring, where whoever is about to hit it will read it.

*The heading's real complaint is answered, not just its example.* It objected that a docstring contradicting its own =defcustom= "is invisible to every test and to =bin/lint-org=". =claude-code-ide-org-test-no-source-line-claims-the-trigger-is-off= is that test. It scans file *text*, not loaded docstrings, because half the drift was in =config-test.el= comments, which are not docstrings and would otherwise stay unguarded.

*Proved discriminating before being believed*: reintroducing the exact original phrasing fails it at =config.el:3250=, and it passes on either side of that. 422/422.

*Two things it found about itself, both kept in its docstring.* Its needles must be assembled with =concat=, because a literal needle written anywhere in the file is found by its own search -- caught on first run. And the needles are phrase-level, so the rule they actually enforce is narrower than it looks: *say when instead*. One of the historical rewordings made in this same commit -- "off by default for the day between 2026-08-18 and 2026-08-19" -- tripped it and had to be reworded again. That is the right rule anyway: the phrasing is what a reader takes as current, whatever clause follows it.

*Not covered, stated so nobody trusts it further than it goes.* It pins two phrasings that actually drifted, not the meaning; the same falsehood in new words passes. *Not filed as residue*, deliberately: a semantic prose-versus-code lint is not a thing anyone knows how to build, and the general form of "a declared thing the code infers some other way" is already this slice's whole subject.

*Left undone by choice*: this heading's prospective body was not wrapped into a =:PLAN:= drawer. Its DONE is queued, not applied, so the heading still reads NEXT on disk, and a finished-heading treatment ahead of the keyword would misreport it. Available to the next ceremony.

*Kept deliberately short, and the tension is worth naming.* CLAUDE.md asks a =DONE= heading for an outcome summary before archiving; the slice convention says a slice's body is one sentence, the checklist and the revision links, "and nothing else". For a slice those pull against each other, and the checklist wins: what shipped is twenty-five member headings each carrying its own debrief, and restating them here would be a second copy that can disagree with the first. What follows is only what is true of the *slice* rather than of its members.

*It grew by half while it ran*, from twenty members to twenty-seven, and every addition came from work found *while* doing the planned work rather than from the plan. Three arrived on the last morning. That is the shape the prompt kept warning about -- "the job is to finish the current slice, not to grow it" -- and the warning was right about the risk and wrong about the outcome: the additions were the parts that made the ceremony actually run.

*The slice mechanism grew up during its own first use.* It began as a checkbox list nothing maintained. It ends with a =:KIND:= declaration, a derived =:BLOCKER:=, a lint assertion, a regenerator, and -- as of [[id:a0abf97d-0f98-42df-9749-e1647b723596][a0abf97d]] -- an automatic refresh in apply's settle phase, so the staleness this slice was hand-repaired for five times on its final day cannot recur. Eight prompt revisions are linked below.

*What it was actually for.* The review pass is the one activity this project depends on and had never measured. It now records when each event was applied, repairs the drift it causes, prompts its own ceremony once a day, and clocks the human who runs it. Every one of those was invisible when the slice opened.

*No residue.* Everything named as unfinished during its life was filed as a heading before the heading naming it closed -- a rule this slice produced by breaking it once ([[id:aa1ba915-ee68-48df-afea-197ae60aac63][aa1ba915]]) and then writing it into CLAUDE.md.

*The story these three share, noticed 2026-08-24 while surveying what the session had captured.* They were filed separately, into three different categories, and each reads as a small independent defect. Together they are one thing: *the ceremony has four steps, two of them have a tool, and nothing composes them or reminds anyone.*

The sequence, from =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md=: *apply the queue, consolidate every drawer, then archive* -- plus re-separating headings, which applying always disturbs.

| step | state |
|--------------------------+-------------------------------------------|
| apply the queue | human-only by design, and permanently so |
| consolidate the drawers | [[id:7ae6562d-25c8-453e-b78b-920e036c5665][7ae6562d]] -- not built |
| re-separate the headings | [[id:e1284bdb-0a18-402a-81cb-1ac8d09fb8a2][e1284bdb]] -- built, must be re-run by hand |
| archive | manual |
| *remember to do any of it* | [[id:aa1ba915-ee68-48df-afea-197ae60aac63][aa1ba915]] -- not built |

*The shape of the problem is not "these are unbuilt".* It is that each one only helps if a human remembers it at the right moment, and the moment is the same moment for all of them. A normaliser that must be recalled separately from the pass that disturbs the file is a normaliser that will drift -- measured on [[id:7ae6562d-25c8-453e-b78b-920e036c5665][7ae6562d]] itself, where 13 of 25 drawers archived since consolidate-on-apply shipped are still out of order, and observed three times today with the separation normaliser, which had to be re-run after every apply.

*Why the ritual heading is not a child of this one, though it is the same subject.* [[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]] carries a repeater, and =bin/lint-org= refuses a repeater under a completable ancestor -- correctly, since such an ancestor could never reach =DONE=. So the ritual stays where it is and this heading covers only the *tooling that makes the ritual cheap*. That constraint is worth stating: it is why an obvious "everything about the ceremony" subtree is not the right shape.

*Done when* a human runs one command, answers the prompts apply asks, and the file comes out consolidated, separated and archived -- with the prompt to do so arriving on its own.

*This heading carried no TODO keyword until 2026-08-25*, and the user asked whether that was deliberate. It was not: there is no =:LOGBOOK:= on it at all, so no state was ever set. It was written directly as a parent in =4b115d8=, rather than captured and then given an initial state, which is how every other container heading here got one. Seven of eight carry a keyword; this was the only exception.

*The exception falls exactly on the emergent/declared axis*, which is why the question was worth asking rather than just fixing. The other seven all *acquired* their children -- emergent epics, detectable and never declared. This one was created to bundle three headings that already existed, filed under three different categories; its opening line says so. So the corpus accidentally encoded "emergent gets a keyword, declared does not", in a sample of one, with nothing written down and no mechanism enforcing it.

*Keywordless is not a defensible marker for a declared grouping, though, and the reason is mechanical.* A story composed by reference is a checkbox list blocked on its members ([[id:8ca6541d-0fc7-45a2-a4d3-76e1608f658d][8ca6541d]]), and =org-depend= blocks on an *unfinished TODO keyword*. A member with no keyword can never be unfinished, so a checkbox naming it is inert -- the same inertness CLAUDE.md already records for a =:BLOCKER:= written in the session that captured its target. Found while the user was drafting exactly such a list against this heading, which is the only reason it surfaced at all.

*Set to =TODO= rather than =DOING=, deliberately.* A transition to =DOING= obliges a clock, and a container's own clock measures nothing -- the work clocks on [[id:aa1ba915-ee68-48df-afea-197ae60aac63][aa1ba915]], which is the child actually in progress.

*The cost of the omission was narrower than assumed, and worth recording so it is not overstated later.* =org_outline= with =active_only= keeps a keywordless heading, since the filter drops only =DONE= and =CANCELLED= -- verified against this subtree. What it actually forfeits is narrower: it can never be nominated =NEXT=, never appears in a TODO agenda, and its =[0/3]= cookie can never reach =DONE=.

*Measured 2026-08-24, over both files.* =claude-code-ide-org-consolidate-on-apply= is =t= and works -- but it only fires on a heading that an apply pass *writes to*. A drawer disturbed by anything else keeps its disorder, and archiving ends the only thing that would have repaired it.

Counting drawers with two or more timestamped entries, and asking whether their entries ascend:

| file                     | drifted | of  |
|--------------------------+---------+-----|
| TODO.org                 |       9 |  62 |
| DONE.org                 |      43 |  60 |

*The split by =:ARCHIVE_TIME:= is what makes it a finding rather than a backlog.* Consolidation-on-apply landed 2026-08-13, so anything archived before then is expected to be disordered and is not evidence. Anything archived after is:

| archived            | drifted | of |
|---------------------+---------+----|
| before 2026-08-13   |       6 |  6 |
| on/after 2026-08-13 |      13 | 25 |
| no =:ARCHIVE_TIME:= |      24 | 29 |

*Over half of everything archived since the feature shipped is out of order*, which is not what "consolidate on apply" implies to a reader of the defcustom.

*Cause, and it is structural rather than a bug.* Org inserts =CLOCK:= lines newest-first; =--append-to-drawer= appends annotations before =:END:=; the ascending order [[id:af7d3687-6d1e-4480-a9e2-df772785713f][af7d3687]] chose is neither. So a drawer drifts the moment anything writes to it outside apply -- a hand =C-c C-x C-i=, or =--trigger-auto-clock-in= firing on a hand-set =DOING=. TODO.org stays healthy only because apply keeps returning to those headings. Once a heading is archived, nothing ever touches it again and the drift is permanent.

*Why this rather than reversing the sort.* Newest-first would end the drift by construction, by agreeing with org's insert convention. It was considered and rejected: it reverses the narrative order that was the whole of af7d3687's request, it breaks that heading's byte-identical fixed-point test against =clock-template.org=, and it systematically flips every tie whose adjacency the stable sort was chosen to preserve. The drift is a *coverage* problem, not an *ordering* one, and the coverage fix keeps what was asked for.

*Shape:* a command that consolidates every drawer in the tracked files, reusing =--consolidate-logbook-text= unchanged -- already idempotent and pinned lossless. Worth running before an archive pass in particular, since that is the last moment a heading is ever touched; that makes it a natural companion to [[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]] rather than a separate ritual.

*Shipped 2026-08-25* ([[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::8cd7c57][8cd7c57]]) as =claude-code-ide-org-consolidate-all-drawers=, built to the shape this heading specified: walk the tracked files, reuse =--consolidate-logbook-text= unchanged, and inherit that function's idempotence and lossless guarantee rather than restating either.

*Modelled on =recompute-accumulated-clock-lines=*, its nearest sibling, which already had the whole pattern -- walk =--tracked-files=, find every =:LOGBOOK:=, transform the text, dry-run support, save only touched files, close a buffer this command opened and leave alone one the user already had. Copying that shape rather than inventing one is why this is 60 lines.

*Validated on the real corpus, not only fixtures.* 38 of 221 drawers reordered on a copy of both files, *0* on the immediate re-run -- so it converges in one pass. CLOCK-line counts unchanged at 318 and 239. A sorted-content diff of both files against their pre-run state came back *empty*, which is the strong form of the losslessness claim: not "the counts match" but "no line differs, only its position".

*Note the 38 is not this heading's 52.* The measurement above counted drawers with two or more timestamped entries (122 of them); the command counts every drawer whose text changes (221 scanned). Apply passes have also consolidated some in the intervening day. The two numbers are not comparable and should not be read as a discrepancy.

*Two things the tests found that the design did not, both recorded in the code.*

*The Lisp default is reversed and that is sharp.* =(consolidate-all-drawers)= with no argument *writes*; only a bare =M-x= defaults to a dry run. This matches =recompute-accumulated-clock-lines= exactly, so the two do not disagree with each other -- but a caller reading the interactive behaviour will guess wrong. A test now pins the asymmetry so it cannot be quietly changed.

*The dry-run guard on the write protects exactly one thing, and it took three attempts to find out what.* The save gate blocks the disk write regardless, and a buffer the command opened is killed with =set-buffer-modified-p= nil -- so checking the *file* after a dry run passes even with the guard removed. Two successive assertions failed to discriminate: first a presence check (both orderings contain both timestamps), then an order check on the file (the save gate masks it). The guard's real job is leaving the *human's already-open buffer* unmodified, which is now what the test asserts.

*And one break that is genuinely unobservable, reported rather than hidden.* Removing =(not dry-run)= from the save gate changes nothing detectable: on a dry run the buffer was never modified, so =save-buffer= is a no-op, and the dry-run report omits the file count entirely. It is belt-and-braces, redundant with the write guard. Two of three attempted breaks are caught; this one cannot be, and the honest claim is that the code is robust to it rather than that a test covers it.

*Live reload done and confirmed*: =fboundp= t, =commandp= t, arity =(0 . 1)= in the running Emacs, so this is usable now and not merely on disk.

*Where it belongs, per this heading: before an archive pass.* Archiving is the last moment a heading is ever touched, so a drawer disordered when it moves stays that way permanently -- which is how DONE.org reached 43 of 60. Wiring it into the ceremony alongside the heading-separation normaliser is [[id:edd47f32-e6c9-4ab3-8e8a-46a37ea29605][edd47f32]]'s remaining work, not this heading's.

*Shipped 2026-08-24* (=b6619e5=). Every heading's content now ends with exactly two blank lines before the next heading.

*Two, and the number is not a matter of taste.* Org hides the blank line between a collapsed subtree and the following headline unless there are at least =org-cycle-separator-lines= of them, and that variable is 2 by default here. Two in the file buys exactly one visible line of air when folded; one buys none. So the convention is calibrated to a setting that already existed, and needed no configuration change.

*Before every heading, not only before same-level ones,* and the corpus settled that. The gap you see before =** B= in a folded outline is the trailing space of A's *last child*, not of A's own body: 7 of 88 level-2 headings are preceded by a deeper heading, and 31 of 134 gaps sit between different levels. A same-level rule would skip exactly those.

*=claude-code-ide-org-normalize-heading-separation= touches only the run of blank lines immediately preceding a heading*, found by walking back from the next heading and stopping at the first non-blank line. That is the safety property: the edit cannot reach text. Verified on the first run -- 224 insertions, 37 deletions, and *zero* changed lines carrying any character. The last heading in each file is left alone; there is nothing after it to separate from.

*Re-run twice since,* because applying queued events inserts lines without the convention. That is the shape of the thing: it is a normaliser, not a one-time migration, and it belongs in the same sitting as the consolidation sweep [[id:7ae6562d-25c8-453e-b78b-920e036c5665][7ae6562d]] rather than being remembered separately.

*Not yet written down as a convention anywhere* -- neither =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= nor CLAUDE.md mentions it, so nothing tells a session to preserve it and no lint asserts it. That is this heading's remaining work.

*Written down 2026-08-25* ([[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::d542382][d542382]]), in two places rather than one, split on the test CLAUDE.md already uses: what is true of org generally goes in the portable skill, what is true of this repo goes in the path-scoped rule.

*It was not a gap -- it was a contradiction, which is the part this heading did not know.* =.claude/skills/org/SKILL.md= already carried a blank-line rule, and it said the opposite: two blank lines *"before a level-2 heading that has no TODO keyword"*, everywhere else one, with the explicit judgement that *"doubling it everywhere would just be noise"*. So a session following the skill would have actively undone the normaliser's work. The measurement recorded above is what falsifies it -- 31 of 134 gaps sit between headings of *different* levels, which is exactly the set a level-2 rule skips. The skill's rule is corrected in place, and carries the reason so it is not re-derived the other way later.

*The generic half went to the skill*: two lines, why two (=org-cycle-separator-lines= defaults to 2, so two in the file buy one visible line folded and one buys none), and why every level. None of that is specific to this repo.

*The project half went to =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md=*: the normaliser command, that the count is =claude-code-ide-org-heading-separator-lines= (default 2, and setting it below =org-cycle-separator-lines= makes the convention invisible where it was meant to be seen), the walk-back safety property, and that it belongs in the same sitting as the consolidation sweep rather than as its own ritual.

*Drift is now measured rather than asserted*, using the normaliser's own dry run rather than a hand-rolled count -- the two were written independently and agree exactly:

: TODO.org: 18 heading(s) re-separated, 150 already had 2 blank line(s).
: DONE.org: 0 heading(s) re-separated, 104 already had 2 blank line(s).

*The asymmetry is the mechanism showing itself*, and is the clearest evidence that this is a normaliser rather than a migration. DONE.org is written by archiving, which moves whole subtrees and carries their separation along; TODO.org is where applies and =org_amend= land, and both append without the trailing lines. Some of today's 18 were created by this very session's amendments.

*The normaliser was deliberately not run.* Three reasons, in order of weight: TODO.org is open in the user's live Emacs, and a batch write behind that buffer is the desync hazard [[id:53b0047d-c55c-486c-8eed-ba4994d97a1a][53b0047d]] describes; the file also holds the user's own in-flight edits; and the fix belongs in the ceremony, which is where the convention now says it goes.

*The lint assertion is not built, and that is why this is =REVIEW= rather than =DONE=.* This heading's remaining work was named as two things -- nothing telling a session to preserve the convention, and no lint asserting it -- and only the first is addressed. What the second would now cost is no longer a guess: 18 sites, all in one file, against a checker that already walks every heading. That is a small enough blast radius to decide cheaply, which was the point of measuring it before proposing a rule.

Asked 2026-08-24: can the daily ceremony ([[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]], now =<... 07:00 ++1d>=) be scheduled in the agentic CLI so a prompt arrives at the first opportunity each day and the agent performs it?

*Measured against the actual tool surface, not assumed.* Two schedulers exist and neither fits:

- =CronCreate= is *session-only* -- in-memory, nothing written to disk, gone when the session exits, recurring jobs auto-expire after 7 days, and jobs fire only while the REPL is idle. A standing daily ritual outlives any session, so this is the wrong shape by construction rather than by degree.
- The =schedule= skill creates *cloud* routines. A cloud agent cannot reach =localhost:45571=, and every MCP tool in this project goes through =emacsclient= to a local Emacs server. It could not perform a single step.

*And the first step of the ceremony cannot be delegated at all.* Apply is human-triggered by design: org's native state-change logging only completes inside a genuinely interactive command. So "performed by the agent" is unavailable for the pass as a whole no matter which scheduler is used. What is available is *prompting* plus the steps after apply -- consolidate and archive.

*The mechanism this repo already has is the right one, and it is the =SessionStart= hook.* =bin/hooks/session-start-recovery-check= already fires at session start, already injects =additionalContext= that the session relays to the user as a question, and is already *self-limiting to first thing each day* -- it reports only intervals opened before today, so it goes quiet once handled. That is precisely the requested behaviour: a prompt at the first opportunity each day, no nagging, and nothing at all on a day with no session.

It also already has the right manners for this: [[id:7771fc63-9374-4c8a-9e80-24ceec21977c][7771fc63]] established that the report *asks and never proposes*. A ceremony line should follow that -- state what is waiting (pending item count, headings ready to archive, drawers out of order) and let the human decide, rather than announcing an intention to act.

*The one design question to settle before building:* what counts as "already done today". Candidates -- a stamp file, on the model of the =block-open= sentinel; the existence of a day node for today; or the pending-queue count having dropped since the last pass. The stamp file is the cheapest and the only one that does not conflate "ceremony performed" with "work happened".

*Not to be confused with a nag.* The org repeater already makes the item show up in the agenda daily. This heading is only about the *agentic* prompt, for the case where the agenda is not what the user is looking at.

*Audited 2026-08-24, prompted by the user asking whether the report has ever actually asked them anything.* It has not, and that is correct behaviour rather than a fault.

*The mechanism works.* Verified today by running a synthetic stale interval through the real path in batch Emacs: =--session-start-hook-json= returns well-formed =hookSpecificOutput= / =additionalContext=, and the text does ask what time work stopped while explicitly forbidding the relaying session to propose one. So this is *not* [[id:c5b02503-1700-47fd-bf89-bd3296b24af2][c5b02503]] -- the report was never suppressed in relaying, it was never generated.

*Its single condition has never held.* The report fires only for an unclosed =CLOCK:= line whose open timestamp *predates today*. Scanning every commit that touched TODO.org: unclosed lines were routine between 2026-07-28 and 2026-08-17, and *every one of them was closed the same day it opened*. Not one survived overnight.

*Two things see to that.* =kill-emacs-hook= and =suspend-hook= both run =claude-code-ide-org--clock-out-if-clocking=, so a clean quit or a sleep closes an open clock -- which covers everything short of a crash or power loss. And since the 2026-08-11 cutover =org_clock_in= queues rather than opening a clock at all, so the only live clocks left come from a human clocking by hand or =--trigger-auto-clock-in= firing on a hand-set =DOING=. The feature is a net for an unclean death, not a routine check.

*A correction worth keeping, because the first answer was the opposite one.* The initial scan reported overnight-stale intervals throughout, up to and including today. It was wrong: the pattern matched =CLOCK: [date= without anchoring the end of the line, and a *closed* line begins identically -- =CLOCK: [start]--[end] => H:MM=. So every closed interval from a previous day counted as an open one. Anchoring with =$= reversed the finding completely. The same shape of mistake as [[id:f4b07fc0-187a-4975-aa3b-b9bd4b1c0799][f4b07fc0]]'s prose-quoting one, hours apart: a pattern that matches more than it names, over text where the extra matches look exactly like real hits.

*Comment corrected in* =bin/hooks/session-start-recovery-check=. It still described injecting "an educated guess ... based on =claude-code-ide-org-working-hours=", retired 2026-08-14 with [[id:7771fc63-9374-4c8a-9e80-24ceec21977c][7771fc63]], and still mentioned =:SESSIONS:=, retired 2026-08-11. The behaviour was right; only the comment lied. It now also says to *expect silence*, with the audit's reason -- so the next reader does not go looking for a bug in a feature that is working.

*Shipped 2026-08-25* ([[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::3c2a72e][3c2a72e]], with CLAUDE.md corrected in [[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::ae98b0e][ae98b0e]]). The prompt rides in the existing =SessionStart= payload, exactly where this heading's analysis said it should.

*The open design question is settled: a stamp file*, and the reasoning is the one this heading recorded rather than a fresh preference. The test that decides it is whether the signal means *the ceremony was performed* or merely *something happened*. A day node is created by any meta-work clock-in; the pending count falls whenever anyone applies a single item. Both conflate the two. An explicit stamp means only what it says.

*One file, not one per day.* =ceremony-last-run= in the queue directory, whose *mtime* carries the date -- an mtime is already a date, and a dated-filename scheme accumulates forever and needs a reaper. =M-x claude-code-ide-org-mark-ceremony-done= writes it, and a test backdates the stamp to prove yesterday's does not silence today.

*Deliberately not stamped from the apply path.* Apply is one step of the ceremony, not the whole of it; stamping there would go quiet on exactly the days when someone applies two items and archives nothing.

*It asks and never proposes*, on the footing =7771fc63= established. It names the three counts -- pending items, drifted drawers, unarchived finished headings -- and then instructs the relaying session to ask, saying outright that apply is the human's alone. A test asserts the "do not announce that you will" clause survives, because a report offering to run the pass would be *wrong* before it was unwelcome: the first step cannot be performed by an agent at all.

*One hook, one payload.* The stale-clock report and this are independent questions wanting the same moment, and =additionalContext= is a single string -- so they concatenate rather than justifying a second =SessionStart= hook and a second Emacs round-trip per session. Either half may be absent; the payload is ={}= only when both are.

*=--consolidate-drawers-1= was extracted from [[id:7ae6562d-25c8-453e-b78b-920e036c5665][7ae6562d]]'s command* so the ceremony can have the drifted-drawer *count* without parsing prose back out of a message string. The public command's contract is unchanged and its four tests pass untouched.

*One real bug, and the test found it rather than the reading.* When the ceremony has already run -- the *common* case, not an edge one -- =--ceremony-status= returns nil, and the formatter did =(+ nil nil nil)=. That would have errored the whole =SessionStart= payload and taken the stale-interval report down with it on every second session of the day. Guarded now, and the guard is asserted.

*Verified end to end in batch against a copy of the real corpus*, not only fixtures: =(:pending 0 :drifted 38 :archivable 62)=, well-formed JSON carrying the right manners, and ={}= immediately after marking done. Live-reloaded and confirmed in the running Emacs.

*Three of four attempted breaks are caught* -- the stamp ignoring the date, the report announcing it will act, and the ceremony half dropped from the payload. The fourth, removing the =(and status ...)= guard, is redundant with the =(or ... 0)= defaults and is *unobservable*; recorded as robustness rather than claimed as coverage.

*What this does not do.* It prompts; it does not perform. And nothing yet *calls* =mark-ceremony-done= automatically at the end of a pass -- the report asks the session to, which is a instruction to a model rather than a mechanism. Wiring it into the review command's exit is the honest completion, and belongs to [[id:edd47f32-e6c9-4ab3-8e8a-46a37ea29605][edd47f32]].

*Split out of [[id:e1284bdb-0a18-402a-81cb-1ac8d09fb8a2][e1284bdb]] 2026-08-25*, which was closed having done the other half: the convention is now written down in both the org skill (the generic part -- two lines, why two, why every level) and =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= (the normaliser, its defcustom, its safety property, where it sits in the ceremony). Nothing asserts it, so it holds only as long as =claude-code-ide-org-normalize-heading-separation= is actually run.

*The blast radius is already measured*, by the normaliser's own dry run rather than a hand count, so a decision here is cheap:

: TODO.org: 18 heading(s) re-separated, 150 already had 2 blank line(s).
: DONE.org:  0 heading(s) re-separated, 104 already had 2 blank line(s).

*The asymmetry is the argument for a check rather than against one.* DONE.org is written by archiving, which moves whole subtrees and carries their separation along; TODO.org is where applies and =org_amend= land, and both append without the trailing lines. So drift is *structural* -- it arrives every time the queue is applied, not occasionally through carelessness.

*Open, and the reason this is not obviously worth doing:* the fix is a normaliser that already exists and is idempotent, so a lint rule reporting 18 sites is 18 lines of noise telling a human to run one command. A =warn= that never becomes an =error=, or a pre-commit hook that simply *runs* the normaliser rather than complaining about it, may both be better than an assertion. Decide which before building.

*Do not reach for the count as a threshold.* The separator count is =claude-code-ide-org-heading-separator-lines= (default 2, matched to =org-cycle-separator-lines=); any check must read that variable rather than hard-coding 2, or it will disagree with the normaliser the moment either moves.

*Answered 2026-08-26 by rejecting the question* ([[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::395d233][395d233]]). No lint assertion was added. Apply now repairs the drift it causes, in its settle phase, beside the slice refresh.

*The three recorded options share a flaw this heading had already half-noticed.* An error, a warning that never escalates, and a pre-commit hook that runs the normaliser all *report* -- or at best prompt for -- a condition whose repair is one idempotent command. The body above says it plainly: "18 warnings telling a human to run one command is noise." The fourth option is to run the command.

*It became available only because the drift was measured rather than assumed.* "Structural -- it arrives every time the queue is applied, not occasionally through carelessness" is what makes this a defect apply can fix. A drift arriving from carelessness would need a check; a drift arriving from a known mechanism can be repaired at that mechanism.

*Ordered after [[id:a0abf97d-0f98-42df-9749-e1647b723596][a0abf97d]]'s refresh*, which rewrites member lines and can itself disturb separation. That ordering is asserted *against the call site* -- reading =--review-apply='s own definition -- and not by calling the two in sequence inside the test. The first version did the latter and passed with the call site reversed, which a break-it pass caught. A test that only proves its own ordering is worse than none, because it reads like coverage.

*It runs for real, not as a dry run*, and that is pinned by its own test: passing =DRY-RUN= would silently turn the repair back into the report this heading declined to build.

*The count is untouched, as instructed.* Nothing here hard-codes 2; the normaliser reads =claude-code-ide-org-heading-separator-lines= as it always did, so the two cannot disagree.

*Known gap, stated rather than left implicit.* =org_amend= causes the same drift and is not an apply, so prose added between passes stays unseparated until the next one. Acceptable while applies are frequent -- and the residue to revisit if that stops being true.

*What this means for the original ask:* =bin/lint-org= still does not assert the separation convention, and now should not. There is no drift for it to find that apply has not already repaired, and a rule reporting a self-healing condition is a rule that will only ever fire on the window between a stray edit and the next pass.

*Split out of [[id:aa1ba915-ee68-48df-afea-197ae60aac63][aa1ba915]] 2026-08-26, and it should have been filed when that heading closed rather than a day later.* The debrief named this gap in prose and said it "belongs to [[id:edd47f32-e6c9-4ab3-8e8a-46a37ea29605][edd47f32]]" -- but nothing was filed, so the only record sat in a finished heading's body, which readers are told to treat as history and which =org_wrap_plan= will eventually sweep into a drawer they are told to skip. The user caught it by asking whether the heading was really done.

*The mechanism exists; only the trigger is missing.* =claude-code-ide-org--ceremony-done-today-p= reads the stamp, =claude-code-ide-org-mark-ceremony-done= writes it, and both are tested. What invokes the writer is a *sentence in the injected prompt* asking the session to call it once the pass is finished.

*Why that is weaker than it looks.* Much of this project does run on standing instructions to a model, so an instruction is not disqualifying on its own. But the instruction lands in =additionalContext= at session start and has to survive until the pass is finished, which may be an hour and many turns later -- and its own parent heading has today's evidence that per-response discipline decays exactly that way ([[id:2758f3a0-3c47-405e-9662-a7669dcb60cc][2758f3a0]], 41 of 45). An instruction that must be remembered across a long turn is the shape that measurably fails here.

*And the failure is the one the heading explicitly disclaimed.* [[id:aa1ba915-ee68-48df-afea-197ae60aac63][aa1ba915]]'s body says "not to be confused with a nag". Unstamped, the prompt fires at *every* session start for the rest of the day. Observed 2026-08-26: it fired correctly at 08:2x, and would fire again on the next session, and the next, until someone remembers.

*The obvious hook is the review command's exit*, since apply is the one step that must be interactive and is therefore the one moment a human is provably present. Not chosen: apply is *one step* of the ceremony, and stamping there would go quiet on the days when someone applies two items and archives nothing -- which is the same objection that kept =mark-ceremony-done= out of the apply path in the first place. Whatever is chosen has to distinguish "a pass happened" from "the pass happened".

*Cheapest honest alternative, if the trigger question stays open:* have the prompt itself decay -- report at most once per day per *machine* by stamping when the report is *emitted* rather than when the ceremony completes. That is strictly worse as a record and strictly better as a nag guard, and it needs no new trigger at all.

*Shipped 2026-08-26* ([[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::d56e1ac][d56e1ac]]), and the answer is neither of the two options recorded above -- because [[id:961f15b6-d782-40b8-8ceb-ba086d188a3b][961f15b6]] landed in between and changed what was available.

*The trigger question dissolves once a pass leaves evidence.* The review command now opens a real clock on the attention heading, so "a pass ran today" is *derived from the act itself* rather than from anyone remembering to announce it. =--ceremony-reviewed-today-p= reads that clock, and either it or the stamp silences the prompt. Nothing has to be called at the end of a pass for the prompt to go quiet.

*Both recorded candidates are superseded rather than chosen between.* Stamping on the review command's exit was rejected here for going quiet on a day when someone applies two items and archives nothing -- and that objection still holds *for the record*, which is why the stamp keeps its old meaning. Making the prompt decay on emission was rejected as "strictly worse as a record" -- also still true, and now unnecessary, because the derived signal is about the pass rather than about the prompt.

*The two signals answer different questions and are deliberately kept apart.* The clock says a pass was *run*: derived, unforgettable, and reason enough not to ask again today. The stamp says the ceremony was *completed*: a claim spanning consolidate, normalise and archive -- steps nothing observes -- which only a human can make. Conflating them is what made the original design hard; keeping both costs one =or=.

*So the report now names the last completion, "never" included.* Silence after a pass must not read as the ceremony being finished, and without that date it would. Stated rather than implied, on the same footing as the rest of this report's manners.

*Verified live against the real corpus*, not only in fixtures: after reload, =(:reviewed-today t :stamp-today nil :status nil)= -- quiet today because a pass genuinely ran, with =mark-ceremony-done= never called. Three real =CLOCK= lines sit on the attention heading from today's passes, including one the user created minutes earlier.

*Both attempted breaks discriminate*: removing the clock derivation, and dropping the last-completed date from the report.

*What remains, and it is smaller than it was.* Nothing yet calls =mark-ceremony-done= automatically -- but that is now only about the *record*, not about the nagging, and a record of a human judgement arguably *should* need a human act. The honest residue is that the record will be sparse until someone habitually marks it, and the report makes that visible by printing the date every time it asks.

*Filed 2026-08-26 at the user's request*, after they asked whether they still have to refresh the slice by hand. They do.

*The regenerator exists and nothing calls it.* [[id:0acc1df2-6916-4180-867a-99bfa551806b][0acc1df2]] shipped =claude-code-ide-org-refresh-slice=, which rewrites every member line from its referent, recomputes the cookie and regenerates the =:BLOCKER:=. It is invoked only by a human typing =M-x=. On 2026-08-26 alone it was run five times by hand between us.

*Why that is worse than an ordinary missing convenience.* Every field on a member line except the id is *derived*, and the whole point of that design is that a line which disagrees with its referent means the slice is stale rather than that someone formed a second opinion. But nothing detects the staleness: =bin/lint-org= compares the =:BLOCKER:= against the checkbox list, and both are regenerated together, so they go stale in step and agree with each other while disagreeing with reality. A slice is therefore *stale by default* between passes, and silently so.

*This is the third step in the ceremony that depends on someone remembering*, alongside [[id:806ff394-3ede-4d67-82aa-9c44fe1cf86e][806ff394]] (nothing stamps the ceremony done) and [[id:601c885c-7d8c-46d4-af14-0d8d3ea69ba8][601c885c]] (nothing asserts the separation convention). The pattern is worth naming as such: the ceremony is a sequence of idempotent commands, each individually cheap, none of them wired to anything.

*The obvious trigger is wrong, and [[id:798bb7a1-d5a6-4c08-8cf0-cc91a82d08e6][798bb7a1]] is why.* Refreshing *during* apply would hit members whose keyword is still queued -- keywordless on disk -- which leaves the member line unrewritten *and* manufactures a =:BLOCKER:= lint error naming a keyword-less heading. Observed the same day. So the trigger has to be after the batch has fully landed, not per item.

*The right seam probably already exists:* =--review-settle-auto-promote= runs once after apply's loop finishes, against the batch's finished state, precisely because per-item evaluation was wrong for the same reason ([[id:c8a6c5d2-8777-44d2-9900-e56eb03aa2d9][c8a6c5d2]]). A slice refresh wants exactly that phase, and adding it there costs one call rather than a new mechanism.

*Open:* whether to refresh *every* slice or only ones whose members the batch touched. Every slice is simpler and idempotent; touched-only is cheaper and needs the batch to report which ids it wrote. With one live slice the distinction does not yet matter, which argues for the simple version until it does.

*Shipped 2026-08-26* ([[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::9761cdf][9761cdf]]). =--review-settle-slices= runs from the same seam as =--review-settle-auto-promote=, immediately after apply's loop and before the watermark is written.

*The seam this heading identified was the right one, and both open questions resolved in the direction it guessed.* After the batch rather than per item, and every slice rather than only touched ones -- the latter because =refresh-slice= is idempotent and there is one live slice, so a touched-only variant would buy machinery before the distinction costs anything.

*The per-item alternative is worse here than it is for auto-promote*, which is worth stating because the two look symmetrical. A member whose =todo= event has not landed yet is *keywordless on disk*, so a mid-batch refresh leaves its line unrewritten *and* manufactures a =:BLOCKER:= lint error naming a keyword-less heading. That is [[id:798bb7a1-d5a6-4c08-8cf0-cc91a82d08e6][798bb7a1]], observed the same day this was filed.

*Errors are swallowed, deliberately.* This is bookkeeping *after* the work. A slice that cannot be regenerated leaves staleness that is the status quo ante rather than new damage; an error escaping would report a pass that genuinely landed as a failed one.

*The tests assert the invocation, not the regeneration.* =refresh-slice= is already covered by [[id:0acc1df2-6916-4180-867a-99bfa551806b][0acc1df2]]'s tests, and re-testing its output here would pass whether or not anything called it -- so these count calls: none for an empty batch, exactly one for a batch of three. Proved to discriminate by disabling the call site.

*One test was wrong before it was right, in a way worth recording.* The failure test first asserted =should-not= on the return value; the function returns whatever =message= hands back, so it failed against correct code. It now asserts on whether an error *escapes*, which is the actual property.

*Verified live after reload*: =--review-settle-slices= is bound and =claude-code-ide-org--review-apply='s definition contains the call. The first probe reported =nil= only because it named =--review-apply-items=, a function that does not exist -- a reminder that a negative from a hand-written probe is worth checking before it is believed.

*What this closes.* Three ceremony steps depended on someone remembering; this was the third and last of them to be wired. The remaining one, [[id:601c885c-7d8c-46d4-af14-0d8d3ea69ba8][601c885c]], is not a missing trigger but an open decision about whether a lint rule is wanted at all.

*Measured 2026-08-24 over this session's own transcript*, after the user observed the footnotes had gone spotty. 132 assistant messages, 32 of which cited an org =:ID:=.

*Coverage: 37 of 85 citations footnoted -- 43%.*

Two findings, and the second is the actionable one.

*It is all-or-nothing per message, not sloppiness within one.* 25 of the 32 messages either footnoted every id they cited or none of them; only 7 were partial. So nothing is being forgotten mid-paragraph -- a per-message decision is flipping.

*It decays on re-mention, and every offender was correct the first time.*

| id | missed | of | first footnoted |
|----------+--------+----+-----------------|
| cbe282ec |      9 | 13 | yes             |
| 8bcd56f4 |      5 |  9 | yes             |
| 3063c3e5 |      4 |  7 | yes             |
| cc0c17a7 |      3 |  4 | yes             |
| 7771fc63 |      3 |  4 | yes             |
| aa1ba915 |      3 |  4 | yes             |

*The mechanism, stated plainly:* once an id has been footnoted, it stops reading as opaque *to the writer*, who has just looked the title up and is holding it. But the rule is per *response*, and the reader of message 122 does not have message 44 on screen. The rule's own wording -- "one footnote per distinct identifier, ordered by first appearance" -- is silent on whether "distinct" means within the response or within the conversation, and the failure lives exactly in that silence.

*Three fixes, and they are complementary rather than alternatives.*

1. *Say the quiet part in the rule*: distinct **within this response**, regardless of whether it was footnoted earlier in the conversation. One clause, aimed precisely at the measured failure. Cheapest, and it is what the data says is missing -- but memory alone is what just produced 43%.
2. *Enforce it at =Stop=.* Verified against the Claude Code hook docs rather than assumed: a =Stop= hook can prevent the turn ending, either with exit 2 or with =continue: false= plus =hookSpecificOutput.stopReason=, and the reason is shown to the model. Crucially it receives *=last_assistant_message=* as a Stop-specific input field, and the docs explicitly direct hooks needing the current turn's final text to use it rather than =transcript_path=, which lags. So the check is: scan for =\b[0-9a-f]{8}\b=, scan the footnote block, block if any cited id is unfootnoted. This is the project's standing answer to a convention that recurs -- the same instinct as =bin/lint-org= and the =org-trigger-hook= guards.
3. *Make compliance cheap.* The real cost is looking up an exact title per id, which is why the discipline degrades exactly when a response cites five of them. [[id:478d6ec9-1b99-4c6c-88e9-c793ad4b2f22][478d6ec9]] and its child [[id:2d9eeebd-4375-4790-8485-92b244236a21][2d9eeebd]] are already this: resolve an 8-character prefix and read front matter without a whole-body read. A batch prefix→title lookup makes footnoting nearly free, and a rule that is free to obey does not need enforcing.

*The one hazard in (2), and it is not incidental:* the docs describe *no* loop guard for a blocking =Stop= hook -- no =stop_hook_active= flag. A hook that blocks on a condition the model then fails to satisfy loops forever. It needs its own sentinel, one fire per turn, on the model of the =block-open= file [[id:f4e628ce-e653-429a-8f3c-0f5d4241b139][f4e628ce]] already uses.

*Related but a different surface:* [[id:d2a0f54c-b59a-4855-ae3d-c93a6d3aa177][d2a0f54c]] generalises convention checking over *files* at pre-commit. This one checks *response prose* at turn end. Same instinct, no shared code.

*Shipped 2026-08-24* (=9fcc08b=): =bin/hooks/footnote-check=, wired to =Stop=, with =bin/footnote-check-test= covering it. 8 of 8 pass.

*Reads =last_assistant_message=, not =transcript_path=.* The hook docs are explicit that the transcript is written asynchronously and may lag the in-memory conversation, so a hook needing the current turn's final text must use that field. Reading the transcript would have checked the *previous* response and blocked on the wrong thing -- a bug that would have looked like flakiness rather than like a mistake.

*Candidates are validated against the org files rather than pattern-matched.* An 8-hex token is not necessarily an =:ID:=; a git short hash is the obvious collision and this repo's prose is full of them. Only tokens appearing as =:ID:  <token>= in a tracked file are enforced, which turns a heuristic into a lookup and makes a false positive nearly impossible. Two of the eight tests pin that: =deadbeef= and an 8-digit number are both ignored.

*The loop guard is load-bearing, not defensive.* The docs describe no =stop_hook_active= flag, so a hook that blocks on a condition the model then fails to satisfy blocks forever. It fires at most once per turn via a per-session sentinel on the =block-open= model, written when it blocks and cleared by =bin/hooks/session-resume= when the next prompt starts a new turn. Clearing it from the =Stop= hook itself would reintroduce the loop exactly.

*The first draft failed every case that should have blocked,* and the cause is already on record here: =mapfile=, an unguarded ="${arr[@]}"= under =set -u=, and array append -- all bash 4, while macOS ships 3.2 and =#!/usr/bin/env bash= resolves to it. The same three constructs, in the same order, that [[id:7e9aa4ea-4757-4e58-bac3-3c3e67fc4cb1][7e9aa4ea]] recorded hitting. Rewritten for 3.2. Worth noting the tests caught it immediately, which is the only reason it cost minutes rather than a silently non-firing feature -- the failure mode [[id:f4e628ce-e653-429a-8f3c-0f5d4241b139][f4e628ce]] lived in for weeks.

*Two failures measured while testing were my test's fault, not the code's,* and both were the same mistake: =VAR=x cmd1 | cmd2= scopes VAR to =cmd1= only, so the hook under test read the default queue directory and appeared not to clear its sentinel. Recorded because it will recur -- every hook here takes its payload on stdin through a pipe, so the natural way to write the test is the wrong one.

*Known interaction, accepted rather than engineered around:* a blocked turn fires =Stop= twice, so =session-pause= writes two =pause= guideposts with no =resume= between them. The second is the true turn end; the first does not pair, since =--span-work-runs= only pairs =resume= -> =pause=. So a span ends where it should and the cost is one unpaired point.

*Not live in this session.* Hook configuration is read once at session start, so the new =Stop= entry takes effect in a new session only. This heading's own claim to work cannot be verified until then -- the first real test is whether the next session's responses carry their footnotes.

*Still worth doing, and it is the half that removes the problem rather than policing it:* [[id:478d6ec9-1b99-4c6c-88e9-c793ad4b2f22][478d6ec9]] and [[id:2d9eeebd-4375-4790-8485-92b244236a21][2d9eeebd]] make a prefix→title lookup cheap. A rule that is free to obey does not need enforcing, and the enforcement exists because looking up five exact titles mid-response is not free today.

CLOSED: [2026-08-26 Wed 10:27]
:PROPERTIES:
:ID:       5787bfc6-3ba5-4d94-802c-f8a7879de68d
:CREATED:  [2026-08-25 Tue 11:57]
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
