  observed twice; the hook blocked and said nothing
CLOCK: [2026-08-26 Wed 09:44]--[2026-08-26 Wed 09:48] =>  0:04
- State "DOING"      from "TODO"       [2026-08-26 Wed 09:44] \\
  find where the stopReason is lost
- [2026-08-26 Wed 09:44]--[2026-08-26 Wed 09:48] check hook docs, fix the delivery half
- State "REVIEW"     from "DOING"      [2026-08-26 Wed 09:48] \\
  fix shipped; awaits one observed block
- State "DONE"       from "REVIEW"     [2026-08-26 Wed 10:27] \\
  exit 2 + stderr; observed delivering
:END:

*Observed 2026-08-25, twice in one session.* The hook fired and the text that reached the model was exactly =Stop hook stopped continuation: Stop hook prevented continuation= -- no ids, no instruction, none of the =stopReason= the hook composes. The model continued without correcting anything, because it had nothing to correct *from*.

*The hook itself is fine, and that was checked rather than assumed.* Fed a body citing two tracked ids with one footnoted, it emits well-formed JSON naming the missing one and carrying the full instruction. Both real blocks were genuine violations -- =46e4ce2b= and =98c302e0= cited and unfootnoted in one response, =8ca6541d= and =aa1ba915= in another. So the *detection* half is verified in production; it is the delivery half that is missing.

*Why that matters more than it sounds.* A gate that blocks without saying why converts a corrective nudge into an unexplained stall: the turn ends, the model is re-invoked, and the violation is still there. The loop guard means it costs one extra continuation and never hangs, so the failure is quiet -- which is how it survived two occurrences without being noticed as a defect rather than as the feature working.

*What is not yet known* is where the text is lost. Candidates, none tested: =stopReason= may be surfaced to the *user* rather than to the model; the field may need to sit somewhere other than =hookSpecificOutput= for a blocking Stop hook; or the harness may summarise any block to a fixed string. Worth checking against the hook documentation before changing the hook, since the JSON shape currently matches what was designed from those docs.

*Blocks judgement on* the parent [[id:2758f3a0-3c47-405e-9662-a7669dcb60cc][2758f3a0]], which is in =REVIEW= awaiting exactly this evidence: it fires, it is accurate, and it cannot yet tell anyone what it found.

*Cause found 2026-08-26, in the hook documentation as this heading advised, and it is not a delivery failure.* =stopReason= is an *enum*: the reference gives it as accepting =user_request=, =max_turns=, =model_stop_token= or =completion=, and describes it as replacing the stop reason rather than carrying a message. The hook was putting a paragraph of prose into a status code, so the prose was discarded and the harness default appeared verbatim. None of the three candidates guessed above was right -- the text was not surfaced to the user instead, nor misplaced within the payload, nor summarised. It was *type-rejected*.

*The right channel is =systemMessage=*, documented as "text shown to Claude in the next turn as a system message, allowing you to provide feedback or corrections before Claude continues" -- exactly what this needs. =reason= is deliberately not used: it is documented as shown to the *user* only, and the user is not the one who has to fix the footnotes.

*Emitted in both positions, top level and inside =hookSpecificOutput=.* Two passes over the documentation disagreed about which the harness reads. Emitting both costs nothing; guessing wrong costs another silent block, which is a defect that took six occurrences to be noticed. Drop whichever proves redundant once a session has been *observed* receiving it.

*A second defect fell out of probing it, in the loop guard the script's own header calls not optional.* =: > "$sentinel" 2>/dev/null= does *not* suppress failure when the queue directory is absent: bash processes the output redirection before the stderr one, so the error prints *and the sentinel is never written*. A Stop hook that blocks on a condition the model cannot satisfy then blocks forever. =mkdir -p= first, and the probe that found it now passes with zero bytes on stderr.

*Four assertions added and proved to discriminate* by reverting to =stopReason= on a copy: 12 passed / 0 failed becomes 8 / 4.

*Corrected while writing this up, because the first version of the claim was wrong.* The fix is live *now*, not next session: the hook *script* is read fresh on every invocation, and only the *wiring* in =.claude/settings.json= is read at session start -- which is unchanged. So the next block in any running session is the test, and the six-block history says one will come along.

*What this leaves for the parent.* [[id:2758f3a0-3c47-405e-9662-a7669dcb60cc][2758f3a0]] sits in =REVIEW= awaiting exactly this: it fires, it is accurate at 41 of 45 measured over a real transcript, and the reason it could not report is now understood and addressed. What it still lacks is one *observed* block carrying its message -- which is a matter of waiting rather than of building.

*Verified end to end 2026-08-26, by deliberately tripping the hook at the user's instruction.* A response cited =806ff394= with no footnote block, and what came back was:

: Stop hook feedback:
: [${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/bin/hooks/footnote-check]: This response cites
: tracked org :ID:s without footnoting them: 806ff394. Append a footnote
: for each, superscript-marked in the prose ...

The id, the instruction, the rule. The first of eight blocks to say anything at all.

*The deliberate trip is what settled it, and it took two of them.* The first trip *falsified* the =systemMessage= fix -- the block arrived as the bare default, unchanged -- which is the only reason the exit code was examined at all. Waiting for a natural block would have produced the same evidence eventually and much later; asking for one produced it in a turn. Worth remembering as a technique: a gate that fails silently can be *made* to fail on demand.

*The final diagnosis, after two wrong ones.* =stopReason= is an enum and discards prose -- true, and not the cause. =systemMessage= is a real field -- true, and not the cause either. The cause was =exit 0=: "Stderr from a hook that exits 0 goes to the debug log only, never the transcript, and Claude never sees it." Both earlier attempts rearranged fields inside a channel that was shut. Now it is =exit 2= with the text on stderr and no JSON at all, which the docs give as the blocking path for =Stop=.

*A bug in the test harness fell out of the rewrite and is worth keeping.* =run= is always used inside =$(...)=, which is a subshell, so its =RC=$?= could never reach the caller -- four tests that should have blocked silently reported "allowed". The exit status now travels as the first line of =run='s own output. Reverting to the JSON/exit-0 form takes 12 passed to 6 passed / 6 failed, so the assertions bite.

*Honest note on the record.* The build interval for this fix was not clocked -- it happened across the same stretch as the =Review attention= corruption repair, and neither was clocked at the time. Recording that rather than backfilling a guess, per [[id:4f6a6bb1-7773-4657-949e-1fe1ba9484be][4f6a6bb1]].

*What this releases.* [[id:2758f3a0-3c47-405e-9662-a7669dcb60cc][2758f3a0]] has been in =REVIEW= waiting on exactly this. It fires, it is accurate at 41 of 45 measured over a real transcript, and it can now tell the model what it found. There is nothing left for it to wait for.



**** DONE Track the human's review attention, clocked by the review command itself :code:research:
CLOSED: [2026-08-26 Wed 09:35]
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Apply
:ID:       961f15b6-d782-40b8-8ceb-ba086d188a3b
:CREATED:  [2026-08-24 Mon 16:32]
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:16
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Apply
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "NEXT"       from              [2026-08-24 Mon 16:33] \\
  design settled except where to file it
- State "TODO"       from "NEXT"       [2026-08-25 Tue 08:33] \\
  Auto-demoted: superseded by sibling [[id:6cc71c36-0fa6-4773-9b35-c0582f4cee82][Six defects in one day, all the same: the code knew more than it said]] becoming NEXT.
- State "NEXT"       from "TODO"       [2026-08-26 Wed 09:07] \\
  last large slice member; unblocks active spans
CLOCK: [2026-08-26 Wed 09:30]--[2026-08-26 Wed 09:35] =>  0:05
- State "DOING"      from "NEXT"       [2026-08-26 Wed 09:30] \\
  build the review-attention clock
- [2026-08-26 Wed 09:30]--[2026-08-26 Wed 09:35] clock the human's review pass natively
- State "DONE"       from "DOING"      [2026-08-26 Wed 09:35] \\
  own heading, no datetree; bury ends the pass
- [2026-08-26 Wed 09:36]--[2026-08-26 Wed 09:44] assigned at review
:END:

*Proposed by the user 2026-08-24, reviewing a live queue.* The review pass is the one activity this project has never measured, and it is the one the project most depends on: nothing reaches an org file without it. Its cost is currently invisible, so "the review-apply cycle seems pretty straightforward lately" ([[id:361e2708-8124-4bd1-9c44-f97ca97aca4a][361e2708]]) is an impression rather than a number.

*It is a different quantity, not an exception.* The user framed this as a first exception to the union-overlapping-intervals convention, since the agent may be busy elsewhere while the human reviews. It is not: [[id:7d739afd-f879-445c-b0b6-65e295585a94][7d739afd]] unions concurrent *turns* because they are the same quantity measured twice. Human attention and agent activity are different quantities and should never have been added together, so they are simply separate totals and the convention does not reach them. That is a cleaner resolution than an exception, and it is the framing to build against.

*The project already cut this seam.* =claude-code-ide-org--review-format-annotation= records that the queue captures *agent* activity and nothing else, and that an active timestamp inside =:LOGBOOK:= -- the kind org's agenda absorbs -- is "reserved for intervals a human logs themselves" ([[id:b8e6007a-ae13-4b13-bb2e-a5df39435af0][b8e6007a]], [[id:4f8500e6-b468-4fd4-a0f6-ebf04c7a57ba][4f8500e6]]). So the mechanism for human attention was decided before there was anything to put in it. This is that thing.

*No, it does not begin with an arbitrary prompt, and that is the design's main improvement on the proposal.* The user's contract was "tell you to clock me in, then clock me out when I report the outcome". That works, but it depends on a person remembering to say a sentence at both ends -- the discipline half that [[id:eaeeb4ee-ceee-4094-8598-bbcdc8214b66][eaeeb4ee]] proved insufficient even when followed twelve times correctly.

=M-x claude-code-ide-org-review= *is the event*. It is an interactive command in this project's own code, it is the documented and only entry point to the pass, and it cannot be invoked by accident. Starting the clock there needs no utterance and cannot be forgotten.

*And it should not go through the queue at all.* The queue exists because concurrent agent sessions cannot touch a live buffer safely. A human running an interactive command in Emacs has none of those constraints -- they are already inside the interactive session the whole design routes toward. So this writes a native =org-clock-in= directly, with an *active* timestamp, which is exactly what the annotation rule reserves for human-logged intervals.

Three consequences follow, and each removes a problem the queue framing created:

- *No lane collision.* The obstacle noted in conversation was that =org_clock_out= closes whatever the session last opened, one slot per lane, so a human clock would clobber the agent's. Writing natively sidesteps the queue's slot entirely; org's own clock is a separate mechanism.
- *No attribution guesswork.* There are no guideposts to cluster and no span to suggest, because the interval is bracketed by two real events.
- *It reaches the agenda.* An active timestamp is what makes "where did my attention go" answerable there, which is [[id:4f8500e6-b468-4fd4-a0f6-ebf04c7a57ba][4f8500e6]]'s whole question.

*Where the interval ends is the real design question, and it is not obvious.* Three candidates, none clean:

- *Buffer killed.* Automatic and precise about the buffer, wrong about the person: leaving it open over lunch clocks lunch.
- *Apply completes.* Precise about the work, but a pass that ends in dismissals applies nothing and would record no time at all -- and reviewing carefully enough to dismiss everything is the *most* expensive outcome, not the least.
- *The user says so.* Their original contract, correct and unforgeable, but back to depending on a sentence.

*Recommended: start on the command, end on the user's word, with the buffer's death as a backstop.* The start needs no discipline because the command is unambiguous; the end genuinely requires judgement -- "I am done thinking about this" is not observable -- so ask for it rather than infer it. A killed buffer with the clock still running is the stale-interval case [[id:7771fc63-9374-4c8a-9e80-24ceec21977c][7771fc63]]'s recovery report already handles, which is why it can be the fallback rather than needing a new mechanism.

*The iterate-while-open case the user raised is handled by construction:* asking questions about what the buffer shows does not close it, so the clock keeps running across the conversation. That is the behaviour they described wanting, obtained without a rule.

*Its own datetree, or the existing one?* The user asked for a separate one. The reporting question is genuinely different -- "where did my attention go" against "what was the agent doing" -- and mixing them in one tree makes both harder to read. But a second =:DATE_TREE:= category doubles the scaffolding [[id:e30d52d7-960b-44f3-ab92-93846c81a1bd][e30d52d7]] had to teach the lint about, and [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] is still open on whether this project wants more datetrees at all. *Undecided, and it should be decided against a report someone actually wants* rather than in advance -- the same discipline CLAUDE.md states for the whole attention-tracking goal.

*What this does not do.* It measures the review pass only. It is not general human time tracking, and it should not grow into it without a separate decision: the review pass earns measurement because it is the project's own bottleneck, not because measuring people is generally good.

*How the backstop is actually detected, worked out 2026-08-24 rather than assumed.* "Buffer death" sounds like one event and is three, and the obvious mechanism misses the common case.

*=kill-buffer-hook= is the right hook and =q= never fires it.* =q= in the review buffer is inherited from =special-mode= and runs =quit-window=, whose own docstring is explicit: "Quit WINDOW and *bury* its buffer. ... With prefix argument KILL non-nil, kill the buffer instead of burying it." Verified live: =(key-binding (kbd "q"))= in =*org-review*= is =quit-window=. So the ordinary way anyone leaves the buffer buries it, the buffer stays alive, and a naive =kill-buffer-hook= implementation would clock straight through until the buffer was next killed explicitly -- which in practice is never. The failure would present as a clock running all night.

*Three layers, and two of them already exist:*

| how the pass ends | mechanism | state |
|--------------------+---------------------------------------------+----------------|
| buffer buried (=q=) | advice on =quit-window= -- see below | to build |
| buffer killed | =kill-buffer-hook=, buffer-local, runs before the kill with the buffer current | to build |
| Emacs quits | =kill-emacs-hook= -> =--clock-out-if-clocking= | already live |
| crash or =kill -9= | stale-interval detection -> the =SessionStart= report asks when work stopped | already live |

That last row closes a loop worth naming: the recovery report has never fired in this repo's entire history, because every agent clock is queued and every clean shutdown closes what it opened ([[id:aa1ba915-ee68-48df-afea-197ae60aac63][aa1ba915]]'s audit). A *human* clock left open by a crash is exactly the case it was built for, and would be the first thing it ever had to say.

*DECIDED 2026-08-24 by the user: treat burying as ending the pass* -- option 2 of the three considered, advising or wrapping the quit path rather than rebinding =q=.

Rejected: rebinding =q= to =(quit-window t)= so it kills. It would make =kill-buffer-hook= sufficient, but it changes the behaviour of a key every =special-mode= buffer in Emacs shares, to serve a clock -- a surprising cost paid by someone who is not thinking about clocks. Also rejected: relying on the user's word alone with kill and crash as the only backstops, which loses precisely the walked-away case the backstop exists for.

*The reasoning for burying is that it matches what happens.* Burying *is* how a person leaves this buffer; it is not a lesser form of closing it. So the clock stops when the buffer stops being visible, and the user's word remains the primary signal for the case where they say so before leaving.

*Refresh is safe and was checked rather than assumed.* =g= rebuilds contents through =get-buffer-create= on the same buffer -- =claude-code-ide-org-review= is =(let ((buffer (get-buffer-create "*org-review*"))) ...)= -- so it neither kills nor buries, and the clock correctly survives a refresh mid-pass. That matters because =g= is the command a human runs when confused, which is exactly when the pass is most expensive and least should be under-recorded.

*AFK/BAK supplies the one bit no hook can observe* -- proposed by the user 2026-08-24 and measured the same evening.

Verified against the hook documentation rather than assumed: Claude Code exposes 31 hook events and *none* fires during composition. There is no keystroke, input-change, draft or idle event. =UserPromptSubmit= fires after submission. So the gap between two prompts is irreducibly ambiguous -- the user thinking about a design and the user making coffee produce byte-identical records, and no configuration, hook or instrument will ever separate them. The human is the only possible source of that bit.

*The machinery already exists, which is why this is small.* An AFK/BAK pair is structurally identical to =block_start=/=block_end=: a bracketed interval *excised* from a span rather than counted. =--block-intervals= pairs by position, =--time-within-any-p= drops guideposts inside, =--aggregate-guideposts= splits spans across them, and the =exclusions= argument added for clock brackets ([[id:eaeeb4ee-ceee-4094-8598-bbcdc8214b66][eaeeb4ee]]) generalises it. A third kind of excision is an addition, not a mechanism.

=BAK= is the established complement in the idiom -- "back at keyboard", from IRC and gaming. =BTK= is not a thing.

*First real measurement, 2026-08-24:* =AFK= at 18:06:10, =BAK= at 18:46:57 -- *41 minutes*. Both endpoints came from =resume= events the =UserPromptSubmit= hook had already written, with no new instrumentation at all.

*And the measurement immediately showed where it does and does not earn its keep.* Those 41 minutes were *already* excluded: no guideposts fired while the user was away, so the gap never entered a span, and the adjacent item is a lone point at 19:02. The span before it ends at 18:06 exactly.

So AFK/BAK is *not* needed for a gap that ends the working stretch -- silence handles that by itself. It earns its keep for a gap *inside* one: the user steps away while a turn is running, or between two prompts that bracket a span, where the guideposts either side make the interval look continuous. That is a narrower case than it first appeared, and worth knowing before building for the general one.

*The datetree question's main objection weakened 2026-08-25, without the question being answered.* It was recorded as: a second =:DATE_TREE:= category "doubles the scaffolding [[id:e30d52d7-960b-44f3-ab92-93846c81a1bd][e30d52d7]] had to teach the lint about".

*That cost is about to become close to zero.* [[id:2e660571-26df-41e4-bb64-b9d74a3d7efe][2e660571]] proposes replacing =--datetree-node-role='s title-regex inference with =:KIND: datetree-year|month|day=. Once a node declares what it is, a *second* tree costs the lint nothing extra -- there is no per-tree scaffolding to teach, only a property to read. So the argument that was doing most of the work against a separate tree is the one being removed.

*The other argument stands, and it is the one that should decide.* "Decide against a report someone actually wants, rather than in advance." Nothing has appeared that wants the separation -- no report has been asked for that mixing the two trees would make harder to read. So this stays undecided, but for a smaller reason than before: not because a second tree is expensive, but because nobody has yet needed one.

*Worth re-reading once [[id:82df2a6c-881d-4117-a752-5b3b04c9656d][82df2a6c]] lands*, since that is the heading whose whole purpose is to produce evidence about which org lenses this corpus can support -- which is exactly the "report someone actually wants" this decision is waiting on.

*Falsified 2026-08-26, before building: =org-clock-in= cannot write an active timestamp.* The design above says this "writes a native =org-clock-in= directly, with an *active* timestamp, which is exactly what the annotation rule reserves for human-logged intervals". Run in batch on org 9.8.7, =org-clock-in= followed by =org-clock-out= produces:

: CLOCK: [2026-08-26 Wed 09:31]--[2026-08-26 Wed 09:31] =>  0:00

Inactive, and it is org's own grammar rather than a setting -- there is no configuration that makes =CLOCK:= active. So the sentence naming the active timestamp as what native clocking buys is wrong, and every consequence drawn from it needs restating.

*What survives, and by a different route.* Clocked time *does* reach the agenda -- through =org-agenda-log-mode= and clocktables, which read =CLOCK:= lines regardless of bracket style -- not through active timestamps. So "it reaches the agenda" is true and the mechanism named for it is not.

*Where the active timestamp actually lives.* Beside the CLOCK line, on the annotation the review pass writes (=- [ts]--[ts] assigned at review=). That is a plain list item, it can be active, and =--review-format-annotation= is precisely where the active branch was dropped. This also explains the user's request in [[id:01849bef-fdc9-4c30-b467-00ca8606e8e0][01849bef]]: what is tedious to flip by hand is the *annotation*, because the CLOCK line above it never could be flipped.

*Consequence for the undecided datetree question, which this makes decidable.* Human and agent time both land as inactive =CLOCK:= lines, so a clocktable *cannot tell them apart* by bracket style. Sharing the existing meta-work tree would make the two quantities inseparable in exactly the report [[id:82df2a6c-881d-4117-a752-5b3b04c9656d][82df2a6c]] produced -- which is the report the decision was waiting for. Separation therefore has to be *structural*: a different heading.

*And structural separation is cheaper than the heading feared.* A second =:DATE_TREE:= was priced at doubling the lint scaffolding =e30d52d7= had to learn, and at prejudging [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]]. Neither is necessary: measured 2026-08-26, a clocktable with =:step day= reports per-day totals from CLOCK lines on *one ordinary heading*, with no datetree at all --

: Daily report: [2026-08-24 Mon]   *Total time*  *0:25*
: Daily report: [2026-08-25 Tue]   *Total time*  *0:42*
: Daily report: [2026-08-26 Wed]   *Total time*  *0:30*

*So the recommendation is: one dedicated heading, native =org-clock-in=, plus an active annotation line beside each interval.* Structural separation is what makes the two quantities separately reportable; the active annotation is what puts the human's own time in the agenda. The datetree question does not need answering to proceed, which was the only thing gating the build.

*Shipped 2026-08-26* ([[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::82416ad][82416ad]]). =claude-code-ide-org-review= now opens a native clock on a dedicated heading, and three layers close it.

*The datetree question is answered rather than deferred, and the answer is "neither".* It was gated on "a report someone actually wants", which [[id:82df2a6c-881d-4117-a752-5b3b04c9656d][82df2a6c]] produced -- and the report made the case for *structural* separation, since inactive CLOCK lines cannot be told apart by style. But a second =:DATE_TREE:= turned out to be unnecessary: =:step day= reports per-day totals from one ordinary heading. So the recommendation above stands, the cost that made it hard is gone, and =29439196= is not prejudged either way.

*What was built.* =claude-code-ide-org-review-attention-heading= (a =defcustom=, "Review attention", nil to disable) names a level-2 heading created on first use under the meta-work category. =--attention-start= is idempotent within a pass; =--attention-stop= closes the clock and writes an *active*-timestamped annotation beside the interval, carrying a reason.

*Ending it, per the decision above: burying counts.* The advice is on =quit-window=, not a rebinding of =q=, and a test pins the distinction that makes that necessary -- quitting *any other* =special-mode= buffer must not end the pass, which without the mode guard it would, since every such buffer shares that function. The other two layers are a buffer-local =kill-buffer-hook= and the =kill-emacs-hook= that was already live.

*Three attempted breaks all discriminate*: dropping the mode guard, writing the annotation inactive, and making start non-idempotent. Each fails exactly one test and no others.

*Live-reloaded and confirmed inert*: the advice is installed on =quit-window=, no marker is open, nothing is clocking. So it is armed and will start on the next real pass rather than having quietly begun measuring something already.

*What is deliberately not done.* The user's word remains the *primary* stop signal and nothing here asks for it -- the mechanism ends a pass on burying, killing or quitting, and a person who says "I am done" before leaving the buffer still has to be listened to by a session rather than by code. That is the same shape as [[id:806ff394-3ede-4d67-82aa-9c44fe1cf86e][806ff394]], and it is the honest boundary: "I am done thinking about this" is not observable, which is why the design asks for it rather than inferring it.

*Also not done: nothing reports on it yet.* The clocktable that makes this legible -- =:step day= over the attention heading -- exists as a measured technique and not as anything anyone runs. Whether that belongs in the ceremony alongside the other steps is [[id:edd47f32-e6c9-4ab3-8e8a-46a37ea29605][edd47f32]]'s question, and it is the fourth thing there that nobody invokes.

=org_amend= appends to the end of a heading's body and can do nothing
else. Its description says so — "the text lands at the end of the
heading's own body" — but frames it as *placement*, not as a
constraint, and nothing at the call site suggests what it costs.

*What it costs.* Every correction, every outcome summary, every "this
turned out to be wrong" lands furthest from where a reader starts. That
is the mechanism behind
[[id:b07df584-3adc-433c-ab49-e104f88aecf7][b07df584]]: 226ed53b reached
274 lines with its summary nowhere, because the only tool available put
each addition at the bottom. Writing that summary where it belonged took
a hand edit through =emacsclient=, and the first attempt corrupted a
sibling heading.

*The shape of the gap*, stated so it is not confused with a formatting
preference: a journal genuinely accumulates and appending is right for
it. What has no tool at all is *revising* — correcting a claim in place,
or putting a summary first. So the question is not whether =org_amend=
should insert elsewhere, but whether a second operation is wanted beside
it.

*Options, none chosen:*
- A =position= argument on =org_amend= — cheapest, and the least
  honest, since "append or prepend" is not the distinction that matters.
- A separate tool for *replacing* a delimited region, which is what a
  correction actually is.
- Neither: keep appending and let the closing action fold history into a
  drawer, which is the direction
  [[id:b07df584-3adc-433c-ab49-e104f88aecf7][b07df584]] was heading
  before it was gated on the task lifecycle.

Filed 2026-08-20 as the one mis-advertisement from
[[id:420816ec-677e-45a5-b898-fb5db70d214b][420816ec]] with no home of its
own. It is also the capture that proved
[[id:bd482c92-a71a-4d7d-88df-47678ee94c79][bd482c92]] fixed: this heading
was filed with =target: "Skill logic"=, a category title, which was
refused outright the day before.

*Decided 2026-08-20 by the user: =org_amend= should allow wholesale revision of a body, not only append.* This closes the three-option question above by rejecting its premise — the problem is not where a correction lands, it is that append-only forces every body to be a transcript.

The objection that append-only protected against was losing the evolution of a body. It does not need protecting: *git already holds every revision*, so the discipline is simply to commit before revising. That makes revision cheap and reversible, and it is the same argument =plans/= already rests on.

*What an open heading's body is for, stated positively:* the problem, the latest intended approach, and relevant verified facts. Not the stream of consciousness of how we got there. The body describes the current state of the question, not its history.

*What a closed heading's body is for:* a concise debrief — what the problem was (a slightly elaborated restatement of the title) and what the actual solution turned out to be. The original problem statement and plan of attack move into a drawer rather than being deleted.

*Two additions offered against the user's \"keep it short\" constraint, both already in DONE.org's house style:* how it was verified, in a clause; and any claim that was *falsified*, because that is what stops the same wrong turn being taken twice. This project's own evidence supports the second — three headings carried confident design claims later found wrong, while no journal claim needed correcting in the same period. Four short items total, not four paragraphs.

*Under consideration, not decided:* a timestamped commit log in a drawer, giving a reader an index into the git history for the rare \"how did we get here?\" question, so that the body never has to carry that answer itself.

This heading is now a *dependency of* [[id:b07df584-3adc-433c-ab49-e104f88aecf7][b07df584]] rather than a neighbour of it: the retention policy cannot be applied to an existing body without a tool that can rewrite one.

*Filed 2026-08-20, not built. An interim convention landed 2026-08-21 and does not close this.*

*A workaround now exists in =.claude/skills/org/SKILL.md= ("Body prose and the task lifecycle").* It cannot put the outcome first -- append-only forbids that -- but it stops the body *contradicting* the keyword, which is the half that was actually costing time. The rule: the keyword owns the status, completion vocabulary (=Shipped=, =Fixed=, =Verified by mutation=) is reserved for outcome prose, and investigation words (=Measured=, =Observed=, =Reproduced=) are what a capture may use.

*The word that broke it was =Verified=,* which fits both stages. Written on 2026-08-21 in two opposite senses within one hour: =Verified on org 9.6.15= (the investigation is sound, heading still TODO) and =Verified by mutation= (the fix works, heading DONE). Nothing distinguished them, and the user reported mistaking filed headings for resolved ones the same day.

*Measured, since the cost had only been asserted:* TODO.org is ~118,000 tokens. Across 72 active headings the median body is *50 lines*, the longest 404, and *44 bodies of 40+ lines carry 86% of all active body text*. That is the context every session re-reads to understand a heading.

*The deletion objection is weaker than this heading's neighbourhood assumed.* CLAUDE.md calls deletion "the one irreversible half of the practice", but justifies it by =plans/='s history being *bounded*. That justification does not transfer to =.org= files, which are version-controlled in full -- as the user pointed out, superseded prose stays recoverable from the commit history. Revising in place is therefore reversible here, and the case against building this tool is correspondingly thinner. The residual risk is only prose written and deleted inside one uncommitted window.

*It blocks [[id:b07df584-3adc-433c-ab49-e104f88aecf7][b07df584]]*, which is the user's standing concern -- raised 2026-08-18 as "I am questioning the long-term utility of capturing this quantity of minutiae", and repeated 2026-08-21 with the added observation that the accumulated prose is costing *working context*, not just readability. Machinery gates the policy: what to stop capturing is hard to settle while nothing can revise what was already captured.

*The cheapest mitigation needs neither this tool nor that decision:* write shorter bodies. That is standing user guidance -- economise on body prose, never on heading count -- and 2026-08-21's own output did not follow it.

*The policy was applied by hand to one closed body, 2026-08-21* ([[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::f0cdc90][f0cdc90]]). [[id:cc0c17a7-a554-426d-afeb-09cbee7339f0][cc0c17a7]] went from 138 lines to 34: the four items, one live loose end, and the original problem statement plus plan of attack moved into a drawer. It was a good test case because its body *contradicted itself* -- "Still open: the apply-side half" forty lines above "The apply-side half needed nothing, because the premise was wrong" -- so a reader stopping in the middle came away with a false belief. That is the append-only defect in its most expensive form.

*So the answer to "can this be done programmatically" is yes, and the answer to "should it be done this way" is no.* Locating a heading by =:ID:=, taking the range to the next heading and rewriting it is a dozen lines of script. The hazard is not the rewrite, it is the range.

*The first attempt corrupted the file, and this is the second recorded instance.* The next-heading test was =startswith("*")=, which matched a *bold prose line* (=*Cause.*=) rather than a headline, so it replaced 6 lines of a 123-line body and left the remainder orphaned below the new text. The body above already records that an earlier hand edit through =emacsclient= "corrupted a sibling heading". Two corruptions, two different range bugs, both from hand-rolling the same operation -- which is the argument for a tool that owns the range logic once, rather than for care.

*And =bin/lint-org= did not catch it: 0 errors on the corrupted file.* The lint checks structure, and the corruption was prose-level -- orphaned paragraphs under an otherwise well-formed heading. Nothing mechanical would have caught it. *Git was the only safety net*, and =git checkout -- TODO.org= restored all 136 lines exactly. That converts "commit before revising" from ceremony into the load-bearing precondition, and it is the concrete vindication of the deletion-reversibility argument recorded above.

*The drawer is =:PLAN:=, chosen by the user 2026-08-21.* The trial first used =:ORIGINAL:=, which I coined on the spot from the policy's own wording -- not from any source, and without grepping first, which is the search-before-coining rule failing in the one place it was most obviously due. =:PLAN:= is the project's existing word (=plans/=, Plan Mode, the Plan link, =org_log_background_plan=) and was free: zero prior occurrences in the repo. It belongs in =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md=, and =bin/lint-org= can then assert that a closed heading's planning content lives in it.

*Immediate consequence worth sequencing on:* this operation is what [[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]] is blocked on. Archiving stalls because CLAUDE.md requires an outcome summary before a =DONE= heading is archived, and there are 30 of them; producing those summaries *is* this revision applied 30 times.

*Shipped 2026-08-24, the wrapping half only* (=8170ddd=). =org_wrap_plan= wraps a body's prospective part in a =:PLAN:= drawer, with an optional =until= marker naming the first line that stays in the body -- the retroactive case, where a body written before the convention already holds both halves.

Two insertions at computable positions, never a range replacement, and no boundary comes from a regexp of ours: =outline-next-heading= and =org-end-of-meta-data= decide, so a line org would not parse as a heading cannot be treated as one. *Verified by reintroducing the bug*: swapping in the =startswith("*")= next-heading test that orphaned 117 lines on 2026-08-21 fails exactly two of the five new tests and nothing else. Refusals rather than guesses on a missing, duplicated or first-line seam, because a silently-wrong seam is the one mistake here no later reader will catch -- the drawer is one readers are told to skip.

*This heading is not done.* Its title names the real problem -- =org_amend= can still only append -- and general in-place revision, which *continuous paring* needs, is untouched. What shipped is the separable half the completion transition needs, split out deliberately so [[id:8bcd56f4-22a8-4673-bad6-a99433027b81][8bcd56f4]] and [[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]] stop waiting on the harder one.

*Shipped 2026-08-26* ([[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::28d68db][28d68db]]). =org_amend= takes =replace=true= and rewrites the body's prose wholesale, which is the decision recorded above rather than a fresh reading of the three options -- the premise that a correction's *placement* was the problem was already rejected.

*The safety case is structural, and it was measured before anything was written.* =--heading-body-bounds= begins after =org-end-of-meta-data=, which skips *every* leading drawer. Probed 2026-08-26 against =:PROPERTIES:=, =:LOGBOOK:= and =:PLAN:= in combination: the returned region begins below all of them. So there is no reachable input that destroys a drawer, and a finished heading can be revised without endangering the plan it was wrapped with. That is what made offering a destructive operation defensible at all.

*Revision defers on a busy file exactly as an append does*, and here the gate is load-bearing rather than merely prudent: racing the human's unsaved edits is the one case where replacing a body destroys work git has never seen. A heading with no body degrades to an append *and says so*, rather than silently doing nothing -- the worst of the three possible behaviours, since the caller would believe the text had landed.

*Both attempted breaks discriminate, but only after the tests were tightened, and the miss is the interesting part.* Deleting from =OPEN= instead of =BEG= leaves every drawer intact -- so all three drawer assertions passed -- while silently butting the new prose against =:END:=. The safety assertions could not tell correct behaviour from a cosmetic corruption. The test now pins the blank line between the last drawer and the body, which is the only observable difference.

*Live-reloaded and confirmed*: =(func-arity 'claude-code-ide-org-amend)= reads =(2 . 4)= and =--replace-body= is bound, with the tools server still on 45571.

*One precondition that a reload does not satisfy.* This adds an MCP *parameter*, and a client's tool schema is negotiated at session start -- so the session that shipped it still holds the three-argument form and cannot call =replace= itself. The elisp is live; the tool surface is not, until a new session. Worth knowing before anyone concludes the argument was ignored.

*What this unblocks, stated because it was the reason to build it.* [[id:b07df584-3adc-433c-ab49-e104f88aecf7][b07df584]]'s retention policy could not be applied to an existing body without a tool that can rewrite one; this heading was its dependency rather than its neighbour. The rules that follow from the decision -- an open heading's body is the problem, the latest intended approach and verified facts; a closed one is a concise debrief with the prospective half wrapped rather than deleted -- are now enforceable rather than aspirational.

The missing half of [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]], which is entirely cost analysis and mechanism comparison with no statement of what the change would *buy*. That asymmetry is the likeliest reason it has sat parked since 2026-08-19 instead of resolving either way.

*Why the features are unused, stated by the user 2026-08-21, and it is not neglect.* It is this project's founding motivation arriving one level up. CLAUDE.md's opening goal is "natural-language manipulation of =.org= files from within Emacs ... without needing to internalise Emacs chord sequences" -- and judging an agenda view, a sparse tree or a column view currently *requires* exactly that fluency, because you cannot evaluate a feature you cannot yet invoke. Nor was there, until this project, a corpus over which exercising them would show anything.

*The corpus now exists, measured 2026-08-21:* TODO.org 8433 lines across 8 categories; DONE.org 9554 lines and 63 archived entries; 353 =[[id:]]= links between the live documents; roughly 200 headings carrying nine TODO keywords and four tags; a =:DATE_TREE:= subtree; and clock data on most active headings.

*Advertised features to point at it, all read-only:*
- =org-agenda= tag/property/TODO matching across =org-agenda-files=, with =org-agenda-custom-commands= to save composite views
- sparse trees (=org-match-sparse-tree=, =C-c /=), which fold away non-matches in the buffer itself
- column view (=org-columns= plus a =COLUMNS= property) -- properties as a table, with summary roll-ups
- =:CATEGORY:= as an inherited agenda label, and statistics cookies: both already verified working here by 29439196, and both unused
- =org-ql=, already a dependency -- =org_query= wraps it, so its query language is reachable from a session today

*The decisive reframing: none of this requires the refactor.* Agenda views, sparse trees and column view all run against the structure exactly as it stands. So 29439196's implied sequencing -- settle the tier mechanism, then get the views -- is backwards. Look through org's own lenses at the corpus first. The views either show something worth having or they do not, and only then is there a real question about whether tiers must move to get more of it.

*What it would buy if they do earn it.* A story or slice becomes a *query* rather than a subtree, composable without relocating headings -- which is the shared problem behind 29439196's membership table and [[id:9651d4c8-6887-4b0a-91d9-562c3bc49a75][9651d4c8]]'s plan-coverage question. Both would largely dissolve.

*And Claude is how they get evaluated without the chords*, which closes the loop: a view or column spec can be built, run and rendered on request, so muscle memory stops being a precondition for the judgement. That is the founding goal applied to org's own feature set rather than to task edits.

*Run 2026-08-25.* Every lens was pointed at the real corpus in batch Emacs (org 9.8.7, loaded from Doom's straight build so this is the same org the live session uses, not the bundled one). Reads are read-only; the two experiments that had to *write* properties ran against copies of TODO.org in a scratch directory, and the real files were never opened for writing.

*The agenda works today, unmodified*

=org-todo-list= renders all 99 lines with no configuration, and keyword restriction works even though global =org-todo-keywords= is only =((sequence "TODO" "DONE"))= -- org reads the file-local =#+TODO:= line, so =org-todo-list "REVIEW"= correctly returns the two =REVIEW= headings. =org-tags-view= handles both a tag query (=research/-DONE= -> 13) and a *property* query (=KIND="slice"= -> 1) natively.

One gotcha, since it will bite: =/-DONE= excludes the =DONE= keyword only, not the done *set*. The =research/-DONE= view listed a =CANCELLED= heading. =/!= or an explicit =-DONE-CANCELLED= is what "unfinished" actually spells.

*The decisive result: the prefix column, and what :CATEGORY: buys that :EPIC: does not*

*Today the agenda's category column carries no information.* Across all 274 headings in both files it holds exactly *two* distinct values -- =TODO= and =DONE= -- because with no =:CATEGORY:= anywhere org falls back to the file name. Twelve columns of every agenda line are spent restating which file you are looking at.

Stamping =:CATEGORY:= on each level-1 group -- exactly [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]]'s proposal, nothing else changed -- immediately populates it, and it inherits down the subtree with no configuration:

: Slices:     NEXT Read a heading's front matter, and take a partial :ID: ...
: Clock lifecy:NEXT Apply consumes queue events with no way to roll one back
: Observabilit:NEXT Six defects in one day, all the same ...

Nine distinct values over the active headings. The same file with =:EPIC:= instead renders =corpus-copy:= on every line.

*Three separate things were measured, not one*, because they do not all go the same way:

- *Display.* =:CATEGORY:= populates the prefix column and inherits; =:EPIC:= does not, and there is no configuration that makes an arbitrary property fill that column.
- *Matching.* =CATEGORY="Observabilit"/-DONE= matched *10* headings with property inheritance *off*, which is the default -- org inherits =:CATEGORY:= specially. =EPIC="Observabilit"= matched *1*: only the heading carrying the property. Add =org-use-property-inheritance= and it also matches 10. So this difference is one line of configuration, not a capability gap.
- *Filtering.* =org-agenda-filter-by-category= -- the =<= key -- works on the displayed category: six =NEXT= items across five categories filtered to two visible and four hidden. There is no equivalent key for an arbitrary property.

*So the choice is not "overloaded versus clean", which is how it has been framed.* It is: =:CATEGORY:= buys a populated prefix column, free inheritance, and an interactive filter key, at the cost of the overload [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] objects to. =:EPIC:= costs one =org-use-property-inheritance= entry and gets *only* matching -- no column, no filter key.

*A cost of flattening that was not on the list*

The level-1 tree is what makes the clock report group. =#+BEGIN: clocktable :maxlevel 2 :scope file :block untilnow= produces a per-epic roll-up today, with no changes at all:

: | *Total time*                    | *1d 5:42* |
: | Slices                          |      6:21 |
: | Clock lifecycle & visibility    |     12:11 |
: | Observability                   |      0:45 |
: | Bigger swings                   |      0:11 |
: | Skill logic                     |      0:45 |

That grouping is structural -- it comes from the epics being level-1 *headings*, not from any property. Flattening the tier into a label, which is the direction [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] proposes, removes the thing =:maxlevel 2= groups by. Clocktable has =:match= but no group-by-property, so the report above would have to be rebuilt rather than inherited. That is a real trade the cost analysis did not include, and it points the opposite way from the prefix-column finding.

*Column view cannot see a slice*

Pointed at [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]] with =%25ITEM %TODO %8CREATED %KIND=, the columnview block renders exactly *one* row: the slice heading itself. Its 23 members are =[[id:]]= links, and column view walks the *tree*. This is [[id:95c27fca-136c-46f6-b454-fe94261e0e5d][95c27fca]]'s problem one level up -- there, a slice is not recognised as a container; here, it is not traversable as one either. Any native lens that walks children is blind to a slice by construction, which is the price of declaring membership by reference.

Over a real *story* it works and rolls up correctly. [[id:edd47f32-e6c9-4ab3-8e8a-46a37ea29605][edd47f32]] with =%40ITEM %TODO %CLOCKSUM=:

: | Make the daily ceremony cheap enough that it actually runs    | TODO  |     0:19 |
: | Consolidation only reaches drawers an apply pass touches      | TODO  |          |
: | End every heading with two blank lines                        | NEXT  |          |
: | Prompt the daily ceremony automatically ...                   | DOING |     0:19 |

The parent's 0:19 is entirely [[id:aa1ba915-ee68-48df-afea-197ae60aac63][aa1ba915]]'s, summed by org.

*Sparse trees are the strongest result per unit of effort*

Against the 10,856-line file, =org-match-sparse-tree= leaves visible:

: research/-DONE      29 lines   (0.3%)
: TODO="NEXT"         23 lines   (0.2%)
: KIND="slice"        16 lines   (0.1%)

Better than 99.7% hidden in every case, in the buffer itself, with no agenda buffer and no configuration. This is the lens the founding "without the chords" argument most clearly applies to: it is one keystroke plus a query, and the query is the part a session can supply.

*org-ql already expresses a story, and the obvious spelling is wrong*

=--container-heading-p= finds 10 story headings. The natural org-ql translation =(and (todo) (children (todo)))= finds *8*; =(and (todo) (children (or (todo) (done))))= finds *9*. The exact equivalent is:

: (and (or (todo) (done)) (children (or (todo) (done))))

which returns 10. The two misses are real headings, not rounding: a story whose children are *all* finished (=[1/1] Clearing a buffer's read-only flag=) and a story that is itself =DONE= (=[3/3] Enforce org structural hygiene=). Worth recording because "org-ql can already do this" is true and the naive form silently under-reports -- which is [[id:6cc71c36-0fa6-4773-9b35-c0582f4cee82][6cc71c36]]'s pattern again.

*One measured cost, easily fixed*

=org-agenda-prefix-format='s todo entry is =" %i %-12:c"=, and 6 of the 9 level-1 titles are longer than 12 characters -- =Clock lifecycle & visibility= renders as =Clock lifecy=. Either the format widens or the titles shorten; it is a real cost of adopting the column, not a blocker.

*What this settles, and what it does not*

*Settled:* the lenses do earn their keep, and [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]]'s implied sequencing was backwards, as this heading predicted -- everything above ran against the structure exactly as it stands. Sparse trees and the clocktable are usable today with no changes whatsoever.

*Narrowed but not settled:* =:EPIC:= versus =:CATEGORY:=. The evidence cuts both ways and is now quantified rather than argued: =:CATEGORY:= wins on display and filtering, =:EPIC:= loses only matching and only until one variable is set, and *flattening either way* costs the grouped clock report. That last point is new and belongs in [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] before it resolves.

*Still open, and not answerable from here:* whether review attention wants its own datetree ([[id:961f15b6-d782-40b8-8ceb-ba086d188a3b][961f15b6]]). The clocktable above is a report someone would actually want, which was that heading's stated precondition -- but it groups by epic, so what it says about review time depends on where review time is clocked, not on how the table is built.

*The scripts are not archived.* Four probe scripts produced everything above and were left in the session scratch directory deliberately: they are throwaway instrumentation, and the numbers they produced are here. Anything worth re-running belongs in =bin/= as a real check, which is a separate decision.

The conventions went to =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md=; the ritual stayed; this is the backlog.

*The first pass is a backlog, not a cadence.* Clearing the existing 36 should not wait for the repeater -- the schedule is for the steady state afterwards. Re-measured 2026-08-24 against both terminal keywords: *36* closed headings in TODO.org, 35 =DONE= and 1 =CANCELLED=. (An earlier count of 30 was =DONE=-only, which is exactly the omission that makes a =DONE=-filtered sweep strand abandoned work.) [[id:4c0044bf-1b6c-44ea-807a-8f9e3523e3fd][4c0044bf]] made the same observation on 2026-08-07 at 13 headings and was cancelled partly for it.

*A direct cost, not housekeeping.* Those bodies are read into context by every session that opens the tracker, which is [[id:b07df584-3adc-433c-ab49-e104f88aecf7][b07df584]]'s complaint with a number attached.

*DECIDED 2026-08-21 by the user: sweep the old bodies into =:PLAN:= unedited.* The backlog does not get the faithful paring a newly written heading will; the existing body is wrapped as-is and the debrief written beneath it. That splits the migration into one mechanical step and one cheap one. *Wrapping* is now a tool -- =org_wrap_plan=, shipped 2026-08-24 -- and needs no judgement at all. The *debrief* is still per heading, but far cheaper than the [[id:cc0c17a7-a554-426d-afeb-09cbee7339f0][cc0c17a7]] trial suggested: the expensive judgement there was deciding what to *discard*, and sweeping discards nothing.

*Consequence, accepted rather than overlooked:* old drawers will be raw transcripts where new ones are pared plans. The ignore-the-drawer rule covers both, so the inconsistency is invisible in normal reading, and any heading touched again can be pared then.

*Why it stalls, and what changed.* CLAUDE.md requires a prose outcome summary on a =DONE= heading before it is archived, so this was never mechanical. That is still true and is the whole remaining cost -- but the two things that used to block it are gone: the wrapping tool exists, and the ordering it depends on is written down in the rules file rather than in a task body nobody would find.

*Sequence, from the rules file:* apply the queue, consolidate every drawer ([[id:7ae6562d-25c8-453e-b78b-920e036c5665][7ae6562d]]), then archive. Never archive first.

*Note the lint will start reporting these as they close.* =bin/lint-org= now warns when a heading closed on or after 2026-08-24 has a substantial body and no =:PLAN:= drawer. The 36 here are all closed before that date and are deliberately exempt, so the backlog stays silent rather than shouting 124 findings a day.

*Latent, not firing yet, and found 2026-08-24 by running the sweep rather than by reading the rule.*

[[id:8bcd56f4-22a8-4673-bad6-a99433027b81][8bcd56f4]]'s lint rule warns when a heading closed on or after 2026-08-24 has a substantial body and no =:PLAN:= drawer. It assumes every finished heading has a prospective half to wrap. *Six do not.*

Those six refused =org_wrap_plan= with =Seam marker is the first body line; nothing would be wrapped= -- their bodies are *entirely debrief*, written outcome-first since the convention landed. A heading written after the convention often has nothing to wrap, which is the convention working, not a heading missing a step.

*Only a threshold is keeping the rule quiet.* =--lint-substantial-body-p= requires ten prose lines and those six carry five to eight. A debrief-only heading with a longer outcome -- and this project writes long outcomes -- would warn, and the only way to satisfy the warning would be to wrap a debrief into a drawer readers are told to skip. That is the inversion the whole lifecycle exists to prevent, arrived at by obeying the lint.

*The signal already exists and is cheap.* =claude-code-ide-org--plan-seam='s "first body line" condition is exactly the test for "no prospective half", so the rule can ask before it warns rather than inferring from body length. A body whose first line is an outcome marker needs no drawer.

*Not fixed now* because it fires on nothing today, and a rule changed while quiet cannot be seen to improve. Worth doing before the next long-bodied heading closes.

*Shipped 2026-08-25* ([[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::5e6ab98][5e6ab98]]). A debrief-only heading can now answer the lint's question, by declaring that it has no prospective half: pass the debrief's first line as the seam and =org_wrap_plan= writes an *empty* =:PLAN:= drawer. The whole body stays visible.

*Two of this heading's own claims were wrong by the time it was worked, and both were measured rather than reasoned about.*

*First: the rule is not quiet.* It fires *seven* times today. "Latent, not firing yet" was true when filed on 2026-08-24 and stopped being true as headings closed after it. So the stated reason for deferring -- "a rule changed while quiet cannot be seen to improve" -- had already lapsed, and the change could be demonstrated instead of argued.

*Second, and more useful: the proposed signal is not reachable from the lint.* This body says =--plan-seam='s "first body line" condition *is* the test, "so the rule can ask before it warns". It cannot. =--plan-seam= takes a *marker* naming the debrief's first line, and the lint has no marker -- identifying where a debrief starts is the very judgement being asked for. Nothing was salvageable by moving the test into =bin/lint-org=.

*What the corpus said about inferring it instead.* Scanning every finished heading with a substantial body and no drawer: debrief-only bodies open =*Shipped ...*=, =*Found ...*=, =*Filed ...*=, =*Observed ...*= -- and bodies with a genuine prospective half open the same way, e.g. =*Two words, deliberately, and they are not synonyms.*= on [[id:8ca6541d-0fc7-45a2-a4d3-76e1608f658d][8ca6541d]] and =*A slice line renders its referent and declares almost nothing.*= on [[id:0acc1df2-6916-4180-867a-99bfa551806b][0acc1df2]]. A bold lead is not the discriminator, and no vocabulary of outcome verbs separates the two sets. Inference was the wrong shape, not merely inconvenient.

*So it is declared, which is what this project already does with every grouping it cannot derive.* The conventions file's own rule -- that inferring a declared thing is an error mirrored -- applies exactly here. Running the wrap *is* the declaration, and it lands where a marker actually exists.

*The lint needed no change at all*, which is the part worth noticing. It already asks the one right question -- is there a drawer? -- and what was missing was a way to answer "yes, and it is empty on purpose". No threshold was touched, so nothing else it reports moved.

*Uniqueness is still enforced under the new flag*, and a test pins it. =EMPTY-OK= relaxes only "there is nothing to wrap"; "the marker appears twice" and "the marker is absent" still error with it set. Without the flag the original refusal stands unchanged, so a caller that cannot represent the answer keeps refusing rather than silently producing an empty drawer.

*Verified end to end on a copy of the real corpus, not only in fixtures.* Seven =:PLAN:= warnings before, six after wrapping one debrief-only heading ([[id:49557477-e50c-496f-85df-82c65109832b][49557477]]), =Text preserved: yes=, and the debrief still first in the visible body. =bin/test= 399/399.

*The tests were proved to discriminate* by breaking =config.el= three ways on a copy: restoring the unconditional error failed both new tests and nothing else; dropping the flag at the call site failed only the wrap test; and letting =EMPTY-OK= swallow the ambiguity error failed the seam test and the pre-existing refusal test, which is the assertion that keeps the relaxation from becoming "never refuse anything".

*Live reload done and confirmed*, so this is not merely on disk: =(func-arity 'claude-code-ide-org--plan-seam)= reads =(3 . 4)= in the running Emacs and the MCP server is still on 45571.

*Not done here, and not this heading's work:* the seven headings currently warning are still warning. Wrapping them is the archive/ceremony backlog ([[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]], [[id:7fbab3b3-7843-4290-94a5-d421413f2be4][7fbab3b3]]); what this heading owed was a way for the debrief-only ones to be satisfiable at all.



**** DONE Apply consumes queue events with no way to roll one back :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-25 Tue 17:06]
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Apply
:ID:       21c91613-76e0-4590-affe-e2af9f1321ca
:CREATED:  [2026-08-24 Mon 19:08]
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:16
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Apply
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "NEXT"       from              [2026-08-24 Mon 19:08] \\
  cheap fix, found the hard way
CLOCK: [2026-08-25 Tue 16:58]--[2026-08-25 Tue 16:59] =>  0:01
- State "DOING"      from "NEXT"       [2026-08-25 Tue 16:58] \\
  starting the applied-at build
- [2026-08-25 Tue 16:58]--[2026-08-25 Tue 16:59] record apply time per consumed event
CLOCK: [2026-08-25 Tue 16:59]--[2026-08-25 Tue 17:06] =>  0:07
- [2026-08-25 Tue 16:59]--[2026-08-25 Tue 17:06] record apply time per consumed event
- State "DONE"       from "DOING"      [2026-08-25 Tue 17:06] \\
  applied-at shipped, 397/397, breaks proved
:END:

*Found 2026-08-24 while recovering from [[id:7148cddc-aca3-416e-8bcb-f164d4d2bba0][7148cddc]]*, which is the only reason it was noticed: nothing had ever needed to undo an apply before.

An apply writes to the org file *and* marks its events consumed in =<session>.applied=. The two are independent writes with nothing tying them together, so when the file has to be restored from git the queue still believes the work is done -- and the events are never offered again. Restoring the file alone silently discards them.

*No backup is written.* =git checkout HEAD -- TODO.org= is a one-keystroke undo for half the operation, and the other half has none. (A stray =2d057349-....applied.bak= exists in the queue directory from a hand-made copy months ago; nothing in the code produces one.)

*What the recovery actually required,* recorded because it is not obvious and had to be worked out under pressure: the applied set is a *set of event timestamps*, not a watermark, and carries no record of *when* each entry was consumed. So "un-apply the last pass" is not answerable from the file. It was reconstructed from a =org_pending_updates= report captured minutes before the bad apply -- 54 events, cut at 13:14:41.

*The obvious heuristic is wrong,* and nearly cost more than the incident. "Un-apply everything since the last commit" looked right and would have rolled back 85 events, because a *third* apply had landed at 16:42 and was already committed. Its work was correct and would have been re-offered and re-applied.

*Directions, none chosen:*

- *Write =<session>.applied.bak= before each apply,* one file, trivially restorable. Cheapest, and covers exactly the case that occurred.
- *Record the apply time alongside each consumed event* -- =("ts" . "applied-at")= rather than a bare list -- which makes "un-apply the pass of 17:17" answerable directly, and costs one field.
- *Make apply transactional with the file* -- attractive and much larger, since the file write is org's and spans several buffers.

The second is the one that would have made this recovery a single command instead of an archaeology exercise, and it is nearly free.

*The two recorded directions are no longer a toss-up, 2026-08-25, and the tie is broken by this heading's own incident rather than by preference.*

*A =.applied.bak= snapshot can only undo the **most recent** pass.* That is exactly the case the incident was *not*. The recovery record above says the obvious heuristic "un-apply everything since the last commit" would have rolled back 85 events instead of 54, "because a *third* apply had already landed at 16:42 and was already committed". A snapshot has the same shape of blind spot: it restores the ledger to a moment, and if anything landed after that moment, restoring it un-applies correct work too. The cheapest option is cheapest only for the failure that did not happen.

*Recording the apply time per consumed event answers the question that was actually asked under pressure.* "Un-apply the pass of 17:17" becomes a filter rather than a reconstruction. The recovery had to rebuild the consumed set from an =org_pending_updates= report captured minutes earlier, which is available by luck rather than by design.

*Its cost was re-checked against the file rather than assumed.* The ledger is =\{"applied": [ts, ts, ...]\}= -- a bare list of event timestamps, confirmed by reading it 2026-08-25 -- and it is rewritten wholesale on each apply. So pairing each entry with its apply time is one field and no new write path; the structure is already replaced every time.

*One data point on how often this bites, since it argues for doing the cheap thing well rather than urgently.* A pass failed the same day with "Applied 0 item(s); 1 failed" ([[id:c8a97d9d-8b13-4b6a-a8b9-1a3f24b5e00b][c8a97d9d]]), and the ledger was verified unchanged before and after -- so a failed *write* did not consume. The two-operation hazard is real but did not fire; what fired was a plain failure that rolled nothing forward.

*Still the user's decision.* This narrows it to one recommendation with the reasoning attached, rather than making it.

*Decided 2026-08-25 by the user: record the apply time alongside each consumed event.* =("ts" . "applied-at")= rather than a bare list. The =.applied.bak= snapshot is not taken, and the reasoning above is why -- it covers only the most recent pass, which is the case this heading's own incident was not.

*So this is no longer a decision, it is a build*, and the recovery record above is its requirements document rather than background. Two things it specifies that a fresh reading might otherwise miss: the applied set is a *set*, not a watermark, so nothing about ordering can be assumed from it; and the file is rewritten wholesale on each apply, which is why adding a field costs no new write path.

*The unit to record against is a pass, not an event.* "Un-apply the pass of 17:17" is the question that was actually asked under pressure, and it only becomes a filter if every event consumed in one apply carries the *same* stamp. A per-event =now= would make the values differ by milliseconds across a batch and answer a subtly different question.

*Sequenced first in the next session*, ahead of the ceremony work, on the grounds that it was carrying a decision and no longer is.

*Built 2026-08-25* ([[orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::4c18cc2][4c18cc2]]). =applied= is now a JSON object of =ts -> apply-time=, mirroring =dismissed= exactly, so both fields on this file share one serialization idiom rather than two that can drift. The stamp uses the queue's own =%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z= format, so an apply time and an event =ts= compare without conversion.

*The stamp is taken once per pass and pushed down*, as this heading specified. =--review-record-applied= computes it and passes it to =--queue-mark-applied=; a =now= taken inside the latter would differ across the sessions the former loops over, and would answer a subtly different question.

*Two edges the design did not name, both found by reading the callers and both now tested.* =--queue-mark-dismissed= round-trips =--queue-applied='s return straight back into the writer, so a reader that normalised its values to =t= would have erased every apply time the *first* time anything was dismissed -- and the ledger would have looked perfectly well-formed afterwards. And re-marking an already-consumed event now keeps its original stamp: the event was consumed once, by the pass named, and overwriting would rewrite the history the field exists to preserve.

*Legacy files read, and upgrade in place.* Every =.applied= on disk today holds a bare array; each such entry reads as =""=, never a fabricated time -- the same reasoning that retired the stale-clock guess (=7771fc63= in DONE.org). The upgrade needs no migration step because the file is rewritten wholesale on every apply, which is what made this cost one field and no new write path.

*Verified, not just implemented.* =bin/test= 397/397. The four new tests were then proved to discriminate by breaking =config.el= on a copy three ways and re-running: normalising the reader's values to =t= failed all four and nothing else; dropping the pass stamp from =--review-record-applied= failed only the one-stamp-per-pass test; letting a re-mark overwrite failed only the round-trip test. Consumers were checked before the shape changed -- =grep -rn '\.applied' bin/ .claude/hooks/= returns nothing, so every reader is elisp in this file.

*One test could not have discriminated as first written and was rewritten.* Stamps carry second resolution, so a per-session =now= and a per-pass one agree whenever a batch takes under a second -- which is always, in a test. It now stubs =format-time-string= and counts the calls, asserting the mechanism rather than a coincidence.

*Reload precondition, unmet at the time of writing.* =bin/test= spawns a fresh batch Emacs and loads =config.el= from disk, so the suite is real evidence. The user's *live* Emacs still holds the old definitions; the next real review pass writes the old bare-array shape until =config.el= is reloaded there. Nothing breaks either way -- the new reader accepts both -- but the field will be missing from that pass.
