*A slice line renders its referent and declares almost nothing.* =- [X] [[id:...][49557477]] DONE Expand an 8-character prefix ...= holds a link target, a keyword, a title and a checkbox -- and every one of the four is derivable from the referent. What the slice actually declares is *which* headings are members and *in what order*, which is exactly what a declared grouping should assert and nothing more.

*The checkbox maps from the referent's keyword, totally.* Four rows were given by the user; the rest follow the same logic and are marked as inferred rather than agreed:

| referent keyword          | checkbox  |                  |
|---------------------------+-----------+------------------|
| =DONE=                    | =[X]=     | given            |
| =CANCELLED=               | no cookie | given            |
| =DOING=, =REVIEW=         | =[-]=     | given            |
| =TODO=, =NEXT=            | =[ ]=     | inferred         |
| =PLANNING=, =WAITING=     | =[-]=     | inferred: work started, clock opened then closed |
| =MAYBE=                   | no cookie | inferred: deferral, same treatment as cancellation |

*So the tool is a pure regenerator and the lint rule collapses.* Walk each slice's checklist, resolve each =[[id:]]=, rewrite keyword, title and checkbox from the referent, leave the ordering and any trailing prose alone. Nothing needs to detect contradiction, because nothing independent is stored to contradict.

*The trigger is apply, not a schedule.* Applying the queue is the only thing that changes referents' keywords in bulk, so a slice is stale exactly when a review pass ends. That makes this a fifth step in the ceremony [[id:edd47f32-e6c9-4ab3-8e8a-46a37ea29605][edd47f32]] already sequences -- apply, consolidate, re-separate, archive -- and it inherits that sequence's argument: a normaliser recalled separately from the pass that disturbs the file is one that will drift.

/This heading first claimed the checkbox was slice judgement that a normaliser must not touch, and proposed lint warnings to catch contradictions between it and the referent. The user asked what there was to judge, and there was nothing./ /The claim was tested against all 22 members: 19 matched a pure keyword mapping and the three that did not were all mine --/ =edd47f32=, =e1284bdb= /and/ =961f15b6=, /each marked/ =[-]= /because I knew work had happened. A search for a second derivation rule for the parent case found none: org left parent checkboxes untouched in every configuration tried, including all-children-done./

*And the three mismatches were information about the referents, not about the slice*, which is the part worth keeping. [[id:e1284bdb-0a18-402a-81cb-1ac8d09fb8a2][e1284bdb]] is =NEXT= while its normaliser shipped 2026-08-24; [[id:961f15b6-d782-40b8-8ceb-ba086d188a3b][961f15b6]] is =TODO= while its design was written up in full. Both keywords under-report what happened. A hand-set =[-]= papered over that in the slice and made it invisible; a mechanical rule surfaces it as a question about the *referent's* keyword, which is where the fix belongs. That is an argument *for* the mapping, not a cost of it.

*Membership staleness needs nothing new.* A referent archived into DONE.org still resolves, since =org-id= spans files, and a deleted one already produces =bin/lint-org='s existing "id: link resolves to nothing" error -- which caught two fabricated links today.

*Rejected, with a reason, so it is not re-proposed:* a custom =slice:= link type whose =:activate-func= renders the referent's live keyword and title as display properties. Nothing would be stored, so nothing could go stale -- but it is honest only inside Emacs, and a =git diff=, a =grep= or a web view would see a bare id. This project keeps its files legible as plain text on purpose; that is the founding premise of the event queue.

*Already demonstrated twice.* [[id:46e4ce2b-fdc8-447b-ad09-b4845602540f][46e4ce2b]] was retitled *after* [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]] was drafted -- had it been a member, the slice would now carry a title that no longer exists anywhere.

*Measured 2026-08-25 by simulating the next apply on a copy*, in answer to the user asking whether a slice's checklist changes when its referents do. It does not, and the more useful half of the answer is that *nothing says so*.

Applying the two pending state changes to a copy of TODO.org leaves [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]] reading:

: - [ ] [[id:8ca6541d-0fc7-45a2-a4d3-76e1608f658d][8ca6541d]] TODO Compose slices by reference: ...

against a referent that is now =DONE=. Three stored facts are wrong at once -- the checkbox, the copied keyword, and the =[9/21]= cookie -- and both available checks stay quiet:

- =bin/lint-org= is silent. Its slice rule compares =:BLOCKER:= against the *checkbox list*, and both are unchanged, so they still agree. It has no rule comparing a checkbox against its *referent*, which is the axis that drifts.
- =org-update-statistics-cookies= is silent too, and necessarily: it recomputes the cookie from the checkboxes, and the checkboxes did not change. Org agrees with =[9/21]= because org is answering a different question.

*So the slice is at its most misleading precisely after a review pass*, which is the moment someone is most likely to read it -- and it is misleading in the flattering direction, showing less progress than exists rather than more.

*The =:BLOCKER:= needs no refresh in this case*, worth stating so the manual repair is not cargo-culted. A member going =DONE= keeps its cookie, so the blocker set is unchanged and org-depend simply stops blocking on a finished id. The refresher is only needed when a member's cookie is *deleted* -- cancellation or deferral -- which changes the set.

*Manual repair until this is built:* tick the box, correct the copied keyword, and let =C-c C-c= recompute the cookie.

*This strengthens the case for the trigger being apply rather than a schedule.* The staleness is not gradual; it is created in one step, by one command, at a known moment.



**** DONE A container entering DOING when a child does is nowhere written down :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-25 Tue 16:17]
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Skill
:ID:       241a4c54-ed59-4780-b602-2a86efee978a
:CREATED:  [2026-08-19 Wed 19:24]
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:16
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Skill
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-08-25 Tue 16:17] \\
  codified by the DOING recalibration
:END:

Asked by the user 2026-08-19 of
[[id:aded703f-8110-439e-b470-5e0375121c95][aded703f]], which should have
entered DOING the moment its first child did and did not: /"is that not
codified anywhere?"/ It is not. Verified by grep across =CLAUDE.md=, the
path-scoped rules and the org skill — the transition table governs a
heading's own state and clock, and nothing mentions a container reacting
to a child at all.

*Why it is not merely an omission.* Writing it down collides with the
rule immediately below the table: /any transition to DOING must open a
clock/. A container must /not/ open one —
=claude-code-ide-org--container-heading-p= exempts containers from
auto-clock-in precisely because a parent's own CLOCK line lands inside
the total org already rolls up from its children, measured on
[[id:b5f7c5c7-7ad6-4c68-9cce-3479db1f1644][b5f7c5c7]] as a parent
claiming 14:52 against children summing 13:44.

So the rule cannot be stated as "a container goes DOING like anything
else". It needs its own clause: a container enters DOING when its first
child does, *without* a clock, and leaves it when no child is active.

*Unclear, and worth deciding before writing it:* whether leaving is
symmetric. A container whose children are all DONE is finished; one whose
children are all WAITING is blocked, not done, and DOING would be a lie.
Also whether this should be a hook at all — it is mechanical enough for
=org-trigger-hook=, which already carries two sibling-state triggers, and
unlike "is this conversation about that task" it needs no judgement.

Backdated by hand this time, which the queue cannot express: it stamps an
event when written, not when it was true. =--format-log-state-line= now
takes an optional TIME for exactly this.

*Proposed by the user 2026-08-20, and it dissolves this heading's problem rather than solving it.* Scope the clock rule to leaves: *a clock opens when a leaf enters DOING, and only then.* A container may then enter DOING freely, because DOING on a container no longer means \"I am working on this\" — it means \"something is happening inside\", and costs nothing.

This is better than the exception it replaces. The rule currently reads \"any transition to DOING must open a clock\" with a container carve-out bolted on ([[id:517a4290-4c66-43e7-b42e-dad7167b9c41][517a4290]] exists because CLAUDE.md never grew that carve-out). Scoping to leaves removes the carve-out: there is one rule, and containers simply are not in its domain. =claude-code-ide-org--container-heading-p= already exists and the auto-clock-in trigger already consults it, so most of the code is written.

*Leaving condition, settled:* all children DONE or CANCELLED. Terminal, machine-checkable, no judgement.

*The WAITING propagation as stated over-triggers, and this is the one part to change before implementing.* The proposal was \"when any child is WAITing then the parent should be also WAITing.\" But a container with one WAITING child and two DOING children is not blocked — work is happening inside it, which is exactly what DOING on a container was just defined to mean. Marking it WAITING would assert the opposite. The rule that carries the intent is *every non-terminal child is WAITING* — nothing inside can progress. The two readings coincide whenever a container has a single unfinished child, which is probably why \"any\" felt right; they diverge as soon as it has two.

*One caveat worth naming, not blocking.* Containment is emergent, so a heading clocked as a leaf can later acquire TODO children and become a container. Its own historical CLOCK lines then sit inside a subtree that also rolls up its children's — the [[id:b5f7c5c7-7ad6-4c68-9cce-3479db1f1644][b5f7c5c7]] double-count in miniature. The lines are honest records of real work; the risk is only in how a clocktable totals them.

*Accepted by the user 2026-08-20:* the WAITING propagation rule is *every non-terminal child is WAITING*, not "any child". Implement that reading; the "any" wording above is recorded only so the distinction is not re-litigated.

So the full rule set, settled and ready to be written down:

1. A clock opens when a *leaf* enters DOING, and only then.
2. A container may enter DOING to mean "something is happening inside", at no clock cost.
3. A container leaves DOING when all children are DONE or CANCELLED.
4. A container is WAITING when every non-terminal child is WAITING.

*Codified 2026-08-25, and this heading was not consulted while it happened* -- which is the part worth recording.

*The answer, now in CLAUDE.md beside the transition table.* =DOING= on a container means "at least one member is in the mail" -- one level up from the leaf sense of "started and owed a return". It takes no clock, is plural, and is derivable from the members rather than asserted. =--trigger-auto-clock-in= already implements the no-clock half by exempting containers; the gap is that a slice is not recognised as one ([[id:95c27fca-136c-46f6-b454-fe94261e0e5d][95c27fca]]).

*So the question this heading asked -- "is that not codified anywhere?" -- now has the answer "yes", and it got there by a route that never mentioned this heading.* The recalibration was driven by a conversation about what =DOING= should mean, written into CLAUDE.md, the org skill and [[id:c954f650-b92f-4920-9967-ab6c44577b30][c954f650]], and this heading sat open through all of it asking for exactly that.

*Found only when the user asked whether =org_outline= should have been used*, which is the lesson rather than the outcome. The preceding search had been =grep= for ids already in mind, and a search like that can only return what the searcher already remembers. One =org_outline= call with =active_only= surfaced this heading immediately. CLAUDE.md says to start there and gives the reason; the reason is not compactness, it is that the index shows what you were not looking for.

*The collision this heading warned about did not materialise, and that is worth stating since it was the reason for hesitating.* Writing it down was said to collide with the transition table's per-heading framing. It did not: the table now carries a note that it describes a heading acting for itself, and the container sense sits beside it as a separate paragraph rather than as another row.

- State "CANCELLED"  from "TODO"       [2026-08-25 Tue 14:12] \\
  tag was a manual edit, not a writer
:END:

*Observed 2026-08-25.* [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]]'s tag line became =:code:slice:blocked:=. The =slice= tag was written deliberately; =blocked= was not written by anything in this repo -- =grep '"blocked"'= over =config.el= returns nothing.

*Not reproduced, and that is the state of knowledge rather than a conclusion.* It entered in =ed2aca6=, the commit that tagged the slice and ran =claude-code-ide-org-refresh-slice-blocker= against the *live* Emacs. Two candidates were tested in batch and both cleared: =org-depend-tag-blocked-tasks= is void, and =org-entry-blocked-p= leaves =org-get-tags= untouched and was verified to do so on a fixture. So the writer is something loaded in the live session that =emacs --batch -Q= does not load.

*Why it matters more than one stray tag.* Blocked-ness is *derivable* -- =org_outline= computes it per read, and =org-entry-blocked-p= answers it on demand. A tag is *stored*. The moment the last blocker finishes, a stored tag says "blocked" about a heading that is not, and nothing in this repo would notice: the tag is undeclared in =#+TAGS:=, =bin/lint-org= is silent about it, and no test covers it. That is the same second-copy-that-can-disagree failure the slice design spent this session eliminating from checkboxes and blocker lists, arriving from outside the design.

*Left in place deliberately.* Removing it without knowing the writer would most likely see it return on the next operation, and the churn would be a worse signal than the tag. Find the writer first.

*Two ways it could resolve, and they point opposite directions.* If a package is maintaining it *correctly* -- adding and removing in step -- it is a useful visible marker and should be declared in =#+TAGS:= and left alone. If it is write-only, it is a bug and should be turned off rather than linted around.

*Cancelled 2026-08-25, hours after being filed.* The user identified the tag as inadvertent -- a side effect of hand-drafting the slice heading in Emacs -- and deleted it along with the others. There is no writer to find, so the heading's premise is withdrawn rather than answered.

*The evidence is consistent with that and was not consistent with much else.* Two mechanical candidates had already been tested and cleared in batch: =org-depend-tag-blocked-tasks= is void, and =org-entry-blocked-p= leaves =org-get-tags= untouched on a fixture. The tag entered during a window in which the user was editing the same heading by hand. Direct knowledge beats an unreproduced hypothesis.

*What was actually right here survives elsewhere, and is worth separating from the wrong part.* The reasoning -- that a *derived* fact written down is a second copy that can silently disagree with the thing it derives from -- was sound; it was aimed at the wrong instance. It is the same argument that removed judgement from slice checkboxes and made =:BLOCKER:= a regenerated list, and it now applies to the tag mechanism as a whole.

*Because the tags went with it, and that had a sharper consequence than the tag itself.* =--slice-p= detected a slice by a =slice= tag, so deleting the tags left [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]] undetected and the new =:BLOCKER:= lint assertion *silently inert* -- =bin/lint-org= reported zero errors because nothing was a slice, which is indistinguishable from nothing being wrong. The detector is now a =:KIND: slice= property, and the episode is recorded on [[id:8ca6541d-0fc7-45a2-a4d3-76e1608f658d][8ca6541d]], whose tag proposal it falsifies.

CLOSED: [2026-08-25 Tue 12:56]
:PROPERTIES:

- [2026-08-25 Tue 12:36]--[2026-08-25 Tue 12:45] assigned at review

- [2026-08-25 Tue 12:50]--[2026-08-25 Tue 13:00] assigned at review
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-08-25 Tue 12:56] \\
  blocker half and lint assertion built
:END:

*Two words, deliberately, and they are not synonyms.* A *story* is a parent heading whose children are the work -- declared by refiling things under it, and able to span epics only once [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] makes categories a label rather than a place. A *slice* names its members *by reference* and sequences them, so it can pick a whole story or one task inside one, and needs nothing moved. This heading is about the slice; where "story" appears below it means the parent-heading sense.

*A slice is a fourth heading class, and that -- not the slice -- is the finding.* The user's point 2026-08-21, made in the vocabulary of the time, when this object was still called a story: "story" becomes another category, qualified by its members having a particular structure, which deserves its own convention-enforcement definition. Taking it seriously exposes a pattern this project has been repeating without naming.

Four classes exist, each detected by a *different, bespoke* mechanism, and not one of them declared:

| class             | detected by                                  | asserted of it                                          |
|-------------------+----------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------|
| category          | heading *level* (= 1)                        | no =:ID:=, no =:CREATED:=, no keyword, no tags; has =:ARCHIVE:= |
| container / epic  | =--container-heading-p=, a descendant scan   | carries a statistics cookie                             |
| datetree node     | =--datetree-node-role=, position *plus* a title regex | day node carries =:ID:= and =:CREATED:=            |
| slice             | -- nothing yet --                            | checkbox list of id links; blocker ids match those links; cookie present |

A level test, a descendant scan, and a position-and-regex test: three answers to one question, and a fourth class would need a fourth. That is a sharper argument for [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] than either overload of heading level -- the problem is not that depth carries too much, it is that there is *no way to say what kind a heading is*, so every class invents its own tell. Verified 2026-08-21: no =:KIND:=, =:TYPE:= or equivalent property exists anywhere in this repo.

*And a slice cannot be emergent, which is the substantive break from the container.* =--container-heading-p= can *derive* container-ness because "has a TODO-carrying descendant" is an unambiguous structural fact. "Has a checkbox list of id links" is not -- an ordinary body may hold one for reference, and inferring slice-ness from it would misclassify. So the slice class must be *declared*. That does not contradict the emergent/declared dichotomy; it is that dichotomy doing its job, and it is why epics stay derived while slices are marked.

*A tag is the likely mechanism, and it is already sanctioned.* =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= holds that tags are free-form beyond the four declared, so =#+TAGS:= gains one word. A tag is also natively agenda-matchable (=+story=), which is exactly what [[id:82df2a6c-881d-4117-a752-5b3b04c9656d][82df2a6c]] exists to evaluate -- so choosing it would put a first real query in front of that heading rather than a hypothetical one. One detail to check rather than assume: =org-use-tag-inheritance= defaults to =t= and is unset in the Doom config, so a slice's tag would be inherited by any subheading it ever acquired. Harmless while slices have no children by design, but it is the shape that bites later.

*The enforcement definition belongs in =bin/lint-org=*, beside the category, container-cookie and datetree rules it already carries -- not in [[id:d2a0f54c-b59a-4855-ae3d-c93a6d3aa177][d2a0f54c]]'s proposed =bin/check-conventions=. That split is [[id:3bd3402b-3ab6-4ace-b20b-3ff84caa3fb2][3bd3402b]]'s: check-conventions checks claims *about* the system, =bin/lint-org= checks the org files' *own* structure. A slice's qualification is the latter.

*This heading's premise is conditional, and the condition is [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]]* -- established by the user 2026-08-25, and it changes what this is about rather than whether it is right.

The reasoning above is sound *given today's structure*: "a story whose members sit in different categories cannot be expressed without moving a heading across a category boundary". That constraint exists only because categories are *structural* -- a level-1 heading is a place, so belonging to one means living there.

29439196 removes it at the root. Flatten the categories into a label carried by a heading rather than a place it lives, and a *story becomes an ordinary parent heading that can span epics*. It stops needing composition by reference, because refiling stops being the cost.

*What still needs by-reference composition is a slice,* and that is a different object than this heading describes. A slice picks off open work *at either level* -- a whole story, or one task inside one -- and *sequences it intentionally*. Its members already live somewhere, its ordering is the payload, and the same task may appear in one slice and not the next. A checkbox list of id links fits that exactly, and fits a story only as a workaround for structure that 29439196 proposes to remove.

*The prototype exists, and it is [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]].* Built 2026-08-25 under =* Slices=: twenty members as =[[id:]]= links in a checkbox list, a =:COOKIE_DATA: checkbox recursive= property so the cookie counts nested members, cancelled members with their cookie *deleted* so they neither count nor inflate, and one =orgit-rev:= link per revision of the prompt that drove it. Its body carries the composition rules inline -- membership, checkbox derivation, why several plan links rather than one -- so read it rather than re-deriving them here. The convention extracted from it lives in =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md=.

*The title's "stories" became "slices" on 2026-08-25*, at the user's instruction, and this paragraph is what it replaced. Asked directly earlier the same day whether the current parlance already made it "slices", the answer was measured from corpus usage and came back *no*: 33 uses of "story" against 5 loose uses of "slice", with the tiers naming "level 1 epic, level 2 story, level 3". That measurement was accurate about established usage and blind to an intended model being revised -- *frequency cannot see where a word is going*, which is the lesson worth keeping and the reason the wrong answer is recorded rather than deleted.

*The sequencing claim was falsified by events, not by argument.* It read: "Building this first delivers by-reference composition for stories and then discovers that stories no longer need it while slices do. 29439196 is upstream: decide flattening, and this heading's scope follows from the answer."

*A working slice shipped 2026-08-25 with flattening undecided*, which is the falsification. [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]] is upstream of *stories* -- a story is a parent heading, so it needs categories to stop being places before it can span epics. It is not upstream of *slices*, because a slice never moves anything: its members stay where they live and it names them. The gating was inherited from the story framing and did not survive the split.

*So what remains here is scoped to slices*, and three of its four parts are now settled elsewhere: composition is prototyped ([[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]]), rendering is designed ([[id:0acc1df2-6916-4180-867a-99bfa551806b][0acc1df2]]), and the predicate problem is measured and filed ([[id:95c27fca-136c-46f6-b454-fe94261e0e5d][95c27fca]]). What is genuinely unbuilt is the =:BLOCKER:= half -- a slice that refuses DONE until its members finish -- and the lint assertion that its blocker ids and its checkbox ids are the same set.

*Unaffected:* the fourth-heading-class finding above. Flattening removes one bespoke detector -- heading level -- which makes the inconsistency smaller without answering how a story or a slice declares itself.

Proposed by the user 2026-08-21, as what flattening the categories ([[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]]) would enable. A *slice* is a composite task whose members are named *by reference* -- a checkbox list of =[[id:]]= links -- rather than contained as children. No nested copies at a lower level; tasks keep their own subtasks exactly as now.

*Why the archive orders it correctly for free.* Archiving files by =CLOSED= (measured on 29439196), and a slice cannot close before its members, so it lands *later* in the datetree than everything it references. The archive then reads as narrative: the constituent work, then the slice summarising it. Day-granular only -- within one day node entries append in archive order, not by =CLOSED= time.

*Two halves are already native, verified 2026-08-21:*
- A headline =[/]= cookie *counts body checkboxes*, not just TODO children -- =* TODO A slice [/]= over three items became =[1/3]= with no children present. So progress is visible and self-maintaining, and =bin/lint-org='s container-cookie rule is satisfiable.
- =:BLOCKER: ids(...)= already refuses DONE until every named id is finished, via =org-depend=, which this project loads. "Closes only once its checklist completes" therefore needs no new machinery -- it is the blocker list.

*What was recorded here as "one gap, and it is the whole build" -- that nothing ticks a checkbox when the referenced heading closes -- dissolved rather than being solved.* The premise was that a checkbox is independent state something must maintain. It is not: every field on a slice line, the checkbox included, is *derived* from the referent's keyword, so nothing ticks anything and the line is re-rendered instead. =:TRIGGER:= was read from =org-depend.el= and confirmed to act on headings by id with no checkbox facility, which was accurate and is now beside the point.

*The seam identified here was right, though*, and survives into the design: the apply path is where it belongs, because applying the queue is the only thing that changes referents' keywords in bulk ([[id:0acc1df2-6916-4180-867a-99bfa551806b][0acc1df2]]).

*This answers 29439196's own objection to the shape.* That heading's membership table calls a container-declared link list the *drifting* form, "one edit point nobody revisits". Two things change that here. The blocker list is the machine-readable half and the checkbox list the human half, so neither carries the burden alone; and a lint assertion that the two id sets *match* makes disagreement loud rather than silent. =bin/lint-org= already validates that every =:BLOCKER:= resolves and would actually block, so this is one more assertion in an existing harness rather than a new guard.

*Emergent vs declared, reconciled rather than contradicted.* The epic stays emergent -- a subtree that acquired TODO-carrying children, detected by =claude-code-ide-org--container-heading-p=. The slice is explicitly *declared*. Separating them stops one mechanism serving two masters: today a container is simultaneously "what happened to grow children" and "what you would want to slice by", and those are rarely the same set.

*Consequence for the predicates, which must not be missed -- and was not.* =--container-heading-p= scans descendants for TODO keywords, so a slice holding only checkboxes is *not* a container by that test, making it eligible for auto-clock-in and for auto-promotion to NEXT -- precisely the defect [[id:42808717-2736-4bf4-872e-887f990203ca][42808717]] fixed for containers. Confirmed on the first real slice rather than left as a prediction: =(:container-p nil :auto-clock-in t :would-clock t)=. Filed as [[id:95c27fca-136c-46f6-b454-fe94261e0e5d][95c27fca]], which also records the sharper form of the problem -- the predicate tests a mechanism ("has keyworded descendants") while its callers want a meaning ("is a grouping whose time lives elsewhere"), and a slice is the first case where those two part.

*Closely related and not a duplicate:* [[id:9651d4c8-6887-4b0a-91d9-562c3bc49a75][9651d4c8]] asks which of a container's children were in its original plan. A declared slice answers that question by construction, since membership is written rather than inferred from what accumulated.

*Built 2026-08-25.* The two halves this heading still owed after the prototype -- a slice that refuses DONE until its members finish, and an assertion that its two member lists agree -- both shipped. 389 tests, 0 lint errors.

*The declaration mechanism is the tag proposed above*, unchanged: =#+TAGS:= gains =slice=, and =claude-code-ide-org--slice-p= tests the heading's *own* tags via =(org-get-tags nil t)=. The inheritance caveat recorded above was checked rather than assumed -- =org-use-tag-inheritance= is =t= live -- and the local-only test is what neutralises it, with a test asserting a tagged grandchild does not make its parent a slice.

*Blocker ids are the members that still carry a cookie, and that identity is the design.* A member whose cookie was deleted is cancelled or deferred, and deferral is the case that forced the rule: a deferred member is *unfinished*, so blocking on it would hold the slice open forever for work it explicitly decided not to do. Cookie and blocker are therefore the same set by construction, which is exactly what the lint asserts -- =seq-difference= both ways, since an implementation comparing one direction only would pass the other.

*The lint is an error, not a warning.* The correct value is computable from the body, so a mismatch is never a judgement call, and the message names the command that fixes it. Blast radius was measured before the rule was allowed to matter: with nothing tagged it fired on zero, and it grows only as slices are declared.

*Verified end to end on the real file rather than only in fixtures.* Tagging [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]] produced the error naming all 20 members; refreshing produced =:blocked-p t= with 20 blocker ids; adding a twenty-first member re-broke the lint within one command, and the refresher fixed it. That round trip is the answer to [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]]'s objection that a link list is "one edit point nobody revisits" -- nobody has to revisit it, and nobody can forget to.

*One bug, found by the data and worth recording because the tests would not have caught it unaided.* The first parser treated an empty =[ ]= as an absent cookie, so the first real run proposed 12 blocker ids instead of 20. An unstarted member still blocks; only a *deleted* cookie does not. The fixture now carries all five member shapes -- ticked, unstarted, nested, cookie-deleted, and an =orgit-rev:= revision link that is a cookie-less list item but not a member -- and reintroducing the bug fails exactly three tests.

*Not included, and filed rather than forgotten:* teaching =--container-heading-p= about slices, which this heading correctly warned would otherwise reintroduce [[id:42808717-2736-4bf4-872e-887f990203ca][42808717]]. Measured on the prototype and filed as [[id:95c27fca-136c-46f6-b454-fe94261e0e5d][95c27fca]].

*Where =:KIND:= came from, asked by the user 2026-08-25 because it had only ever been argued in a commit message.* That is the real defect the question exposed: a vocabulary decision was made in passing while fixing something else, and never written where anyone would meet it.

*It was taken from this heading, but from the wrong sentence.* The line above reads "Verified 2026-08-21: no =:KIND:=, =:TYPE:= or equivalent property exists anywhere in this repo" -- a statement of what is *missing*, offered as evidence for the four-heading-classes finding. This heading's actual *proposal* was a tag. So =:KIND:= was not invented, but neither was it proposed; the tag was tried, failed within an hour, and the name was reached for from the sentence that had named the gap.

*Why not =:CATEGORY:=, which is the obvious org-native candidate.* Because it is already spoken for, by [[id:29439196-bbb8-4b64-b8d5-3bf9d457bf6c][29439196]], whose membership table assigns it to *epic assignment*: "a *label* -- tag or =:CATEGORY:= -- carried by headings, not a place they live". That is the same mechanism the user described leaning toward, and 29439196 has already verified it works here, including inheritance by a level-3 grandchild.

*Sharing the property would make it undecidable.* If epics are categories, then reading =:CATEGORY: X= you cannot tell whether =X= names an epic or a kind. That is one mechanism serving two masters, which is the failure this heading's own four-classes table exists to name -- arriving from the other direction, by *merging* detectors rather than by multiplying them.

*And the two answer different questions.* A category says what a heading is *about*, or where it belongs. A kind says what sort of thing it *is*. A slice belongs to no epic by design, since it cuts across them, while it certainly *is* a slice -- so the one property that would be empty for a slice is exactly the one being proposed to carry its declaration.

*Inheritance points the same way, though it is the weakest of the three reasons.* Org inherits =:CATEGORY:= down a subtree by design. That is the latent hazard already recorded here for tags, and =:KIND:= avoids it by being read with =org-entry-get= without the inherit flag.

*Reversible if the user prefers otherwise*: the detector is one =equal= in =claude-code-ide-org--slice-p=, plus fixtures in four tests.



**** CANCELLED Snapshot the next-session.md that drove each slice, the way plans are archived :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-25 Tue 11:46]
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Slices
:ID:       637ee73d-e1b7-4a84-9213-830c49a400b4
:CREATED:  [2026-08-25 Tue 11:10]
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:16
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Slices
:ARCHIVE_TODO: CANCELLED
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "TODO"       from              [2026-08-25 Tue 11:10] \\
  first snapshot taken by hand; the mechanism is not built
- State "CANCELLED"  from "TODO"       [2026-08-25 Tue 11:46] \\
  superseded by orgit revision links
:END:

*=.claude/commands/next-session.md= is reused in place*, rewritten once per slice, so the text that drove slice N is overwritten when slice N+1 is planned. The first snapshot was taken by hand on 2026-08-25 -- =slices/2026-08-24-harden-the-review-pass.md=, linked from [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]]. Nothing automates it, and nothing notices when it drifts.

*The analogy to =bin/sync-plans= is close but the reason is different, and getting that backwards would misdesign it.* =plans/= exists because =~/.claude/plans= is *outside the repo* and would otherwise have no history at all. =next-session.md= is inside the repo and already has ten commits of history, so history is not what is missing. What is missing is *identity*: a stable, immutable path a slice heading can link, so "the plan that drove this slice" is a link rather than an archaeology exercise through commits that all touch the same path.

*What carries over unchanged* is the membership rule, which is the part of =sync-plans= worth copying: a file belongs to the archive iff some org heading links it. That keeps the directory from accumulating and makes an unlinked snapshot visible rather than silently included.

*What differs*: the copy is taken at slice *close* rather than continuously, since a slice's plan is edited throughout its life and only the final text is the record of what drove it. That makes =--check= mean something different too -- not "the archive is stale" but "a closed slice links a snapshot that does not exist, or a live one has none yet".

*Open:* whether =.githooks/pre-push= should refuse a push on that, as it does for plans. The plan case is stricter because the source can vanish with a home directory; here the source is committed, so a missing snapshot loses ordering and attribution, not content.

*Cancelled 2026-08-25, hours after being filed*, superseded by a better answer to the same problem: a slice links =orgit-rev:= commits instead of a copied file, and links *several* of them -- one per revision of the prompt.

*The reason it was cancellable is the finding this heading itself recorded.* It argued that the =plans/= analogy was imperfect because =next-session.md= already has history and what it lacks is *identity*. An =orgit-rev:= link is exactly identity and nothing else: this path, at this commit, resolvable through Magit. Once that was said out loud, the copy under =slices/= was doing no work that the link does not do better, and it brought a sync script, a =--check= mode, a drift definition and a pre-push question along with it. All of that existed to keep a copy honest, and the copy was the part that was not needed.

*Two things the link form gains that the copy could not.* A slice can carry *many* links rather than one, so the evolution of the plan across a slice's life is legible instead of collapsed into its final text. And because a slice can then span sessions -- a CLI restart or a cleared context is a revision, not a new slice -- there is far less pressure to defer unfinished members into a successor slice, which was proliferating mentions of tasks that were planned and never reached the top of the stack.

*=slices/= was removed in the same commit*, its single snapshot replaced by the four =orgit-rev:= links now on [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]]. Nothing is lost: the file is recoverable from any commit, which was always true and is the reason the copy was redundant.



**** DONE Every orgit link a body adds costs a permanent lint warning :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-25 Tue 11:46]
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Dev
:ID:       43201e64-3fe8-4fa6-81f5-d2ab5b65d191
:CREATED:  [2026-08-21 Fri 16:07]
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:16
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Dev
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
CLOCK: [2026-08-21 Fri 17:11]--[2026-08-21 Fri 17:17] =>  0:06
- [2026-08-21 Fri 17:11]--[2026-08-21 Fri 17:17] assigned at review
- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-08-25 Tue 11:46] \\
  stub link types registered in the lint
:END:

The commit-reference convention shipped 2026-08-21 ([[id:7b54c439-ab2c-4398-b332-2b2cc0d98ac9][7b54c439]]) says to link commits in org bodies as =orgit-rev:=. Its *first actual use* -- one link on [[id:3063c3e5-0dd0-4354-8985-271b0313c5d1][3063c3e5]] the same evening -- pushed =bin/lint-org= from 23 warnings to 24: =org-lint: Unknown fuzzy location "orgit-rev:claude-code-ide-org::f0cdc90"=. The two earlier occurrences in TODO.org are inside =verbatim= markup and are never parsed as links, so nothing had exercised the convention until now.

*Cause.* =orgit= is a Doom package present in the live Emacs, but =bin/lint-org= runs =emacs --batch -Q= with only org and =config.el= loaded. With no =orgit-rev= link type registered, org-lint falls back to treating it as a fuzzy internal link and cannot resolve it.

*Why it matters more than one warning.* The cost is per-link and permanent, so following a documented convention makes the report grow monotonically -- and a report that accumulates stops being read, which is the exact failure [[id:5ff5a4b8-2fee-472a-b5e1-c9de8cf96704][5ff5a4b8]] measured and the lint's own error/warn split exists to prevent. Candidate fixes, none chosen: load orgit in the lint's =emacs_args=, register the link type with a stub =org-link-set-parameters=, or filter this org-lint check. The first is honest but adds a package dependency to a batch script that deliberately has none.

*Fixed 2026-08-25* by the second of the three candidates recorded above -- registering the link types with a stub =org-link-set-parameters= in =bin/lint-org=, rather than loading orgit or filtering the check. 29 warnings to 28, and zero =orgit= matches in the report.

*The first candidate was rejected on the reason this heading already gave.* =(require 'orgit)= would drag magit into a batch script that deliberately carries no package dependencies, to buy nothing the lint uses: org-lint does not need the link to *work*, only to know the scheme exists so it stops guessing the location is fuzzy. The stub is three lines and registers =orgit-rev=, =orgit-log= and =orgit-status= together, so the two link types nothing has used yet are covered before their first use rather than after.

*Guarded with =unless (assoc type org-link-parameters)=*, so the stub can never clobber a real registration if the lint's environment ever does load orgit.

*Forced by [[id:c44c2119-dbf8-4510-99e2-6aaa7f259d94][c44c2119]] rather than chosen*, which is worth recording because this heading predicted it. It was filed as "small; worth doing before the convention is used much more", and sat unworked for four days. The slice's revision-link design adds four orgit links at once and one per slice thereafter, so the monotonic growth this heading warned about arrived as a concrete number the same afternoon the design was proposed.

:PROPERTIES:

:ID:       df1cf43c-749f-435c-9f45-3d8df1d725ad

CLOCK: [2026-08-24 Mon 19:50]--[2026-08-24 Mon 19:53] =>  0:03
- [2026-08-24 Mon 19:50]--[2026-08-24 Mon 19:53] assigned at review
- State "DONE"       from              [2026-08-24 Mon 19:51] \\
  instrumentation shipped and tested
:END:

*Shipped 2026-08-24* (=f1dcec9=), and filed after the fact -- the user asked for a heading and got one only for its sibling proposal, which is its own small instance of the same defect.

*The measurement.* An apply reported:

: Applied 0 item(s); 5 failed: Error: Before first headline at position 1 in buffer TODO.org; Error: Before first headline...

Five times, identically. Every word true. Between them they identified *nothing* -- not which heading, not which kind of item, not which timestamp, not where in the stack. Three hypotheses were raised and withdrawn against that message before anyone could act on it, and the state that produced it was gone by the time it could be probed.

*Why the information was thrown away, which is the part worth keeping.* =--at-id= converts every error to a string, deliberately: that is what lets a caller report a failure without unwinding a whole batch. But conversion happens at the boundary where the stack still exists and the caller's identity is still known, and both were discarded there. The design decision was right; the *lossiness* was incidental to it.

*What shipped.* =--at-id= records =--last-error-backtrace= -- =(:id :message :backtrace)= -- on every conversion. =--review-apply= snapshots it per item and annotates each failure with the item's type, short id and timestamp, so the report reads =[state ff92700e 15:56]=. The stack goes to =*Messages*= rather than into the returned string, because the return value is rendered in the review buffer where a stack would bury the summary.

*An item with no =:ID:= identifies itself as "unassigned"* rather than erroring. That case is not hypothetical: the five failures could each have been an unassigned span, and a describer assuming an id would have replaced a bad diagnosis with none.

*One real mistake, recorded because it was nearly shipped.* The first draft used =condition-case-unless-debug=, which broke four existing tests -- ERT binds =debug-on-error=, so errors stopped being converted at all. =--at-id='s contract is that it *always* converts; the capture had to be additive, not a change to when it catches. The suite caught it in one run.

*Still unverified against the original failure.* By the time the instrumentation was live, the five items had been dismissed as stale -- the partial applies had moved their headings to the states the events described. So the message that motivated this has never been seen through it, and the underlying cause of "Before first headline at position 1" remains unknown.



**** DONE The promotion trigger re-entered itself; one apply made 1201 mutations :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-24 Mon 19:07]
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Apply
:ID:       7148cddc-aca3-416e-8bcb-f164d4d2bba0
:CREATED:  [2026-08-24 Mon 19:07]
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:16
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Apply
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "DONE"       from              [2026-08-24 Mon 19:07] \\
  guard shipped, cascade cannot recur
:END:

*Shipped 2026-08-24* (=7c7d992=), filed after the fact because the incident is worth keeping even though the fix took twenty minutes.

*What happened.* A single apply of ~12 queued state changes produced *1201 mutations across 114 headings in nine seconds*, sustained at roughly 240 writes per second. Seven level-1 categories acquired TODO keywords, five headings ended up holding each other's states, and ~146 spurious =State= log lines were written into =:LOGBOOK:= drawers. Read from the audit log rather than inferred: every record attributed to =org_review_apply=, 50 of them on headings with no =:ID:= at all.

*The mechanism.* =--trigger-auto-promote-sole-todo= runs on =org-trigger-hook= and, when it promotes, calls =org-todo=. =org-todo= fires =org-trigger-hook=. So the trigger re-enters itself.

Its only guard was =--review-applying=, and that is bound around the apply *loop* and deliberately *unbound* during =--review-settle-auto-promote= -- which is the entire point of suppress-then-settle ([[id:c8a6c5d2-8777-44d2-9900-e56eb03aa2d9][c8a6c5d2]]). So the settle phase ran with no re-entrancy protection at all.

*Why categories.* Once the cascade writes a keyword onto any level-1 heading, the level-1 sibling group satisfies the promotion's own condition -- more than one sibling, none =NEXT=, exactly one carrying a TODO keyword. The condition it tests for is *created by the cascade*, so it feeds itself. [[id:42808717-2736-4bf4-872e-887f990203ca][42808717]]'s container guard should have refused those and did not, but that is downstream: without the cascade it is never asked.

*The fix is the one this project already wrote once.* =--auto-promote-active=, bound around that single =org-todo= call, modelled exactly on =--auto-clock-in-active=, which guards =--trigger-auto-clock-in= against the identical shape and has done since it was written. The promotion trigger never got the equivalent.

*Only one of the two tests discriminates, and that is recorded in the test itself.* A single sibling group cannot cascade into itself -- after the promotion the group holds a =NEXT= and the re-entered call refuses on its own terms -- so no minimal fixture reproduces production. The guard is pinned by asserting that the two guards each stop the trigger independently, which fails when the new one is removed. The write-counting test is a regression guard on the count, not a proof.

*Recovery, and the part worth remembering.* The file was restored from =HEAD= and the queue's =.applied= set rolled back so the events became pending again. The obvious cut -- "un-apply everything since the last commit" -- would have been *wrong*: a third apply had happened at 16:42 and was already committed, so cutting there would have re-offered work that was correctly filed. The seam came from a pending report captured minutes before the bad apply: 54 events, not 85.

*What the rollback cost, which was under-described at the time.* Assignments and edited intervals live in =--review-items=, in memory, never in the queue. Rebuilding items from the queue restores the *events* and discards the judgement applied to them. The user lost a hand-made assignment and an edited interval, and was told the rollback would "cost the review pass again" -- which sounded like keystrokes and meant decisions.


**** DONE A repeater never reaches DONE, so its body is never pruned :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-24 Mon 16:00]
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Skill
:ID:       ff92700e-1713-4862-a3fe-8fd972ad96fa
:CREATED:  [2026-08-24 Mon 13:10]
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:16

:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Skill
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "TODO"       from              [2026-08-24 Mon 13:11] \\
  captured keywordless, setting initial state
- State "DOING"      from "TODO"       [2026-08-24 Mon 15:56] \\
  build the repeater body cap
CLOCK: [2026-08-24 Mon 15:56]--[2026-08-24 Mon 15:59] =>  0:03
- [2026-08-24 Mon 15:56]--[2026-08-24 Mon 15:59] build the repeater body cap
- State "DONE"       from "DOING"      [2026-08-24 Mon 16:00] \\
  cap shipped; direction 1 chosen
:END:

*Found 2026-08-24 while paring [[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]]*, whose body had reached 47 lines against a 35-line median.

[[id:8bcd56f4-22a8-4673-bad6-a99433027b81][8bcd56f4]]'s lifecycle prunes a body at *completion*: the prospective half is wrapped into =:PLAN:= when the task is carried out, leaving the debrief. Every pruning event in the design is tied to reaching =DONE=.

*A repeater never reaches =DONE=.* Its keyword resets and its =SCHEDULED= stamp advances; that is the whole mechanism. So a recurring heading accumulates body prose indefinitely and *nothing in the convention will ever collect it* -- not once, not on a schedule, never. The lifecycle has no event for it.

*It is not a small class.* Every ritual heading is one, and ritual headings are exactly the ones re-read most often, since they are the ones a session opens to find out what to do.

*And the accumulation has a specific shape rather than being general growth.* =cbe282ec= grew because a recurring heading is where cross-cutting decisions get written down -- there is nowhere else obvious, and it is the heading being edited at the time. It had collected three different things: the ritual itself, a one-time backlog ([[id:7fbab3b3-7843-4290-94a5-d421413f2be4][7fbab3b3]]), and a set of standing conventions that turned out to belong in =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md=. The pruning gap is what let that go unnoticed; the *cause* is that a repeater attracts prose that is not about the repetition.

*Directions, none chosen:*

- *A repeater's body is capped by convention* -- say a dozen lines -- with anything longer required to move out to a rule, a linked heading, or a one-time task. Mechanically checkable by =bin/lint-org=, which already knows =org-get-repeat=: it uses it to refuse a repeater under a completable ancestor.
- *Prune at the repeat*, treating each firing as a completion for lifecycle purposes. Attractive symmetry, but wrapping a ritual's standing instructions into =:PLAN:= would hide the very text the ritual exists to state, which inverts the drawer's purpose.
- *Accept it and rely on the periodic review* to notice. This is what happened, and it worked only because a human read the heading and asked.

*The lint direction is the one worth measuring first,* since it is the project's usual answer to a convention that would otherwise recur and it needs no new concept -- just a length threshold on headings carrying a repeater.

*Decided and shipped 2026-08-24* (=6e0aef9=): the lint cap, direction 1 of the three recorded above. =bin/lint-org= warns when a heading carrying a repeater exceeds =claude-code-ide-org-repeater-body-max= body lines, default 25.

*Direction 2 stays rejected on its own terms* -- treating each firing as a completion would wrap a ritual's standing instructions into =:PLAN:=, hiding the very text the ritual exists to state. Direction 3 is what had been happening, and it worked once because the user happened to ask.

*The cap fires on nothing today, and that is stated rather than glossed.* The three repeaters hold 3, 7 and 9 body lines. It is a forward-looking guard on the same footing as [[id:8bcd56f4-22a8-4673-bad6-a99433027b81][8bcd56f4]]'s rule, and the honest claim is that 25 would have caught [[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]] at 47 lines, shortly before it had to be split three ways by hand.

*A mismeasurement worth keeping, because it nearly set the threshold.* The first survey reported an 80-line repeater -- [[id:96a51c2f-ce11-4b40-bdff-11223d3d4eb7][96a51c2f]] -- and the cap was proposed *because* of it, framed as "flags exactly one heading". The real figure is *7*. The survey counted drawer contents as body prose, which is precisely what =--lint-body-prose-lines= exists to exclude, and 96a51c2f's =:LOGBOOK:= is long.

Two things follow. A body-size rule calibrated against a body-size measurement that does not use the rule's own counter is calibrated to nothing -- so the counter is now shared with =--lint-substantial-body-p=, and the fixture asserts the drawer case directly. And the recommendation that reached the user was wrong in its evidence while right in its conclusion, which is the more uncomfortable half: it would have been accepted either way.

1. [[id:98700ea3-6770-429b-84dd-1fddde60afed][98700ea3]]: an unassigned span's group heading rendered an *error string* where a title belonged.
2. A =:DATE_TREE:= category target rendered as the first eight characters of its own title -- literally ="Review a  (unresolved)"=. =--review-heading-title= could not resolve a title through =org-id=, and =--short-id= truncates to eight.
3. A *pending capture* rendered as ="(unresolvable :ID:)"= -- of an id whose heading is *supposed* not to exist yet, because apply is what creates it.

*The shape was the defect.* The =cond= branched on whether =org-id= happens to resolve an id, which admits exactly two states and calls everything else broken. The real question is what *kind* of id it is: unassigned, a resolvable heading, a destination that is not a heading, a heading not yet written, or genuinely unknown. It now branches on that, and the final branch keeps its meaning rather than being a catch-all for anything unusual.

*The capture case is not cosmetic.* The human is being asked to *approve* that item, and ="unresolvable"= reads as a fault in the thing they are approving -- the wrong prompt for an item whose entire purpose is to create the heading it names.

*Note where instances 2 and 3 came from:* both were introduced by features that made an =:id= mean something new. [[id:9575e65b-b589-465a-830c-286541780f96][9575e65b]] made a category title a legal target, and the queued-capture path made an =:ID:= forward-referencing. Neither touched the render, and neither had reason to -- which is the argument for the render asking what an id *is* rather than enumerating what it has seen.

*Tested across all four kinds together*, because the failure each time was a case falling into a branch that describes something else, and only comparing them shows that.

*Reported by the user 2026-08-21, reviewing a real batch:* a suggested span rendered =(nothing for 10m, 10:37-10:47)= beneath a header already reading =10:37--10:47=, and the first question it prompted was whether the line was a defect.

*It is not. It is [[id:5ff5a4b8-2fee-472a-b5e1-c9de8cf96704][5ff5a4b8]]'s deliberate empty case*, and the reasoning there is sound: a span with no evidence used to render *no lines at all*, so "nothing was found here" was visually identical to "nobody looked". Making the absence visible is the whole point and should not be undone.

*What is wrong is only the degenerate form.* When the gap covers the entire span, the line prints the same two timestamps the item header prints, one line apart. Redundancy at the top of an item reads as malfunction rather than as information -- which is why the first response to it was to ask whether something had broken, rather than to decide what the span was.

*This is the answer to a question 5ff5a4b8 left open on purpose.* Its body declined to claim the fix worked: "whether gap lines actually induce evaluation is unknown until the next batch is reviewed, and the honest test is to ask again afterwards rather than to assume." A batch has now been reviewed. The finding is partial -- the line *did* draw attention, so the mechanism works; it drew attention to itself rather than to the decision, so the rendering does not.

*Proposed fix, small and preserving the intent:* when the gap's interval equals the span's, drop the timestamps and say only that no evidence was found in the window. The absence stays visible, the "nobody looked" ambiguity stays resolved, and nothing is printed twice. Interior gaps -- the case where a stretch inside a span is empty while other stretches are not -- keep their timestamps, because there the times are the information.

*Do not raise =claude-code-ide-org-span-evidence-gap= to suppress it.* The threshold exists to filter *interior* gaps by significance; using it to hide the empty case would restore exactly the "nothing found is indistinguishable from nobody looked" defect 5ff5a4b8 fixed, and would do so silently for short spans only.

*Shipped 2026-08-24* (=078bf65=), as the body proposed and for the reason it gave: when the gap's interval equals the span's, the timestamps are dropped and the line says only =(no evidence found in this window)=.

*The line still appears,* which is the load-bearing half. Suppressing it entirely would restore [[id:5ff5a4b8-2fee-472a-b5e1-c9de8cf96704][5ff5a4b8]]'s "nothing found is indistinguishable from nobody looked" defect, and raising =claude-code-ide-org-span-evidence-gap= to hide it would do the same thing silently and for short spans only. Both were rejected here before the fix was written, and the fix took neither.

*An interior gap keeps its timestamps,* and that distinction is now pinned by its own test. There the times *are* the information -- they say which stretch inside the span was empty, which cannot be recovered from the span's endpoints. A fix that dropped timestamps unconditionally would satisfy this heading and quietly destroy the case the feature exists for.

*Two existing tests asserted the redundant form* and were updated. They had encoded the defect: =test-span-with-no-evidence-says-so= and =test-span-gaps-ignore-the-slack-window= both matched on =(nothing for 14m, 17:18-17:32)=, the exact string this heading calls a bug.

*Reported twice before it was fixed* -- 2026-08-21 when it was filed, and again 2026-08-24 while the user was working through a live review buffer. Worth noting against the "real but cosmetic" label it was filed under and carried on the next-session prompt's off-the-critical-path list: a cosmetic defect that gets re-reported is costing attention every pass, which is the cost the label was implying it did not have.



**** DONE The review buffer truncated lines the human had to read :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-24 Mon 13:08]
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Apply
:ID:       111ca40a-3fdb-4106-ad52-991e30737ece
:CREATED:  [2026-08-24 Mon 13:08]
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:17
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Apply
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "DONE"       from              [2026-08-24 Mon 13:08] \\
  wrap default shipped and verified live
:END:

*Shipped 2026-08-24* (=5de3948=), from the user asking whether the review command could open its buffer wrapped "as I have it now".

*Diagnosed by reading their live buffer rather than guessing which wrap was meant.* =truncate-lines= is =t= in the *global* value -- their Doom config sets it -- and =nil= *buffer-locally* in the live =*org-review*= buffer, with =(local-variable-p 'truncate-lines)= true. That combination is the signature of =toggle-truncate-lines=: they had been turning it off by hand on every review buffer. =word-wrap= is globally =t=, which is why the result was word wrap rather than a mid-word break.

*Why it matters more here than in an ordinary buffer.* Every line in the review buffer is prose someone reads *in order to decide something* -- an annotation label, a heading title, the reason an item writes nothing. A truncated line hides the tail, and the tail is where the deciding information sits: ="writes nothing (34s of turns, none crossing a minute)"= is entirely tail.

=word-wrap= is set alongside =truncate-lines= rather than left to the global value. With truncation off but =word-wrap= nil the break lands mid-word, which reads worse than either extreme -- and a different machine, or this one after a config change, would get exactly that.

*Both are buffer-local, and that is asserted rather than assumed.* The point is to change one buffer, not the editor; the test pins =(local-variable-p ...)= for both and runs with a global default of =t= so it is testing the case that actually occurs.

*One test assertion was written and removed in the same pass*, worth recording because it is a tempting mistake: it asserted =(default-value 'truncate-lines)= was =t=, which is a claim about *the user's Doom config*, not about this code. It passed nowhere but this machine and failed immediately in batch, where Doom is not loaded. A unit test may not assert the environment it happens to run in.

*Note for anyone verifying this:* reloading =config.el= updates the mode definition but does *not* change an already-open review buffer, whose locals were set when its mode ran. Only a newly created review buffer picks it up -- which is why the live check was done in a fresh buffer.

*Shipped 2026-08-24* (=413e737=), at the user's request after they edited a number of 0-minute spans up to 1 minute by hand during a review pass. Instituted in =--apply-idle-floor= rather than at review, so every path that writes a CLOCK line gets it and nobody has to remember.

*The line drawn, and both halves matter.* A run with *positive* duration was observed -- 34 seconds of agent time is work that happened, and org's minute precision is the only reason it renders =0:00=. Recording it as =0:01= is a rounding error; discarding it is a false statement that nothing occurred, which is the erasure [[id:293ac49e-3324-421c-8495-de1a46fc04ac][293ac49e]] was filed against. A *zero-width* run is still dropped: nothing was observed there, and promoting a single timestamp into a minute is the class of guess [[id:7771fc63-9374-4c8a-9e80-24ceec21977c][7771fc63]] retired.

*The first version was wrong, and the real queue caught what the unit test did not.* It promoted on duration alone, testing =(zerop (round (/ secs 60)))=. But =round= goes to *nearest*: 34/60 is 1, not 0. So a 34-second run did not read as zero, survived the duration test, and was then dropped anyway for rendering =[11:17]--[11:17]= -- the *other* drop condition. The unit test happened to use an 11-second run, which does round to 0, so it passed and proved nothing. The failure only appears for runs of 30-59 seconds inside one minute, and it surfaced when a live item on =aa1ba915= reported "34s of turns" while producing =work-runs=nil=.

The two conditions are now named once as =--renders-as-nothing-p= and used for *both* promoting and dropping, so they cannot drift apart again. That is the actual fix; the promotion was only half of it.

*Three tests asserted dropping,* and rewriting them was the interesting part. They asserted it as a *means* to an end -- "rather than written as =>  0:00=" -- and that end still holds, so they are rewritten around the surviving invariant: whatever leaves this function, no interval renders as nothing. =--review-nothing-reason='s "none crossing a minute" branch is now unreachable by construction; it is kept as a guard that says so rather than deleted, because if it ever fires the two functions have diverged and that is worth hearing about.

*Measured on the live queue:* 16 CLOCK lines to 17, 88.3 to 89.3 minutes, items writing nothing 13 to 12, and zero lines rounding to =0:00= either way. Small today because the backlog was applied an hour earlier; the point is that it applies from here on without anyone editing by hand.

*Carried in the same commit:* =--lane-clock-intervals= hoisted out of the per-group loop in =--review-items-from-queue=, where it ran once per heading -- 53 groups against ~250 events, re-filtering and re-sorting the full history each time -- for an answer that does not vary by group. Introduced by [[id:eaeeb4ee-ceee-4094-8598-bbcdc8214b66][eaeeb4ee]] this morning. It is *not* the cause of the Emacs hang that followed the apply: that process sat at 0.0% CPU, which rules out anything computing.

:END:
:PLAN:

Designed by the user 2026-08-21/22. A heading body has two lives, and today they are the same text in the same place, which is why bodies become transcripts.

*Prospective, while the task is open.* The body holds motivation, observations and speculation -- everything leading up to the moment of implementation. It is *pared and revised continuously*, from creation right up to realization, so that it stays concise and internally consistent. It describes the current state of the question, never the history of how the question moved. The plan-file link, when one exists, goes at the *end* of the body the moment it is composed: the plan can supersede any statement above it, so it must be read last.

*Retrospective, once the task is carried out.* The whole prospective body -- plan link included -- is wrapped in a =:PLAN:= drawer, which sits beside =:PROPERTIES:= and =:LOGBOOK:= rather than below the prose. The body is then the debrief alone: problem restated, what the solution turned out to be, how it was verified, what was falsified ([[id:3063c3e5-0dd0-4354-8985-271b0313c5d1][3063c3e5]]'s four items). A folded heading therefore shows the debrief and nothing else.

*Relocation, never deletion.* The plan link moves into the drawer with the rest of the planning content because it *is* planning content -- and a forward-looking pointer inside a retrospective readout invites a reader to treat the plan as current. CLAUDE.md's "not removed at =DONE=" is a rule against losing the link, not against moving it, and must be reworded to say so.

*Readers skip the drawer.* The org skill should tell agentic readers to ignore =:PLAN:= entirely until a retrospective "how did we get here" question is actually asked. The debrief and the source code describe present reality; the plan describes an intention that may not have survived contact.

*Two mechanisms, and only one of them is missing.* Measured 2026-08-21 on [[id:cc0c17a7-a554-426d-afeb-09cbee7339f0][cc0c17a7]]: =org_amend= already appends *below* a =:PLAN:= drawer that sits at the top of a body, so the debrief needs no new tool at all. The only new operation is *wrapping* -- insert the drawer at the end-of-drawers boundary, close it after the last body line -- which is two insertions at computable positions rather than a range replacement. That distinction is not cosmetic: both of that day's file corruptions were range bugs, and neither was caught by =bin/lint-org=, which sees structure and not prose. Continuous paring still needs general in-place revision, which is why this is blocked on 3063c3e5 rather than merely related to it.

*What it enables mechanically:* =bin/lint-org= can assert that a =DONE= heading with a substantial body carries a =:PLAN:= drawer -- the project's usual answer to a convention that would otherwise recur ([[id:3bd3402b-3ab6-4ace-b20b-3ff84caa3fb2][3bd3402b]]'s split puts this in the lint, not in =bin/check-conventions=).

*Deliberately deferred until the wrapping tool exists*, so that a rule never describes something no session can perform: CLAUDE.md's plan-link wording, and the org skill's "Body prose and the task lifecycle" section, which is explicitly an interim workaround for append-only ("Until that is fixed") and is superseded wholesale by this. =.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= gains =:PLAN:= beside the other drawer conventions in the same pass.

*Migration of the existing backlog is settled and is not this heading's work:* sweep old bodies in unedited, recorded on [[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]]. Old drawers will be raw transcripts where new ones are pared plans; the ignore-the-drawer rule makes that invisible in normal reading.

:END:
*Adopted 2026-08-24* (=44b7020=, =fe376db=). All five deferred edits landed, once [[id:3063c3e5-0dd0-4354-8985-271b0313c5d1][3063c3e5]]'s wrapping half made them describable without describing something no session could perform.

1. *CLAUDE.md's plan-link wording* now says the link is *relocated into* =:PLAN:=, not deleted, at =DONE=. The old "not removed at =DONE=" was a rule against *losing* the link and was being read as a rule against *moving* it.
2. *=.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= gains a =:PLAN:= section* beside the other drawer conventions: what goes in it, that =org_wrap_plan= makes it, and that readers skip it.
3. *The org skill's "Body prose and the task lifecycle" section is reframed* -- and this is where the plan and the outcome diverge, deliberately. This heading anticipated the section being "superseded wholesale". It is not, and saying so would have thrown away good rules: the completion-vocabulary table, the date-stamping rule and the brevity rule each stand on their own and are kept. What is superseded is the *framing* -- the section opened by stating that =org_amend= appends and can do nothing else, so an outcome always lands furthest from the reader, and cast everything below it as interim "until that is fixed". That premise is now half-false. The date-stamp rule's stated justification is adjusted too, since it leaned on nothing later needing revision.
4. *The ignore-the-drawer rule is in both files*: treat =:PLAN:= as absent unless the question is explicitly retrospective. Reading it for current fact is how a superseded design claim gets repeated as though it still held -- which is the reason the two halves were separated at all.
5. *=bin/lint-org= asserts it*, and this was the one that needed measuring first.

*The lint rule's scoping is the whole of whether it is usable.* Measured before writing it: unscoped it fires on *124* headings at once -- 30 in TODO.org, 94 in DONE.org -- taking the report from 24 warnings to 147. That is exactly the drowning [[id:e30d52d7-960b-44f3-ab92-93846c81a1bd][e30d52d7]] had to rescue this lint from once already. Scoped by =CLOSED:= date to headings finished on or after the convention landed, it fires *zero* times today and grows only with new work.

*And that scoping is only possible because of a few hours earlier.* [[id:f4b07fc0-187a-4975-aa3b-b9bd4b1c0799][f4b07fc0]] backfilled 58 =CLOCK=-derived =CLOSED:= markers this morning; before that, "closed after date X" was not a question these files could answer. The backfill was filed as housekeeping and turned out to be the enabling step.

*Because the rule reports nothing on the real files by design, the positive case is a fixture* -- a rule never seen to fail proves nothing. Removing the date scoping fails the exemption test and takes the real report to 147 warnings, so both the rule and its scoping are pinned. =--lint-substantial-body-p= excludes drawer contents, so thirty =CLOCK= lines cannot make a short heading look substantial.

*Still open, and not this heading's:* the backlog itself. 124 finished headings carry a substantial body and no drawer, which is [[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]]'s sweep. The lint is deliberately silent about them rather than counting them daily.

*=:BLOCKER:= dropped 2026-08-24*, having read =ids(3063c3e5)=. It was set because adoption could not describe an operation no session could perform; =org_wrap_plan= shipped this morning, so the thing it guarded exists. [[id:3063c3e5-0dd0-4354-8985-271b0313c5d1][3063c3e5]] stays open for the *revision* half its title names, which adoption never needed -- that half serves continuous paring, not the completion transition.

Left in place it would have blocked this heading's own =DONE= at apply: =org-depend-block-todo= refuses a =DONE= whose =:BLOCKER:= names a heading still carrying a keyword, and 3063c3e5 is =NEXT=. So the property had gone from a true statement to a false one that would fire as a real refusal.

*Nothing was invented for the 39.* =:ARCHIVE_TIME:= is the obvious substitute and is a *different fact wearing the right shape* -- when the subtree moved, not when the work stopped. Wiring that fallback in fails two of the three new tests, which is what makes them worth having rather than merely present. Those 39 are [[id:b7b46a26-2fd6-4784-bed3-d0112a917c0a][b7b46a26]]'s question.

*One correction worth keeping, because it changed the answer.* The estimate quoted before the tool existed was "59 of 97", produced by scanning each heading's whole body for a =State= line. The real figure is *58*. [[id:3d93021d-1d8a-4657-bc5c-77734f91fb9d][3d93021d]] has no =:LOGBOOK:= at all, but quotes =- State "DONE" from "NEXT" [2026-08-07 Fri 08:19]= *in prose*, while diagnosing the bug that produced that very line. A body-wide scan reads it as evidence and dates the heading from a sentence about a bug. The shipped code bounds its search to the drawer, so it does not -- and the discrepancy between the two counts is the only reason the difference was noticed at all. Worth reading twice, because the prose that fooled the estimate is *correctly quoted org*, not malformed text, and nothing structural would ever flag it.



**** DONE The #+STARTUP line is undocumented and the two org files disagree on it :code:
CLOSED: [2026-08-24 Mon 10:08]
:PROPERTIES:
:CATEGORY: Skill
:ID:       bba1088c-d8e1-49f7-bef8-b070860f5257
:CREATED:  [2026-08-21 Fri 10:54]
:ARCHIVE_TIME: 2026-08-31 Mon 11:16
:ARCHIVE_FILE: ~/git/claude-code-ide-org/TODO.org
:ARCHIVE_CATEGORY: Skill
:ARCHIVE_TODO: DONE
:END:
:LOGBOOK:
- State "TODO"       from              [2026-08-21 Fri 10:55] \\
  document STARTUP, reconcile the two files
CLOCK: [2026-08-24 Mon 10:05]--[2026-08-24 Mon 10:08] =>  0:03
- State "DOING"      from "TODO"       [2026-08-24 Mon 10:05] \\
  reconcile the two STARTUP lines
- [2026-08-24 Mon 10:05]--[2026-08-24 Mon 10:08] align STARTUP and document the ordering guard
- State "DONE"       from "DOING"      [2026-08-24 Mon 10:08] \\
  lines aligned, divergence documented
:END:
:PLAN:

=.claude/rules/org-conventions.md= prescribes a file header of =#+TODO:=, =#+TAGS:= and =#+ARCHIVE:=. It says nothing about =#+STARTUP:=, and the two files that exist disagree:

| file     | =#+STARTUP:=                  |
|----------+-------------------------------|
| TODO.org | =logdrawer logdone content=   |
| DONE.org | =logdrawer=                   |

So the line controlling how every one of these files opens -- and, via =logdrawer=/=logdone=, *where org writes state-change logging* -- is undocumented, and a third file created from the template would carry neither setting. =logdrawer= in particular is not cosmetic: without it org writes state notes loose under the heading instead of into =:LOGBOOK:=, which is the shape every reader and every parser in this project assumes.

*Found 2026-08-21 while answering a different question*, namely whether =#+STARTUP: content= caps depth. It does not, and that is worth recording here so nobody re-derives it: =org-cycle-set-startup-visibility= dispatches =content= to =(org-cycle-content)= with *no argument*, and a nil argument selects the regexp =^\*+ = -- every level. The capped variants are separate keywords, =show2levels= through =show5levels=, which call =(org-cycle-content N)=.

*Measured on a fresh open of TODO.org in the live Emacs (org 9.8.7):* 104 headings, *all visible, none hidden* -- 7 at level 1, 63 at level 2, 34 at level 3 -- and no heading carrying a =:VISIBILITY:= property. The mechanism is working; there is nothing to fix in TODO.org's own line.

*Decide, then write it into the template:* whether =content= is the house default for every file or a TODO.org-specific choice, and whether =logdone= belongs everywhere =logdrawer= does. DONE.org arguably wants a *different* answer rather than the same one -- it is an archive, read rarely and in full -- so this is a decision about two files, not a copy-paste.

:END:
*Resolved 2026-08-24, and the disagreement turned out to matter.* The two lines were:

: TODO.org:  #+STARTUP: logdrawer logdone content
: DONE.org:  #+STARTUP: logdrawer content

=#+STARTUP:= is *file-local*, applied at buffer setup, and nothing in =~/.config/doom/config.el= sets =org-log-done= or =org-log-into-drawer= globally -- both sit at their defaults. So the divergence was live rather than notional; the buffers read =:log-done time= and =:log-done nil= respectively. Per org's own =org-startup-options=, =logdone= maps to =(org-log-done time)=, which is what writes the =CLOSED:= planning line. It is a separate record from the =!= cookies in =#+TODO:=, which write the =- State "DONE" from "DOING" [ts]= line into =:LOGBOOK:=.

*The consequence, which is reachable and which* [[id:cbe282ec-10c3-4aa0-8d3a-f30e17a12fa8][cbe282ec]] *walks toward.* Apply resolves a heading by =:ID:= through =org-id=, and DONE.org is in =org-agenda-files=, so a queued =todo= event applies wherever the heading now lives. Archive the backlog first and then apply a pending =DONE= for one of those headings, and the transition executes *in DONE.org* with =org-log-done= nil: the =:LOGBOOK:= gets its =State= line and no =CLOSED:= is written. Silent, and afterwards the heading is indistinguishable from the 97 that never had one.

Measured before deciding: *zero* such post-archive closes have happened yet, checked by comparing every =State "DONE"= timestamp in DONE.org against its own heading's =:ARCHIVE_TIME:= across the 63 headings carrying one. So this is a guard against a case the archive backlog creates, not a repair of one already present.

*Both guards taken.* The ordering one -- apply the queue *before* an archive pass, never after -- removes the case outright and is recorded on cbe282ec where the pass is planned. Adding =logdone= to DONE.org costs nothing when no transition occurs there and makes the ordering a preference rather than a requirement. The two lines are now byte-identical, which is this heading's actual complaint answered.

*Verified after* =org-mode-restart=, not merely after the edit: =#+STARTUP:= is read at buffer setup, so the live buffer kept =:log-done nil= until the mode was restarted, at which point it read =time=.

*Left open, and it is the larger half of the question:* DONE.org holds *97* =DONE=/=CANCELLED= headings and *zero* =CLOSED:= markers, because =logdone= only arrived 2026-08-17 (=7be24df=) and the newest =:ARCHIVE_TIME:= is that same day -- so every archived heading was closed before the setting existed. All 34 markers in TODO.org sit on headings still awaiting archive. Backfilling is only *partly* mechanical: 59 of the 97 carry a =State "DONE"=/=CANCELLED= line to read a time from, and *38 carry no in-file evidence at all*. For those, =:ARCHIVE_TIME:= is a different fact wearing the right shape, and writing it as =CLOSED:= would be the class of guess [[id:7771fc63-9374-4c8a-9e80-24ceec21977c][7771fc63]] retired. Git history is the one honest source left for them.

**** DONE Clock pairs name the heading; the review pass asks anyway :code:
